News.title: Cop who Tasered tragic amputee, 92, ‘posted sick taunt about him after she was made butt of office joke’
News.content:
OAP 'JOKE' Cop who Tasered tragic amputee, 92, ‘posted sick taunt about him after she was made butt of office joke’







Next

A COP who Tasered a tragic 92-year-old amputee told a tribunal she posted a taunt about him after she was made the “butt” of office jokes.

Donald Burgess was filmed screaming out during the horror at Park Beck Residential Care Home in St Leonards-on-Sea, East Sussex.



PC Rachel Comotto and PC Stephen Smith had been called to the residence after the 92-year-old poked a worker in the stomach with a butter knife.

The pair were later found not guilty of assault occasioning actual bodily harm following a trial.



But they are both appearing before a disciplinary panel to answer allegations they used “excessive force” against Donald.

They are accused of “escalating the situation” and failing to treat the “vulnerable and confused” pensioner with compassion.

If the allegations are proven at the disciplinary hearing then both officers could be sacked from the force.

The tribunal heard previously PC Comotto is also accused of placing “inappropriate comments’” on Facebook about the tragic incident.

She had been interacting with a colleague after they posted a message on Facebook saying: “Happy birthday, the care home is getting closer and closer.”

The cop replied: “We all know what happens in care homes” before adding a lightning emoji.



Aaron Rathmell, lawyer for Sussex Police, said said this was in reference to the taser she had used on Donald at the care home.

He said PC Comotto had “made light of the actions” and her response was “inappropriate and unprofessional”.

But giving evidence today, the cop claimed she made the comment after being made “the butt” of the joke by fellow officers who were “laughing and joking” about the incident.



Colin Banham, her lawyer, asked: “They were ribbing you? How far had this joke spread?”

She replied: “They did not know the details but they were laughing and joking at my expense. It was throughout the office.”

Pc Comotto also claimed there was “no humour directed at Mr Burgess” and insisted she was not trying to poke fun at him.

She added: “It was continuation of the joke I was the subject of or the butt of. I am the target of the joke, not Mr Burgess.

“With hindsight and without context it doesn’t look good and I want to extend my apologies to the family.”



Bodycam showed Donald clutching a specially adapted butter knife while sat in his wheelchair when Smith and Comotto entered his room.

PC Smith can be heard saying: ‘Put it down mate. Come on, Donald, don’t be silly.

“We can solve it without having to resort to this…Do as you’re told.”

The footage also showed Smith making his way towards the pensioner with his baton extended before striking him.

PC Comotto then deploys her 50,000-volt Taser as Donald screams out in pain before the officers took the knife from him.



After shooting him, PC Comotto asked Donald how he was feeling, leading him to reply: “I’m dying, I’m dying.”

The tribunal heard the cops massively “escalated the situation” and were confrontational and antagonistic towards him.

Mr Rathmell said that at no point in the use of three separate uses of force had the two officers tried to de-escalate the situation.



He also told the tribunal later the same day, PC Comotto interacted with a colleague after they posted a message on Facebook saying: “Happy birthday, the care home is getting closer and closer.”

The cop replied: “We all know what happens in care homes” before adding a lightning emoji.

Mr Rathmell said this was in reference to the taser she had used on Donald at the care home.

He said PC Comotto had “made light of the actions” and her response was “inappropriate and unprofessional”.

Donald suffered from multiple health conditions including diabetes and carotid artery disease.



He was taken to hospital following the incident and died 22 days later after contracting Covid.

The disciplinary hearing was told that it was not alleged that the actions of the officer contributed to his death.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

After the incident Sussex Police voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

The tribunal continues.

News.title: Manslaughter probe launched after Brit tourist, 66, killed while parasailing in Benidorm as freak storm hit resort
News.content:
HOLIDAY TRAGEDY Manslaughter probe launched after Brit tourist, 66, killed while parasailing in Benidorm as freak storm hit resort







Next

SPANISH police have launched a manslaughter investigation after a British tourist died during a parasailing trip in Spain.

Beverley White, 66, was on a tandem ride with a man in Benidorm when a freak storm swept across the beloved Brit holiday hotspot.



Holidaymakers fled the beach as Beverley flew overhead but before the boat guiding her could return to shore a strong gust snapped the parachute cord.

Beverley and her 47-year-old companion crashed down to the sea but high winds then dragged them along the surface towards rocks.



Dramatic footage taken from the shore showed the speedboat desperately racing after them.

Beverley suffered a heart attack and was treated by paramedics in an ambulance when the boat made it back to dry land.



She was then rushed to Villajoyosa Hospital, near Benidorm, but doctors were unable to save her.

The man she was with suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Spanish police have now released their first detailed statement about the August 10 tragedy and have revealed that a manslaughter probe has been launched.

They are also investigating an alleged cover-up after a dispute over who was at the controls of the speedboat.



A spokesman for the Civil Guard in Alicante said: “The Civil Guard has concluded its investigation into a parasailing accident.

“The accident occurred while both victims were participating in the activity in tandem, being towed by a boat.

“At a certain point, the cable connecting the parachute to the boat broke, causing both of them to be dragged by the wind until they fell into the sea.

“During the investigation, detectives analysed the circumstances surrounding the accident, including the conditions at the time, as the weather was deteriorating with a storm and strong gusts of wind.

“Another aspect was who was actually in command of the boat at the time.



“Initially, a person linked to the company responsible for the activity identified himself to the officers as the boat’s skipper.

“However, he later acknowledged that he was not the person in command at the time of the accident and identified another employee as responsible, with the investigation determining that it was the latter who was operating the boat.”

The spokesman said the second man did have the necessary qualifications to operate the boat but was not listed as crew with the company at the time of the accident.

He went on: “As a result of the probe, two people are under investigation, one of them for the alleged offences of manslaughter and wounding and the second for an alleged offence of concealment.”

The two men have not been arrested but are expected to be summoned for questioning by a court in Benidorm.



Beverley and her companion took off on their 75 euros (£64) tandem trip around 6pm at Rincon de Loix, Benidorm.

Shortly after the weather suddenly changed, the sky turned black and strong winds swept across the resort.

Holidaymaker Kerriann Blagden, 40, from Doncaster, South Yorkshire, watched the tragedy unfold from the balcony of her beachside hotel.

She told The Sun: “We were looking out to sea when it happened.

“The weather just changed all of a sudden and took the parachute off.



“They then dropped to the sea and the wind caught the parachute again and was dragging them across the sea.”

Another witness added: “It didn’t rain but the wind suddenly got up.

“The sudden gust of wind broke the rope and they became separated from the boat.

“The boat tried to chase after them but even going at full whack speed it couldn’t catch up.”

A spokesman for the Civil Guard said at the time: “At 6.50pm on Monday we received an alert about a parasailing accident that occurred in the sea off Benidorm.



“Two British nationals, a 47-year-old man and a 66-year-old woman, were injured and taken to Villajoyosa Hospital.

“The woman’s death was subsequently confirmed.

“The Guardia Civil has carried out the initial steps to clarify the circumstances of the incident, and the investigation is ongoing.”

Beverley’s inquest was opened and adjourned earlier this month at Cornwall’s Coroners’ Court in Truro.

The court heard Beverley went into cardiac arrest after landing in the sea and efforts to revive her were unsuccessful.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A full hearing will be held at a later date.

The parasailing firm declined to comment.

News.title: Three teens killed after car ploughed through barrier into river pictured – as boy, 17, who escaped is quizzed by cops
News.content:
Next

THE three teenagers killed after a car ploughed through a barrier and into a river have been pictured – as a 17-year-old boy who escaped is quizzed by cops.

Shortly before 1.30pm yesterday, police raced to reports that a black Audi A3 had come off the road and crashed into the River Wear in Sunderland.



Jackson Duke, 17, and Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw, both aged 16, were all tragically in the car at the time.

Jackson and Luke were from the Sunderland area, while Zara was from Houghton-le-Spring.





Their next of kin continue to be supported by officers.

The investigation into the circumstances leading to the car entering the water remains ongoing.



Enquiries are at an early stage, but no other vehicles are believed to have been involved.

Another occupant of the car – a 17-year-old boy – reached safety and sustained non-serious injuries.

He was subsequently arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and he remains in police custody at this time.

The black Audi veered off the road near Wearmouth Bridge before plunging into the water, taking its occupants with it, Northumbria Police said.

The bodies of the three teens were tragically recovered from the water following an intensive rescue operation.



Emergency services rushed to the scene, as dozens of stunned onlookers gathered on either side of the river.

Cops cordoned off a section of the metal barrier overlooking the river, as rescue teams in boats scoured the water.

The coastguard and RNLI were seen using poles in their frantic search for the youngsters, as helicopters circled ahead.

A 31-year-old nearby resident, who did not wish to be named, said: “There were loads of ambulances here, we had helicopters here at one point.

“This is the first time I’ve ever seen anything like this around here.



“I’ve lived here for three years, this is sad to see. Some families may get some awful, awful news today.”

He said his neighbour called emergency services after witnessing the incident from his window.

Chief Supt Scott Cowie, Area Commander for Sunderland, said: “First and foremost, our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the teenagers who have tragically lost their lives.



“The last 24 hours have brought unimaginable agony and heartbreak for the loved ones of Luke, Jackson and Zara.

“All three had their whole futures ahead of them and will be hugely missed.

“I know the wider community will want to join me in offering their families’ our heartfelt condolences at this devastating time.

“We will do everything we can to support them, and would continue to ask for their privacy to be respected.

“We also recognise the impact that this tragedy has had upon the people of Sunderland and further afield, and know that you will continue to be there for one another.”



He added: “The investigation into the circumstances leading to the car entering the water remains ongoing.

“We would continue to ask members of the public not to speculate about the incident both on social media and in the community.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“In doing so, please be mindful of the potential impact such commentary could have on the families of those involved in this incident.”

Anyone with information, particularly those with CCTV or dashcam footage, should send Northumbria Police a direct message on social media or use live chat and report forms on the Force’s website.

News.title: Moment naked drug dealer is caught straddling garden fence and arrested by cops after trying to escape through window
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment a naked drug dealer is caught scaling a fence while trying to flee cops, before being arrested.

Jake Lowe was part of a pair found to be selling more than nine kilogrammes of cannabis in just under a month.



Footage captured the moment Lowe was caught escaping out of a window and onto a garden fence.

Surprised officers shouted “get over that wall” after finding the 28-year-old starkers.



Lowe then complained “there’s a big drop” before reassuring the officers he would climb down.

Cops then ordered the nude crook to put his hands behind his back, before he asked “can I have them in front please for my personal sake”.



The ordeal ended with Lowe being taken away in handcuffs, with a jacket tied around his waist for dignity.

The Wigan-based drug dealer was one of two drug dealers jailed for the selling of marijuana between February and June of this year.



The other dealer, Joseph Knockton, was also arrested as part of a larger operation.

After a raid of Lowe’s address, officers uncovered small quantities of cocaine, 4kg of cannabis, mobile phones, a knuckleduster, a taser and cash.

Knockton’s address revealed a Rolex watch and £30,000 in cash.



Both men pleaded guilty to being concerned in the supply of cannabis, with Lowe also admitting to possession with intent to supply cannabis, possession of cocaine and possession of criminal property.

On Monday, September 21, Lowe was sentenced to four years in prison, and Knockton to three years.

Detective Chief Inspector Gary Stratton, from Project Medusa, said: “This was a sophisticated drug-dealing operation set up by Lowe and Knockton.



“We found bin bags full of plastic containers bearing their drug branding, which they used to sell drugs online.

“The turnover they generated is estimated to have been in the region of £150,000 a month, so this is a great result.

“We have intercepted two drug dealers who thought they were above the law and who were prepared to peddle their filth online.

“Serious organised crime groups are a massive blight on our communities. Drugs are closely linked to serious violence, including firearm and knife crime.

“We will continue to target criminals by thoroughly examining any evidence, messages and images we uncover.”

News.title: Iran WERE involved in RAF Fairford ‘terror plot’, suggests Burnham – as mystery grows around foiled ‘base attack’
News.content:
Next

PRIME Minister Andy Burnham has said there are “strong indications” Iran played a part in the alleged RAF Fairford terror plot as the mystery continues to grow.

His comments come as cops continue to investigate the bizarre series of events outside the Gloucestershire airbase, where five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday.



The suspects, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, have since been released on bail.

Burnham told GB News: “So what I can say is there are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend.



“It is, though, still an ongoing and very serious police investigation.

“So I hope you’ll understand that I don’t say more at this point, but I wanted to confirm what we could say.”



He added: “It’s obviously a very serious investigation involving our colleagues in the United States, and we are working very closely with them.

“And I will say more when I can.”



The development comes after counter-terror cops searched three white vans found blocking a road near RAF Fairford.

No improvised explosive devices were found, although a quantity of petrol was recovered.

The Sun understands large plastic barrels of fuel were found inside the vehicles and were initially thought to contain chemical explosives.

Cops are now examining a number of possible explanations for why the men were there, including whether they were acting as Iranian proxies.

Other lines of inquiry include whether they were carrying out surveillance, testing the base’s security in a “dry run” or attempting to send a message to the British Government.



The case took another bizarre turn after The Times reported that one of the suspects had called 999 himself before the arrests.

It is not known why the man made the call and only deepens the mystery engulfing the case as question marks are raised over the suspect’s motives for calling the police on themselves.

The reported call could explain why cops were responding at around 12.45am, before a local farmer raised the alarm at around 1.36am.



The farmer had spotted three vans blocking the road near Whelford as she drove home with her husband.

She told The Sun: “We had to turn around and drive away.

“When we did that, we saw a group of men with masks and balaclavas running in front of us.”

She tried to contact the airbase but was unable to get through before calling 999.

Around 85 homes in nearby Whelford were evacuated as armed cops descended on the scene.



Exclusive footage shared with The Sun showed one of the white vans travelling towards RAF Fairford at around 11.15pm on Saturday.

The vehicle was captured on a resident’s doorbell camera less than a mile from the airbase, just hours before the arrests.

RAF Fairford is used by the US military and has been involved in operations against Iran.



US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticised the decision to release the five suspects on bail.

He previously said he was “surprised” by their release and that he would not have granted them bail.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also previously said a “foreign actor” was involved, while pointing towards Iran.

Counter Terrorism Policing has stressed that the investigation remains ongoing and that officers are keeping an open mind.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said searches of the vans had concluded and confirmed that no viable explosive devices had been found.



Speculation grew that the men could have been fuel thieves, after the head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said a “quantity of petrol” was found.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In a statement yesterday he said: “As part of the investigation, we have searched properties in London which I can confirm have concluded.

“We can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found [in the vans]. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered.”

News.title: Sarah Everard killer Wayne Couzens’ life behind bars – wife’s final words, fears of Huntley-style attack & shock perks
News.content:
Next

THE abduction and murder of Sarah Everard by a serving cop horrified Britain, sparked angry protests and led to a public inquiry.

And after a harrowing trial that heard how he abducted, raped and murdered Sarah, 33, Met Police officer Wayne Couzens was handed a rare whole-life prison term.





Judge Lord Justice Fulford imposed the sentence after calling the murder “grotesque” and saying its seriousness – after Couzens staged a fake Covid arrest as Sarah walked home in South London – was “exceptionally high”.

And now – five years after the fiend was handed the whole-life order on September 30, 2021 – we can reveal Couzens is “withering away” in his prison cell.

The monster is said to be “haunted” by loneliness and does not have any visitors or contact with friends and family.

His wife Olena is understood to have visited Couzens, 53, four years ago to say ‘goodbye’ to him.

And he is barred from contact with – or having pictures of – the couple’s two daughters.

Couzens has no current visiting orders listed at tough HMP Frankland, County Durham where he is held alongside killers including Levi Bellfield, Vickrum Digwa and nail bomber David Copeland.

He is also “petrified” of leaving his cell to mix with other lags, after the death of Soham killer Ian Huntley at Frankland in February.

But – due to good behaviour behind bars – Couzens is on the highest-level enhanced regime, meaning he gets £33 per week to spend in the canteen plus extra TV, DvD, and Xbox rights.





A source said: “Couzens might be on enhanced, but his life at Frankland is pretty grim.

“He is terrified of leaving his cell after what happened to Huntley and is withering away in there.

“He has lost loads of weight and is haunted by loneliness and what he has done.

“He now comes across as like an old man and cuts a pretty pathetic figure.

“Couzens does not have any visitors and it is rare that he gets a letter or makes a phonecall.

“His wife did come to see him, but that was to say goodbye and tell him she and their daughters would not be coming back.

“That was a while ago but other prisoners still remember him breaking down and apologising for the crime and being devastated when she left.

“Now he doesn’t have anyone coming to see him, which is quite unusual for prisoners even at a place like Frankland.



“He is not even allowed any photos, so his cell is pretty grim and he is on his own in there with his own thoughts.

“Couzens is basically wasting away in his cell and spends hours playing Xbox games and watching TV.

“He is allowed TV 24 hours per day as he is on enhanced, and watches it late into the night.

“A lot of people would be horrified that he gets taxpayer money to spend and can lounge around watching telly.

“But Couzens’ life inside is not enjoyable.

“He is unpopular because of his crime and his job and is hiding away from other inmates most of the time.

“He has a huge target on his back and is extremely worried someone will get to him after what happened to Ian Huntley.

“So he is wasting away surround by people who hate him – not that anyone has much sympathy for him.”



Couzens kidnapped marketing executive Sarah, using his Met Police-issue warrant card to stage the fake Covid arrest on March 3, 2021.

He used his knowledge to Covid patrols to trick her into his car for breaching strict stay-at-home guidelines.

He handcuffed Sarah before driving to a remote rural area of Kent where he raped and murdered her, using his police belt to strangle her.

He later returned to the scene and doused her body with petrol before burning it.

But Sarah’s remains were found days later in a woodland stream, close to land owned by Couzens near Deal.

He was handed the whole-life order – the first in England and Wales for a single murder of an adult – due to the abuse of his police powers.

After he was sentenced then Police Commissioner Dame Cressida Dick admitted Couzens had “brought shame on the Met” as she apologised.

She added that his crime was a “gross betrayal of everything policing stands for”.



The case sparked protests over violence towards women – including a vigil in Clapham – with activits demanding “radical change” in the Met.

An Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) report discovered misogyny, bullying and sexual harassment were rife within the force.

And an inquiry published in 2024 ruled Couzens should never have been a cop and opportunities to stop him were missed.

The Anglioni report said police “repeatedly failed” to spot warning signs during his 20-year career.

He was a repeated ‘flasher‘ but probes into indecent exposure by Couzens in 2015, 2020 and 2021 were marred by police failings.

We told last November how Couzens had been banned from receiving photos in jail after being sent racy snaps by warped “admirers”.

Bosses found inappropriate images of women in his cell in a search.

The fiend is also barred from all contact with under-18s.



And we revealed last year how Couzens was whisked from jail for non-emergency surgery on his spine in an operation that would have cost around £19,000 including transport and security.

The Prison Service said it could not comment on individuals.

News.title: Teen admits trying to have sex with Shetland pony named Cheeky after ‘breaking into farm’
News.content:
SICK ACT Teen admits trying to have sex with Shetland pony named Cheeky after ‘breaking into farm’







Next

A TEENAGE boy has admitted to trying to have sex with a Shetland pony named Cheeky after allegedly breaking into a farm.

Thomas Mikaelson, 19, pleaded guilty to attempting to allow sexual penetration by a living animal today at Leeds Crown Court.



The court heard the charge relates to an incident on August 24 last year against Cheeky at Gledhill Farm in Almondbury, West Yorkshire.

The attempted attack on the pony has impacted the farm and its workers “in more than one respect”, the court was told.



Mikaelson, of Huddersfield, denied a second offence of recklessly trespassing to commit a relevant sexual offence, Yorkshire Live reports.

Prosecutor Robert Galley told the court the pleas were acceptable to the Crown.

Mr Galley said that he had been instructed to invite the second charge to lie on file.

Judge Phillips KC told the court: “The farmer concerned has supplied a victim impact statement and I think that he ought to be given the opportunity of attending court at sentencing.

“It clearly has had an impact in more than one respect upon the farm and those involved in its operation.”

He told Mikaelson: “You pleaded guilty to the offence at count one. I’m not going to pass sentence today. Your case will be listed for sentence on the 17 November. There will be a 30-minute time estimate.”



Mikaelson was bailed with instructions to attend court for his sentencing.

The judge added: “The fact I’m adjourning the sentence in order for the Probation Service to prepare a report on you to address the risk you pose to the public in future should not be taken by you as an indication of what the sentence will be.”

The 19-year-old left court in a large black head covering, supported by two women.

He will be sentenced on November 17.

News.title: ‘I enjoy every piece of you’ boast & ‘can’t stop’ sex confession…sick reign of paedo teacher before dirty secret exposed
News.content:
Next

ON the surface, school teacher Emily Drury was the picture of respectability.

A fun, vivacious and dedicated maths teacher based in the quiet seaside town of Mablethorpe, Lincolnshire, she was trusted by anxious parents to guide their children through GCSE exams.



And to the delight of one schoolboy’s mum and dad, Drury offered to personally tutor their struggling son.

But behind the bedroom doors of the vulnerable 15-year-old, the attractive blonde was hiding a dark, predatory obsession.

Exploiting her position, the married teacher launched into a campaign of sexual abuse, manipulating her young student into a secret physical relationship between May and June last year.



When the illicit affair finally unravelled, police discovered a chilling paper trail left by the predator – including a handwritten note to the boy, tucked beside some cash.

In the twisted letter, the 26-year-old confessed: “I enjoy every piece of you. I don’t know how to stop, or what this is. Here’s £20 just in case… Your Em xoxo.”

Last month Drury was brought to justice at Lincoln Crown Court, weeping in the dock as a judge handed down a four-and-a-half-year prison sentence.

Now The Sun examines every shocking twist in yet another disturbing female paedophile teacher scandal that has shocked Britain.

Drury’s sickening crimes mark the latest in a deeply troubling trend of female educators abusing their power over underage boys in British classrooms.



The nation has previously watched in horror at high-profile scandals involving PE teacher Bronwen James, found guilty last month of sexually abusing a vulnerable 16-year-old schoolboy after previously admitting offences against two teenage girls.

In March last year a teacher in Northern Ireland was sentenced to two years in prison for grooming and sexually exploiting an underage male pupil.

Last week we told how maths teacher Rebecca Joynes was jailed in 2024 for grooming and having sex with two 15-year-old boys, falling pregnant to one.



Like those before her, Drury hid behind a veneer of professional trust – before dismantling every ethical boundary expected of an educator.

Court proceedings revealed that Drury began to assist the 15-year-old victim as he prepared for his GCSEs.

Instead of focusing on algebra and exam technique, Drury began grooming the young lad, using intimate personal disclosures to win him over and draw him into her adult world.

Reading the boy’s devastating victim impact statement, prosecutor Amber Hobson told the court how Drury systematically manipulated his emotions.

The victim revealed that Drury would unload her personal life onto him, telling the teen that her and her husband didn’t really talk, they weren’t having sex, and that marriage wasn’t what she expected.



As the grooming intensified, Drury’s inappropriate emotional demands quickly turned into repeated physical abuse.

The court heard how Drury engaged in sexual activity with the schoolboy on multiple occasions over a two-month period.

The lad recalled the troubling emotional pressure he felt while trapped in the teacher’s web: “She told me she was obsessed with me.

“I realised I had been manipulated.

“I was put into a situation where I was experiencing emotions and situations no child should have to experience.”



The grooming campaign reached a sinister peak when Drury turned to the teen and whispered: “You can’t tell anyone about this.”

Bound by confusion, guilt, and fear, the boy initially agreed to keep her dirty secret.

But the immense psychological burden proved too heavy for the young victim to carry alone.

He confided in two close school pals about the relationship, sending them a picture of Drury to prove his claim.



Word rapidly spread through the playground, sending “rumours running” through the corridors of the boys’ school.

Recognising the gravity of the allegations, school staff intervened immediately and alerted Lincolnshire Police, sparking a swift safeguarding probe.

When the police interviewed the stressed youngster, he handed over his mobile phone.

On it officers found communications from Drury, including a text message referring to a love note she had left him.



Armed with the damning evidence, Lincolnshire Police arrested Drury at her home in June last year.

Facing a mountain of digital and forensic evidence, Drury eventually broke down and pleaded guilty to five counts of sexual activity with a child.

However, it’s understood the ex-teacher cruelly chose to do so at the very last opportunity, meaning her victim spent months living with uncertainty.

At Lincoln Crown Court, disgraced Drury dabbed tears from her eyes as details of her predatory behaviour were read aloud to a packed courtroom.



In his victim impact statement the boy said that the teacher had become emotionally close to him.

“She was kind to me.

“She would say positive things to me, buy me clothes, she would talk to me and made me feel better about myself,” he said.

“I trusted her and told her very personal things.”

He also described how he was overwhelmed with feelings of shame and fear that others might blame him.



“I felt judged. I felt that people blamed me.

“I felt unable to simply be a child.”

He added that he had feared that his experience would not be taken seriously because he was a boy.

“I believed there was a stigma against men who are victims of sexual abuse, and this fear made it even more difficult to cope with the situation.”

Drury was supported in the public gallery by her husband – the very man she had disparaged to her teenage victim during her grooming sessions.



Her defence barrister, Jeremy Janes, argued that Drury had embarked on an “uncharacteristic, fantastical and unreal relationship” with the child as a form of “escaping the reality of her life”.

But Judge James House KC offered no sympathy for her claims of a lapse in judgment, sternly reminding the court that the legal and moral responsibility lay entirely on Drury’s shoulders.

He said character references showed her “kindness and compassion”, but said the offending had come from a place of “her own selfish desires”.

And Judge House refused to allow the defence to frame the abuse as a romance, emphasising: “She was the adult, he was the child.”

He added that Drury had “failed to fully accept the magnitude of harm caused” to the boy.



Passing down a four-and-a-half-year prison sentence, the judge said: “She abused a position of trust, and her offending was so serious that only a jail sentence was appropriate.”

Following the sentencing, Lincolnshire Police issued a scathing statement condemning Drury’s actions and praising the young victim for his bravery in coming forward.

Detective Constable Julie Jode, of Lincolnshire Police, branded the disgraced teacher’s behaviour as nothing short of “despicable.”

“Drury abused her position of trust and exploited the access she had to a vulnerable young person for her own purposes.

“As an adult in a position of authority, she was expected to provide guidance, support, and protection.



“Instead, she used that position to target and manipulate someone who should have been able to trust her implicitly.”

She continued: “Offences of this nature can have a profound and lasting impact on victims, particularly when they involve a significant imbalance of power and an abuse of trust.

“The victim in this case was forced to navigate an incredibly difficult and challenging period of his life while also facing the uncertainty of a lengthy criminal justice process.

“The fact that the offender delayed accepting responsibility only added to that ordeal.”

As well as her prison sentence, Drury was placed on the Sex Offenders’ Register for life.



She was also slapped with a five-year Sexual Harm Prevention Order (SHPO) and a five-year Restraining Order strictly prohibiting her from contacting her victim or his family ever again.

As Drury begins her lengthy stretch behind bars, her brave young victim continues to process the severe emotional scars left behind.

His words in court serve as a stark, final reminder of the devastating human cost of female teacher abuse.

“I was put into a situation where I was experiencing emotions and situations no child should have to experience,” he said, adding that he lives with the consequences of what happened “every day”, still finds it hard to trust people and avoids social situations.

News.title: 'We've just taken control': Passengers describe what happened on flight
News.content:
A pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai flight stabbed another pilot and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said.

The plane was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes, before being diverted to Saudi Arabia.

Eyewitnesses inside the plane described the moment the incident happened, with one man calling for help in a video shared on social media.

Follow this story live.

News.title: UK believes Iran involved in RAF Fairford incident, PM says
News.content:
The government believes that Iran played a part in the RAF Fairford incident which resulted in five men being arrested and then bailed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," he told the BBC. He did not provide further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

Burnham's comments come after it emerged that one of the five men had dialled 999 himself before the group were arrested.

Asked why the suspects had been released on bail - a decision which has been openly questioned by President Donald Trump - the prime minister insisted the men were subject to the "strictest possible bail conditions" and added that UK authorities "have this under the strongest grip and closest control".

Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump said: "I will tell you, I would have said, 'don't let them have bail'. I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that."

But Burnham said: "I think people need to understand that when it says released - that isn't as people might think. It's obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions.

"The authorities have this under the strongest grip and closest control, and I can assure you of that."

Burnham's comments come after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that the incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor".

News.title: China funding UK research and sending it to Beijing's spies, MI5 warns
News.content:
More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China's espionage operations against the UK via a front company working for its intelligence and security services, MI5 has warned.

In the highly unusual public alert, the UK's internal security service warned universities and academics that continuing ties with China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) could ultimately lead to criminal charges for aiding a foreign state.

Security minister Dan Jarvis said MI5's warning exposed attempts by Chinese intelligence agencies to use British academic research to undermine UK national security.

He said he had now written to all university vice-chancellors to end relationships with the organisation.

In June, MI5 and its closest partners in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, issued a joint warning that China's military intelligence services were targeting professional networking sites and online job platforms.

This new UK-specific alert goes further, revealing what the service says is a threat that has been growing within British academic institutions.

MI5 says that the CGTRI, sometimes translated as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), has "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS).

"MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage," it says.

"More than 100 UK-linked academics have contributed to projects funded by MSS via CGTRI," adding that in some cases the researches would not be aware of the front company's role in their project.

UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object.

"This activity supports Ministry of State Security espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security," MI5 said.

The security alert said that many academic institutions and individuals will have engaged with the CGTRI "in good faith" because the link back to Chinese state security had been "obfuscated".

It continued: "UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions."

The public alert raises the prospect that British academics who do not act on it immediately could ultimately fall foul of the law.

It stressed that the National Security Act, a key piece of legislation passed in 2023 to counter state espionage, created a new offence of assisting a foreign intelligence service where the individual ought to reasonably have known what they were doing so.

Jarvis said: "This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies."

News.title: Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, Burnham tells BBC
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" a future Labour election manifesto could promise a new in-out referendum on the European Union.

The prime minister told the BBC a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now" but the UK needed to "consider the options" for its relationship with the EU as "where we are isn't good enough".

It comes after he pledged in his Labour conference speech on Tuesday to explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year.

The move could set up a huge dividing line at the next general election, with the Conservatives accusing Burnham of trying to "reopen old wounds by restarting the battles of the Brexit years".

As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In an interview with BBC political editor Chris Mason, Burnham was challenged over whether he was reopening divisive arguments about rejoining the EU, despite promising not to in May.

In response, the PM said: "No, I'm not proposing that, am I? I am saying that in a context when we're looking at a 10-year plan for Britain, Britain needs to consider the options as to where we will be.

"That is way before you even get to anything that's put before the public, this is about now just looking at what are the broad options for our relationship."

He suggested these options could include staying "exactly as we are", a closer relationship similar to that being discussed by the EU and Canada or rejoining the EU customs union.

However, Burnham stressed that "to leap back to a proposal and a referendum on it wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".

Pressed over whether including an in-out referendum in a future Labour manifesto was a possibility, Burnham said: "Yes, things are possible. I think where we are isn't good enough."

News.title: We fear for our lives after being told our abusive exes will be freed from jail early
News.content:
Dame Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, called the scheme "shameful" and said she's had "no assurance that the danger perpetrators pose has been properly considered and assessed with meaningful input from victims".

"Ultimately, we cannot ignore the fact that the early release scheme has caused untold damage to victims' confidence in the justice system," Dame Nicole added.

She said Prime Minister Andy Burnham "must take urgent steps to address this" and called on the probation service to be given "the resources it needs to safely manage more offenders in the community". She also called for additional funding for domestic abuse services to support victims.

A recent report raised serious concerns about electronic tagging, which can be used to monitor offenders' movements in the community. It found almost half of tags were not fitted on time.

Alice told the BBC she had been looking to buy a doorbell with a camera fitted to help make her feel safer, but said she cannot afford one. "I don't feel prepared in the slightest and I don't feel safe," she added.

"I think the early release scheme is a joke to victims and survivors, who spent years preparing for trial, going through evidence and re-traumatising themselves to go to court, just for the perpetrator of their crimes to be released after just 33% of their sentence".

The MoJ said: "Anyone who is released faces the toughest-ever controls on their movements, including world-first restriction zones and the largest expansion of electronic tagging, with victims having a say in their perpetrators' licence conditions."

News.title: Teens who died in car that entered river named
News.content:
Two teenage boys and a teenage girl who died when a car they were in ended up in the River Wear have been named by police.

Northumbria Police said a black Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, in Sunderland, and went in the water just before 13:30 BST on Tuesday. Four people were in the car at the time.

The three who died have been named as Jackson Duke, 17, Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw, both 16.

A 17-year-old boy who managed to reach safety has been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving, the force said.

The force said the investigation into the circumstances leading up to the car entering the water, including who was driving, were ongoing.

Jackson and Luke were from Sunderland, while Zara was from Houghton-le-Spring, a town about seven miles (11km) from the city.

News.title: Sussexes condemn 'reckless intrusion' after photographer spotted near Archie and Lilibet's school
News.content:
The BBC understands that the two men were observed by both private security and school staff on Monday morning, stopping at various points and looking into the school grounds, before returning to a van which police later established was a rental vehicle.

One of the men was later identified as photographer for a European press agency.

"The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless," Harry and Meghan's spokesman said.

"There is a world of difference between legitimate media activity and photographers walking the perimeter of a school, stopping to look into the grounds and monitoring children as they go about their day."

The spokesman continued: "Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school."

The children began school in the UK at the start of September, but changed after a few days after security concerns were raised about traffic during the school run.

Earlier this month, it emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their move back.

News.title: Oasis take legal action to stop sale of unheard tapes
News.content:
A set of unheard Oasis recordings valued at between Â£1.2m and Â£1.6m have been pulled from an auction after the band filed an injunction.

Earlier this month, it was announced that Littleton Auctions, in Evesham, were selling a set of recordings which included 63 live shows, as well as soundchecks and more than 100 hours of Noel and Liam Gallagher in the 1990s.

They were collected by Oasis sound engineer Huw Richards, who worked with the band from the release of their debut album Definitely, Maybe in 1994, until 2001.

However, the auction house said the sale of the recordings had been suspended after the band intervened.

Managing director Ben Homer said: "Littleton Auctions confirms that the Oasis recordings known as The Desk Tapes have been withdrawn from our October 3 auction in light of legal proceedings.

"We are very disappointed that we cannot offer this significant archive as planned."

News.title: Residents near RAF Fairford left 'like sitting ducks'
News.content:
A couple, who asked not to be named, claims Whelford villagers were warned to stay home on Saturday night - hours before the alarm was first raised by a farmer.

The pair were evacuated from their home the following morning, after the vans were found abandoned at the end of their driveway.

But when the husband stepped outside, he said he was confronted by armed police.

"I was trying to get my wallet out to say, 'look I'm a resident here'," he said.

"Then one of them got out of the vehicle and put a gun on me, in my direction.

"Then the other officer also got out, put a gun on me, and said 'Who's asked you to leave?'."

The couple said they and and their terrified child were briefly trapped inside their home before managing to escape through a neighbour's property.

After being allowed to return home, the pair saw the van doors had been "blown off" and their contents emptied, with water butts and oil drums strewn on the ground.

"All of a sudden, you see on the news the five suspected terrorists have been released," the husband said.

"You're thinking, 'Is this for real?'.

"We've all been panicking for the best part of a day and a bit. Are our homes going to get blown up? Could we have been blown up?"

The family say they are "angry" over an absence of communication from authorities in the days leading up to the incident, alongside the lack of reassurance afterwards.

News.title: Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.

The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester.

An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

It comes as the Independent Football Regulator â set up by the government in 2025 â said the case had raised "serious issues".

The regulator suggested it would be exploring options â including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club â once the disciplinary process was completed.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing â which could take months to convene â to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.

The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period.

Some fans and pundits have questioned how the club's owners can carry on if they deliberately breached rules over the course of nine years.

Asked by the BBC's political editor Chris Mason if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burham said on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

News.title: Met hands Grenfell fire investigation file to CPS
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has submitted its final investigation file into the Grenfell Tower fire to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), seeking charges against 54 individuals and 20 companies.

These include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office.

Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC) and the Department of Housing have both been referred to the CPS following the fire which killed 72 people at the tower block in North Kensington, west London.

The CPS said charging decisions would be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster, which is on 14 June 2027.

RBKC said it had been informed by the Met that it had referred the council to the CPS for three offences: corporate manslaughter, section 3 of Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, and acting contrary to the Regulatory Reform (fire safety) Order 2005.

The council said in a statement on Wednesday: "They have told us that the CPS will now independently review the evidence, and they will decide whether to charge the council of those offences."

Elizabeth Campbell, leader of the council, said their "commitment to candour, openness, and accountability has not changed".

News.title: 'Rock, paper, scissors' decides London Marathon dates
News.content:
A game of rock, paper, scissors was used to determine when the elite female and male races will take place during next year's unique two-day London Marathon.

After confirming they were playing for the right to race on the traditional Sunday, women's wheelchair world record holder Catherine Debrunner beat men's world record holder Sabastian Sawe - both 2026 London Marathon champions in their respective races - in the contest.

As a result, the elite men and men's wheelchair races are set for Saturday, 24 April, with the women's races the following day.

Hugh Brasher, chief executive of London Marathon Events, said: "Sabastian and Catherine's rock, paper, scissors battle was an entertaining way to decide which day would host each elite race.

"Splitting the elite races will allow us to shine an even brighter spotlight on the extraordinary athletes taking part."

Earlier this year, organisers of the event confirmed the London Marathon will be held across two days in what is said to be a momentous one-off edition of the event.

The decision was made to enable more people to take part, after a record 1.33 million people entered the ballot for next year.

In 2027 a record-breaking 100,000 participants will take part and it is estimated that more than Â£150m will be raised for charitable causes.

The women's championship categories will line-up behind the women's elite field for the first time in the London race.

"Our outstanding elite women's wheelchair field will begin the action just ahead of them, creating a true celebration of women's marathon racing," Brasher added.

The main events on both days will be a mixed field of male, female and non-binary participants.

News.title: Greggs to shut four factories and cut 740 jobs
News.content:
High street bakery brand Greggs has announced plans to shut four of its factories and cut 740 jobs.

It plans to close manufacturing sites at North Lakes near Penrith, Cumbria, Pettigrews in Kelso, Scotland, Seaham in County Durham and Enfield, Greater London, though distribution operations would continue to run from the latter.

The proposals will also impact manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will also continue as a distribution centre for the business.

The chain, which has headquarters in Newcastle, said its retail shops would not be affected by the proposed changes and like-for-like sales had grown across its managed stores.

It said the plans would save it about Â£20m across the 2028 and 2029 financial years.

The changes would take place over the next two and a half years, with parts of Greggs' manufacturing processes relocating, the firm said.

The range of products manufactured at its Clydesmill Glasgow and Manchester locations would be reduced and production of tinned bread at Gosforth would be stopped.

Some products would also be sourced from specialist suppliers.

The general secretary of the Bakers, Food and Allied Workers Union (BFAWU) Sarah Woolley said the union was "deeply concerned" about the announcement.

She said: "Our immediate priority is our members, their jobs, their families and the communities that could be affected by these proposals."

She added Greggs was clear in its own announcement the business continued to "perform strongly".

News.title: Grooming gangs inquiry expanded to Birmingham and Wales
News.content:
A national inquiry into child sexual abuse by grooming gangs has announced that targeted investigations will take place in Birmingham and Wales.

The inquiry said the probes would "examine the sexual abuse and exploitation of children by grooming gangs and the response of organisations responsible for protecting children" in both areas.

Oldham in Greater Manchester, Bradford and Keighley in West Yorkshire and London were announced as the first locations for investigations earlier this year.

It is unclear whether further locations will be selected. Some survivors have expressed frustration that their area has not yet been included and said they were concerned about expanding the inquiry's scope.

Fiona Goddard, who was sexually abused as a child by groups of men in Bradford, said there was clearly evidence from Birmingham and Wales "that needs to be properly heard" and welcomed their inclusion.

But she told the BBC that the scale of the inquiry "must not come at the expense of the depth of investigation". This was especially concerning, Goddard added, given "we are already almost a year into the inquiry with relatively little progress".

Carly, not her real name, was 12 years old when she was first groomed in Huddersfield in 2004. She said she could not understand "how an investigation covering an area as enormous and complex as Wales can be described as a deep dive".

"How are survivors in Huddersfield supposed to have confidence that our experiences will not simply be absorbed into a much bigger national picture and effectively watered down?"

Meanwhile, Welsh grooming gang victim Emily Vaughan, not her real name, welcomed the announcement - saying it marked "a day that has been needed for a very long time".

"It's about institutions that failed children and the questions that have remained unanswered. The expansion of the inquiry means those failures can no longer simply be brushed aside."

News.title: BBC commentator thanks Cardiff City legend for saving him after heart attack scare
News.content:
Blake, who played 131 times for City as well as winning 29 Wales caps, credited his actions to his mum's nurse training.

The 54-year-old, who also played for clubs including Sheffield United, Bolton Wanderers, Blackburn Rovers and Wolves, said: "She always used to say to me 'if someone loses colour like that call an ambulance'."

It had been business as usual for Phillips alongside him in the commentary box, as Cardiff lost "having played really well", he told BBC Radio Wales.

Thierry Gale had scored a 90th-minute header at the Toughsheet Community Stadium in the Championship match, and after completing the post-match interviews, Phillips said he started "having severe chest pains" as he got back to the press box.

He added: "I said to Nath 'I'll be fine now', but he told me I'd lost all my colour."

Phillips said he was still laughing and joking around when he was taken to see the Bolton club doctor, adding: "He casually said to me 'Rob, I can't be sure, but I think you're having a heart attack'."

Within an hour he was on an operating table with a pipe up his arm, as doctors tried to unblock his artery.

News.title: NHS trust admits 'failing families' over stillbirths
News.content:
An NHS trust has apologised after an independent review found that eight babies might have survived with better maternity care, admitting it has "failed families".

The stillbirths all occurred at the East Kent Hospitals NHS Trust's hospitals between June 2025 and March 2026.

An independent review ordered by the trust found systemic issues lay at the heart of the failures. These included failures to manage high risk pregnancies, provide appropriate triage, identify foetal growth concerns, and make appropriate use of interpreter services.

Since the report, a further seven stillbirths have occurred, including three last month. A review into those deaths has now been ordered.

All the stillbirths occurred after 34 weeks gestation.

Three years ago, the Kirkup report found 45 babies might have survived at the trust's hospitals if they had received better care.

The East Kent NHS trust runs the William Harvey Hospital in Ashford and the Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother Hospital (QEQM) in Margate.

News.title: Pilot stabs co-pilot in attempted hijacking of Israel flight - before hero passengers avert disaster

A pilot who stabbed his co-pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv in an attempted hijacking wanted to crash the plane and kill everyone on board, Israel has said.

Israeli intelligence believe the pilot is an Omani jihadist who wanted to carrying out a midair terror attack, that was only prevented by the brave intervention of passengers on the Flydubai flight. An off duty British pilot also stepped in to help land the plane safely in Saudi Arabia after chaos broke out in the cabin on Wednesday.

With their clothes still covered in blood, a number of the 170 people on board described the terrifying ordeal after the plane veered off course and dramatically descended around 17,000 feet in two minutes.

Flight FZ1073 passengers managed to overpower the attacker, “narrowly avoiding a major disaster” an Israeli official said. They broke into the cockpit with members of the crew after the aircraft entered a tailspin, only to find the co-pilot trying to sabotage the systems.

If you or anyone you know have been impacted by this incident and would like to share your story, please email alex.croft@independent.co.uk

open image in gallery Passengers gather round an injured man, who appears to be one of the pilots ( Social media )

open image in gallery The other pilot was also seen with injuries and using a gas mask ( Social media )

“We’re here during the hijacking of an airplane,” said one passenger with blood running down his face, in a plea posted to social media during the melee.

“At this point we’ve subdued the terrorists, we’re approaching landing. Whoever is hearing me, we need help.”

Yasmin Abu Kasis, the mother of one of the passengers, said her daughter Miriam heard screaming and saw a man with a knife put the pilot on the floor, with blood everywhere.

“The plane start to lose control. So all the people, they scream,” she told The Associated Press.

The wounded pilot, covered with blood and lying on the floor, had managed to click open the release on the cockpit door so help could get through.

open image in gallery Passengers covered in blood described the chaos onboard ( Israeli media )

open image in gallery With blood pouring down his head, one passenger posted a video asking for help ( Social media )

“Someone shouted ‘stabbing’ and my husband immediately understood what was happening and rushed to the front of the plane, and along with other Israelis they neutralized the terrorist,” Meital, a passenger whose husband was involved in the onboard brawl, told Israel’s Channel 12.

“There were stabbings and a lot of blood. We’re very emotional and under terrible stress, it’s very difficult for me to talk,” she adds.

Graphic footage from inside the flight shows the two pilots covered in blood and wearing gas masks in the aftermath of the horrifying incident.

A second set of pilots on board, who were due to replace the first pair, landed the plane safely at Tabuk Airport in north eastern Saudi Arabia.

One passenger, Almog Itali, has told media that one of the off-duty pilots onboard who stabilised the plane was British.

open image in gallery Passengers applauded after the flight safely landed on diversion in Saudi Arabia ( i24 Israel News )

open image in gallery The FlyDubai plane was missing its rudder when it touched down in Saudi Arabia after an emergency landing ( Social media )

In a short translated clip on the BBC, Mr Itali said: “There were two pilots in the front, one stabbed the other, and there were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight.

“The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered (the cockpit) and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.”

A spokesperson for the airport said both the wounded pilot and co-pilot involved were hospitalised after the plane landed. The passengers, none of whom were injured, were greeted by their friends and family later on Wednesday

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one pilot has been arrested and was being interrogated by Saudi authorities, after stabbing the other pilot and allegedly trying to crash the plane.

“I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage,” the prime minister added. “They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster.”

open image in gallery This Flightradar24 map shows the flight’s path when it was diverted to Saudi Arabia ( Flightradar24.com )

Defence minister Israeli Katz described the incident was a “jihadi terrorist attack attempt”.

However, the airline said in a statement that the underlying reasons for the event remained unknown and warned against premature speculation. The cause of the altercation between the pilots is not yet clear.

Katz said it the attack was “thwarted only thanks to the bravery of several Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit, overpowered the terrorist and, with their own hands, restored control of the plane to another flight crew who was present there”.

Netanyahu has ordered tighter security on both Israeli and non-Israeli carriers flying into the country, amid growing tensions in the region due to the ongoing war with Iran.

The incident has also further heightened security fears weeks before Israelis vote in the first election since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks.

open image in gallery Family members and loved ones of the passengers on the FlyDubai aircraft wait for their arrival at Ben Gurion International Airport ( Reuters )

Israel’s national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir said “a terrorist who planned to crash a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board”, using the incident to call for continued military action in “Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, and Judea and Samaria [the West Bank”.

“Terrorism is a devil with whom no agreement must be reached,” he added.

A spokesperson for Flydubai told The Independent that an “altercation occurred in the flight deck” before the aircraft was “secured by on-duty Flydubai crew”.

“Everyone onboard is safe and accounted for and will be picked up by two replacement aircraft that have been sent to Tabuk”, it said, adding that the motives remain unknown and “subject to a formal investigation”.

Flydubai operates daily flights between Dubai and ‌Tel Aviv, a route that is popular ⁠among Israeli nationals.

A second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, flight FZ1081, afterwards diverted and is heading back to Dubai, according to FlightRadar. It is unclear whether this was precautionary or the result of another incident.

Energy debt in the UK has reached a record £5bn, new official figures have revealed, as household bills are set to rise further in the coming months.

Data from Ofgem shows that domestic customer debt and arrears outstanding for 91 days hit £5.02bn by the end of June, up 4.8 per cent from the previous quarter and 13 per cent year-on-year.

The increase during the summer months comes despite the back-to-back heatwaves experienced across Europe this year, which brought temperatures to record highs.

Experts have warned that winter threatens to continue pushing the UK’s energy debt levels, as rising fuel costs and lower temperatures drive up household bills.

Nearly a third (29 per cent) of UK adults are now concerned about their ability to pay their energy bills over the next six months, a poll from debt charity StepChange has found. The charity adds that the average energy arrears for its clients now stands at £2,676.

open image in gallery Energy costs will increase on Thursday, with another hike expected in January ( PA Archive )

Peter Tutton, director of policy, research and public affairs at StepChange, said the latest figures show “yet more evidence of sustained pressure on household budgets and an inability to pay regular costs”.

“With further price rises expected in the new year, things stand sadly only to worsen,” he added.

"What is most alarming is the 5 per cent increase in total arrears during a period where people tend to use less energy in the warmer spring and early summer months. With winter still to come and the price cap set to rise, financial pressures are highly likely to intensify in the coming months.”

StepChange has urged the government to introduce a new social energy tariff, means-tested to support the most vulnerable, alongside implementing Ofgem’s debt relief scheme.

Last year, the regulator announced a consultation on a scheme to tackle debt built up between 2022 and 2024 to help 195,000 customers write off up to £500m. However, the scheme has not yet received a fixed launch date.

The debt figures come as energy bills are set to increase by £60 on average from October, when Ofgem’s energy price cap rises to £1,723. This will partially offset by Andy Burnham’s move to cut VAT from electricity bills, saving £45 on average.

Ahead of the increase, Cornwall Insight has predicted that bills will rise another £276 from January, up to an average £1,999 a year.

The trusted forecaster says its figure is based on the ongoing US-Iran conflict, which has hit energy prices worldwide.

Responding to the latest debt figures, TUC General Secretary Paul Nowak said: “Energy costs are crushing households up and down the country – with many getting into debt just to keep the lights on.

“The government are rightly prioritising help for households with the cost of living. But with energy prices set to rise in October as a result of Trump’s reckless warmongering – and no end in sight to war in the Middle East – ministers will need to go further and faster to protect households.

“That's why the government should cut household energy bills with a social tariff – paid for by taxing banks' enormous profits.”

The government was approached for comment.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has stated that it would be incorrect to "leap to judgment" over Manchester City, expressing confidence that his past interactions with the club will hold up under examination.

Addressing the team's conviction over financial regulation violations spanning from 2009-10 to 2017-18, he argued they ought to be permitted to "contest the situation if they don’t think it’s fair".

However, Burnham maintained he would "keep my distance" if representatives from the United Arab Emirates government approached him regarding the conflict after City vowed to appeal.

According to the Premier League, an independent panel concluded that City setup "sham" commercial agreements with several sponsors throughout that timeframe as part of a covert funding system, in which the firms only covered a fraction of the agreed sponsorship costs.

It was established by the panel that the outstanding amounts were provided by the club's parent entity, Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG).

open image in gallery Man City chiefs have denied any wrongdoing ( Reuters )

Expressing gratitude to City Football Group - the parent organisation of the club - for its investment in the local area, the Prime Minister noted he would be "really concerned to lose them" if they chose to divest.

Speaking to 5 News, he remarked: "I think it’s only right that Manchester City and Manchester City supporters have that opportunity to continue to contest the situation if they don’t think it’s fair."

Previously, the Prime Minister spoke out against the Premier League's penalty docking points from Everton for financial rule infractions.

The Merseyside club successfully appealed their initial 10-point sanction in 2024, seeing it lowered to six points.

Burnham, a fan of Everton, informed the news outlet: "I think it’s only right to say that it is still contested now.

"The Premier League proclaimed (Everton) guilty and I never accepted that and therefore it would be somewhat wrong of me to leap to judgment on another football club. But they’re very serious charges, don’t get me wrong."

He added: "But I think it’s only fair from my own experience fighting for my club that I take that position at this stage."

When questioned by the BBC on whether his historical interactions with Manchester City would survive public scrutiny, he replied: "Oh indeed, I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad and the campus around it but also into the city, but yes of course."

In response to queries about a potential sale of the team, he stated: "I would be really concerned to lose them. They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester.

"Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

On whether he would entertain dialogue with the UAE government concerning the ongoing case, he explained to the BBC: "I am not getting directly involved in the process. I’ve not spoken to anybody directly about that.

open image in gallery Burnham would not be drawn on whether City should be relegated after years of dominance ( Getty )

"I have to keep my distance from it. It would be wrong for me to do anything else. It’s an independent legal process that has to play its course through.

"…There’s a lot at stake. Let’s be honest about that, for the football club, for city supporters, for the city of Manchester."

The Prime Minister declined to comment on whether Manchester City ought to face relegation from the top flight.

For its part, the club plans to challenge the ruling "on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

Following the confirmation of the breaches, the Premier League indicated that potential penalties will be considered at a subsequent hearing held by the independent panel.

A public statement from the Premier League added that additional "sham arrangements" allowed the club to report artificially suppressed operating costs.

Over the period in question, the illicit scheme served to boost recorded income and trim expenditure by in excess of £900 million.

In its final judgment, the panel declared: "By its conduct the club clearly intended to circumvent the Premier League rules."

Polling guru Professor Sir John Curtice has emerged as the favourite to lead Andy Burnham’s commission on electoral reform that could see the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system scrapped.

The commission to change the voting system for parliament was announced by Andy Burnham amid a series of startling policies in his first speech as prime minister at a Labour Party conference in Liverpool.

It will consider changing the way people cast their votes in Westminster elections, with the prime minister himself supporting a switch to a proportional representation (PR) model, in a move that could prove seismic for the future of British politics.

While Sir John told The Independent that he has not been approached, Labour sources have said he is the preferred name to chair the commission on electoral reform in the hope it will provide it with authority and command trust from the public.

The 72-year-old Strathclyde University academic and UK’s leading polling expert was awarded a knighthood by former prime minister Theresa May and has become a well known face for the public over decades of commenting on polling.

Sir John is no stranger to the electoral reform debate and has sat on panels for campaign groups pushing for proportional representation such as Make Votes Matter and the Electoral Reform Society.

Professor Sir John Curtice (Andrew Matthews/PA) ( PA Wire )

One senior Labour figure told The Independent: “John Curtice is the obvious person to chair this commission. The public know and trust him and will respect the conclusions if it is fronted by someone with his authority.

“Andy Burnham doesn’t have many options to chair this commission. Curtice is a no-brainer.”

A Downing Street source said they “are not at the stage” of approaching anyone yet.

Sir John has regularly commented on the way that the traditional FPTP system, where seats are decided by the party which gets the most votes in a constituency rather than a majority of the overall votes is becoming increasingly out of date.

In an article for the BBC in May said: “Historically, the [first past the post] system has also given whoever is the victor in the electoral battle between Conservative and Labour a boost in seats. The two parties thus both get the chance of securing a period of untrammeled majority government rather than having to negotiate the rocky shores of minority or coalition government.

“However, [last May's] election results raise questions about whether first-past-the-post will continue to benefit the Conservatives and Labour in future. Rather, they have shown that the system is colour blind in how it operates.

“The results confirmed that Britain has now entered an unprecedented era of multi-party politics.”

He also pointed out that “fewer than three in five people voted Conservative or Labour in the 2024 general election. That was the lowest proportion since and including 1922, when Labour first became the Conservatives' principal competitors.”

Speaking on a panel for Make Votes Matter in May, Sir John also highlighted the unfairness of the current system where a party can win many votes but still come away with very few seats.

He said: “If at the same time your vote goes down and becomes more geographically spread, the system will murder you.”

However, writing in The Times, Sir Johnwarned that Mr Burnham’s plans to introduce a more proportional system "would come at a price" for the party.

"Electoral systems vary in their degree of proportionality, but virtually any conceivable alternative would have treated Reform much more favourably," he wrote.

"While electoral reform might make it much difficult for a future Reform leader to become prime minister, it would make it easier for the party to establish the significant parliamentary presence it currently lacks."
