Electric car drivers using Gridserve chargers on October 1 will get a 20 per cent discount, as the company cuts its prices for one day. This is highlight the difference in VAT between charging at home and using the public network.

The price reduction comes on the same day that VAT on qualifying domestic electricity in Great Britain falls to zero until March 31, 2027. Public EV charging, however, will continue to attract VAT at the full 20 per cent rate.

Gridserve normally charges between 85p and 92p per kWh for ultra-rapid charging at speeds of up to 400kW. On October 1, those prices will fall by 20 per cent to between 68p and 73.6p per kWh.



open image in gallery Gridserve's ultra-rapid charging costs will drop from 85p and 92p per kWh to between 68p and 73.6p per kWh on October 1 for one day ( Gridserve )

For a typical 40kWh top-up, that works out at a saving of between £6.80 and £7.36. It might only be the price of a couple of coffees on the day, but for someone doing the same charge once a week the savings would add up to between £353.60 and £382.72 over a year.

The one-day offer is Gridserve’s way of highlighting what it sees as an unfair difference between drivers who can plug their cars in at home and those who have to rely on public chargers.

The company says drivers living in flats, rented homes or properties without off-street parking can face higher charging costs simply because they don’t have a driveway. It estimates that 10 million British households have no potential for off-street parking.

Rebecca Trebble, chief customer officer at Gridserve, said: “On 1 October, millions of households will see VAT removed from their electricity bills. For EV drivers who cannot charge at home, however, the tax treatment of electricity is very different.

“We want to make that difference tangible. Rather than simply talking about what cheaper public charging could look like, we are giving drivers the opportunity to experience it for themselves.

“Gridserve has been clear that if the gbovernment reduces the VAT burden on public EV charging, we believe the benefit should be passed directly through to drivers. Our 1 October initiative demonstrates this principle in practice: when the cost of charging comes down, drivers will see those savings at the plug.”

Public charging operators argue that VAT is only part of the reason public charging can cost considerably more than plugging in at home. They also face the cost of installing and maintaining high-powered chargers, land rents and expensive grid connections.

open image in gallery Gridserve's Chief Customer Officer, Rebecca Trebble: "Rather than simply talking about what cheaper public charging could look like, we are giving drivers the opportunity to experience it for themselves." ( Gridserve )

Independent analysis from Cornwall Insight found that standing charges for ultra-rapid charging hubs have increased by up to 462 per cent since 2021.

Gridserve has previously called for the tax treatment of home and public charging to be brought closer together. Research commissioned by the company in 2025 found that 49 per cent of non-EV drivers surveyed said they would switch to an electric car sooner if public charging attracted the same VAT rate as charging at home.

The Government is reviewing the cost of public EV charging, with its findings expected later this year.

Shane Brennan, chief executive of ChargeUK, said: “Cutting VAT on home electricity is the right call at the right time, it will relieve some pressure on what will be a tough winter for energy consumers, including EV drivers.

“However, it will also entrench the driveway divide for those current and want-to-be EV drivers who pay the full 20 per cent VAT to charge their cars at the worst moment.

“With diesel prices topping £2 a litre this week, and petrol not far behind, encouraging all drivers to go electric is the right thing to do, let’s make it fair and accessible for all.”

Khaldoon Al Mubarak, chairman of the scandal-plagued Manchester City soccer club, sat with Donald Trump in Davos this year, signing on to the U.S. president’s Board of Peace on behalf of the United Arab Emirates government.

He was with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Palace of Versailles in June at a signing ceremony for a business summit.

Al Mubarak, 50, also is a UAE special envoy to China, and welcomed Xi Jinping to the club when the Chinese leader visited England in 2015.

Why the head of an English soccer club — albeit one of the wealthiest, most successful and now highly controversial — should be a key player at such political events is easily explained.

Al Mubarak, the public face of the 2023 Champions League winner now embroiled in one of soccer's biggest scandals, is a member of the ruling elite in Abu Dhabi — part of the United Arab Emirates — and the head of a $385 billion sovereign wealth fund.

His family has a long tradition of public service that he has continued with a long list of roles serving his nation's interests, including as a strategy advisor to its president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, known as MBZ, and a board member of both Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank and Abu Dhabi National Oil Company.

Before entering European soccer, Al Mubarak was a key liaison with F1 when the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix joined the circuit.

When Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, now a deputy prime minister of the UAE, bought the long-time underachieving soccer club in 2008, Al Mubarak was installed as chairman to oversee what became a turnaround that was barely believable to an older generation of fans.

The story of sporting and financial success was, according to the verdict by an investigatory panel, too good to be true.

While under Al Mubarak's leadership, Man Ci ty was found to have broken financial rules

The Premier League announced Tuesday that its most successful club over the past 15 seasons, and current standings leader, systematically broke financial monitoring rules for years.

An independent panel of judges appointed by the league said City orchestrated “sham” contracts with commercial partners to disguise secret funding of more than 830 million pounds ($1.1 billion) by the Abu Dhabi ownership between 2009-18. Club witnesses also gave evidence “they knew to be untrue."

That money helped pay high-value transfer fees and wages for players, some signed from City’s biggest rivals, that fueled the club’s trophy-laden rise to become a European power.

For City it was a virtuous circle: winning titles led to earning more prize money and building a global brand that led to attracting more of the world’s best players, like today’s superstar goal scorer Erling Haaland.

Al Mubarak held firm when the story of the judgment leaked

The devastating judgment, which City can appeal, said the club broke Premier League rules designed to keep clubs financially stable and secure, and which rivals like Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United complied with.

Reports of the pending verdict leaked Friday to The Athletic, and the club responded a day later with a statement from Al Mubarak.

“Here’s what I said to my family,” he said. “The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the Club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.”

Al Mubarak says the club represents Abu Dhabi's values

In a rare interview in 2009, with British daily The Guardian, he spoke of City as representing Abu Dhabi's values. "These are loyalty, commitment, discipline, long-term thinking, respect, appreciation of history.”

“This is showing the world the true essence of who Abu Dhabi is and what Abu Dhabi is about,” he said.

Al Mubarak was an elegant, articulate embodiment of a project many saw as an extension of Abu Dhabi soft power as much as a sheikh’s personal investment. He also is chairman of City Football Group, the global network of 12 clubs anchored by Man City that includes New York City FC.

A graduate in economics from Tufts University near Boston, he oversees the Mubadala wealth fund among a slew of key government positions.

His family suffered personal tragedy in public service

Al Mubarak's father, Khalifa Al Mubarak, was a diplomat who served as the UAE’s ambassador to France.

He was assassinated in Paris in February 1984, shot on a street outside his residence close to the Eiffel Tower. Khaldoon Al Mubarak was 8. The killing was linked to the Abu Nidal Organization, a violent group calling for Israel's destruction.

Gulf media has reported that the young Khaldoon was mentored by the royal family in the wake of his father's death. In 2018 a street in Abu Dhabi was renamed for the slain diplomat.

Hacked emails revealed the malfeasance

As Man City's finances and compliance with soccer's rules came under more scrutiny, including by UEFA investigations judged in 2014 and 2020, Al Mubarak's public comments were limited to end-of-season interviews filmed and conducted by the club's own staff.

A landmark UEFA case in 2020 — won by City on an appeal that overturned a two-year ban from the Champions League — and the Premier League case were sparked by internal club emails and documents obtained by a hacker-whistleblower.

They were published in a series of articles by German magazine Der Spiegel in November 2018, that gave insight into the City chairman's resolve for a legal battle.

In 2014, when UEFA's then-general secretary, now FIFA president, Gianni Infantino, was in talks with Man City about settling a rules breach with a fine, the club's lawyer Simon Cliff sent an email with a line yet to be forgotten.

“Khaldoon said," Cliff wrote, "he would rather spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years.”

Russia has warned NATO that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military bloc try to cut off its western exclave from the rest of the country.

The warning sent to NATO echoed statements issued by several Russian embassies in Europe this week which said that Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing (an) air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and Kaliningrad region.”

The embassies in the U.K. and Ireland posted their statements on their Telegram channels, and the embassy in Belgium released it to the Tass news agency.

The statements accused European leaders of “playing a dangerous game” by warning that Russia might attack another country or ramp up a campaign of destabilizing attacks in Europe using drones and sabotage. Moscow has called the allegations absurd.

“There should be no mistake — Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country,” the Russian Embassy in Ireland said in its statement on Tuesday.

NATO slams 'irresponsible' nuclear rhetoric

NATO spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed on Wednesday that Russia had sent a written message to the U.S.-led military alliance. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she said in a statement.

Hart insisted that NATO is not targeting Kaliningrad and had sent a reply, “noting that NATO is a defensive alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia.”

The Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad is surrounded by NATO members Poland and Lithuania. It is home to Russia’s main Baltic navy base and other military assets. Nuclear-capable Iskander missiles are deployed there.

Western military officers have said that key military installations in Kaliningrad would be a likely first target should Russia ever launch an attack on any NATO ally.

NATO allies have conducted a series of military exercises in the Baltic Sea region in recent months. More are planned in October. It launched Operation Baltic Sentry there last year to protect communication cables and pipelines.

Europeans have warned that Russia could strike another country

Asked Wednesday about Russia’s warning, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov pointed to what he said were “rampant statements” from Poland and other European nations regarding Kaliningrad.

“It’s only natural that our diplomats are trying to remind the hotheads in Europe about our policy documents regarding this matter,” Peskov said in a call with reporters.

European leaders and intelligence services have warned that Russia is ramping up its hybrid campaign and could be ready to strike at another country within a few years, especially if it wins its war on Ukraine.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said last week that he believes the rising number of incidents shows that Russian President Vladimir Putin is losing the war, now in its fifth year, and that the best way to respond is to give more weapons to Kyiv.

“Russia’s use of hybrid tactics is a sign of desperation,” Hart said. “But we will not be dissuaded from our support to Ukraine. We have what it takes to defend every inch of Allied territory and remain strong, ready, and able to counter any threat.”

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

News.title: Lethal Trent Alexander-Arnold sends Tuchel a statement in England victory
News.content:
Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

I knew exactly where I wanted to go, where I needed to go but I needed some guidance. I think the same way as him [Jude]. We don’t think there’s any limit on what we can achieve, wanting to win, wanting to win in a good way by going for the throat. Fearlessness.

It ate me up for a good couple of weeks after [losing the semi-final]. I’d scored… on the same pitch as Messi, the man I idolised as a kid. It was the highest possible moment of my entire life. And within 20 minutes it had come completely crashing down. There’s been a lot of controversy, a lot of talk about that. Going forward, if we are going to lose a game, it’s going to be like how we lost to Spain. We went for their throats, we missed a penalty and lost the game. But the way we went for them, no regrets. I want to stay as far away from that [regret] as possible.

[Did you ever think you would sign for Barcelona?] Yes. No one ever achieves anything in life by playing it safe. My personality is based on being bold, taking risks and going for whatever you want.

At this level we’re all as talented as each other but only the most mentally competitive and driven people can maintain success for a long time.

I always thought in England that people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never respected my quality and people are starting to take notice that I’m not just quick. In Barcelona if you’re not technical, if you’re not smart, you’d stand out like a sore thumb.

[Where do you see this squad in two years?] European champions.

News.title: How vaccines and antibiotics can beat some cancers
News.content:
At least one in eight cancers worldwide are caused by viruses and bacteria, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 – out of a total of 20 million recorded worldwide – were caused by common infections, almost all of which could have been prevented with treatments such as antibiotics or vaccines.

Almost half of infection-linked cancers, around 760,000 cases, were caused by H. pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach, researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer found.

The pathogen, which is typically ingested through contaminated food and water and is carried by around 60 per cent of the world’s population at any given time, can remain relatively undetected in the gut for between 20 and 40 years without causing any symptoms.

If left untreated, it can trigger chronic inflammation in the stomach and cellular mutations that, in some cases, lead to gastric cancer.

Cases of stomach cancer linked to H. pylori are particularly common in East Asia, where roughly 80 per cent of the population carries the bacterium. This is due in part to the prevalence of a more aggressive strain of the pathogen, known as CagA, which is endemic to the region.

East Asian diets – which typically include salty, pickled or smoked foods – can also damage the stomach’s protective lining and accelerate the inflammatory processes that can contribute to stomach cancer, researchers have found.

While H. pylori infection is treatable with a course of antibiotics, its symptoms often mimic those of other digestive problems and can be difficult to distinguish without testing.

This means the infection can remain undetected for years, allowing inflammation and damage to progress.

News.title: ‘Pooled’ TB testing could save money and improve diagnosis, study finds
News.content:
Mixing phlegm samples from multiple patients in “pooled tests” for tuberculosis could halve costs and help find millions of missing cases, according to a major new study.

While most advances in fighting TB come with a large price tag, the shift in strategy could dramatically boost access to diagnosis and save money, experts said.

TB is the deadliest single infection globally, killing around 1.3m people every year, despite being both preventable and curable.

The gold standard in diagnosis is rapid molecular testing, which detects genetic material from the bacteria causing TB in patient sputum samples within hours. But each sample needs a specialist diagnostic cartridge that costs around US$8, beyond the budget of many poorer countries even before recent aid cuts.

In a pooled test, samples from multiple individuals are tested in one cartridge. If the result is negative then all of them are reported to be negative, but if the result is positive each is re-tested individually.

Results published in The Lancet Global Health found the strategy, with up to four patients in each pool, used half as many cartridges as individual testing – 7,028 compared to 14,362. It detected 84.9 per cent of people with TB compared with 88 per cent for individual testing.

The study involved more than 14,000 people whose symptoms suggested TB in Bangladesh, Brazil, Cameroon, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria and Vietnam.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2007 after Middle East tensions pushed oil prices above $108.

Yields on 10-year gilts, which determine the price the treasury pays to borrow money, rose above 5.43pc on Monday, before edging back to 5.42pc.

These are levels not seen in almost two decades, underlining the challenge facing John Healey as he prepares for next month’s Budget.

The Chancellor is coming under pressure to slash spending or raise taxes to bring Britain’s borrowing costs under control, against a backdrop of growing debt and rising inflation.

The surge in 10-year gilt yields pushes them above the 19-year high of 5.41pc recorded earlier this month, threatening to put a dent in Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom – a self-imposed guardrail to guide public spending.

Economists said high costs reflect the scale of Britain’s near-£3tn national debt and the rise in inflation facing the country.

“The uncomfortable truth for the PM and his Chancellor, John Healey ... is that the wide spread of gilt yields over peers is fair, in our view, given the UK’s dire fiscal position and the inflationary pressures stemming from high energy prices,” said Elliott Jordan-Doak, at Pantheon Macroeconomics.

“Gilt yields will fall if energy prices drop, but investors will continue to be driven by the economics and the Government’s willingness to take tough fiscal decisions, both of which point to yields staying high.”

UK borrowing costs are growing amid a wider bond market sell-off after Donald Trump rejected a peace deal with Iran over the weekend, pushing oil prices higher.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 3pc to just over $108 a barrel on Monday, adding to global inflation pressures. Bond traders reacted by demanding higher yields from governments to lend them money.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds rose to above 5.24pc, the highest level since 2007.

News.title: Taylor Swift becomes most-awarded artist in MTV history
News.content:
Taylor Swift broke records at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs) on Sunday, becoming the most-awarded artist in VMA history.

The pop star, 36, was previously tied with Beyoncé for the title, with 30 VMAs each. However, Swift took home three awards at the ceremony, bringing her career total to an unmatched 33.

The Fate of Ophelia, ⁠Swift’s first single from her record-breaking The Life of a Showgirl album, claimed the top trophy – Video of the Year – and she dedicated the honour to the late country music legend Dolly Parton.

During her speech, Swift praised Parton as “the ultimate showgirl” who told stories that were “so vivid and so rich”.

“I think that we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time,” she said.

Parton, an award-winning country singer, died in August at the age of 80.

Swift also received the inaugural Artist Director Honors, a new award meant to recognise artists “whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling”.

The 36-year-old has written and directed 18 videos of her roughly 60 videos during her career. The ‌most recent, for ‌her new single Patient Zero, debuted during ⁠the ceremony.

Sports.title: World’s biggest football stadium set to host 135,000 fans taking shape as new photos emerge of 80-METRE tall towers
Sports.content:
Next

THE world’s biggest stadium is continuing to take shape after pictures showed off the incredible arena after nine months of construction.

The VinFast Trong Dong Stadium is being built in Hanoi, Vietnam and is set to host 135,000 spectators.



Workers are operating around the clock in a bid to complete the project by July 2027.

The initial completion date was the summer of 2028.



The stadium, which is named after a traditional Vietnamese bronze drum, will feature the biggest fully retractable roof.

Designs suggest it will have a stunning circular gold dome that will be shaped like a trong dong drum.



And now new images have shown huge 80-metre towers dotted around the site as constructions moves towards the next step.

A series of cranes are visible as the incredible vision of the ground begins to become a reality.

The project is said to be part of a £26million development to create an Olympic Sports City that will host global events.

The development will cover around 22,200 acres on the outskirts of Hanoi, according to Reuters.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

The 135,000 capacity will comfortably make it the largest football stadium globally.

That will make it more than twice the size of Arsenal’s Emirates Stadium.



The current biggest ground in the world is the Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in Pyongyang, North Korea, which can host around 114,000.

The second largest is the Nou Camp at 99,354 – though it will expand to 105,000 after its ongoing renovations are completed.

The Soccer City Stadium in Johannesburg – which hosted the 2010 World Cup final – comes in third at 94,736.

Rounding off the top five are the New Administrative Capital Stadium in Egypt at 93,940 and Wembley Stadium at 90,000.

The Grand Stade Hassan II in Morocco – which is currently under construction ahead of the 2030 World Cup – will have a 115,000 capacity when it’s ready.

Sports.title: Man City fans ashamed by guilty verdict and fear relegation – but don’t hold it against Sheikh Mansour ownership
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER CITY fans are fearing relegation from the Premier League – but are adamant they will not turn against Sheikh Mansour after being found guilty of breaking financial rules.

An independent commission ruled the Sky Blues had failed to comply with spending regulations following a four-year investigation into alleged breaches between 2009 and 2018.



And a stunning statement released by the Premier League revealed City hid a wallet-busting £900MILLION in “sham” deals.

Ashamed supporters are now fearing the worst as they wait to discover the sanctions.



But they are refusing to hold City’s rule-breaking against Mansour, 55, and other influential figures behind the scenes.

One diehard fan said: “I’m very disappointed but not surprised. The rules were brought in for the elite clubs after Mansour came in. We’d become one.

“I don’t think we’ve cheated on the sport but it looks pretty damning. I would imagine a fine is coming our way and enough points deducted to be relegated.

“But look at what the owners have done to the club. There is the Pep Guardiola Stand, Medlock Square and the new training ground.

“I have no anger at all and don’t blame the board. They were trying to compete with Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United – and they did it.

“Only Leicester did it and there will probably never be anyone else who does it except from them three and maybe Chelsea.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

“The likes of Newcastle, Aston Villa and Everton – proper clubs – will never win the Premier League with these rules.”

Liverpool legend Jamie Carragher has ruthlessly demanded for City to be stripped of their titles and the club’s mega-rich owners to be kicked out.

But another fan who visited the Etihad just days after his beloved Sky Blues had been found guilty of more than 100 charges vowed to back Mansour.

He added: “They touched up quite a wide aspect of our area as well as the stadium.



“They paid homage and I didn’t really estimate their wrongdoings. The owners should definitely be allowed to stay.”

But David Kogan, who is the chief of football’s new independent regulator, has warned he could boot City’s owners out of the sport.

Sports.title: Man City badge outside Etihad Stadium DEFACED with X-rated slur after club found guilty of financial rule breaches
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER CITY’S badge outside the Etihad Stadium has been defaced with an X-rated slur following the club’s bombshell financial verdict.

The giant crest was targeted in the aftermath of an independent commission finding the Premier League giants guilty of serious breaches of financial rules.



An offensive message was daubed across the badge outside City’s home ground as the fallout from the explosive ruling continued.

It comes during one of the most turbulent periods in the club’s recent history, with City facing the prospect of a major sporting sanction if their appeal is unsuccessful.



The Premier League confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission had found City guilty of all charges relating to serious breaches of its financial rules over a nine-season period between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

The commission found City had arranged “sham” contracts with commercial partners as part of schemes which artificially inflated revenues and reduced costs.

It concluded the arrangements distorted the club’s finances by more than £900million over the period in question.

City were also found guilty of the majority of charges relating to their failure to co-operate with the Premier League’s investigation.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said the decision established that the club had “systematically” broken the competition’s rules for almost a decade.

The punishment will be decided separately, with Premier League rules allowing the commission to impose sanctions including fines and points deductions.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

City, however, have vehemently rejected the findings and insist they remain innocent.

The club immediately confirmed its intention to appeal, claiming the commission’s opinion contains “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact” and describing the decision as “unsafe”.

City said: “The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.”

They added that they would be “relentless” in pursuing the regulatory and legal avenues available to them.

The club have until Friday, October 2, to exercise their right to appeal the commission’s findings.



No sanction has yet been imposed, with a separate hearing set to determine City’s punishment while the unprecedented battle between the club and the Premier League continues.

Sports.title: Man City chiefs could face criminal charges over Premier League breaches – with up to TEN YEARS in jail
Sports.content:
Next

INDIVIDUALS implicated in the Manchester City scandal could face criminal charges – as well as further action by the football authorities.

The bombshell summary of the independent commission’s guilty verdict on all but one of the charges City faced opens up the possibility of figures in the club being sentenced to up to TEN years in jail for fraud.



The police, financial regulators and the taxman are being urged to look at the wider implications of the club’s systematic breaking of Premier League financial regulations over a nine-season period.

Former City and Football Association chairman David Bernstein is among those to raise whether the case needs to be “looked at by outside authorities”.



Meanwhile Conservative party peer Lord Cruddas today said: “Surely the Man City findings are now a police matter.

“If accounts have been falsified and auditors have been misled, then it is potentially a criminal matter.”



The names of those responsible for City’s cheating are redacted from the summary. But the full version of the verdict includes appendices which spell out who knew what in the Etihad and City Football Group hierarchy.

The club continues to deny all wrongdoing and say they are confident of vindication.

But the commission found City guilty of disguising more than £800m of cash injections from their Abu Dhabi owners as commercial income, with the state-controlled Abu Dhabi United Group providing massive top-ups to the much smaller sums that came from sponsors.

The full verdict includes a whole section, Appendix 22, showing how City’s auditors remained in the dark.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Under section 501 of the 2006 Companies Act, it is a criminal offence to make “misleading, false or deceptive” statements to auditors, with a maximum prison term of two years for offenders.

But things could get even more serious for City and those who oversaw the cheating.

Section 2 of the Fraud Act 2006 says anyone who dishonestly makes a false representation – such as incomplete or inaccurate accounts – with the intention of making a gain or avoiding a loss can face up to 10 years in jail and an unlimited fine.

HMRC will surely take an interest in another strand of City’s cheating.

The club gave side contracts to individuals, in addition to their salary for working for the club, and paid inflated image rights deals to players via a company called Fordham.



When Portsmouth collapsed into administration for the first time in 2010, HMRC decided image rights payments to players including Sol Campbell were higher than their value, using the legal term “sham” to describe the agreements.

Similarly, the commission verdict on City describes the image rights deals and separate contracts as “shams”.

Like HMRC in the Portsmouth case, the commission believes the payments were effectively income which should have been subject to income tax and National Insurance contributions.

What are Man City charged with? THE Premier League claim Man City hid £900m in 'sham' deals across a nine-year period. They were found guilty on 114 of the initial 115 charges – with the number now up to 130 charges – which fit into six categories… Failing to give accurate financial information over sponsorship revenue, related parties and operating costs between 2009-10 and 2017/18. Total charges: 50

Failing to provide full details of managerial remuneration between 2009/10 and 2012/13. Total charges 8

Failing to provide full details of player remuneration between 2010/11 and 2015/16. Total charges 12

Failing to comply with Uefa Licencing and Financial Fair Play regulations between 2013/14 and 2017/18. Total charges 5

Breaching Premier League Profitability and Sustainability rules between 2015/16 and 2017/18. Total charges 25

Failing to co-operate with the Premier League investigation between 2018/19 and 2022/23. Total charges 30

Total charges: 130

Tax evasion is a criminal offence, carrying a penalty of up to seven years in jail.



If any City employee were convicted of criminal wrongdoing, they would immediately be disqualified from involvement in the club under the terms of the Premier League’s Owners’ and Directors’ Test.

The summary also accused some of those who gave evidence on City’s behalf of lying to the commission.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They are in danger of separate disciplinary action by the PL and/or the Football Association and Independent Football Regulator.

But such proceedings may end up being the least of their worries, if the authorities outside football also take an interest in the City saga.

Sports.title: How Man City case is different to Chelsea’s after Blues got off lightly over 74 breaches – thanks to hated owners
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER City fans are pointing to Chelsea’s lenient punishment as a sign that the Etihad club will not be thrown to the wolves.

The Blues admitted to 74 breaches of football regulations and escaped with a £10m fine and a rap across the knuckles.



While City have pledged to fight on, accusing the commission and League chiefs of serious failings, supporters recognise a major sanction is coming their way unless their appeal is successful.

It seems unlikely that City will be so lucky as Chelsea after the damning findings of the independent commission. SunSport explains why…



BASIC DIFFERENCES

In 2022, following the forced sale of Roman Abramovich’s stake in the club, Chelsea’s new owners BlueCo became aware of irregularities in previous financial figures.

Abramovich had sanctioned illegal, off books payments to agents, totalling millions of pounds, to grease the wheels on transfer deals, securing the likes of Eden Hazard, Willian and David Luiz to the club.



But rather than hiding this information, Chelsea reported their findings to both Uefa, which handed out a fine, the FA and Premier League.

The allegations against City, by contrast, were triggered by the 2018 Football Leaks data dump, a cache of emails and other documents relating to the club’s financial dealings between 2008-09 and 2017-18 and published by German magazine Spiegel.

From the outset, City vehemently and vigorously denied all the allegations, condemning the “illegal hacking and out-of-context publication” of their emails, maintaining their innocence would be confirmed by their “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence”.

Despite that, the club was hit by, initially 115 charges alleging breaches of financial and co-operation rules in 2023, later amended to a total of 130 allegations.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

RESPONSIBILITY

The Chelsea allegations were over transfers made by the club between 2012 and 2019, under the Abramovich ownership model.

A significant aspect of Chelsea’s mitigation for the 74 offences, to which they admitted guilt, was that Abramovich was no longer involved with the club in any way.

City have been under the current Abu Dhabi ownership throughout the entire period in question, with the money routed into the club by the Abu Dhabi United Group.

Club bosses were also accused of failing to co-operate with the inquiry up until 2022.



NATURE OF THE ALLEGATIONS

Chelsea’s breaches of the rules were in regard to payments made OUT of the club but which were not entered into the official books.

However, it was found that, even had the payments been declared, Chelsea would not have been in breach of Premier League financial loss-making rules.

City were accused of systematic financial deception including hiding the true source of sponsorship income, paying managers and players through secondary off-books contracts, disguising owner funding through company vehicles and breaching both Uefa and Prem financial regulations.

The independent commission, in its brutal findings, said City recorded “sham” contracts to cover £830m of income from Abu Dhabi.



HELP

After admitting to the malfeasance that they had discovered, Chelsea offered full help to the investigation, with all documentation handed across and guilty pleas.

BlueCo might not be particularly popular among the Chelsea fans, but their actions likely saved the club from far worse sanctions.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

City were found guilty of the vast majority of the non-cooperation charges laid in 2023 and failing to file accurate financial details.

A number of City’s witnesses were found to have given “false”, knowingly “untrue and dishonest” evidence.

Sports.title: ‘We will use these powers’ – Man City owners warned they could be forced to SELL club by independent regulator
Sports.content:
Next

FOOTBALL’s new independent regulator has warned he could boot Manchester City’s owners OUT of the game.

In a dramatic response to the initial findings of the Premier League commission which ruled City chiefs had overseen a near £1bn scheme to break financial rules, chairman David Kogan confirmed the range of his powers.



Kogan said: “The independent commission’s decision raises serious issues.

“The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives.



“We will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals.

“This includes taking account of findings made by the Leagues.



“However, as the proceedings remain ongoing between Manchester City and the Premier League we will await further developments.

“We hope it can be resolved quickly for the sake of fans. For now, we have no further comment.”

Kogan’s comments underline the threat to City’s Abu Dhabi ownership if they fail to overturn the commission verdict.

The Manchester-based IFR was initially drafted by the Conservative government but brought into existence with more powers during Keir Starmer’s spell at No10.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Kogan will now sift all the evidence and findings made by the commission.

But his intervention at this stage signals the scale of the threat to City and the club’s executives.

Sports.title: Man Utd cult hero Chris Smalling, 36, ‘on brink of Champions League return on free transfer’ after two years in Saudi
Sports.content:
Next

FORMER Manchester United defender Chris Smalling is set to land one last big move.

The 36-year-old has spent the last two years in Saudi Arabia with Al-Fayha after his successful spell with Roma came to a close.



Now, the 31-time England international is a free agent and is set to sign with Portuguese giants Porto.

Smalling arrived in Portugal on Wednesday to discuss a deal with Primeira Liga champions, according to Portuguese outlets.



With ex-Premier League stars and Polish internationals Jan Bednarek and Jakub Kiwior as the main options in central defence, Smalling will become another experienced option for the position.

Nehuen Perez is currently sidelined due to injury, which has caused coach Francesco Farioli to have a look around the market.



The Greenwich-born star had returned to the UK this summer as he plotted his next move, but it seems he’s now heading abroad once again.

Despite racking up more than 580 senior club appearances and winning silverware with Manchester United (including two Premier League titles) and Roma, Smalling admits football was never even on his radar growing up.

Speaking to BBC Sport, he said: “It wasn’t even plan D. I had everything set out. I already had my A levels, and I was looking at other non-league clubs near Leicester because I still wanted to play.”

Everything changed when Fulham offered him a contract after Roy Hodgson watched him in a practice match.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Smalling added: “It wasn’t even a full week. I didn’t have any time to get my head around it. I was just in total shock.”

Now, as a seasoned centre-back, he is still able to draw the interest of clubs playing in the Champions League.

Having played under Sir Alex Ferguson and Jose Mourinho during his career, the ex-England star was one of the steals remaining on the open market.

And he’d be joining a good club. Porto are a perfect seven wins from their opening seven league games this season.

Sports.title: As Schmeichel jokes about new ‘Uber’ career, seven wildest careers stars took on after retiring including Netflix star
Sports.content:
Next

PETER SCHMEICHEL joked that he felt like an Uber driver after he was forced to swap football stadiums for school runs after his early retirement.

And while the comments about ferrying his kids around like an Uber driver were in jest, it would be far from the strangest career change that the beautiful game had seen over the years.



Some players are simply not content to sit on their football fortunes, and have instead found themselves new lines of work that range from the glamorous to the bonkers.

Whether it be the worlds of entertainment, politics or more adult industries, it seems there is no limit on industries that footballers can make the leap into after hanging up their boots.



Eric Cantona – Actor/Singer

Manchester United legend Eric Cantona is best known for his iconic moments on the pitch, whether that be any of his spectacular finishes or his controversial leap into the crowd to confront a fan.

But since retiring he has taken his penchant for entertaining fans and channelled it into creative endeavours, including careers in acting and in music.

The Frenchman has starred in a number of primarily French films and TV series, and he even released his first official album, Perfect Imperfection, in March.

Michael Owen – Horse Racing

Michael Owen is the second-youngest Ballon d’Or winner ever at 22 years and four days, behind only Brazil‘s Ronaldo – but he has no interest in second-place finishes in his new line of work.

The former Liverpool star is the co-founder of Manor House Stables, an elite horse-training facility helmed by Hugo Palmer.

The horses are even becoming a family business, with Owen’s daughter Gemma making her debut as a jockey in a charity race at Goodwood in July, and the entire endeavour being featured on brand new Amazon documentary Meet the Owens.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Vinnie Jones – Netflix star

Another star undaunted by the small screen is Vinnie Jones, whose post-playing career as an actor has soared to new heights this year.

The former Wimbledon and Leeds star made his acting debut in Guy Ritchie‘s Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels in 1998, and has collaborated with the director a number of times since.

But it is arguably their new work together in smash hit Netflix series The Gentlemen that has really seen Jones flex his acting abilities, featuring as a main character in both seasons of the show so far.



Tino Asprilla – Condoms

Faustino “Tino” Asprilla is a cult hero in Newcastle, and his iconic larger-than-life personality has clearly carried over to his post-playing days as well.



The Colombian wowed fans in 2014 by becoming the face of Tino Condoms, explaining: “You know, sex has always been important to me. I am Asprilla: lots of sex, no rules and pure life.”

He even sold a stockpile of 3.5million of the flavoured condoms in 2020 to help combat a global shortage brought on by the Covid lockdown.

Steve Lomas – Bed & Breakfast owner

West Ham legend Steve Lomas has chosen a more low-key lifestyle since retiring than some of his fellow Premier League stars.

Anyone enjoying a trip to the gorgeous County Antrim coast could find themselves having their breakfast cooked for them by the ex-Manchester City star.



He co-owns the 13-bed B&B Causeway Guest Accommodation, and isn’t afraid to muck in to the daily running of the venue, joking: “We get a lot of visitors from Spain, Germany, America and China. I love football and it’s no hardship to talk about it, but I’m usually slaving over the stove.”

Daniel Agger – Tattoo artist

Liverpool star and former Denmark captain Daniel Agger is a man of many hats, taking up not one but two bizarre careers after retiring.

The 41-year-old is a qualified tattoo artist and is virtually covered in ink himself – turning his interest into a business opportunity by investing in Tattoo giant Tattoodo alongside his friends around ten years ago.

And in an even weirder move, the former defender launched a sewage management company alongside family members in 2013, called KloAgger.



George Weah – President

Former Paris Saint-Germain and AC Milan star George Weah had possibly the highest stakes post-retirement career of any football star as he became the president of his home nation.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Weah, 59, is the only Ballon d’Or winner that Africa has produced, and he made another first when he made the switch into politics, and eventually became the 25th President of Liberia.

He spent six years in the role before being defeated in a re-election campaign by Joseph Boakai, who took over from the former footy star in 2024.

‌



He has gone on to become a key player for Napoli, scoring 27 goals in 82 appearances, helping the club to win Serie A in his debut campaign.

‌

Sports.title: Andy Burnham 'concerned' over losing Man City owners in fallout to Premier League scandal
Sports.content:
Andy Burnham 'concerned' over losing Man City owners in fallout to Premier League scandal

The prime minister has addressed the unfolding scandal at Manchester City, who have been found guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has been asked about Manchester City's breaches of Premier League rules (Image: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Andy Burnham says he will keep his distance from the Manchester City scandal, but admitted he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners were forced out.

‌



City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled against them by the Premier League. The independent commission found they had broken the league's financial rules, arranging "sham" contracts to disguise secret funding of more than £830million over a nine-year period.

‌



City have continued to plead their innocence and plan to appeal against the verdict, but the Independent Football Regulator has now threatened to turn their attention to the "suitability" of the club's owners. It means that the Abu Dhabi United Group and Sheikh Mansour are now in the spotlight.

‌



The story has escalated in recent days, going well beyond just football, and Burnham was asked his opinion in an interview with the BBC. The prime minister is an Everton fan and made a comparison with their six-point deduction for breaking the Premier League's profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour faces being STRIPPED of club in brutal punishment READ MORE :

Pep Guardiola breaks silence on Man City charges with clear message to owners READ MORE :

"I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time, and you know, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn't fair the way that was handled," he said. "So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."

Burnham has another obvious link with the story, having previously been Mayor of Manchester, where he came into contact with City's owners. "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad and the campus around it but also into the city," he said.

‌



He then added: "I would be really concerned to lose them. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

View 2 Images Man City owner Sheikh Mansour (centre), chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (right) and chief executive Ferran Soriano (Image: Getty)

"I can't intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail, but obviously it's ongoing, and because it's still contested by Manchester City, then I think it's right that I don’t say much more."

‌



After a lengthy process, City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. They have until October 2 to submit an official appeal and Burnham refused to be drawn on offering his opinion, given the process is likely to remain ongoing for much longer.

"I have to keep my distance from it," he said. "It would be wrong for me to do anything else. It's an independent legal process that has to play its course through.

"So for the reasons I gave at the start, you know, I was involved in one myself in relation to Everton. I think it's frustrating when people rush to judgment and proclaim people guilty. I think the thing has to be allowed to run its course."

Sports.title: Man City charges LIVE: Pep Guardiola statement, punishment latest, dressing room leak
Sports.content:
The latest news on Manchester City's charges after the club were found guilty of alleged breaches of Premier League financial rules

Hello and welcome to Mirror Football's Manchester City charges live blog for Wednesday, September 30.

The Premier League officially announced the club's guilty verdict on 114 breaches of financial rules on Tuesday afternoon, four days after media reports broke the news.

A statement from the league read: "An independent Commission has found Manchester City FC guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period, and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the League’s investigation."

As a result, City have until Friday to appeal the decision, which the club are likely to do as they continue to protest their innocence.

Manchester City also released a statement of their own in the wake of the Premier League's confirmation. It read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence. The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Stay tuned for the latest news and updates in our live blog below as the saga continues to unfold...

Sports.title: Man Utd's crisis meeting that led to Erik ten Hag sacking as Michael Carrick under pressure
Sports.content:
Man Utd's crisis meeting that led to Erik ten Hag sacking as Michael Carrick under pressure

Manchester United have consistently found themselves in managerial chaos

View 3 Images Michael Carrick is under pressure at Manchester United (Image: Getty Images)

The managerial merry-go-round at Manchester United has served as a constant source of chaos. The Red Devils are now led by Michael Carrick after the former United midfielder signed a deal until 2028 with the option of a further year after impressively leading the club to Champions League qualification last season.

‌



Carrick's initial appointment as interim boss saw him lead United to 12 wins in their last 17 Premier League games. However, the honeymoon period is well and truly over at Old Trafford after just one win in their opening five fixtures, alongside their shock EFL Cup exit against Brighton earlier this month.

‌



Carrick, 45, will no doubt be feeling the pressure of the hot seat, but club bosses will surely be keen to bypass the mayhem that has existed in the previous situations of Ruben Amorim and Erik ten Hag.

‌



The Portuguese boss is now at the helm of AC Milan after being sacked from United in January 2026, ending his tumultuous 14-month reign. Amorim began his second season in charge under instant pressure, having guided United to a record-low 15th-place finish in the Premier League in the 2024/25 campaign.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

The club went without an away win until their 2-1 victory over Manchester City in December, while their embarrassing exit from the Carabao Cup at the hands of League Two side Grimsby Town earlier that season led to intense speculation over Amorim's position.

‌



Reports at the time suggested club executives had held discussions with key United players to get a sense of the mood in the dressing room. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox were believed to have consulted captain Bruno Fernandes, among others, in their aim to gain better insight into the squad's views.

View 3 Images Ruben Amorim was sacked after a miserable 14-month spell with Man United (Image: Getty Images)

The situation within United was similar to the circumstances behind the seven-hour meeting between Ten Hag and his former bosses in October 2024, with the Dutchman's firing coming later that month.

‌



The discussions were held at Sir Jim Ratcliffe's Knightsbridge offices in London, with co-owner Joel Glazer, chief executive Berrada, then-sporting director Dan Ashworth, and director of football Wilcox all meeting to confer over the state of United.

Board member Jean-Claude Blanc, chief operating officer Collette Roche and chief financial officer Roger Bell were all understood to have been present for the conference. While a meeting of such magnitude doesn't seem to be on the horizon when it comes to Carrick's position, the United boss must turn his side's fortunes around and fast to prevent such a situation.

View 3 Images Erik ten Hag was sacked in October 2024 (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

Article continues below

United currently sit 12th in the league and face fellow strugglers Tottenham Hotspur at home in their first game following the end of the international break. Over the next month, fixtures against Leeds United, Bournemouth, Chelsea and Aston Villa will further test the resolve of Carrick's squad.

Man Utd suffer third injury blow during international break as star forced off

Manchester United defender Noussair Mazraoui came off injured for Morocco to give Michael Carrick yet another concern during the international break. Mazraoui, 28, went down holding his back following a challenge with Lesotho midfielder Neo Mokhachane during Morocco's 2-0 victory in Africa Cup of Nations qualifying on Tuesday.

‌



His team-mates signalled to the Moroccan bench that he couldn't continue and he was brought off in the 69th minute. Mazraoui, who scored in Morocco's 2-0 win against Gabon last Friday, able to get back on his feet and slowly made his way off the pitch to be replaced by Achraf Hakimi.

‌



The ex-Bayern Munich and Ajax star became the third player to suffer an injury while representing their country this month. Bruno Fernandes was ruled out of Portugal's clash with Norway on Sunday before Patrick Dorgu picked up a suspected hamstring injury while playing for Denmark.

‌



United captain Fernandes is understood to have played through pain in recent weeks but could return when Portugal face Dorgu's Denmark on Thursday. Prior to the international break, the trio of Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Benjamin Sesko pulled out of their respective country's squads because of injury.

Sports.title: The truth behind Man City CEO not blinking for 3 minutes in 'unusual' announcement video
Sports.content:
EXCLUSIVE: The truth behind Man City CEO not blinking for 3 minutes in 'unusual' announcement video

Manchester City CEO Ferran Soriano addressed staff in a new video, and his body language was very telling

View 2 Images Ferran Soriano has sent a video out to Manchester City staff (Image: Getty)

A body language expert has described Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano's announcement video as "unusual". Soriano sent a video message to club employees after the club were found guilty on 114 of their Premier League charges.

‌



A bombshell statement from the Premier League on Tuesday confirmed that Man City were guilty on all but one charge between 2009 and 2018.

‌



The independent commission's judgement ruled that City "overstated [its income] by over £830m" during the nine-year period covered by the investigation and arranged "sham commercial deals" with several sponsors.

‌



Man City responded with a fiercely defensive statement of their own, with Soriano hitting back at the verdict on video. The City CEO reiterated the club's intention to fight on through every available legal avenue and labelled it a "conspiracy theory".

The Spaniard spoke confidently for three and a half minutes, with many viewers online noting his lack of blinking throughout the now-viral message.

Body language expert Judi James spoke to Mirror Football about the video, claiming Soriano's body language is "unusually textbook impeccable", with his hand gestures and facial movements matching his words perfectly. James also explained that the City chief's lack of blinking could be down to extreme focus on the message he was trying to deliver.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

Micah Richards heartbroken and Jamie Carragher lashes out - Pundits weigh in on Man City charges READ MORE :

She said: "There is what looks like one heavy swallow in preparation but after that any unnecessary movement is negligible. But that includes his blinking. The average blink rate is around 15 - 20 per minute, which is quite a consistent rate, and it might actually be reasonable to expect Soriano's blink rate to speed up a little under the pressure of making what are clearly some emotional points.

"Intriguingly though there appears to be no sign of any blinking here until the only visible cut in the video at 1.54. Even after that it only appears to be at 2.55 that the first blink is seen and then maybe another after that.

‌



"Soriano does use his eyes to register different moods as he speaks here, though, so they are not static, which makes the lack of blinking look even more unusual as he's clearly not hard staring with a frozen eye expression. His left eye wrinkles in a smile at one point; the eye expression gets colder at another, then we see his brows rise in an expression of surprise before there is a hardening that suggests inner anger.

"So, we have the eyes showing expression but no apparent blinking for nearly three minutes, which is unusual. Not blinking is said to sometimes be caused by intense focus, though. Interestingly, there is also no apparent micro-darting of the pupils here that you usually get when someone is reading from an autocue, so the suggestion would be that an unblinking Soriano is able to be this word-perfect but without cues from a script."

James went on to analyse his hand gestures, which transmitted confidence and a sense of authority, likely with the intention of reassuring City's staff.

‌



She continued: "His hand gestures are also textbook. The hands move throughout as though accompanying every point or sentiment made with absolutely no untidy leakage. At the start, he even has a cocked left thumb to suggest confidence.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

"The Precision Pinch is a regular ritual used, and it tends to imply precise thinking. He throws the first when he says, 'I want to explain' and he even raises and drops it as a baton for extra emphasis. This sense of being 'precise' is echoed in his mouth movement when he hikes the left side of his mouth up to then 'bite' at the word 'exactly'. There is a look of rejection as he leans back and widens his eyes to say that this has 'gone on for so long'.

‌



"Then he digs deeper into the visual signals of precision as he performs a double precision pinch using both hands, with his 'this is just not true' coming with a double precision, a baton gesture and his unblinking gaze. There is what looks like a desire to register authority as he raises his left index finger on the word 'Remember…' and then, when he talks about 'in order to win the case', he uses a downward jab point with his right index finger to signal determination.

"When he talks about 'protecting the club', he cups his hands as though holding it protectively, and then at the end, there is a motivational smile as he talks about overcoming adversity 'together.'"

Soriano's message was as follows: "The whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation - that the owner's personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi.

‌



View 2 Images City bosses have until Friday, October 2 to appeal the verdict (Image: Getty)

"This is just not true. Irrefutable evidence has been provided to the Premier League commission that shows it could not happen and that it did not happen. This includes bank statements, money transfers, witnesses and everything necessary to categorically demonstrate the money did not come from the owner.

"Every other false charge that has been thrown at us comes from that simple, central and completely false accusation. Surprisingly for us and our lawyers after nearly two years the commission has issued an opinion that supports the Premier League’s conspiracy theory.

Article continues below

"To do so, the opinion had to ignore the extensive evidence provided by the club in order to reach a conclusion that is clearly wrong. Our lawyers will now file an appeal that sets out the opinion contains clear, material errors of law, principle and fact and that it is unsafe."

City have until Friday, October 2 to appeal the verdict. Sanctions have yet to be applied.

Sports.title: Why F1's return to 'intense' Sepang offers 'chaotic' race potential
Sports.content:
Ask a Formula 1 driver or fan anytime over the last nine years what track they would most like to see return to the sport's calendar, and there was a good chance that Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit would get mentioned.

So those who have been hoping that Sepang would one day return get their wish this weekend as, for the first time since 2017, Formula 1 cars will race on the fast, flowing 3.44-mile track on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur.

We take a look at how that has unexpectedly come about and what to expect from the race weekend...

Why is Malaysia hosting the Bahrain Grand Prix?

The first thing to explain is how Malaysia has ended up as the host of Bahrain's Grand Prix.

The Bahrain Grand Prix at the Gulf country's own Sakhir track had been scheduled to take place on April 12 but the war in the Middle East saw both their race and Saudi Arabia's, which was scheduled for the week after, called off.

But a subsequent agreement in July between the Bahrain and Malaysian governments, plus F1 and the FIA, paved the way for the Bahrain GP to still take place, albeit over 3,000 miles from its usual location, at Sepang.

It has been slotted into what was a free weekend in the schedule between last week's race in Azerbaijan and next week's in Singapore, which neighbours Malaysia.

With Bahrain covering most of the cost, the event runs under the official title of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Formula 1 has added Malaysia to its 2026 schedule to host the Bahrain Grand Prix that was postponed earlier in the season.

"It makes sense because the relationship between Bahrain and Malaysia has been strong. Malaysia's fantastic, Sepang's fantastic," said Sheikh Salman bin Isa Al Khalifa, chief executive of the Bahrain International Circuit to Sky Sports F1.

"For us and F1 it's important that we are on the calendar. We went from 24 races to 22 then there were concern about other races so it's important for everyone, not just for F1 but the sponsors and the teams."

What is the Sepang International Circuit like?

The track - located in the town of Sepang to the south of Kuala Lumpur and close to the capital's international airport - proved a gamechanger for modern Formula 1 venues when it staged the inaugural Malaysian Grand Prix in October 1999.

It was the first F1 layout to be designed in full by Hermann Tilke, who has subsequently gone on to pen most of the sport's many new tracks, and is perhaps still his best in terms of absolute driving challenge.

The 15-turn track features a combination of medium-high speed corners, two long straights and wide braking zones, offering both a stern challenge for car and driver, plus the possibility of overtaking.

Image: Sepang's iconic main grandstand offering views of both the back and main straight

"The track itself has got a really nice flow to it," explains Sky Sports F1's Jamie Chadwick, who raced at Sepang in the F3 Asian Championship.

"I think the track itself is kind of one that I think all the drivers are going to enjoy. It's got a little bit of China in it, a little bit of Budapest I think in a couple of places.

"You've got two decently long straights kind of into each other so the way that they'll manage the energy deployment for the racing I think will be good.

"A lot of the drivers will know it and remember it well from when F1 previously went there. Although the younger ones maybe not, a lot of the drivers will know it and feel familiar quite quickly."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Craig Slater with the latest update on the 2026 F1 calendar season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

What 'shock' factor does racing in Malaysia provide?

Then there is the aspect that often made F1's annual visits to Sepang memorable: the weather.

Malaysia's tropical, humid climate means conditions can quickly shift from searing sunshine to torrential rain.

High track temperatures in dry conditions provide an intense workout for drivers, tyres and engines, while in 2009 the race was red-flagged with 25 laps remaining and never restarted after a huge downpour left cars undriveable and saw several aquaplane off the track.

"Physically it will be a bit of a shock. The humidity is pretty intense!" said Chadwick.

"Obviously they've got Singapore in and around the same time, so it's going to kind of hit them all at once, that kind of temperature and physicality of the race.

"I don't think it's going to be an easy race by any means. Like I say, the physicality, the tyres, everything is all going to be a factor."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton had to retire from the race lead after an engine failure as his title hopes were damaged at the 2016 Malaysian Grand Prix.

What are the F1 drivers expecting?

It's fair to say that Formula 1's drivers are excited for the sport's return in Malaysia, irrespective of whether they have driven at Sepang before or not.

Lewis Hamilton has raced there 11 times in F1, claiming a joint-record five poles and winning once in 2014, and the Ferrari driver is looking forward to re-familiarising himself with both the country and track.

"I always loved going to KL," said Hamilton.

"Had lots of great experiences there with my previous team [who are title sponsored by Malaysian oil firm Petronas] and the track is awesome. It is a circuit that does give good racing.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player In 2014, Mercedes driver Lewis Hamilton claimed his one and only win at the Malaysian Grand Prix.

"When it comes to deciding what tracks to go to in the year, that should be a part of the decision making. We want good races for fans, not ones that that you don't see any overtaking in, so I'm very much looking forward to it.

"It's a super hot circuit, one that's physically massively demanding, so I look forward to that challenge."

Red Bull's Max Verstappen was the last winner in 2017 and agrees it presents a demanding track for driver and car.

"It's a great track," said the Dutchman. "I really enjoy being there.

"It's very tough, I think just from the heat already, but also degradation will be really tough on the tyres."

Image: Malaysia 2017 was Max Verstappen's second win in F1

Ten of the 2026's 22 F1 drivers were on the grid the last time F1 raced at Sepang (with Charles Leclerc driving for Sauber in Friday practice), while Alex Albon and Liam Lawson experienced the circuit in junior series.

Reigning world champion Lando Norris is among those whose Sepang experience is limited to the simulator.

"I'm excited for it," said the McLaren driver.

"I've seen many races when I was younger and I was growing up. I remember doing simulator support for Fernando [Alonso] and Stoffel [Vandoorne] when they raced there.

"I remember going into the factory at midnight and driving until 7am in the morning, so it's not completely new to me, but it'll be a first time going to the circuit itself, which is exciting.

"The only thing that's not exciting is because you have no battery, the two high-speed corners that should be high-speed, you run out of battery and it's flat, so that takes away a little bit of the character that I think you should have on such an incredible track.

"Otherwise, it's a new place, and I'm looking forward to another new challenge for us."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sebastian Vettel and Lance Stroll crashed into one another following the 2017 Malaysian Grand Prix!

The same inexperience is true for world championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who was only 11 years old the last time F1 raced there.

"It's always very nice as a driver to discover a new track," said the Mercedes driver, whose title lead over team-mate George Russell, another Sepang rookie, was cut to 66 points last week in Azerbaijan.

"I've done it on the sim and it looks like a pretty cool track - very fast flowing, long corners, not easy, especially to put it all together.

"I think it's going to be very interesting as well with tyre degradation. We might see two or three stops because tyre degradation is going to be big."

So what will the racing be like in Sunday's 56-lap Grand Prix, which starts at 8am live on Sky Sports F1?

"Malaysia will be pretty chaotic in terms of racing because of the straights and corner setup that you have there," predicted Norris.

"In some ways, a similar vibe to Monza."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli and George Russell go wheel-to-wheel for the Italian Grand Prix lead in several epic team-mate battles.

The track will reward those teams who find the right set-up compromise between cornering performance and straight-line speed. Although, should it rain, all bets would be off.

"Another question mark is going to be the weather," added Antonelli.

"I've seen the forecast and it seems to rain pretty heavily at a certain time, at a specific time of the day, so there's going to be a lot of unknowns."
