Sports.title: Who wins the Arc? Jamie Lynch's big-race runner guide
Sports.content:
Our Senior Form Analyst looks ahead to Europe's most prestigious contest, live on Sky Sports Racing on Sunday, and reveals his big-race fancy.

This is everything a Qatar Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe should be, first and foremost a clash of nations and generations, and not just a defining race but a deciding race, to decide the best around, while a returning champion always adds an extra layer of motivation and invigoration.

Let's take a deep dive into the field for Sunday's 2026 edition, live on Sky Sports Racing, of what is, by common consent, the greatest Flat race in the world.

Daryz

Trainer: F Graffard

"If you're going to be a star, you have to look like a star," and Daryz has worn the daunting mantle of Arc winner very well this season, looking suitably starry… Apart from that one time. After Royal Ascot, for Daryz and his devotees, a reported bad blood test was music to the ears, before the Prix Foy's feast for the eyes and its in-built assurance of all systems go for a second Arc, which has been done eight times in history, but only once in history has the Arc winner added the nine-furlong Prix d'Ispahan on the way, though the horse in question, the outstanding mare Allez France ('the best I ever rode', said Yves Saint-Martin), didn't do it so strikingly in it as Daryz, who topped 42mph when powering up, prompting a 10.68 second furlong. When such a strong stayer is able to reach those speeds, it explains in simple terms the complex combustion engine of Daryz, as well as outlining the overwhelming task for his rivals, up against such a refined and defined racehorse on his home patch.

Image: Daryz (Photo: Debbie Burt/Racingfotos.)

Saddadd

R Varian

Roger Varian's fourth runner in an Arc, after Kingston Hill's fourth in 2014 and Postponed's fifth (as favourite) in 2016, and Defoe was done by stall 18 in 2018. Saddadd isn't rated nor decorated like any of those, but he's still pushing upwards, a master of marginal gains, taking him from a London Gold Cup to a German Group One, and the Grosser Preis von Baden has had a happy habit of readying Arc winners, like Marienbard, Danedream and Torquator Tasso. That was only his first go at the trip, yet he was fastest at stages of both the Tattersalls Gold Cup and the Coral-Eclipse, Group Ones at a mile and a quarter, and the systematic skin-shedding qualifies him as a lively longshot.

Chestnut Rocket

Alicja Karkosa

Polish Derby winner of 2025 and has done better still operating in France as a four-year-old, splitting Al Aasy and Arrow Eagle on his latest start in the Group Two Grand Prix de Deauville. That still leaves him out of his depth in an Arc.

Admire Terra

Yasuo Tomomichi

His claim to fame is that he finished ahead of Calandagan and Masquerade Ball in the Japan Cup. Sadly, he was riderless at the time, having stumbled leaving the stalls, but he went off a 45-1 shot which rather sums up his position in the pyramid, 0/4 in Group Ones.

Meisho Tabaru

Mamoru Ishibashi

There has been little news or noise around the Japanese challenge for the Arc this year but Meisho Tabaru is a bona fide Group One horse, highlighted by back-to-back wins in the Takarazuka Kinen, this year beating Croix Du Nord, who was 14-1 for last year's Arc having edged out Daryz in a trial, and Danon Decile, former winner of the Sheema Classic (from Calandagan). He seems very straightforward, able to front run, as he did on his one venture outside of Japan so far, though it got him only fifth (behind compatriot Soul Rush) in the 2025 Dubai Turf. In summary, he doesn't appear to have anything different from the previous 38 from Japan who've tried and failed in the Arc over six decades.

Arrow Eagle

J C Rouget

Two Arcs and 14 French Classics are the decorative adornments to the metaphorical monument that's fixed in French racing for Jean-Claude Rouget, for whom Arrow Eagle will be his last ever runner, without any pretensions of doing any better than 2025 when a staying-on sixth to Daryz at 150-1.

Bay City Roller

George Scott

He's viable on good ground, but invincible in the mud. Unfortunately for him, conditions won't be the same at ParisLongchamp as they were at Epsom for the Coronation Cup which he won by ten lengths from two Classic winners and Calandagan. His class is conditional and he was just a plaything for Daryz in the Prix Foy.

Minnie Hauk

A P O'Brien

The widest winning margin in Arc history is six lengths, and Minnie Hauk was five-and-a-half lengths clear of all the other 15 runners when her and Daryz had their ding-dong a year ago. Her standards have slipped this season during which time she's been hitting the notes without playing the music, but there are precedents for sleepy mare setting the alarm clock in time for their second Arc attempt, such as Treve and Found, the latter having an identical campaign as a four-year-old. Nonetheless, as a would-be winner, she's easy to explain but hard to back.

Kalpana

A M Balding

Vive la evolution! The draw did for Kalpana in last year's Arc, but Calandagan did for Kalpana in last year's King George and there was a role reversal this time around because she has evolved into an even more powerful and purposeful five-year-old. As many as fifteen horses have won an Arc the year after they were beaten in it, and the software updates which have added an extra layer of speed and steel to Kalpana's classy core makes her the leading lady for ParisLongchamp, with a rating (of 125) that's higher than Found, Alpinista or Bluestocking ran to in winning an Arc.

Image: Kalpana won the 2026 King George in the hands of Colin Keane

Friendly Soul

J and T Gosden

It has taken some time and training to overcome the holes in her career and holes at Haydock to recover the whole of her ability and then some, successful as a three-year-old in the Pretty Polly (from Kalpana no less) and Prix de l'Opera, but hitting new heights last time out with an all-the-way win in the Prix Vermeille on her first go at the trip, in the fastest overall time of the three trials that day. This, however, is a different ball game, taking on the big boys for the first time in her life.

Varandir

F Graffard

Two of the last three Arc winners were unraced at two, shining a specific spotlight on Varandir, who actually won the very same newcomers race in April that Daryz had 12 months earlier. His only defeat so far came in the Grand Prix de Paris and that was a matter of heads and necks when a close fourth to Maltese Cross, though his rebound in the Prix Niel owed something to a subdued Benvenuto Cellini rather than any great improvement on his part, meaning his upside is more in profile and potential: but it's the modern Arc profile and Graffard grade potential.

Image: Varandir (M. Barzalona) wins Qatar Prix Niel Gr.2 in ParisLongchamp, France, 06/09/2026, photo: Zuzanna Lupa

Benvenuto Cellini

A P O'Brien

There was a while there when it felt like he was the "chosen one" for the Ballydoyle three-year-olds, but he hasn't added as much as hoped to the coffers, before becoming one of the coughers in that spell when the stable had some downtime, explaining in part his dull display in the Prix Niel. He looks of similar standing to Maltese Cross from their defeat of the same two horses, in the Irish Derby for him, but there's a big difference in momentum at this stage and Benvenuto Cellini is stuttering into the autumn, from chosen one in the spring to third string in the Arc.

Image: Benvenuto Cellini, ridden by Ryan Moore, on the way to winning the Dubai Duty Free Irish Derby at the Curragh

Bright Light

Andreas Suborics

German-trained three-year-old who has been placed in Group Ones at home, behind British raiders, Tiffany at Hoppergarten and Saddadd at Baden-Baden, an element of him being in the right place at the right time in those events. A race like this is out of his reach.

Maltese Cross

W J Haggas

The Maltese Cross cocktail has been purified and clarified over 393 days and seven refining races, making for a fortified blend which is now similar in strength to a drop of Daryz. And there's still a bit of shaking and stirring to be done with him yet, a three-year-old who's peaking for Paris, after resisting the temptation to mix a Classic cocktail for the Leger. The brilliance-bordering blend is the stamina that got him a Great - in literal terms - Voltiguer and the speed that got him out of a spot in the Grand Prix de Paris, in which he clocked an even faster speed (43.1mph) than Daryz had at ParisLongchamp in the Prix d'Ispahan. His ingredients and improvements have earned him a robust rating which is higher than Daryz and Ace Impact packed pre-Paris amongst recent three-year-old Arc-winning colts, and the fullest Maltese Cross is still in the future tense.

Image: Maltese Cross

Thundering On

J P O'Brien

What she's done is impressive, but it's more who she is that could win her an Arc, a flourishing three-year-old filly often greater than the sum of her parts when it comes to Arcs, as wild winners Zarkava, Danedream, Treve and Enable all symbolize in recent times, while Minnie Hauk went mightily close last year. Thundering On, whose 117 rating is within a pound of Minnie Hauk's at the same stage, passed the eye test in the Oaks and the time test in the Blandford at the Curragh where her closing two furlongs were faster than any winner on that Super Sunday bar the Group One sprinter Commanche Brave. The form-lines and data points booked her a ticket but, above all, it's the badge she wears that could win her it, the wind of a three-year-old filly a specialist sirocco that regularly blows through ParisLongchamp.

Image: Thundering On struck gold in the Oaks

Diamond Necklace

A P O'Brien

Without the Prix Jean Romanet, I'm pretty sure Diamond Necklace would be second-favourite for the Arc, as a hitherto unbeaten dual Classic winner who gave a subsequent Prix Vermeille winner a good thrashing in the Nassau. On that basis, she's rated higher than Thundering On, and trained by the Daddy, but there's no doubting the dent that defeat by Aventure did to her Arc claims, begging the question of a bump in the road or the end of her developmental road? The recent market momentum would suggest bump and, a half-sister to Irish Oaks winner Chicquita amongst others, there's plenty to propose that she'll improve for this trip let alone stay it: don't forget what a mile and a half did for three-year-old Daryz at the first attempt last year.

Image: Diamond Necklace (RL Moore) wins Emirates Poule d'Essai des Pouliches Gr.1 France, 10/05/2026, photo: Zuzanna Lupa

Jamie Lynch's Verdict

We've got a true A-lister in Daryz who has an air and aura of horse about to force his way into Arc folklore, though for now scales are weighted slightly more in style than substance for his season so far, with extra marks for artistic impression, but it can't be completely forgotten how he fell flat at Royal Ascot. There's still a sense that the best version of Daryz will leave this lot or any lot for dead, but the market rather underestimates quite what a heavyweight MALTESE CROSS is becoming, with a strong case for saying he's the best three-year-old in Europe. His budding brilliance is in his blend, of overt stamina and hidden speed, and that's the magic mix which wins Arcs.

Watch every race from Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe weekend at ParisLongchamp live on Sky Sports Racing (Sky 415 | Virgin 512) on Saturday 3rd and Sunday 4th October.

Sports.title: Djokovic lands first win since Wimbledon at China Open
Sports.content:
Novak Djokovic returned to action in Beijing 11 years after his last appearance and extended his incredible record to 30 consecutive wins at the China Open on Wednesday.

Djokovic, a six-time winner in the Chinese capital, received a medical timeout in the second set but did enough to defeat Portugal's Nuno Borges 6-3 7-6 (7-2) and reach the second round.

Next up for Djokovic is home favourite Buyunchaokete Bu, who beat Juan Manuel Cerundolo 6-2 5-7 6-4.

"In the second set he started playing better and I struggled a little bit physically to stay fresh," said Djokovic, who arrived in Beijing having suffered opening-round exits at the US Open and at the ATP Masters 1000 event in Cincinnati.

"When I was serving, I was dominating and going through my games quite comfortably. It was helping getting those first serves in, that high percentages makes my life easier in my service games and I played a great tie-break to close it out in two, so I am very happy about that."

Djokovic, 39, was treated on court by the physio at 3-2 down in the second set, but he didn't appear to be hindered by the issue as he saw out his next two service matches to love and played some of his best tennis of the match.

There was only one break of serve during the match, by Djokovic in Borges' first service game.

Djokovic raced ahead in the tie-break and swiftly racked up four match points, but needed only one as Borges found the net.

"That was a really competitive match by the end of it," Annabel Croft told Sky Sports Tennis.

"Djokovic managed to find a way towards that finishing line and actually his service games became more and more efficient. So much of what we talked about in commentary was the physicality of the match and how uncomfortable Djokovic felt."

Image: Selected matches on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+ this Thursday

Tale of the Tape

Boulter sets up Muchova tie

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the China Open match between Mai Hontama and Katie Boulter

Katie Boulter opened her campaign in Beijing with a 6-3 6-4 victory against Japanese qualifier Mai Hontama.

The British No 1 will now go on to face seventh seed and Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova which will mark a third career meeting between the pair, and second this year following Muchova's straight-sets victory over Boulter in the second round of the US Open.

US Open semi-finalist Karen Khachanov continued his recent domination of Felix Auger-Aliassime 6-3 6-3.

Sports.title: Man City charges Q&A: Appeal, EFL, independent regulator and more answered
Sports.content:
Kaveh Solhekol has answered your latest questions on Manchester City after they were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission.

City continue to deny the breaches and have confirmed they will appeal against the ruling - they have until Friday October 2 to do so.

Answering your questions live on Sky Sports News, the chief correspondent discussed a range of topics, from when there will be an appeal outcome, to a potential drop into the EFL, player contracts and much more.

Read on for his answers in the latest Q&A...

'We should have appeal outcome in new year'

RhydonDN asked: How long is the appeal process expected to take? Could we be in a scenario where Man City appeal and this whole process takes additional months or even years to be resolved?

Solhekol said: "The football process will be done relatively quickly. If Man City take it to the High Court though, it could run for years and years.

"But with the Premier League process, City have until Friday to appeal, then that would need to be wrapped by Christmas, I think - 12 weeks.

"We would then get a judgement in 30 days of that 12-week period being over. We will get the judgement of the appeal in the new year and well before the end of the season.

"That appeal will be heard by a new three-person panel."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher believes stripping Manchester City of their titles should be part of their punishment after they were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of financial rules. The club continue to deny the breaches.

Potential punishment and would the EFL accept Man City?

Josh asked: Could the Premier League deduct Man City the maximum amount of points they could earn this season to ensure they are relegated to the EFL?

Secondly, would the EFL accept them into the Championship?

Solhekol said: "What is going to happen is, we will have a sanctions hearing. The same three people who delivered the judgement and were on the original commission will decide what the punishment will be.

"They have a range of options. City could be expelled from the Premier League, could be a points deduction, transfer ban or big fine. We have to wait and find out what the punishment will be.

"If they just get a points deduction, which means they are relegated this season, then I imagine the EFL would accept them.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News senior reporter Rob Dorsett outlines the possible punishment that could be handed to Manchester City by an independent commission. The club continue to deny the breaches.

"If they are expelled, the EFL does not need to necessarily accept them. They would have to apply to be admitted to the EFL and it would be up to the EFL's 72 clubs to decide.

"You would imagine the EFL would want to admit them as City are a big club. Wherever they go, there will be big interest and big support."

Jonty asked: Could the EFL refuse City entry into their system? Where would that leave them?

Solhekol said: "Technically they could. If they are expelled from the Premier League, the EFL may decide they don't want Man City in the EFL, but I don't understand why they would not want City in the EFL."

Would City get parachute payments if they were relegated?

Ash asked: If City are effectively relegated by points deduction, will they receive automatic parachute payments? The mechanics of relegation are set up to support teams not punish them as far as I'm aware. I'd also be keen to know if 2019 onwards will also be investigated.

Solhekol said: "I don't see any reason why they wouldn't receive parachute payments, just like any other club if they were relegated from the Premier League. That is the simple answer."

What role could the Independent Football Regulator play?

Owners test asked: Surely there's something in the owners' charter about this, could they be forced to sell? Could criminal charges happen as they submitted fraudulent accounts?

Solhekol said: "Now we have an Independent Football Regulator, it may well be the case that the regulator takes an interest in this, once the whole process has run its course.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Jamie Redknapp has his say on the guilty verdict handed out to Manchester City and is concerned by the effect it could have on football as a whole. The club continue to deny the breaches.

"They do have the power to disbar people from owning clubs or having senior roles, for instance being directors of clubs.

"That is a possibility. But again, let's make it clear, City say it is never going to get as far as that because we will prove that we are innocent."

PolarBear asked: Can the independent football regulator force the current owners out?

Solhekol said: "We've had a lot of questions like this and yes, the regulator has the power to force an owner to sell a club, but we are a long way away from the possibility of that happening."

'The evidence submitted only went up to 2018'

Gooner2526 asked: Considering how damning the verdict appears to have been for the seasons 2009/10 to 2017/18, surely the subsequent seasons would warrant investigation next? Why isn't this a topic?

Solhekol said: "I can only assume that the evidence put in front of the tribunal only went up to that season.

"What we do know is a lot of the evidence came in material obtained by a Portuguese hacker, Rui Pinto, who hacked into City's email servers and handed that information on to German magazine Der Spiegel.

"They first reported their investigations in a series of articles that were published in 2018 and that is what promoted UEFA's investigations and also triggered the Premier League's investigation.

"The short answer is - the evidence that was presented to the tribunal only went up to 2018."

'HMRC might take an interest - but we have to wait and see'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dave Reed takes a look the independent commission's key findings on the 'Disguised Funding Scheme' used by Manchester City. The club continue to deny the breaches.

Dan asked: The scale of the judgement goes beyond football and suggests that Man City could be guilty of a massive corporate fraud. What is the likelihood of a criminal or regulatory investigation into the evidence of fraud/false accounting by Man City?

Solhekol said: "We have to wait and see. What I do know is that when you file company accounts, you have a legal duty to make sure the financial declarations you make are true and accurate.

"If you fraudulently misrepresent the figures, then you could be charged under the Fraud Act of 2006 and that is a serious issue. I imagine the relevant authorities will be looking at that.

"There's also the possibility that HMRC - the tax man - might take an interest in this as well because we know from what the commission has said that Man City were paying people in a roundabout way off the books.

"That could mean the National Insurance and the tax that had to be paid wasn't paid. But again, that's something we have to wait and see if HMRC take interest in that.

"Man City still to this day say they have done absolutely nothing wrong and they are very confident that their name will be cleared and their innocence will be established."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Following Man City being found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission, Paul Merson shares what he believes should happen next. The club continue to deny the breaches.

Player contracts and potential clauses discussed

MattC asked: If City's punishment is severe - e.g. relegation - would players have a right to cancel their contracts due to the club's irresponsible behaviour?

Solhekol said: "Good question. I don't think you can just rip up your contract but I think you could seek legal advice.

"If you could establish that you signed the contract and the other party to the contract did not make you fully aware of the situation at the club when you signed the contract, then you may be able to walk away from your contract.

"That is something players would need to get legal advice on. It is not something I would totally discount.

"That may or may not have happened [clauses in contracts]. I don't think there would be clauses in the contract about whether, if this judgement goes against us, they can go away [leave].

"No player is going to show me or you their contract."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Barristers and lawyers across the country are working with Premier League clubs over the prospect of bringing further litigation against Manchester City. City continue to deny all the charges and will appeal by Friday's deadline.

Why the hearing was conducted in privacy

Matt H asked: Why was the hearing conducted in complete privacy? If it had happened in a High Court, for instance, there would be witnesses, press in attendance and more clarity to what was being said, what was being witnessed and what wasn't being witnessed?

Solhekol said: "This is a point being made by sports lawyers. They say that these proceedings should be open and transparent.

"The issue here is that this is a private matter. Effectively, the Premier League is a very exclusive club, made up of 20 member clubs.

"They have their own rulebook. This is what it says in the rulebook, so why would they open their doors to the likes of you and me to sit in on some very private and confidential proceedings."

Sports.title: Guardiola sends message to Man City amid calls for titles to be taken away
Sports.content:
Pep Guardiola has posted a message of support to Manchester City's players, staff, fans and ownership saying: "We will get through this together. I love you all."

Man City were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission.

The independent commission found that between 2009/10 and 2017/18, Manchester City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

The club continue to deny the breaches, with chief executive Ferran Soriano calling the process a "Premier League conspiracy theory" in a video message to players and staff. The club have confirmed they will appeal against the ruling and have until Friday October 2 to do so.

Guardiola, who was City manager between 2016 and 2026, posted on social media: "I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here; more than ever. I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran, the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters.

"Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."

Dates for a potential Man City appeal According to Premier League rules, any Man City appeal would have to be concluded 12 weeks after it is filed.



Man City have until Friday to make their appeal.



The appeal hearing can only last a maximum of five days. The board will then have 30 days to come to its decision.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol answers your questions after Manchester City were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission.

News and analysis after Man City guilty verdict

As the football world continued to digest news of Man City's guilty verdict, on Wednesday:

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher believes stripping Manchester City of their titles should be part of their punishment after they were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of financial rules

The 'disguised funding scheme' used by Manchester City changed the football landscape from 2009. Sky Sports features writer Nick Wright looks at how City's status was transformed through the course of the nine seasons in the investigation.

through the course of the nine seasons in the investigation. Several Manchester City sponsors are standing by the club in the wake of the guilty verdict, with Lucozade, Kellogg's, Revolut, BYD, Joie and PUMA all telling Sky Sports News they are not commenting on the independent commission's findings while the process remains ongoing.

What did the independent commission find?

Manchester City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

The club filed accounts that concealed the true state of its finances.

Manchester City were significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits and broke "well over 100" Premier League regulations.

Manchester City failed to co-operate and act in good faith towards the league during the investigation, with three out of four alleged breaches upheld and one charge not proven

The commission also said it was "regrettable" that a decision had taken so long to reach, with the hearing having taken place between September and December 2024.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Dave Reed breaks down the key findings from the independent commission's 40-page document on the Manchester City charges.

Man City: Process was not impartial

A Manchester City statement released on Tuesday read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News has obtained a video of Manchester City CEO Ferran Soriano that has been sent to internal staff and players at the club after the guilty verdict in relation to allegations of serious breaches of financial rules.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Manchester City's statement erroneously refers to a Premier League commission. It is an independent commission.

Sports.title: Inside Rangers' summer transfer window - but will it deliver success?
Sports.content:
We have passed the 100-day landmark in the Derek McInnes era at Rangers, and it has certainly been a rollercoaster ride.

His first four games were winless, followed by that humiliating European exit to Jablonec.

However, when Rangers return from the international break, they will have their sights set on going top of the Scottish Premiership for the first time this season.

That's down to a new-look squad and six consecutive wins, including back-to-back Old Firm victories. There is a feel-good factor in the stands at Ibrox once again.

Here, we look at how a key summer transfer window helped pave the way for a remarkable turnaround - one McInnes knows he must keep on track against Kilmarnock on October 10.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights as Rangers made it back-to-back wins over Celtic within a week as they won at Parkhead

How do transfers at Rangers work?

Before we get into the fine detail, it's important to take a look at the bigger picture.

This was the second consecutive summer that Rangers signed 14 players. However, the two windows couldn't be more different.

For full context, you need to go back 12 months. It was a new era (yes, another one) at Ibrox. Russell Martin had been appointed head coach, and the club were being led by CEO Patrick Stewart and sporting director Kevin Thelwell. However, that fresh start proved to be a false dawn.

As Rangers went off track, Martin was sacked after 123 days, before Stewart and Thelwell followed soon after. Meanwhile, of the 14 signings sanctioned by the likes of the aforementioned, only four remain. Chairman Andrew Cavenagh admitted mistakes had been made, and after issuing the P45's, he took a more hands-on role at the club.

Image: Kevin Thelwell, Russell Martin and Patrick Stewart were all sacked by Rangers last year

Some might think it was Robbie Thelwell, who has the title "head of recruitment", who was in charge of the signings. In truth, his title does not reflect his responsibility, and he works in the scouting team.

Instead, fast-forward 12 months and working alongside Cavenagh were the likes of CEO Jim Gillespie, who joined in March, now outgoing technical director Dan Purdy, Paraag Marathe and Gretar Steinsson of the 49ers, plus Stig Inge Bjornebye, who was appointed performance director in June following a spell as consultant.

Image: Former Everton head of recruitment Dan Purdy has stepped down from his role as technical director but will continue assisting Rangers this season after helping rebuild the squad

Rangers were not only looking at players' attributes, but also how they'd fit in the dressing room, their injury history, trading value and so on. Things which in the past were not always prioritised but are now all part of the equation.

The likes of Purdy would identify the options, Cavenagh and Gillespie were among those signing off on the deals, all done with the backing of the 49ers and ultimately the manager.

While there will always be successes and failures, this time Rangers had a united approach.

Image: CEO Jim Gillespie joined in March and led the search for manager Derek McInnes who both played a key role in summer transfers

So what was the plan this summer?

Rangers' initial target was to sign fewer players than they did the previous summer, but opportunities and injuries saw that number rise from around 10 to 14.

The club's leadership group set the parameters, the model of how Rangers should play both domestically and in Europe was in place, and it was over to the new powers that be to sign the players - just like they did in January when Tuur Rommens, Tochi Chukwuani and Ryan Naderi were permanent additions.

Image: Ryan Naderi and Tochi Chukwuani have impressed after joining Rangers in January

Rangers' goal this season - under McInnes, who knows the Scottish game inside out - was to taste domestic success once again.

So what was the plan to end Celtic's Premiership stranglehold? Well, rather than trying to copy their Old Firm rivals' possession-based style of play, Rangers were focussing on physicality and speed. The view was that to beat Celtic, they couldn't be like Celtic - they had to work differently.

Furthermore, following the departures of captain James Tavernier, vice-captain Jack Butland and co, they needed leaders in the squad, plus wanted to reduce the overall age of the group - something they had achieved over the previous windows.

Image: Dan Neil was captain at Sunderland and Lawrence Shankland was Hearts skipper before both joined Rangers in the summer

Finally, while chairman Cavenagh was willing to splash the cash for the right players, many signings would still need to have the potential to grow in value and help the club flourish.

Did they deliver?

It was a complex checklist and not everything has been fixed at Ibrox over a few months. This was always going to take multiple windows. However, there are positive signs.

The average age of the team that beat Celtic in their two games before the international break was less than 24 - compared to their rivals, who were closer to 27.

The starting XI in those games comprised of a new-look spine and six summer signings: goalkeeper Ivor Pandur, defender Olwethu Makhanya, captain Dan Neil in midfield along with James Penrice, Minsu Kim out wide and Kevin Kelsy leading the line.

Image: Kevin Kelsy and Olwethu Makhanya, both 22, have impressed since joining Rangers in the summer

At Ibrox in their League Cup quarter-final triumph, Rangers played like a team with an identity and style. They were strong, physical, fast and dominated the battle for second balls. That was reaffirmed at Parkhead in the Premiership a week later, while their rivals changed shape in a search for answers that didn't arrive.

Both in January and this summer, Rangers have been adding to their squad with a clear plan in place. They now have a group boasting speed, physicality, desire and the types of players who could attract interest from bigger leagues across Europe.

That recognition is coming on the international front too, with 13 of the squad selected by their country for this three-week window. Of those away with their countries, 12 of the 13 are 26 or under too - a clear sign of the change in direction at Ibrox.

Rangers starting XI vs Celtic age Ivor Pandur (26); Dujon Sterling (26), Emmanuel Fernandez (24), Olwethu Makhanya (22); Kim Minsu (20), Nicolas Raskin (25), Dan Neil (24), James Penrice (27), Djeidi Gassama (23); Ryan Naderi (23), Kevin Kelsy (22)

There has been significant work to alter Rangers' recruitment process since last summer, and while the early signs are positive, nothing is won in September.

Rangers still need to catch Celtic in the Premiership and face a tough test in Aberdeen, if they're to book a spot in the League Cup final, where Hearts or Hibs would await.

However, for the first time in years, after a busy transfer window and consecutive Old Firm victories - they head into Autumn with a platform that will allow them to deliver.

Sports.title: Ocon to leave Haas at end of 2026 season
Sports.content:
Esteban Ocon will leave Haas at the end of the 2026 Formula 1 season, both driver and team have confirmed.

Confirmation of the Ocon's exit came on Wednesday morning after months of speculation over the 30-year-old Frenchman's future with the team.

Along with confirming Ocon's departure, Haas said that there would be no imminent news on his replacement, despite reports that Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara has been lined up to partner Britain's Oliver Bearman next season.

Ocon wrote on social media: "My time with Haas F1 Team will come to an end at the end of the 2026 season.

"I leave this project with my head held high and proud of my performances in what were not always the easiest of circumstances for various reasons and factors outside of my control."

Ocon joined Haas from Alpine for the 2025 season but has been outperformed by 21-year-old Bearman across their two campaigns together.

"His professionalism and commitment have proved valuable as we continue to grow as an organisation. Together this year we tackled the challenge of a major regulation change, where Esteban's driving experience and inputs were significant as we've worked hard to develop the VF-26 across the season.

'This is not the end of my F1 career'

The timing of the announcement, with just eight rounds of the 2026 season remaining, means Ocon is highly likely to be without an F1 seat next year.

Sports.title: ‘I am here more than ever’: Guardiola backs Manchester City owners over guilty verdicts
Sports.content:
Pep Guardiola has thrown his support behind Manchester City after the club were found guilty of all charges of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, telling fans: “We will get through this together.”

Guardiola left City in the summer after a trophy-laden decade in charge, with his first two seasons falling within the period investigated by the independent commission. The Spaniard remains a close ally of the chief executive, Ferran Soriano, who brought him to England, the pair having previously worked together at Barcelona. City maintain their innocence and are set to appeal against the decision before Friday’s deadline.

“I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here; more than ever,” Guardiola posted on social media. “I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran, the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters. Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all.”

Twenty trophies were won in the 10 years Guardiola managed City and he was frequently asked about the charges that hung over the club for much of his tenure. The 55-year-old has consistently reiterated his faith in what he was told by the club’s Abu Dhabi ownership while the investigation was ongoing, with charges first brought against the club in February 2023. “I trust them,” Guardiola said in May. “I spoke with them and trust how they behave and how they did.”

Upon Guardiola’s departure, it was confirmed that he would continue as a global ambassador for City Football Group, which would involve him giving “technical advice to the clubs in the group, working on specific projects and collaborations”.

Meanwhile, David Bernstein, City’s former chair, has described the situation at City as “beyond awful” and called for the current board to stand down.

“I can’t think of a penalty strong enough for this, really. I mean, this is absolutely ⁠terrible,” said Bernstein, who was City’s chair between 1998 and 2003. “I want to raise another question, and that is the position of the ​board of directors. Because the directors ‌of the club, including the chief executive, who’s been there for years and went ‌through this period, are responsible for the running of the club in every respect.

“If this was a public company of some sort, the directors would have to stand down or be suspended pending the outcome of all this, appeal or no appeal. I don’t ‌think the present management can credibly continue.”

Andrée Jeglertz, the Manchester City women’s head coach, insisted that it has been a case of “business as usual” for his team as they prepare to host Real Madrid in the Women’s Champions League on Thursday. And asked if he echoed Pep Guardiola’s position and if he would back the club, in spite of the Premier League’s guilty verdict, Jeglertz said: “Definitely. I’m working [at] this club now, and that’s definitely what I’m hired for, for sure.”

The Swede declined to comment further when asked if he had been given any assurances that the women’s team would not be impacted by the matter. Jeglertz insisted that his side - who won the Women’s Super League title last season – were focused only on football, saying: “We haven’t changed anything, we just keep on doing everything we normally do.”

Sports.title: Paris FC v Arsenal: Women’s Champions League – live
Sports.content:
Renée Slegers makes just two changes from the 1-0 defeat to Chelsea, with Misa Rodriguez in goal ahead of Anneke Borbe, while Lotte Wubben-Moy replaces Steph Catley in defence. Catley, like Chloe Kelly, is injured and did not travel for the game.

One, zero, one, one, zero – that is Arsenal’s scoring record in five games this season, the Gunners devoid of their usual firepower. Their Champions League opener ended in a fortunate late win over Danish part-timers Køge, but today’s opposition represent a significant step up.

Paris FC edged out PSG to finish second in the French top tier last season, and gave Barcelona a scare in their first game, even if the defending champs did eventually run out 5-2 winners. Arsenal will face Barça and Lyonnes later in this league phase amid a tough domestic fixture list, so tonight would be a good time to rediscover their attacking form.

Kick-off at the Stade Jean Bouin in Paris is at 5.45pm (BST) – stay tuned for all the team news and pre-match chat.

Sports.title: Sham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severe | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
How bad could it be, really? How serious can a breach of arcane financial regulations be, really? Just how damning can accountancy be? Even after Friday’s revelation that Manchester City had been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League, it was perhaps difficult to grasp the scale of what that meant. After the publication of the independent commission’s findings, there can be no doubt: the commission found that Manchester City cheated, that they did so deliberately, and that they have sought to cover that up with a campaign of calculated misinformation.

City continue to maintain their innocence and issued a statement insisting that “the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. It referred, once again, to “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of all of its positions”, and, again, insisted that “the club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence”.

The chief executive, Ferran Soriano, released a video reiterating many of the same points and vowing that the club would appeal – it has until Friday to do so – and pursue “all other legal avenues” to prove its innocence. He dismissed the Premier League’s charges as “a conspiracy theory” – and pointedly referred to the independent commission as a “Premier League Commission” – claiming that they were based on “a single false accusation” of diverting funds from the owner to the club under the guise of sponsorship payments. This, he said, “could not happen and … did not happen”. The commission’s view, it’s fair to say, is very different.

Any sanction will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission, but it is impossible to read the verdict without thinking that it will have to be extremely severe. Everton were docked a total of eight points over two accounting windows for an inadvertent breach of profitability and sustainability rules amounting to around £20m, having cooperated with the investigation. Exactly what City’s breach would turn out to be remains to be calculated, but the verdict found that they overstated income by around £855m and understated outgoings by around £66m. And this was not a cock-up but a calculated attempt to circumvent the rules.

View image in fullscreen The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. Photograph: Carl Recine/Reuters

The verdict makes for astonishing reading. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters, shredded in careful, measured legal prose. The appendices, as and when they are made public, might make it even worse. Even if some technicality is found that mitigates the punishment, their standing cannot surely recover. The findings show this is the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football. This is not breaching the maximum wage and being caught when most clubs were doing similar, which lay at the heart of the three previous huge top-division financial scandals: Manchester City in 1906, Leeds City in 1919 and Sunderland in 1957. This was deception on a massive scale.

Sponsorship deals are described as “shams” to obscure investment and overstated by £830m over the nine years in question as part of “a plan to disguise shareholder funding … as ‘commercial partner revenue’”. The Fordham Agreement, an arrangement by which an entity bought player image rights, was “little more than a front”. Attempts to claim that the Premier League had misunderstood how the sponsorship deals worked were “an ‘explanation’ that the club concocted well after the event in an attempt to conceal and obscure the realities of the disguised funding scheme”.

The level of mendacity identified is extraordinary. In regards to the “sham” sponsorship arrangements there was “intentional conduct” to “disguise the true nature of certain revenues and liabilities/expenses, to give the appearance of minimising the club’s financial dependence on ADUG” and give “a misleading impression in the club’s financial statements that the club’s financial position was better than it in fact was”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Having been charged, City “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation”. The panel found “evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects” and “certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”. On occasions, the panel concluded it “should not accept the opinion of an expert”; the precise reasons why are set out in an appendix but, in context, an inference can be drawn.

The one charge on which City were not found guilty was of breaching “duties of cooperation” with the Premier League in relation to one tranche of accusations. That, clearly, is not the get-out many City fans have hoped for since Friday. The verdict is damning.

The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. They have lied consistently and deliberately. The continued denials only enhance the sense that this is a club that has no respect for the regulations.

There must now be a very good argument for expulsion. How can City, at least under the current ownership, ever be trusted again? How can they go on playing even this season, pretending all is well, awaiting appeal and sanction, when they have been found guilty of charges of such magnitude?

When the club has behaved like this, how can its continued existence in the Premier League be tolerated? And when they have cheated as they have been shown to do between 2009-10 and 2017-18, how can their name appear on the Premier League’s roll of honour?

Sports.title: ‘A lot of lies’: Ireland manager hits out over coverage of Bazunu exit from Israel game
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, has claimed “a lot of lies” were told over keeper Gavin ⁠Bazunu’s decision to withdraw ⁠from the Nations League ​game against Israel last weekend, and he does not anticipate any problems with Sunday’s second match against them going ahead.

Ireland are one of Europe’s most outspoken critics of Israel’s war in Gaza, ⁠and protests calling for the team to boycott the fixture prompted Bazunu to pull out of both games between the two countries.

Last Sunday’s match, which Ireland won 3-0, went ahead after a majority of their squad ⁠voted to play on the eve of the away fixture in Hungary. Media reports indicated a fractured squad after the meeting and ​vote, and that Bazunu had been insulted by teammates ‌over his decision.

The keeper is ‌available for Thursday’s home game with Austria, but will not take part in Sunday’s rematch with Israel, which the Football Association ‌of Ireland (FAI) has moved to Serbia behind closed doors.

“Gavin is a great lad, I’ve always had a good relationship with him and it’s probably tougher for him than the other players, but they have really welcomed him,” Hallgrímsson told a press conference on Wednesday.

“There’s been a lot of lies said around all of this, but we welcomed him back and he’s taking part. Amazing, I think it shows his character, as well, to be with ‌us. So I want to give him praise for that. I want to give the players praise for how welcome they have been with him,” he added. “Life goes on. He’s a ​part of this group and I think that shows how strong the bond is between these players that even a thing like this is not breaking us.”

Ireland midfielder Finn Azaz has also been the centre of attention given his deep Israeli heritage, and remained on the bench for the win over Israel. Hallgrimsson was asked if Azaz would be involved ⁠in Sunday’s fixture.

“We are focusing on this one [against Austria], you can probably ask me that ​question later on,” the manager said. “Finn has ​shown incredible emotional control and awareness. He ​probably is one of the people I admire the most in how he conducted himself ​in all of this.”

Thursday’s ‌game against Austria in ​Dublin is expected to bring ​further protests over Ireland playing Israel.

“I am focused on football, I’ll let others think about security,” Hallgrímsson said. “The FAI has said we are playing both games and we will fulfil that. It has been really, really tough, but I surely think that in time we will have seen that we took more right decisions than wrong ones.”

Sports.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
Sports.content:
In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation mark The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation mark The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo misses Portugal training amid reports of rift with coach Jesus
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo’s continued absence from Portugal team training has led to speculation that the 41-year-old might miss his country’s match in Denmark on Thursday due to a rift with the head coach, Jorge Jesus.

Ronaldo, the all-time leading scorer in men’s international football and pursuing the milestone of 1,000 career goals, was left on the bench on Sunday in Portugal’s 2-1 win at Norway in the Nations League. He has not practised with the team since then, doing only gym work, the Portuguese Football Federation said.

Portuguese media claimed the federation president, Pedro Proença had to travel to meet with Ronaldo and Jesus after reports the forward was unhappy about being left out against Norway. The federation confirmed only that Proença was with the squad, as it prepares for the Nations League game in Copenhagen.

Ronaldo, who has 146 international goals for Portugal, posted a photo of himself on Instagram wearing the Portugal tracksuit on Tuesday, accompanied by the Portuguese flag and a heart emoji.

Jesus, who took over the squad from Roberto Martínez after the World Cup, said before the Norway game that he didn’t want to overuse Ronaldo during the unusually long international break in which Portugal play four games in 11 days.

View image in fullscreen Jorge Jesus conducts Portugal team training on Tuesday … without Cristiano Ronaldo. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/Shutterstock

Jesus added that he planned to give Ronaldo minutes against Norway but the circumstances of the match kept the veteran from being used. Jesus explained after the victory that he would “talk to him”, responding to reports that Ronaldo was upset.

Ronaldo started in Portugal’s 1-0 win over Wales last week and was substituted in the 67th minute.

Sports.title: Football Daily | The big story is of course … Scotland fans pining for another home run
Sports.content:
CURVEBALL

In the four matches they’ve sat through since their unconvincing Geopolitics World Cup win over Haiti, it must rankle among diehard conscripts of the Tartan Army that the only sporting moment they’ve been able to celebrate with genuine wild abandon remains a Wyatt Langford home run biffed out of the stadium for the Texas Rangers at Fenway Park. Away from the diamond, fairly meek surrenders by Scotland to Morocco and Brazil led to Steve Clarke’s resignation, which in turn prompted Sébastien Pocognoli to surf in on a wave of cautious fan suspicion. Following an extremely promising second-half display in his first game against Slovenia – one that obviously featured no goals, a couple of missed sitters and plenty of attacking verve from his side – the Belgian had plenty of reasons to be cheerful going into his first home game as Scotland head coach. After all, as a newbie to the gig he probably didn’t know any better.

He does now. While Hampden Park was far from full for Tuesday night’s match against Switzerland, those who did turn up also had every reason to feel less downbeat than usual ahead of a potentially glorious new dawn of not only qualifying for tournaments, but potentially getting past their group stages. This being Scotland, any optimism evaporated shortly after the 10-minute mark when – “AFTER REVIEW!” – Jack Hendry was sent off for preventing a clear and obvious goalscoring opportunity with a blatant tug on Dan Ndoye’s shoulder. Having first been awarded a penalty for a foul that was actually committed outside the box, the Swiss had to settle for a free-kick and promptly scored it anyway.

“We were ready to deliver the game we wanted from the first minute,” parped Pocognoli at the end of a match in which his 10 men shipped two more and came out on the wrong end of a 3-0 drubbing. “We had an unlucky red card, punished with the free-kick, that’s the worst scenario.” While Pocognoli clearly has a lot to learn about his new role if he thinks that is as bad as things will get on his watch, Scotland now have a trip to Skopje, where they will hope to keep a full complement of players on the pitch and at least trouble the scoreboard operator in a match against North Macedonia.

Fourteen years ago this month, the then Scotland manager Craig Levein was the subject of much abuse from fans when his similarly goal-shy side failed to beat all of Macedonia (yes, that’s a joke) in a World Cup qualifier. “This is going to be really tight indeed,” insisted Levein, of a group in which Scotland would eventually finish 15 points off the pace set by Belgium. While Pocognoli’s reign is in its infancy and he will be afforded far more patience than his unpopular, ultra-defensive predecessor, any kind of win on Saturday will be greeted with far more Scottish delight than anything the Red Sox and Rangers could ever magic up between them.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

The Nations League is taking a night off but Niall McVeigh has piping hot Women’s Bigger Cup action, with Paris FC 1-2 Arsenal live at 5.45pm BST.

QUOTE OF THE DAY I

“I want every single @ManCity fan to know I am here; more than ever. I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters. Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all” – a few months after doing one, Pep Guardiola pops up to tell distraught fans he’s going to battle on through with them after reading the Premier League’s bombshell official guilty verdict and revelation of £900m worth of “sham” contracts. Yep, presumably he agrees with City chief suit Ferran Soriano who has since parped that he thinks the findings are “a conspiracy theory”.

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola has got City fans’ backs. Photograph: Molly Darlington/Reuters

QUOTE OF THE DAY II

“If I was a player, I’d be 100% sticking those medals in the bin. Of course you would, it’s cheating. They won it on the pitch because cheating was going on. [Manchester City] knew it would hurt a lot of people, but they’ve still done it” – Roy Keane, there, not mincing his words and taking a very different view to another former Manchester United captain, Wayne Rooney, who reckons players should not be stripped of their shiny titles.

The most that will happen is that the big five (and Spurs) will be reduced back to the big four (and Spurs). We’ll continue to praise plucky little Brighton and lament how monied Manchester United can’t get it together while preventing the likes of Aston Villa and Newcastle from having the money to sustain any multi-year challenge to the clubs owned by nation states and hedge-fund managers.
