World.title: Why the War in Ukraine Is Making Rice More Expensive in Liberia
World.content:
When we hear about the war in Ukraine, it can feel distant – something happening far away that doesn’t touch our lives in Liberia. It is tempting to view it as a political dispute between foreign nations that has little to do with the daily realities in Monrovia, Gbarnga, or Harper. But in today’s deeply interconnected global economy, no nation is an island. What happens in the Black Sea directly affects market stalls, kitchen tables, and family budgets here in Liberia.

By Zoltan Szalai, contributing writer

Before the war, Ukraine was known as the “breadbasket of the world.” It supplied 15 percent of the world’s corn, 10 percent of its wheat, and half of all sunflower oil. These are not just numbers; they are the ingredients in the food we eat every day. But now, Russian attacks are destroying Ukrainian ports, farms, and grain storage facilities. Ships carrying food cannot move freely. Millions of tonnes of grain sit trapped, at risk of spoiling. Farmers who cannot sell their crops this year may not have the money to plant next year’s harvest. If this continues, food shortages and high prices could stretch well into 2027.



For Liberia, this is a serious problem. While Liberian farmers grow rice, they do not produce enough to feed everyone. Here in Liberia, we rely on imports for rice, wheat, cooking oil, and even fuel. When global food supplies shrink, prices rise – and those higher costs are passed to us consumers. That means the bag of rice you buy at the market costs more. The loaf of bread for your children’s breakfast is pricier. The cooking oil you need for every meal becomes harder to afford. For families already struggling with rising living costs, this is not just an inconvenience – it is a crisis.

The impact goes beyond food. When shipping and fuel prices increase, everything becomes more expensive. The cost of farming goes up. The price of transporting goods rises. Inflation stretches household budgets even thinner. Globally, over 645 million people now face hunger. Liberia, like many import-dependent nations, remains highly exposed to these disruptions. At stake is not merely the challenge is not just fighting against high prices; it is a fight for one’s ability to survive.

Food should never be used as a weapon. Yet right now, attacks on Ukraine’s food infrastructure are doing exactly that – using hunger as leverage in a war. The European Union has created alternative routes, called “Solidarity Lanes,” to help move Ukraine’s food by land and river. But these cannot replace the Black Sea, which normally handles 90 percent of Ukraine’s exports. Without safe shipping lanes, the world’s food supply remains at risk.

Liberia cannot afford to ignore this. The international community must take urgent action. First, the attacks on grain facilities and commercial ships must stop. These are not military targets; they are the sources of food for millions of people. Second, there must be guarantees for safe passage for civilian cargo vessels carrying essential supplies. Third, and most importantly, the only real solution is a lasting ceasefire and peace. Until then, families in Liberia and across the world will continue to pay the price.

This is not just Ukraine’s war – it is a crisis that touches us all. When The European Union demands an end to attacks on food supplies, we are not just standing up for Ukraine; we are protecting our own ability to feed our families. No parent should have to choose between putting food on the table and paying for their children’s school fees. No child should go to bed hungry because of a war they had no part in.

The world is connected, and our struggles are connected. What happens in Ukraine affects the price of rice in Monrovia, the cost of bread in Gbarnga, and the availability of cooking oil in Harper. The time to act is now – before more families are pushed to the brink. We may be thousands of miles away, but this fight is ours too.

About the author

Zoltan Szalai serves as the Chargé d’Affaires a.i. of the Delegation of the European Union to the Republic of Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: MODA Distances Itself from Agriculture Minister Nuetah, Says He Is Not and Has Never Been a Member
World.content:
According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah “is not a member of the Movement for Democratic Alliance, has never been a member of MODA, and has not communicated any intention to become a member of the Movement.”

GBARNGA, Bong County – The Movement for Democratic Alliance (MODA) has clarified that the Minister of Agriculture, Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah, is not a member of the organization. It also rejected claims that his support for a youth training initiative in Bong County signals a political alliance or an effort to form a political party.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

In a press statement issued Tuesday in Gbarnga, MODA said it had taken note of recent public discussions and media reports that sought to link the Minister to the Movement and to present his backing of a youth skills-development program as evidence of political collaboration.



“MODA considers it important to place the facts on record and to correct any misunderstanding surrounding the matter,” said Acting Chairman Lawrence N. Yallah, who signed the statement.

“Not a Political Party”

MODA first clarified its own status, stating that it is “not a political party” but a “political movement.” It then addressed Minister Nuetah’s relationship with the group directly.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah “is not a member of the Movement for Democratic Alliance, has never been a member of MODA, and has not communicated any intention to become a member of the Movement.”

The Movement said it therefore “rejects any representation suggesting that the Minister is a member, official, political leader, financier, or representative” of MODA.

Describing itself as a people-centered movement founded on democratic participation, integrity, unity, equity, inclusion, public service and sustainable development, MODA said it remains open to working with individuals, institutions, organizations and public officials when such engagement serves the legitimate interests of the Liberian people. However, it cautioned that cooperation on a specific development project should not be read as political membership, affiliation or endorsement.

Origin of the Excavator Training Slots

The statement traced the controversy to July 14, 2026, when Minister Nuetah made five excavator-training slots available for young people from Bong County. MODA said this followed an appeal from its Commander-in-Chief, Mr. Jomah B. Dolo, for more opportunities for the county’s youth.

The Movement described the slots as an initial contribution toward skills development.

The five slots reportedly drew 252 applicants, who then went through an independent vetting and selection process.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah made the opportunity available, while the individual who received it, who is associated with MODA’s leadership, chose to place the selection process in the hands of the Movement. MODA said it then facilitated the exercise with the stated aim of ensuring the five beneficiaries were chosen through a transparent and competitive process

MODA stressed that the Minister did not personally select the five beneficiaries and did not set up any political recruitment process through the Movement.

According to the statement, Dr. Nuetah made the opportunity available, while the individual who received it, who is associated with MODA’s leadership, chose to place the selection process in the hands of the Movement. MODA said it then facilitated the exercise with the stated aim of ensuring the five beneficiaries were chosen through a transparent and competitive process.

The Movement added that it was “even more excited” that all five selected individuals turned out to be supporters of the Unity Party, even though party affiliation was not a requirement for applying.

The five young people are expected to begin their excavator training at For Life Zoe in the coming days. MODA said it regards the initiative “strictly” as an opportunity for young Liberians to acquire practical skills that can improve their employment prospects and economic participation.

It noted that the Ministry of Agriculture has itself publicly emphasized youth empowerment, agricultural mechanization and practical skills development as part of its broader agenda.

MODA Dismisses New Party Speculation

The Movement also responded to commentary suggesting that the Minister’s support for the training slots through MODA means he has established a political party to challenge President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s potential bid for a second term.

MODA dismissed the suggestion in strong terms, describing it as “blatant mendacity coming from the mouth of back-door politicians who are afraid of youth progression.”

The Movement called on individuals, commentators, political actors and media practitioners to distinguish between a development initiative and political affiliation.

“A public official providing opportunities for young people does not, by itself, establish membership in MODA or demonstrate an intention to form or lead a political party,” the statement said.

MODA further stated that Minister Nuetah’s political affiliation and future decisions are matters that should be addressed through his own public statements and actions, not attributed to the Movement.

“For the avoidance of doubt, MODA does not claim Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah as a member of the Movement, and the Movement has no authority to speak on his behalf regarding his political affiliation or future political plans,” the statement said. It added that the group has known the Minister only as a people-centered leader, not through “the opinions of agent provocateurs.”

Outlining its position, MODA said the country’s political and development environment should allow people and institutions to cooperate on matters of national and community interest without every act of cooperation being treated as partisan politics. It encouraged public discussion to remain grounded in facts, particularly where individuals, political organizations, public officials and opportunities for young people are concerned.

The Movement also urged everyone discussing the excavator-training initiative to respect the integrity of the 252 applicants and the five young people chosen. “Their opportunity should not be reduced to political speculation,” the statement said.

MODA reaffirmed its commitment to its stated principles and to engaging anyone prepared to support initiatives that advance the interests of the Liberian people, noting again that such engagement does not automatically create political membership or affiliation.

It pledged to continue supporting efforts that expand opportunities for young Liberians, promote skills development, encourage transparency and contribute to national development.

World.title: Liberia: Beyond Survival: WONGOSOL Gives FGM Survivors Dignity Today and Livelihoods for Tomorrow
World.content:
MONROVIA — For women and girls who have survived female genital mutilation (FGM) and other forms of gender-based violence, the road to recovery often extends far beyond the immediate trauma.

By Patience M. Jones

It can mean having access to basic hygiene supplies, clothing and personal-care items while receiving support—and, for some survivors, having the means to earn an income and rebuild their lives.



That is the focus of the Liberia Fight FGM Project, implemented by the Women NGOs Secretariat of Liberia (WONGOSOL) with support from the United Nations Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women.

As part of the project’s third consignment of support, WONGOSOL is distributing more than 600 dignity kits to FGM and gender-based violence (GBV) survivors through one-stop centers across six counties, while also preparing livelihood assistance for 365 women trained in vocational skills, business management and Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) approaches.

Speaking to journalists on Friday, WONGOSOL Executive Director Esther S. David Yango said the initiative is designed to address both the immediate needs of survivors and the economic challenges that can leave women vulnerable.

“The FGM project connects immediate survivor support with long-term economic empowerment, providing dignity today while helping women and communities build safer, more resilient and sustainable futures,” Yango said.

A Kit Designed to Restore Dignity

The dignity packages are intended to provide practical assistance to survivors during periods of vulnerability.

According to the project team, the packages include toothpaste and toothbrushes, sanitary pads, towels, grease, slippers, bath soap and lappa.

Separate packages are being prepared for younger survivors, with additional items such as snacks and toys intended to make their experience at one-stop centers less distressing.

Clothing, including blouses and dresses, will also be provided to survivors.

Jeneba M. Vessellie, Project Officer of the Liberia Fight FGM Project, explained that the materials are meant to respond to survivors’ immediate needs while they access health, psychosocial, legal and protection services.

The intervention, officials said, recognizes that recovery is not only about medical or legal assistance, but also about helping survivors maintain dignity during a difficult period.

From Training to Economic Independence

While the dignity kits address immediate needs, the livelihood component is intended to provide a longer-term pathway toward economic independence.

The project has trained 365 women in livelihood and vocational skills, business management and VSLA approaches. The beneficiaries include FGM practitioners, FGM survivors, single mothers, youth and women leaders.

Livelihood support will include materials for activities such as soap making, tailoring, pastry and baking, among other income-generating activities.

The project team said the assistance is intended to help trained women put their skills into practice, establish or strengthen businesses and build economic resilience after the project ends.

For women involved in agriculture, support will also include farm materials and tools.

The program team cited women survivors involved in agriculture in Bong County as among those expected to receive agricultural support.

The project also links livelihood support to savings.

Officials said beneficiaries trained in savings and loan approaches will be able to save from the income generated through their activities, helping them sustain their businesses beyond the life of the project.

Reaching Communities Across Six Counties

The Liberia Fight FGM Project is being implemented in 38 communities across Bomi, Bong, Gbarpolu, Grand Cape Mount, Margibi and Montserrado Counties, in partnership with local organizations.

The project has also established 40 community coalitions comprising 600 members who have been trained to advocate for the protection of women and girls against harmful practices, including FGM and sexual and gender-based violence.

The coalitions are also supporting advocacy for the passage of the Women and Girls Protection Act.

The implementing partners include Women Care Initiative (WOCI) in Bomi; Community Women Peace Initiative (CWPI) in Bong; Paramount Young Women Initiative (PAYWO) in Gbarpolu; Sister Hands Liberia (SHL) in Grand Cape Mount; Women Education and Development Organization of Liberia (WEDOL) in Margibi; and WEPS and INSURED in Montserrado.

Two Needs, One Intervention

For WONGOSOL, the distribution represents two connected sides of survivor support.

The dignity kits respond to immediate needs, helping survivors meet basic personal-care and hygiene needs and restore a measure of dignity during vulnerable periods.

The livelihood assistance, meanwhile, addresses longer-term economic vulnerability by helping women transform training into sustainable economic opportunities.

Together, the interventions form what WONGOSOL describes as an integrated approach to prevention, protection and women’s economic empowerment.

The project, which began in October 2023, was initially scheduled to end in September 2026. A five-month no-cost extension has now extended implementation through February 28, 2027.

For the women at the center of the intervention, the assistance is therefore about more than receiving a package or business materials.

It is about having something to meet a need today and, through skills and economic opportunities, something to build on tomorrow.

World.title: Catholic Bishops Question Credibility of 2026 Elections as CCZ Demands Kafwaya Probe
World.content:
Catholic and Protestant Churches Close Ranks on Rule of Law, Demand Dialogue and End to Arbitrary Arrests

Zambia’s two largest church bodies have issued separate but closely aligned statements warning that the rule of law, public confidence in institutions and national unity are under strain in the aftermath of the 2026 general election. The Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops (ZCCB) raised concern over the credibility and transparency of the elections, arrests of opposition figures and the presence of military personnel in civilian spaces. It also pointed to reports of excessive or unlawful force, including the loss of civilian lives. The Council of Churches in Zambia (CCZ) called for an independent investigation into the death of former Cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, who was killed in August during a State security operation. Both bodies called for sustained national dialogue and an end to detention without due process.

The Catholic bishops’ pastoral statement followed an extraordinary plenary meeting of eight bishops on September 29. The bishops said they had listened to the concerns, fears and hopes of citizens before reflecting on the situation in the light of the Gospel and the social teaching of the Church. They said their intervention was not intended to deepen political divisions or take sides in partisan struggles. Instead, they said, it was meant to protect human dignity, justice, truth, peace and national unity. The bishops said the moment called for action, not silence.

“The present moment requires not silence or resignation, but responsible action directed towards peace, justice, reconciliation and the common good,” the bishops said.

The bishops warned that increasing political polarisation was weakening dialogue and making it difficult for citizens to put the common good above partisan interests. They expressed concern over the manipulation of ethnic identities and tribal sentiment for political purposes, warning that it threatened the spirit of ‘One Zambia, One Nation’. Many citizens, they said, were living in fear over their personal security, freedom of expression and employment, and over the consequences of voicing political opinions. They also pointed to a narrowing of space for independent media, civil society and dissenting voices.

The ZCCB questioned the credibility and transparency of electoral processes, particularly concerns over the conduct and management of the 2026 General Elections. The bishops said public confidence in elections was essential to the legitimacy and stability of democratic institutions. They raised concern over restrictions affecting access to justice and perceptions that the independence of governance institutions was being weakened. They also flagged debates around the constitutional provisions on presidential terms of office, where such debates raise anxiety about constitutional safeguards and democratic continuity. On opposition politics, the bishops cited reports of harassment, restrictions and arrests, and they defended the right of rival voices to take part.

“Democracy requires space for alternative political voices and peaceful political participation,” the bishops said.

The bishops’ gravest concern was the use of force. They cited reports of arbitrary arrests and detention, the presence of military personnel in civilian spaces and reports of excessive or unlawful use of force, including the loss of civilian lives. The statement did not name any individual case. The bishops said such developments risked eroding trust between citizens and institutions, and they spoke plainly on the value of life.

“Every human life is sacred and must be protected,” the bishops said.

The CCZ was more direct on the one death that has come to define the post-election period. In a communique issued after a Heads of Churches meeting at the University of Zambia Chapel, CCZ president Reverend Ackson Banda called for a thorough, independent, impartial and transparent investigation into Mr Kafwaya’s death. He said the facts must be established and accountability must follow wherever wrongdoing is found. Mr Kafwaya was killed in Lusaka’s Kabulonga area during what police described as an intelligence-led operation by a joint task force. Police said officers came under gunfire and returned fire. That account has been contested by the opposition, and a complaint over the death has since been lodged with the International Criminal Court in The Hague.

The CCZ also raised concern over people being arrested and held without being promptly brought before a competent court. It stressed that every citizen’s constitutional rights must be respected regardless of political affiliation, religious standing or social status. The council called for urgent investigations into allegations of organised groups or militias operating outside established security structures, without saying which groups it meant. Rev. Banda said the moment called for wisdom rather than political triumphalism, restraint rather than provocation, and justice rather than the selective application of the law.

Beyond their concerns, both bodies set out remedies, and these largely overlap. The ZCCB proposed a sustained process of national dialogue, reconciliation and healing across political, ethnic, religious and social lines. It also called for stronger democratic institutions and a review of electoral processes so that citizens can trust their votes are protected. The CCZ urged the Government, opposition parties and civil society to commit to national dialogue, saying reconciliation must be shown through justice, forgiveness and rebuilding trust rather than declarations and ceremonies. The bishops also called for civic and constitutional education for young people, protection for journalists and civil society, and legal and humanitarian support for families affected by violence or arbitrary detention.

“Public institutions must be instruments of justice and service rather than sources of fear,” the bishops said.

The two statements part ways on the economy. The CCZ acknowledged progress in debt restructuring, key economic indicators and free education, while noting that many Zambians still struggle with the high cost of living, unemployment, food insecurity and energy challenges. The ZCCB kept its focus on governance, rights and the conduct of the elections. The CCZ urged leaders to keep constitutional reforms inclusive and people-driven, and said the Church would maintain its independence from partisan political interests.

The statements come in the same week that the Catholic Archbishop of Lusaka, Dr Alick Banda, was released on bail after a night in custody on a charge of possessing a vehicle allegedly obtained unlawfully from the Zambia Revenue Authority. ZCCB president Archbishop Ignatius Chama had earlier accused the ruling party of seeking to silence the Church. The ruling UPND has rejected that charge, describing the Catholic Church as an important voice in matters of governance. The bishops’ pastoral statement did not refer directly to the Archbishop’s case.

The Catholic statement was issued at Kapingila House on the memorial of St Jerome. It was signed by Archbishop Chama, vice-president Bishop Charles Kasonde, Bishop George Lungu, Bishop Clement Mulenga, Bishop Patrick Chisanga, Bishop Edwin Mulandu, Bishop Raphael Mweempwa and Auxiliary Bishop Gabriel Msipu Phiri. The bishops declared October a special month of Holy Rosary prayers for peace in Zambia. They closed with an appeal to the nation.

“We call upon all people of good will to work together so that Zambia may remain a home for all her children, a nation in which human dignity is respected, justice is accessible, differences can be expressed peacefully, and power is exercised as service,” the bishops said.

World.title: Zesco explains Levy Mwanawasa Stadium blackout
World.content:
ZESCO Limited has explained the power disruption that stopped play for 18 minutes during Zambia’s 2-0 win over Togo at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium.

In a media statement issued today, ZESCO says the power disturbance occurred at 18:21 hours and lasted only 0.2 seconds.

However, the utility says the stadium’s floodlights require about 20 minutes to return to full brightness after a power disturbance due to their design.

“ZESCO Limited acknowledges the power disturbance during the Zambia vs Togo match at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium last night. The disturbance occurred at 18:21 hours and lasted 0.2 seconds. However, the design of the affected stadium floodlights requires approximately 20 minutes for them to return to full brightness after a power disturbance,” the power utility stated.

ZESCO says it will engage the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts to redesign the stadium’s lighting system to prevent future disruptions.

“ZESCO will engage the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts to look into redesigning the stadium’s lighting system to minimise the risk of similar disruptions during future matches.”

ZESCO has also congratulated the Chipolopolo Boys on their victory.

World.title: Govt backs public-focused Law reforms
World.content:
Government says it is committed to supporting law reforms that promote public participation and respond to the needs of citizens.

North-Western Province Deputy Secretary Luckson Mulumbi said the expansion of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) is an example of progressive policy reform that has brought resources closer to communities.

Speaking when he graced the Law Reform Talks organised by the Zambia Law Development Commission (ZLDC) in Solwezi, Mr Mulumbi said the expanded CDF has supported the construction of classrooms, health facilities and boreholes, among other community projects.

He said laws and policies should evolve in line with changing technological and economic trends to meet the needs and expectations of society.

Mr Mulumbi said Solwezi and North-Western Province provide an important setting for discussions on law reform due to the region’s significant economic, social and infrastructural development.

He said the developments have created new questions relating to land, livelihoods, investment, community participation, access to justice and the administration of laws.

ZLDC Director Hope Chanda said the Law Reform Talks are a deliberate initiative aimed at providing a platform where legal reform issues can be discussed interactively.

Ms Chanda said the commission had previously participated in the reform of the Gender Act, CDF and Access to Information Act through research and consultations with stakeholders.

Meanwhile, civil society organisations called for reforms to laws governing land ownership.

Caritas Solwezi Director Noel Haaninga called for the harmonisation of laws governing statutory and customary land.

Fr. Haaninga also called for stronger mechanisms to resolve land-related disputes and ensure that vulnerable families are treated fairly.

Fr. Haaninga said there was also a need to address gender disparities in land ownership, noting that men continue to dominate land ownership.

A representative of the Solwezi Legal Aid Board, Joseph Kalimina, urged the commission to intensify sensitisation programmes on ongoing law reforms.

Mr Kalimina also called for laws to be translated into local languages to ensure that all citizens can understand and participate in the reform process.

World.title: UPND USA-Canada Chapter Distances Itself from UN Protesters
World.content:
The UPND United States of America and Canada Chapter has distanced itself from six Zambians who recently staged a protest outside the United Nations building.

UPND USA-Canada Chapter Secretary General Andrew Mwape says only two of the six individuals are Zambians and do not represent the interests of more than 9,000 Zambians living in the United States and Canada.

Dr. Mwape says the chapter supports the development trajectory being pursued by President Hakainde Hichilema.

Speaking to the media in an interview, Dr. Mwape said that before the August General Elections, the chapter conducted a poll among 11,000 Zambians living in the United States and Canada.

Dr. Mwape condemned the conduct of the individuals, saying their actions do not reflect Zambian culture and values.

He said the chapter does not support such behaviour and maintained that the individuals do not represent the views of Zambians living in the United States and Canada.

World.title: Lwandamina Promises Improvements After Chipolopolo Victory
World.content:
Chipolopolo coach George Lwandamina has described the team’s 2-0 victory over Togo in the 2027 AFCON qualifiers as important.

Speaking during a post-match press briefing in Ndola on the Copperbelt last night, Lwandamina said his technical bench and players will continue working to improve the team.

He noted that the players are maturing and encouraging each other in every game, adding that with the likes of Patson Daka and Fashion Sakala leading the team, good things are coming.

Lwandamina called for total commitment from everyone ahead of the next AFCON qualifier matches.

And Togo coach Patrice Neveu said he was disappointed with the result but remained happy with the performance of his players.

Neveu noted that conceding an early goal affected Togo’s game plan.

He said Zambia capitalised on its speed to secure the three points, while his team failed to contain the home side.

World.title: Zambia Opens Talks with IMF on Successor to Extended Credit Facility
World.content:
Zambia has opened talks with an International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission on a successor programme under the Extended Credit Facility (ECF).

Government is seeking to build on restored macroeconomic stability while accelerating investment, exports, economic diversification and job creation.

The IMF mission, led by Edward Gemayel, has started engagements with Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane in Lusaka.

Mr. Gemayel said the successor programme will help preserve Zambia’s macroeconomic stability and debt sustainability while aligning with the Grow Zambia Agenda.

And Dr. Musokotwane said Zambia will maintain fiscal and macroeconomic stability while placing greater emphasis on growth, investment and employment.

The Minister said employment, particularly among young people, remains a major challenge, making stronger investment and sustained economic growth critical.

Dr. Musokotwane said the envisioned growth strategy rests on four key areas: export-led growth, foreign direct investment, human capital development, and a stronger regulatory and governance environment.

The IMF mission will also hold discussions with other public institutions, including the Bank of Zambia, Zambia Revenue Authority and other relevant institutions.

The discussions will focus on economic and structural policy issues that will anchor the proposed programme, including the 2027 National Budget and the 2027–2029 Medium-Term Budget Plan.

The successor programme is expected to build on the stability achieved under the previous ECF arrangement, with greater emphasis on sustainable and inclusive growth, private-sector-led development and export-oriented expansion.

This is according to a statement availed to ZNBC News today in Lusaka by the Ministry of Finance.

World.title: HH Seeks Solutions to Monthly Fuel Price Adjustments
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has called for solutions to Zambia’s monthly fuel price adjustments.

President Hichilema says frequent changes in fuel prices are distorting business planning and complicating economic management.

He says Zambia needs to explore a more predictable fuel pricing system that will give businesses greater certainty and support effective economic planning.

President Hichilema said this in the United Arab Emirates during a meeting with ADNOC Global Trading Chief Executive Officer Ahmed Bin Talith.

He appealed to ADNOC Global Trading to work with Zambia in addressing the factors driving fuel prices, namely international oil prices, the exchange rate and transportation costs.

President Hichilema also disclosed that Zambia is considering moving away from monthly pump-price adjustments to longer pricing periods of two or three months.

He explained that this would help businesses plan better instead of constantly adjusting to changes in fuel prices, while emphasising the need to ensure security of fuel supply.

And Mr. Bin Talith said his company is looking beyond fuel supply by investing in Zambia’s petroleum infrastructure and helping position the country as a regional fuel hub.

Mr. Bin Talith said ADNOC is exploring opportunities to support local companies, such as Indeni, in managing and expanding their terminals while improving operational flexibility and capacity.

He said increased investment in Zambia’s fuel infrastructure could secure the country’s domestic fuel demand while creating a surplus that could be supplied to neighbouring countries.

Mr. Bin Talith added that ADNOC’s interest is based on its previous experience of supplying Zambia, particularly during difficult periods, and its record of honouring contracts in East Africa.

He said ADNOC is also prepared to pursue a long-term partnership with Zambia rather than operating on short-term, month-to-month arrangements.

World.title: Zambia Must Use Digital Platforms to Cut Bureaucracy
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says Zambia must use digital platforms to cut bureaucracy, delays and inefficiencies that are slowing investment and service delivery.

President Hichilema says digital infrastructure should not be treated merely as an enabler, but as an integral part of Government’s efforts to deliver services to citizens and create a more conducive environment for investment.

The President was speaking during a meeting with United Arab Emirates Minister of Cabinet Affairs Mohammed Bin Abdullah Al Gergawi in Abu Dhabi.

He said the need to remove bureaucracy is directly linked to the Grow Zambia Agenda, which seeks to accelerate economic growth and improve service delivery.

And Mr. Al Gergawi said the UAE is ready to work with Zambia in transforming opportunities into practical solutions, including creating opportunities for the private sector.

He said the UAE has already been implementing a programme aimed at reducing bureaucracy, following a directive from the President of the UAE.

Mr. Al Gergawi said the experience could provide lessons for Zambia as it seeks to improve efficiency and create opportunities for private-sector participation.

World.title: Malawi: From Seaweed to Sanitary Pads - Malawian Scientist Pushes to Build Solutions in Africa
World.content:
Malawian scientist and entrepreneur Kennedy Mulungu was selected as one of just 10 young innovators from more than 900 international applicants to attend the United Nations Science, Technology and Innovation Forum in New York, where he engaged directly with the World Intellectual Property Organization and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers on how African biotech can reach global markets.Â Â

"You can have a brilliant solution and still struggle to get it in front of the right people."

For many African innovators, getting access to the funding, intellectual property systems, mentorship and manufacturing networks needed to turn research into products remains a challenge.

Malawian scientist and entrepreneur Kennedy Mulungu is an exception.

Selected as one of just 10 young innovators from more than 900 international applicants to attend the United Nations Science, Technology and Innovation Forum in New York, the opportunity placed him in rooms where global science and innovation priorities are discussed, and gave him the chance to engage with organisations including the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) on how African biotechnology can reach global markets.



Mulungu leads Ubhwando Group Limited, driving sexual and reproductive health initiatives in rural Malawian communities. He is developing biodegradable sanitary pads and wound dressings made from alginate, a natural polymer extracted from seaweed.

His ambition is to eventually commercialise the products locally.

"When I found out that I had been selected as one of 10 young innovators from more than 900 applicants, it was both humbling and deeply emotional. My first thought was Malawi - how far the journey had come, from developing ideas in environments where resources can be limited to having those ideas recognised on an international platform," he said.

"For me, the recognition was bigger than an individual achievement. It was evidence that innovations developed by young Malawians can stand alongside solutions from anywhere in the world when they are given the opportunity to be seen."

He believes that his application stood out because he was not presenting innovation as technology for technology's sake.

His work starts with problems he sees around him in Malawi: women and girls who need affordable, dignified menstrual-health products, farmers facing water scarcity and climate pressure, and researchers whose excellent science too often stops at the publication. Through BioAlgix, he explores how biomaterial science can address some of these challenges. Africa Innovation Brain grew from his desire to help bridge the gap between African research and commercialisation.

Being selected, he said, reminded him that Malawi does not have to be only a recipient of technologies developed elsewhere. "We can build solutions here, validate them here and ultimately take Malawian innovation to the world," said Mulungu.

From local problems to global platforms

Mulungu's journey into biotechnology began with problems he encountered in Malawi.

Growing up in Malawi, he saw how health, poverty, agriculture, and access to basic products are interconnected. A solution might already exist somewhere in the world, he said, but that did not necessarily mean it was affordable, accessible, or designed around the realities of communities in Malawi.

His training in Medical Laboratory Sciences gave him a scientific foundation in health and disease, while his work at the Malawi-Liverpool-Wellcome Research Programme exposed him to biomedical research and the importance of evidence.

But it also raised a question that would shape his career: what happens after the evidence has been generated?

That question became increasingly important as he explored women's sexual and reproductive health, particularly menstrual products.

For millions of girls across Africa, menstruation can still be a barrier to education. UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report estimated that one in 10 African girls miss school during menstruation, with inadequate sanitation facilities among the factors contributing to these absences.

A sanitary pad may look like a simple everyday product, but access, affordability, waste and the materials used to manufacture it raise much bigger questions about dignity, health and environmental sustainability. His interest eventually led him towards biomaterial science and the possibility of using materials such as alginate to develop more sustainable products.

Through the LEA-WH Innovation & Entrepreneurship Fellowship, Mulungu is developing biodegradable sanitary-pad materials that could reduce dependence on conventional plastic and synthetic components.

He said Malawi remains at the centre of that motivation.

"I want a girl growing up in a rural Malawian community to benefit from science not as something distant happening in laboratories overseas, but as something that improves her everyday life," he said.

Turning seaweed into a health product

The Kelp Alginate project grew from a deceptively simple question: what if materials used to solve some of these problems could come from Africa's own natural resources rather than being imported at a cost that many communities cannot sustain?

Kelp alginate comes from brown seaweed; it's a natural polymer known for being biodegradable, biocompatible, and highly absorbent, which makes it well-suited for both sanitary pads and wound dressings.

The project is intended to address two challenges through one locally sourced material: improving access to affordable menstrual-health products while also exploring more accessible wound-care options for under-resourced clinics and households.

Alginate-based materials let us tackle both with one locally sourced input.

"If we can commercialise this locally, it changes the everyday calculus for a girl deciding whether to go to school during her period, or for a mother treating a wound at home without reliable access to a clinic," he said. "These are not small things. Dignity and health access, delivered consistently and affordably, can change school attendance, health outcomes, and how communities see what's possible when products are made for them, by people who understand their reality."

The project is still at the development stage.

He said that the project is currently in the stage of refining the formulation and preparing for the testing and validation needed before the products can move toward local manufacturing at scale. "This is the phase where support like the LEA-WH Fellowship Innovation Track becomes critical, because it connects me with the technical and regulatory expertise to move from prototype to a product that can actually reach the market safely and sustainably," he said. "There's still a distance to cover, but the path is clearer than it's ever been."

Turning scientific ideas into products

The move from scientist to entrepreneur has been "one of the hardest and most rewarding transitions of my life," said Mulungu.

Science trained him to ask questions, test hypotheses, and refuse to make claims without evidence. Entrepreneurship taught him that evidence alone is not enough. A solution must also be manufacturable, affordable, regulated, understood by its users, and supported by a sustainable model.

"The hardest part has been learning to carry both mindsets at the same time: the patience and rigour of a scientist and the urgency of an entrepreneur who knows that real people are waiting for solutions," he said.

This challenge is particularly important in Malawi.

"We have talented researchers and young innovators, but there is still a significant gap between producing knowledge and turning that knowledge into locally manufactured products, companies and jobs. I increasingly realised that I did not want my scientific journey to end with a publication or presentation. I wanted to understand how research becomes something a farmer, patient, woman or young person in Malawi can actually use," said Mulungu.

The African STARS Fellowship at Stellenbosch University became a bridge, exposing him to venture building, bioprocessing, product development and commercialisation.

"My LEA-WH Fellowship has pushed that journey further in women's health innovation," he said. "Through BioAlgix and Africa Innovation Brain, I am now trying to connect those two identities - the scientist who demands evidence and the entrepreneur who asks, 'How do we get this solution into people's hands?'"

"Entrepreneurship has not taken me away from science," he said. "It has made me think much more deeply about what science is for."

The barriers African innovators face

The continent has no shortage of ideas, but innovators can struggle to access intellectual-property systems, early-stage investment, manufacturing capacity and mentorship networks capable of connecting science with business. His engagement with organisations such as the World Intellectual Property Organization and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers reinforced the gaps.

"It's not that African researchers lack good ideas; we have plenty. The barriers are structural. They include limited access to intellectual property systems, difficulty securing early-stage investment, weak local manufacturing capacity and a shortage of mentorship networks that understand both the science and the business of commercialisation," said Mulungu.

"You can have a brilliant solution and still struggle to get it in front of the right people," he said.

Mulungu said developing solutions in Africa can also make them more responsive to the communities they are intended to serve. "We understand our own problems best," he said.

Close 

"Relying on imported solutions often means higher costs, longer delays, and products that weren't designed with our realities in mind. When we develop and manufacture locally, we build economic value, create jobs, and keep the knowledge and capacity here on the continent instead of exporting the problem and importing the fix. It's also about ownership. African innovation competing globally, on our own terms, means we're not just consumers of solutions; we're creators of them."

Bringing the knowledge home

His journey has taken him from Malawi to innovation and scientific platforms across Africa and beyond, including South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, France and the United States. He has presented ideas in New York, learned about biotechnology and entrepreneurship in South Africa, engaged with innovation ecosystems in Kenya and Ghana, and met people and institutions that he could once only read about.

Yet every journey brings the same question: what am I bringing back to Malawi? An award in New York, a fellowship in South Africa, or recognition in France only becomes meaningful to me if the knowledge, relationships, and opportunities created through it eventually improve somebody's life at home.

His ambition is not simply to develop a better sanitary pad.

For an ordinary woman or girl in Malawi, he wants the result to be practical: a girl who can attend school during her period without choosing between dignity and affordability, menstrual products that are affordable, environmentally responsible and eventually made closer to the communities that need them, and young Malawians, especially girls, who see biotechnology and innovation as fields where they belong - not industries reserved for people somewhere else.

He said his bigger dream is to help demonstrate that Malawi can move from primarily consuming imported technologies to researching, developing, manufacturing and exporting its own solutions. "So when my work is recognised internationally, I am proud, but I also feel a greater responsibility," he said. He wants the world to recognise Malawi not only for the challenges we face, but for the scientists, entrepreneurs, women, young people and innovators capable of solving them.

"If, years from now, a woman in a rural Malawian community uses an affordable product developed from our science without ever needing to know my name, that would mean more to me than any international award," said Mulungu.

World.title: Africa: Cholera Deaths Soared in 2025, Africa Having 90% of cases - UN
World.content:
A campaign in the Darfur region of Sudan by WHO, United Nations Childrenâs Fund (UNICEF) and Sudanâs Ministry of Health to deliver the oral cholera vaccines to targeted localities and protect over 1.8 million people

Geneva — Cholera deaths increased globally by 30 percent in 2025, despite fewer cases being reported to the World Health Organization, with five countries in Africa accounting for around 90 percent of all cases, the WHO said on Tuesday.

In 2025, 47 countries reported 451,499 cholera cases and 7,870 deaths to the Geneva-based WHO, the health agency of the United Nations, which also released data on meningitis and the plague.

This is the highest number of annual cholera deaths reported to WHO since 1999.

"No one should be dying from cholera today when we have the tools to prevent and treat this disease," said Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu, executive director of WHO's Health Emergencies Programme.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

WHO said the figures reflect surveillance data reported and not the actual global burden of cholera, which is estimated to be substantially higher as many cases go unreported.

Seven countries – Angola, Bangladesh, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Nigeria, South Sudan, Sudan and Yemen – accounted for around 90 percent of all reported cholera cases and deaths globally.

Cholera deaths soared in Africa

The WHO African region reported the largest burden, with a 34 percent increase in cases and a 58 percent increase in deaths compared with 2024.

Dr Ihekweazu said that the concentration of cases and deaths in a small number of countries shows where targeted investments in safe water, sanitation and hygiene could have the greatest impact.

"Combined with stronger disease surveillance, community engagement, vaccination and access to quality care, these investments can help turn this trend around," said Ihekweazu.

Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae bacteria. The disease spreads through food and water contaminated with faeces, especially in areas without safe water and sanitation.

The WHO said that while cholera is preventable and treatable, it can be fatal if severe dehydration is not rapidly treated.

More than one in five reported cholera deaths occurred outside health facilities, highlighting that too many patients are still not reaching care in time.

Meningitis from Senegal to Ethiopia

Regarding bacterial meningitis, the WHO said that the disease continues to place a substantial burden on countries in the African meningitis belt, an area extending from Senegal to Ethiopia where epidemics occur regularly.

In 2025, 24 of the 26 countries in the region reported 21,526 suspected cases and 971 deaths to WHO, corresponding to a fatality rate of 4.5 percent.

Close 

Among countries reporting data for both years, cases declined by 5.9 percent compared with the previous year.

Meningitis involves inflammation of the tissues surrounding the brain and spinal cord, and bacterial meningitis is the most serious type.

For human plague, the WHO said that between 2019 and 2025, 10 countries reported suspected human plague cases, six of which reported confirmed cases.

Overall, 3,847 suspected cases and 423 deaths were reported to WHO, corresponding to a case fatality rate of 11 percent.

Most cases were reported from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar, where plague remains endemic in some areas.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 30, 2026
World.content:
press review

Ramaphosa Unveils 90-Day Plan to Tackle South Africa's Gender-Based Violence

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has announced a national emergency response and a clean-up of high-risk areas following the discovery of the bodies of 12 women east of Johannesburg over two months. Four people have been arrested, but Ramaphosa said police have found no evidence that a single perpetrator committed the killings. He acknowledged that the government had not done enough to protect women and girls and ordered municipalities to conduct women's safety audits to identify dangers such as broken streetlights, abandoned buildings, unsafe transport routes and poorly secured public spaces. He also announced measures to address alcohol-related violence. He called for deeper changes in attitudes towards women, urging men and boys to take greater responsibility for ending gender-based violence.

Fighting Escalates in Ethiopia's Tigray Region

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia is putting civilians at increasing risk, with reports of deaths, injuries and damage to homes and public infrastructure in Tigray. Communication services remain disrupted, making it difficult to independently verify reports from the conflict zone. Residents said that artillery strikes had killed family members and left wounded people without access to medical care, while local sources reported that 11 people were killed and 15 wounded in an attack on a market in Alamata. The claims could not be independently verified and Ethiopian federal authorities had not responded to requests for comment. The latest escalation began in September after Tigrayan forces and allied armed groups, including Amhara Fano, allied against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. The renewed conflict has raised concerns about the collapse of the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement and the spread of fighting and humanitarian disruption across northern Ethiopia.

Burkina Faso Opens First Gold Refinery

Burkina Faso has opened its first gold refinery as the military-led government seeks greater control over the country's mineral wealth and to reduce its reliance on exporting raw materials. The Raffinor-BF facility in Ouagadougou, which cost more than 11 billion CFA francs, can initially refine 164 tonnes of gold a year, with plans to eventually increase capacity to 515 tonnes. The government said that the refinery will help regulate the informal mining sector, curb smuggling and keep more value from gold production within the country. The project is part of Captain Ibrahim Traoré's broader push for greater state involvement in mining and domestic processing. The government has also linked illegal gold trading to the financing of Islamist armed groups.

Morocco Names First Woman Prime Minister

Fatima Zahra El Mansouri has been appointed as Morocco's first woman prime minister after her Authenticity and Modernity Party won the most seats in the parliamentary elections. Her appointment by King Mohammed VI makes her the second woman to lead a government in the Arab world, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden. El Mansouri, 50, is a lawyer and experienced politician who has served as mayor of Marrakesh and held a cabinet position overseeing housing and urban planning. Her party won 97 of the 395 parliamentary seats and must form a coalition to secure a majority. The Islamist Justice and Development Party, which won 54 seats, has said it will remain in opposition.

Close 

Sahel States Launch TV Channel to Counter Western Coverage

Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have launched Tafouk TV, a new regional television channel intended to promote the military-led Sahel states' own narrative and challenge Western media coverage. Broadcasting from Bamako through Canal+, the channel began official programming on 16 September and plans news, fact-checking and geopolitical programmes in French, English and regional languages. The launch is part of the Alliance of Sahel States' broader effort to build shared political, security and media institutions as the three countries distance themselves from France and strengthen ties with Russia. Tafouk TV has received Russian backing and signed a cooperation agreement with Russia's state-funded RT, while the alliance is also planning a joint news agency. Critics, however, have warned that the new media network should not become a tool for government propaganda and have called for greater media pluralism.

World.title: Kenya: Ruto Accuses Lamu Refinery Court Challengers of Extortion, Urges Kenyans to Invest
World.content:
The Dangote Refinery is located in one of the Free Trade Zones in Nigeria.

Nairobi — President William Ruto has accused individuals challenging the planned Sh2.2 trillion East Africa Oil Refinery in Lamu through court cases of seeking to extort investors, as he urged Kenyans to participate in the project.

Ruto said the refinery should proceed despite legal challenges surrounding the land earmarked for the project, maintaining that the investment would create jobs and stimulate industrial development.

The President made the remarks following the groundbreaking of the refinery on Wednesday. The project is designed to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day and is expected to serve markets in Kenya and the wider East African region.

Ruto has said the refinery will be structured as an open investment in which Kenyans can acquire shares through the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE).



He previously said the government would facilitate the participation of ordinary Kenyans in the investment rather than leave ownership to a small group of investors.

"The refinery investment is open and transparent," Ruto said, according to reports of his remarks.

He said Kenyans should view investors as partners in the country's development and participate in opportunities arising from the project.

The President's call comes as the government seeks to mobilise local and international capital for the refinery, which has been presented as a major investment in Kenya's petroleum and industrial sectors.

Ruto's remarks come against the backdrop of a legal dispute involving residents challenging aspects of the refinery project.

Residents have raised concerns relating to land ownership, compensation and other issues connected to the proposed development. A Kenyan court has issued orders affecting activities at the project site, although Dangote Group has said the legal proceedings will not stop the planned groundbreaking.

Ruto has criticised the legal challenges, alleging that some individuals supporting the project publicly were simultaneously backing court cases seeking to frustrate the investment.

The President described such actions as extortion and said they were unacceptable.

The characterisation is Ruto's, while the residents involved in the legal proceedings have raised claims concerning their land rights and compensation.

The government and Dangote Group have projected that the refinery and associated developments will generate tens of thousands of jobs.

Ruto has said the project could create about 60,000 jobs, while Dangote has also announced plans to establish a training school in Lamu to equip Kenyan engineers with skills relevant to the refinery and related industries.

Close 

The refinery is also expected to support the development of downstream industries, including petrochemicals, chemicals, fertiliser production and packaging.

Ruto has previously pointed to Dangote's refinery in Lagos, Nigeria, as an example of the industrial opportunities that could emerge from large-scale refining investment.

The proposed Lamu refinery is planned as a major regional petroleum facility, with a projected capacity of 700,000 barrels per day.

The project is intended to reduce East Africa's dependence on imported refined petroleum products and strengthen regional fuel security. Construction is expected to take several years, with the facility targeting completion around 2030, according to Reuters.

The project has also attracted interest from regional governments, with a proposed collective 30% ownership stake for regional governments reported as part of the investment structure.

As the refinery moves into construction, the government faces the task of balancing its push for the investment with ongoing legal and community concerns surrounding the project site.

World.title: Malawi: As Ration Cuts Bite, Malawi's Refugees Lose Vital Lifelines
World.content:
Dzaleka, Malawi — An $8 payment barely covers a week's needs. From inside Dzaleka, a refugee describes life as food aid, jobs and other lifelines disappear.

The 60,000 people in Malawi's Dzaleka camp are the frontline casualties of the World Food Programme's (WFP) funding crisis. At the beginning of September, they received approximately $8 per person to last them the entire month - a cash payment that barely covers a week's needs.

Around $28 is actually needed to provide each refugee with a food basket that meets the daily minimum of 2,100 calories. For example, the price of maize, a key staple, has doubled. Yet WFP has rarely met that calorie target, with cash payments fluctuating month to month as the agency struggles with a long-standing cash crunch.



WFP recently offered refugees an alternative: It would target the most vulnerable - people with disabilities, orphans, and older refugees - but would cut everyone else. In a camp meeting also involving the UN's refugee agency, UNHCR, and the Malawian authorities, that option was firmly rejected by community leaders.

Their argument was that vulnerability in Dzaleka could not be reduced to a few categories. There are teenage mothers, widows, single mothers, unemployed young people, and households in which one person's small income supports many others.

Community and zone leaders from all the communities - Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, and countries in the Horn of Africa - spoke in one voice: prioritising only certain groups would be unfair as everyone is struggling.

"There are a lot of people who are vulnerable besides the ones they suggested," said one refugee, who asked not to be named. "All these groups depend entirely on these rations. If they cut them, they will be left out and very vulnerable."

Deciding who is "vulnerable enough" would also create divisions inside the camp, which is located 45 kilometres from the capital, Lilongwe. "It is better to give everyone the little that WFP has," the refugee added. For a refugee population already living with so little, even a small payment can make a difference.

"Remember we exist", refugees in Malawi say as aid is slashed

Drastic cuts to the budget of the UN's refugee agency mean an uncertain future for 56,000 refugees.

What to do with $8

This month, the Dzaleka community must budget extremely frugally over how they will use their $8. Some will buy basic necessities. Others will try and repay debts accumulated over the months of ration cuts.

This is how life works for many in our three-decade old camp. A food payment does not necessarily remain food. It becomes soap, school materials, cooking supplies, clothes, credit repayments. Sometimes it becomes a way to help another family member who has received nothing.

That is why uncertainty surrounding WFP assistance is so frightening. The September distribution has brought relief, but we know that relief can also be temporary. WFP has repeatedly warned that funding constraints could affect future assistance. People are therefore eating today while wondering whether they will eat next month.

The food crisis is only part of the problem. For young people, perhaps the deeper crisis is the disappearance of opportunity. Many have spent years in Dzaleka studying and developing skills, hoping that education will eventually lead to employment or a pathway out of the camp. But opportunities remain limited.

Budget cuts have indefinitely paused the Economic Mobility Pathways Pilot (EMPP), a Canadian immigration initiative - co-supported by organisations like the World University Service of Canada - that connects skilled refugees with economic immigration pathways.

For some refugees, programmes such as the EMPP represented something different from humanitarian assistance -- the possibility of building an alternative future through work.

When such opportunities disappear, the message young people receive is difficult to ignore. Working hard, acquiring skills, and becoming self-reliant may in the end account for very little.

Then came another source of uncertainty. In late August, reports circulated that a new refugee settlement was being constructed at Kailizi in the far northern district of Chitipa. The possibility of being transferred from Dzaleka immediately raised questions. Who will go? When will they go? Will families be moved together? What will happen to the houses and businesses people have built in Dzaleka?

Several sources in the camp said they understood that new arrivals would be the first to go to Kailizi, and could be the first refugees considered for relocation abroad. But beyond that, there is little certainty.

The reason for building a new settlement is understandable. Dzaleka is severely overcrowded. A camp designed for approximately 10,000 people is home to triple that number. Kailizi, on the other hand, covers 445 hectares of land - more than twice the size of Dzaleka.

But for refugees, a new settlement is not simply a new location on a map. It means starting again. Families have spent decades building their lives here. Their children were born here. Their businesses are here. Their neighbours are here. Moving them without clear information could create another layer of uncertainty for people who have already lived with uncertainty for most of their lives.

Hope on the horizon

There is finally, however, one potential bright spot. The government recently indicated it may review its Refugee Act and its strict encampment policy that denies refugees the right to work outside Dzaleka. Civil society advocates of a new proposed bill want it to provide opportunities for refugee integration, as well as the possibility of acquiring citizenship for those who meet the necessary legal requirements.

That will mark a dramatic reversal from 2023, when the government clamped down on refugees working and owning businesses in Lilongwe, with a surge of arrests and forced returns to Dzaleka.

At the time, UNHCR noted that Dzaleka already faced inadequate health services, and water, shelter, and sanitation facilities for the existing population.

"Relocating self-sufficient and productive refugees and asylum-seekers to Dzaleka will only exacerbate these problems as their prospects of rebuilding their lives will dwindle," it warned. "The relocation will also negatively affect refugee children enrolled in schools across the country should they have to join overcrowded classes in the camp."

Close 

As a refugee, I can say many of us are excited about the proposed amendment to the Refugee Act. With WFP and UNHCR struggling to support us, abandoning encampment will allow capable refugees to become self-sufficient.

We have contributed to Malawi's economy for decades. We pay taxes, we create jobs, and we employ many in the host community. If the amended act allows us to work and operate freely across the country, it will be a dream come true for many of us, and it will ease the pressure on already strained resources.

Without the new bill, life will just get so much harder.

What is currently happening in Dzaleka is bigger than a reduction in food assistance. It is the slow disappearance of the systems that refugees have depended on to make our existence bearable.

The feeling is that the safety net underneath Dzaleka is disappearing. We are facing WFP's ration cuts, UNHCR's reduced presence due to its own funding crisis, unemployment, and rising petty crime. Each development might appear manageable on its own, but together this is a cascade of anxiety-inducing change.

For refugees, this is not an abstract problem. It is the mother wondering how she will feed her children, the young man looking for work and finding none, or the widow wondering whether she will qualify for the next food distribution.

Edited by Obi Anyadike.

Ndizeye Innocent, Burundian refugee living in Malawi, with a degree in Business Management from Southern New Hampshire University

World.title: Kenya: Ruto, Dangote Break Ground On Lamu Oil Refinery
World.content:
The ceremony in Lamu has brought together several African leaders and senior government officials, including Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Beninâs President Romuald Wadagni

Nairobi — President William Ruto and Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote have broken ground for the Sh2.2 trillion East Africa Oil Refinery in Lamu, marking the formal start of construction of the massive petroleum project.

The ceremony in Lamu has brought together several African leaders and senior government officials, including Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Benin's President Romuald Wadagni.

Other regional leaders and senior officials are also attending the groundbreaking, which is expected to be one of the largest industrial investment events held in Kenya.

The refinery, being developed by Dangote Industries, is designed to process up to 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day, making it one of Africa's largest planned refining facilities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The project is expected to serve Kenya and the wider East African market, with refined petroleum products targeted for countries including Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, South Sudan, Rwanda, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The groundbreaking comes after the first vessel carrying construction equipment for the project arrived at Lamu Port on September 26. The vessel, MV Da Yang Bai He, delivered about 2,930 metric tonnes of project cargo.

Dangote has said the refinery will be constructed over about three years, while Reuters reported that the project is targeting completion by 2030. The facility is expected to support petrochemical and other industrial activities and create tens of thousands of jobs.

The project, however, faces a legal challenge over land ownership and compensation. A Kenyan court has ordered preservation of parts of the site pending proceedings in a case brought by local residents, although Dangote Group has maintained that the groundbreaking ceremony would proceed.

The refinery is being positioned as a major regional energy investment at a time when East African countries remain heavily dependent on imported refined petroleum products.

The project will therefore be closely watched for its implications for regional fuel supply, petroleum processing, industrialisation and the development of Lamu as an energy and logistics hub.

World.title: Kenya: No, Kenya's President Was Not Issued an ICC 'Red Alert' As Claimed Online
World.content:
IN SHORT: Following calls by Kenya's opposition for the International Criminal Court to initiate an investigation against President William Ruto over political violence, a viral video claims he received a "red alert" from the court. But there is no evidence of any formal action against Ruto.

Posts shared on Facebook and TikTok, as well as a longer video on YouTube are titled: "Ruto Kwisha. Ruto receives ICC red alert hours after Kenya lawyers Lead by Martha Karua Letter ICC."

"Ruto Kwisha" translates to "Ruto finished."

The video features a Citizen TV report on Kenya's "united opposition" coalition calling for the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate president William Ruto over political violence. It is followed by commentary from the video's creator.



The video began circulating around 20 August 2026. Collectively, the posts we sampled have received more than 286,607 views and 9,400 likes.

Background

The ICC previously investigated alleged crimes arising from Kenya's 2007 to 2008 post-election violence. It opened an investigation in 2010 and brought cases against six Kenyans, including Ruto.

The case against Ruto and his co-accused, broadcaster Joshua Arap Sang, was terminated in April 2016, "without prejudice to re-prosecution in future". On 27 November 2023, the ICC prosecutor's office announced that it had concluded the investigation phase into the situation in Kenya.

The ICC has again featured in political debate in Kenya. A rights group has asked the court to put the country on watch ahead of the 2027 general elections, while opposition leaders have on several occasions called for the court to investigate Ruto.

The latest call came on 19 August 2026, when Martha Karua, flanked by other opposition leaders, urged the ICC prosecutor to monitor developments in Kenya and assess whether there was information warranting action under the Rome Statute. This followed violence reported during a Linda Mwananchi rally in Homa Bay on 16 August.

The Rome Statute is the international treaty that established the ICC and sets out its powers, procedures and jurisdiction, while Linda Mwananchi is an opposition formation in Kenya.

The video in question includes footage from the 19 August opposition press conference and claims Ruto received an ICC "red alert" shortly afterwards.

But did the ICC issue such an alert? We checked.

ICC did not issue 'red alert'

The video uses a genuine Citizen TV report, then adds commentary from its creator. At one point, the creator calls for Kenya to be put on the ICC's "red watchlist" and later for leaders to be put on "red alert". But he provides no evidence for the title's claim that the ICC issued Ruto with a "red alert".

Close 

Most importantly, a "red alert" is not a formal ICC legal measure. The court can issue arrest warrants and summonses to appear as part of its legal process. Ruto, for example, received a summons to appear in 2011 in connection with the ICC case that was terminated in 2016.

The phrase may be confused with Interpol's "red notice", a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender or similar legal action. Red notices are based on an arrest warrant or court order. There is no such order against Ruto.

The ICC's public records contain no announcement of a "red alert", new summons to appear, arrest warrant, or any other formal action against Ruto following the opposition's statements.

The claim is false.

World.title: Nigeria: Police Charge Five Men Over 'Tinubu Must Go' T-Shirts
World.content:
The five men were accused of criminal conspiracy, inciting disturbance, disturbing public peace and thuggery.

The Nigeria Police Force in Borno State has charged five men to court after arresting them for allegedly wearing T-shirts bearing the inscription, "Tinubu Must Go."

The five men are Baba Aji Gremami, Mustapha Abba Yemen, Abacha Mohammed Ali, Adam Umar Gubio and Abdulhamid Mohammed.

According to charges seen by PREMIUM TIMES, the men were accused of criminal conspiracy, inciting disturbance, disturbance of public peace and thuggery.



The charges alleged that the five men "conspired together by printing some T-shirts with some inscription written Tinubu Must Go on it, with the intent to cause breach of public peace within the West End Roundabout Community."

The alleged offences were said to be contrary to Sections 60, 78, 79 and 392 of the Borno State Penal Code Law.

Rights group Amnesty International, in a statement, condemned the arbitrary detention of the five men, arguing that wearing a T-shirt expressing political opposition does not constitute a crime.

"Hurriedly remanding them in prison and accusing them bizarrely of 'the intent to cause breach of public peace within West End Roundabout Community Maiduguri' simply for wearing a t-shirt with a message of political dissent is not a crime," the rights group said.

It called on the authorities to release the men and drop the charges against them.

"Authorities in Borno state have resorted to the familiar playbook of using the law to criminalize peaceful dissent and silence opposition," Amnesty International said.

The organisation also accused the Borno State Government and the police of increasingly targeting opposition parties and their supporters through arrests and detentions.

It urged the government of Governor Babagana Zulum to respect freedom of expression and association and uphold the rule of law.

"Political opposition is part of human rights," Amnesty International said, adding that the right to express political opinions should not be limited to supporters of one political party.

The Borno State Police Command has not issued an official statement on the alleged arrests and charges.

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the police spokesperson in Borno, Nahum Daso, for comment. Mr Daso did not answer calls to his phone and has not responded to a text message sent to him as of the time of this report.

World.title: Texas A&M posts blank end zone teaser on social media, internet trolls understand their assignment
World.content:
Posting on social media for a big corporation is a tightrope act these days.

You want to create an engaging post, but you don't want something low hanging that will cause internet trolls to come out of the woods and take pot shots at.

It's even crazier for a high-level college football team, because fans of every other team are just looking for a reason to roast you into oblivion.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

As a former social media manager, I don't envy the position these people are in.

FSU FOOTBALL X ACCOUNT GETS COMMUNITY NOTED FOR CLAIMING 'RECORD GPA' IN SOCIAL MEDIA POST

With all that said, the social media team for Texas A&M's football program posted what is perhaps the greatest opportunity for any internet troll with access to Photoshop that has existed in quite some time.

To the uninitiated, this may just look like a team hyping up their new end zones for Saturday, but to "students of the game," this is basically a blank canvas for trolling opportunities.

Don't believe me? Observe.

FALCONS' TUA TAGOVAILOA GETS ROASTED ON SOCIAL MEDIA AFTER ALLEGEDLY COMMENTING ON HIS OWN POST

You know, if the Aggies were 4-0 right now, this probably wouldn't be going as poorly in the comments section.

But the fact that A&M is 2-2 and reeling after back to back losses to Kentucky and LSU made this almost too easy to see coming.



You just don't get opportunities like this anymore as digital graffiti artists, mainly because social media managers have been around the block a few times before, so I have no idea how anyone on the Aggies' social media team let this one slip through the cracks.

They even left the generic blank Photoshop fill on the end zones, almost as if they wanted this to happen.

Was this a false flag operation by Texas A&M to generate engagement?

I doubt it.

Like I said, this was a top-ten preseason team with College Football Playoff aspirations that is now sitting at 2-2 and on the brink of missing the big dance entirely.

I'm sure their posts are being engaged with plenty, though most of that engagement is coming from angry Aggie fans demanding to know why Marcel Reed is still allowed to touch a football.

I think this was just a rookie mistake committed by whoever is in charge of the phones in College Station.

Let this be a lesson to anyone hiring a social media manager for a big-time sports team or Fortune 500 company.
