One immigrant challenging the policy says he fears being sent to a country where he would not receive treatment for his severe mental illness. ➡️ Mahmoud Khalil, who became a prominent face of Columbia University's pro-Palestinian movement, is also fighting the Trump administration's effort to deport him. He told Fresh Air that 104 days in immigration detention strengthened his resolve to challenge the case.

President Trump says that tech companies can largely self-regulate when it comes to artificial intelligence. After meeting with top AI executives Tuesday, he signed an executive order referring to the technology as "superintelligence" for government agencies and launched an AI-powered website, America.gov.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Trump said the Justice Department or FBI could step in if companies break the law — but NPR's Emily Feng notes there are no new AI laws behind the meeting. Executives from six major AI companies signed a one-page document pledging to monitor their models and prevent harmful uses such as hacking. Asked whether the agreement was enforceable, Trump called it "morally binding" and said the companies would be "policing each other."

Picture show

toggle caption Tommy Trenchard for NPR

In Lesotho, a small mountainous country surrounded by South Africa, young shepherds can spend months tending livestock in remote areas, often missing school. The Good Shepherd School offers flexible evening classes in reading, writing and counting. Check out these photos to see how these shepherds are balancing work and education.

Behind the story

by Meg Anderson , National Desk correspondent

toggle caption Cornell Watson for NPR

Since the 2020 police killing of George Floyd, programs that send unarmed responders to some 911 calls instead of police have quietly grown — from just six in 2020 to nearly 100 today.

I wanted to understand what it takes to do that work well, so I spent a few days with the community response program in Durham, N.C.

From the back of their minivan, I watched responders handle 911 calls about things like trespassing and panhandling. They doled out bottled water, snacks and fresh socks, and defused some tough situations: An agitated man refusing to leave a parking lot, a paranoid man asking to go to the hospital, a woman needing a safer place to live.

But they often had few long-term solutions to offer.

Researchers told me this tension is common. The goal after 2020 was to avoid more police killings, not solve problems like homelessness. Now, Durham and dozens of other cities are wrestling with this bigger question: Is success resolving the crisis? Or is it to offer a path to stability, so that eventually fewer 911 calls are made in the first place?

Sponsor Message

Read my full reporting here. And if you have a story or tip about policing and public safety in your city or elsewhere, you can reach me on the encrypted messaging app Signal at mma.05.

3 things to know before you go

Enlarge this image NPR NPR

NPR staff listened to nearly 1,500 podcasts and picked 20 finalists for this year's Student Podcast Challenge. Hear the finalists and see the honorable mentions. Cathy Tie wants to show that her startup's gene-editing technology could repair disease-causing mutations in embryos and help prevent inherited diseases. Editing genes in human embryos is illegal in the U.S. A saxophonist, a forensic anthropologist and a historian are among this year's 20 MacArthur fellows — each receiving an $800,000 "genius grant." Meet the winners.

This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

World.title: Travel plans? Here's what to know as measles exposures reach trains and games
World.content:
Travel plans? Here's what to know as measles exposures reach trains and games

toggle caption Malte Mueller/Getty Images

The U.S. is in the midst of the worst measles resurgence in decades. Recent outbreaks in several states and exposures in places like bars, sports stadiums and on public transit have some people questioning the safety of travel or how they should prepare for upcoming plans.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists over 3,600 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. as of Sept. 24 — and two deaths as of Sept. 28. Almost all of those cases have been among unvaccinated individuals.

The CDC notes the number of deaths is subject to change as more information becomes available and after it completes more reviews. It's important to note that the Pennsylvania Department of Health has counted four measles-associated deaths so far. The CDC has disputed whether measles actually caused those deaths.

Sponsor Message

In the last two weeks, Pennsylvania, Ohio and New York have had the most cases, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health U.S. measles tracker.

The true number of cases across the country is likely higher, according to Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and a professor of pediatrics at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

"I think if anything, we're underestimating how many people are actually being exposed, and how many people are being infected, and how many people are being hospitalized and dying," he said.

He said that's because many children, parents or adults may not seek medical care if they get infected.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Dr. Kalyani McCullough, who leads the Vaccine Preventable Disease Epidemiology & Control Section of the Immunizations Branch of the California Department of Public Health, said it's important for people to know that measles is not "just a fever and a rash."

"It can affect a lot of different parts of the body, and it can have long-lasting effects as well," she said. "Both with immune amnesia, which means that the measles virus can actually reduce immunity to other infections after being infected with measles."

Sponsor Message

"So I think it's just important for people to realize that getting measles can have some pretty serious consequences," McCullough said.

How do you protect against measles?

People who've had two doses of the MMR vaccine are considered protected against measles.

The disease is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. And you don't have to come in direct contact with someone who has measles to get infected; you just have to be within their airspace within two hours of them being there.

Offit said one person with measles can infect about 15 to 18 other people, if they're susceptible. Offit says "susceptible," in this case, means people who've either never had measles, or who are unvaccinated.

For people in that category, up to 9 out of every 10 exposed will get measles.

What does it mean if there have been measles exposures in my state?

Some states that aren't currently experiencing large measles outbreaks have notified residents of possible exposures.

While an outbreak is a group of cases in one area during a certain time period, an exposure is when a person comes into contact with someone who has measles, according to George Mason University College of Public Health epidemiologist Amira Roess.

The California Department of Public Health notified people of potential exposures after an infected and unvaccinated train and bus passenger traveled across the U.S. and through multiple California counties.

The City of St. Louis Department of Health also encouraged residents to monitor for symptoms after an individual who visited local bars and a sports stadium tested positive for measles.

Measles can be difficult for epidemiologists to track because symptoms — like a fever, cough and rash — usually begin seven to 14 days after a person is exposed or as late as 21 days later.

Once a person is confirmed to have measles, epidemiologists interview that person and try to figure out the places they visited and people they saw while they were contagious. In the case of measles, that's typically four days before the telltale rash appears, according to McCullough.

Sponsor Message

"So it's a really labor-intensive process," she said.

She said anyone exposed to measles is usually advised to seek medical advice and isolate themselves if they develop symptoms within three weeks of exposure. People who are unvaccinated may be asked to quarantine and may be monitored by public health officials to see if they get sick.

What should I do if I'm traveling soon?

All the experts who spoke to NPR said the first and most effective step to protect yourself against measles is to make sure you're fully vaccinated.

That means having had two doses of the MMR vaccine — commonly done in childhood. You can check with your healthcare provider if you aren't sure about your vaccine status. They may recommend a booster depending on your records and recent health.

Offit said this recommendation holds for travelers coming into the U.S. from other countries as well.

"I think anybody who is traveling from another country into the United States should make sure they're up to date on their vaccines, because it's dangerous to be in the United States now if you are not fully immune to measles," he said.

Offit noted many people who are immunocompromised cannot be vaccinated if they haven't been already. Those people may rely on herd immunity — protection from a disease when a certain percentage of people in a community are vaccinated. For measles, this threshold is 95%. Last school year, kindergarten vaccination coverage dipped to 92.4%, according to the CDC.

Children typically get their first dose of the MMR vaccine at around 12 months. But McCullough says if parents are planning to travel internationally with infants or babies 6-11 months old, the CDC's recommendation is to get an early dose of the vaccine.

But the experts we spoke to said that if you have your vaccines, you don't need to worry.

Sponsor Message

"If you've been relatively healthy and you are up to date on your vaccines, and you are up to date on your doctor's visits, then you will be fine," Roess said. "I'm not worried about those individuals."

Roess also said people can wear masks in busy areas if they are concerned.

World.title: GG marks National Day for Truth and Reconciliation with plea for 'understanding the truth'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada marks its sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (also known as Orange Shirt Day). CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault is hosting special live coverage to honour residential school survivors and pay tribute to the children who never made it home.

As Canadians mark the sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said it's important to face an unsettling past in order to build a better country.

This is Arbour's first time observing the day as Governor General. She was sworn in this summer, replacing Mary Simon, the first Indigenous person to serve in the role.

In a statement before the ceremonies kicked off on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Wednesday, Arbour recognized that facing the past "can be painful and unsettling," but "understanding the truth is essential to building a more just future."

Arbour also spoke later in the morning, just before the Survivors' Flag was raised in front of West Block.

She said that while "acknowledging the truth does not change the past, it is a reminder that memory carries responsibility — responsibility to recognize these injustices, to learn from them and to ensure that they are never repeated."

Before taking part in the re-raising of the Survivors' Flag, Arbour reminded Canadians that it is "both a symbol of warning and a symbol of hope."

She said the flag "represents what was lost, but also what endured and what continues to thrive ... the spirit, cultures, traditions and languages of communities that, despite immense hardship, have carried these legacies on from generation to generation across this country."

Arbour urged Canadians to use the sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation to "listen with open hearts and reflect on the experiences shared by the survivors and their families."

Children forced to leave families

Prime Minister Mark Carney will be in Edmonton to mark the occasion and is set to speak at a commemorative event.

In a statement released before his address, Carney said the residential school system "was built on assimilation policies designed to sever children from their languages, cultures, identities and ways of life."

Canada's residential schools operated from 1857 to 1996. Some 150,000 Indigenous children were forced to leave their families to attend the government or church-run institutions.

WATCH | Decades after death, residential school student buried on First Nation: Decades after death, residential school student buried on First Nation | Duration closed caption 2:04 Nearly 60 years after his death, residential school student Percy Onabigon’s remains have been brought from a burial site in Woodstock, Ont., and laid to rest in his home Long Lake #58 First Nation. His family fought for years to repatriate him and are calling for more support for others facing a similar burden.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's (TRC) exhaustive, years-long study of residential schools revealed the devastating impact they had on Indigenous people.

The institutions were designed to assimilate Indigenous children into the dominant Euro-Canadian culture, causing deep intergenerational trauma and harm, the TRC found. They were characterized by widespread abuse and neglect, and led to as many as 6,000 deaths, mostly from malnutrition or disease.

Eleven years after the publication of the TRC report, only 15 of its 94 calls to action have been put into force.

CBC News spoke to residential school survivor Eugene Arcand on Parliament Hill.

Arcand said the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation is sometimes when Indigenous Peoples "have to reveal the complacency" that has set in since the TRC report was published.

"In regards to adhering or even addressing some level of co-operation and understanding of the 94 calls to action, we have a lot of unfinished business here in the residential school history."

In his statement, Carney also said his government owes survivors "more than remembrance."

"We owe them action. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 calls to action remain a roadmap for that work."

World.title: FlyDubai pilot tried to down plane before being subdued, Israel's prime minister says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video address on Wednesday that the Israeli government believes that a FlyDubai pilot tried to crash a commercial plane en route to Tel Aviv after stabbing their co-pilot.

The flight from the United Arab Emirates diverted to Saudi Arabia after transmitting emergency signals earlier in the day. The airport in Tabuk reported that a FlyDubai flight made a distress call at 8:44 a.m. local time, before landing safely at 9:45 a.m.

"According to the preliminary information in our possession, the terrorist had one intention: to crash the aircraft with all its passengers aboard," Defence Minister Israel Katz said in a statement.

The airport in Saudi Arabia said both pilots had been hospitalized after sustaining injuries.

Flight to Israel diverted after 'violent incident' between pilots | Duration 2:46 An apparent fight between pilots on a FlyDubai plane travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel resulted in the plane making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, according to officials. Tabuk Airport says both pilots are in hospital after sustaining injuries. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video address that his government believes the pilot tried to crash the plane en route to Tel Aviv after stabbing the co-pilot.

Netanyahu said the pilot alleged to have committed the stabbing was being questioned by Saudi authorities, though it wasn't clear if that was taking place in hospital.

Netanyahu said he spoke with one of the Israeli passengers on the plane, who relayed that they responded by entering the cockpit, along with a crew member. The alleged attacker was subdued, Netanyahu said, with a separate crew member managing to stabilize the plane.

FlyDubai Flight FZ 1073, from Dubai to Tel Aviv, ​diverted over Jordanian airspace toward Saudi Arabia, transmitting a general emergency signal ​and then another emergency signal that indicated possible unlawful interference several minutes later, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.

The aircraft's data appeared to ⁠show that it had suddenly and rapidly descended by nearly ‌14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the first emergency signal, Flightradar24 said.

The emergency signals triggered a major security response in Israel, which has no official diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed.

About 160 passengers were on board the Boeing 737 plane. The passengers were eventually retrieved by another aircraft, landing in Israel on Wednesday evening.

The incident highlighted the potential risks on a route that has become popular among Israeli nationals since the U.A.E. and Israel normalized ties six years ago.

It also comes as Israel holds elections on Oct. 27, with security among the top issues in the wake of the deadly Hamas-led mass attack of Oct. 7, 2023.

Netanyahu ordered authorities to "ramp up" security on both Israeli and foreign carriers flying into the country.

"Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots' identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check," Doron Spielman, ​a Netanyahu spokesperson, told Reuters.

Israel has not experienced a hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world, including on Israel-bound flights. During the 1960s and 1970s, Israelis were targeted in a string of hijackings and airplane attacks by militants, including a 1972 incident in which Netanyahu, then with the Israeli Defence Forces, was struck in the arm by a bullet during a rescue operation.

All passengers safe

In a statement, FlyDubai said that two replacement aircraft were deployed to Tabuk to transport the passengers and crew, and cautioned against early "speculation" about the incident.

"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation. We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts," the statement read.

The U.A.E. had yet to comment on the incident.

Yasmin Abu Kasis said her daughter Miriam, who was among the passengers on the flight, had told her that she had heard screaming ⁠and that a man holding a knife had forced one of the pilots onto the floor, and that there was ⁠blood everywhere.

People sit in the cockpit of a FlyDubai 737 Max on display at Al-Maktoum International Airport during the Dubai Airshow in this Nov. 20, 2025, file photo. (Giuseppe Cacace/AFP/Getty Images)

Israeli media published a photo purportedly taken from inside the plane, which appeared to show a passenger's blood-soaked shirt. ⁠Reuters ⁠could not immediately verify the image.

FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates airlines. It operates daily return ⁠flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv and normally uses airspace over Saudi Arabia and Jordan.

The low-cost carrier's fleet relies entirely on variants of the 737, a twin-engine, single-aisle aircraft that is widely used by airlines around the world. It has nearly 100 of the planes, including 69 of the Max 8 variant.

Though rare, there have been alleged and confirmed incidents of pilot murder-suicide before. It was concluded that a Germanwings pilot deliberately crashed a plane in the French Alps in 2015, killing all 150 people on the aircraft.

The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board concluded that an EgyptAir pilot in 1999 downed a plane into the Atlantic Ocean after taking off from New York — a finding that the Egyptian government disputed.

World.title: Stelco's U.S. owner to face 'fullest extent of the law' over layoffs: PM Carney
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada's federal government will "use all powers that we have" against the U.S. owner of an Ontario steel plant that announced hundreds of layoffs on Monday .

Stelco, owned by Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs, directly linked its plan to cut up to 500 jobs in Hamilton with U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada.

The Trump administration imposed 50 per cent tariffs on foreign steel under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act last year. Canada has retaliated with duties on many U.S.-made steel products.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Carney singled out the company's CEO, Lourenco Goncalves, for "applauding" Trump's move to impose punishing tariffs on Canadian steel imports to the United States.

"Our thoughts are with the workers and the families who have been betrayed by the company," Carney said at a news conference in Vancouver.

"The company made representations, and has legal obligations for employment. We intend to use all powers that we have, and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law."

The Stelco Hamilton Works production facility is seen in an aerial view. Stelco Holdings Inc. said on Monday that it plans to idle part of its Hamilton plant. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Hamilton-based Stelco in a $3.4-billion Cdn cash-and-stock deal that closed in November 2024. In a news release announcing the deal, Stelco's then-CEO Alan Kestenbaum stated the transaction "keeps national interests at the forefront and recognizes the importance of the workforce."

Carney said he is "very disappointed" by the company's decision to lay off workers.

In a memo obtained by CBC News, Stelco vice-president of sales Frederic Fafard called the situation "an unfortunate but necessary action to help ensure the survival of Stelco in what has become a challenging and unsustainable market."

The prime minister said on Tuesday that there is "money on the table from the federal government" to help companies like Stelco blunt the impact of the ongoing trade war.

In an email to CBC News on Monday, a Cleveland-Cliffs spokesperson confirmed Industry Minister Mélanie Joly had been in touch with Goncalves about financial support.

Pat Persico, Cleveland-Cliffs' senior director of corporate communications, said while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company expects "a significant number of workers" will be absorbed by the company's Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont.

Cleveland-Cliffs did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday regarding Carney's mention of potential legal action against the company.

World.title: Why pro-Trump ads — paid for with public money — are airing on U.S. TV
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With crucial midterm elections just weeks away, the White House is using taxpayer funds to air campaign-style TV ads featuring U.S. President Donald Trump.

The ads have aired in top timeslots on national and local television, including during last weekend's NFL games, costing at least $1.4 million US so far, according to analysis by advertising tracking firm AdImpact.

The White House's decision to spend public money on the campaign is drawing widespread criticism, including from Republicans.

"I like the message, but it shouldn't be paid for by taxpayer dollars," Senate majority leader John Thune told reporters on Capitol Hill on Monday.

The ads are running as Trump's approval rating hits an all-time low and his Republican Party faces what could be a disastrous midterm result on Nov. 3, potentially ceding control of the U.S. Congress to the Democrats for the remainder of his presidency.

Although U.S. law forbids use of government funds for "publicity and propaganda," Trump's officials insist there's nothing illegal about the advertising campaign.

U.S. tax dollars paid for this TV ad, featuring Donald Trump:

"These public service announcements are unapologetically American ," the White House said in a statement. "The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads. President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action."

While it's true that Trump is not up for re-election in the midterms, he did urge the audience watching this month's Republican convention to "pretend that I'm on the ballot," an attempt to boost turnout for GOP candidates in tight House and Senate races.

'Love Me'

Richard Painter, who served as White House ethics lawyer during then-president George W. Bush's second term, says the ads could be an impeachable offence because Trump cannot use taxpayer money to campaign.

"All three ads, they're sheer propaganda," Painter told the Associated Press. "This is increasingly looking like what authoritarian governments do to promote their leaders."

The first ad features rapid-fire montages of photos of Trump, as a choir repeatedly sings the title lyrics of Love Me, a song by musician JMSN.

"If President Trump wants people to love him, he can pay for it himself," a group of Democratic lawmakers wrote to Trump's chief of staff in a letter calling for the ad to be pulled.

'Together we will defeat communism,' says Trump in ad, as choir sings 'Love Me':

"This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and utterly illegal misuse of Americans' hard-earned tax dollars," the Democrats wrote.

The 'Love Me' ad begins with grainy black-and-white video of Trump as his voice is heard saying "Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America."

The 30-second ad then shows slides declaring in all-caps "Largest Tax Cuts in History" and "Reigniting American Manufacturing."

UFC boss praises Trump in ad

It concludes with video of Trump with Dana White, CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship mixed-martial arts empire, as the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" appear at the bottom of the screen.

"He's the toughest, most resilient person that I've ever met, and nothing was going to stop him for fighting so hard for the country he loves," White said in the voice-over, audio from his introduction of Trump at the 2024 Republican National Convention.

Another of the government-funded ads is nearly identical to a Trump campaign ad from 2024.

'We will expel the warmongers from our government,' says Trump in government-funded ad:

" This is the final battle," Trump said in the ad. "With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state, we will expel the warmongers from our government."

Another ad uses clips and video from Trump's speech at Mount Rushmore on July 3, the night before the 250th anniversary of the U.S. Declaration of Independence.

"We are the freest people on earth," Trump said in the minute-long TV commercial. "This is only the beginning of the golden age of America."

The taxpayer money for the ads comes from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, an agency of the Department of Homeland Security, the Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday.

Scott Talan, a professor of communication at American University in Washington, D.C., describes the message of the ads as "love Trump, love his policies" but he's doubtful they will have much impact on the president's sagging polls.

"I can't imagine much movement," Talan told CBC News. "People pretty much have their opinions formed."

He noted that the ads ran heavily during pro and college football games. "I don't know how many people watching those games haven't made up their mind already," he said.

Past administrations have used taxpayer funds on public service advertising, such as a $10 million US campaign under Joe Biden urging people to get vaccinated against COVID-19 and national TV ads promoting government subsidies for health insurance during Barack Obama's time in the White House.

The top Democrat in the U.S. Senate, Chuck Schumer, said the Trump administration's ads are "anything but" public service announcements.

"They were pure propaganda," Schumer said Tuesday on the Senate floor. "Trump is getting you, American taxpayer, to use your dollars to pay for his political ads."

World.title: After 'doom and gloom' decade, Fort McMurray readies for a boom
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Alberta community synonymous with meteoric oil booms and crippling busts is now staring down another potential wave of economic fortune.

Already signs are pointing to a boost in growth in Fort McMurray with rising home prices, increased investment in the oilpatch, widespread hiring and longer lines at the Tim Hortons drive-thru.

Much of the growth is in anticipation of a new oil pipeline to the West Coast, as proposed by the Alberta government. On Thursday, the federal government is expected to declare the project is in the national interest.

As more families and businesses move in, roofer William Gilbert sees his business growing alongside Fort McMurray.

With nail guns and roofing hammers, one of Gilbert's crews finishes up attaching shingles on a black two-storey house on the western edge of the community. His 20 employees are working as much as they can to keep up with demand. Though business hasn't spiked overnight, Gilbert expects steady hiring over the next few years.

"I see us doubling, if not tripling," he said. "We're slowly getting a boom."

A series of federal and provincial announcements aimed at growing oil production over the last 12 months are fuelling the sense of optimism, including a new West Coast oil pipeline being developed by Alberta and Ottawa.

In addition, the federal government has wiped away certain environmental policies such as the oilpatch emissions cap , while speeding up the regulatory process to approve major projects and introducing new financial incentives for investors.

The Alberta government aims to double oilsands production to eight million barrels per day by 2035.

The Syncrude oilsands mining facility operates north of Fort McMurray. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

The last decade in the region has been lacklustre for many businesses, with little economic growth and a declining population. However, the period was useful in allowing the local government to catch up on building roads and other important infrastructure.

Now, people are moving back, pushing the population to an all-time high.

"It's been very doom and gloom here since 2015," said Kyle Vandecasteyen, a councillor with the Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo. "We're ready for growth."

Excitement building

Some construction crews have seen a threefold increase in work, said Dianna De Sousa, the president of the local chamber of commerce.

"It's organized chaos. They have to turn away work," she said.

After several years of a stagnant economy, she said there is excitement and anticipation, mixed with some trepidation.

"The challenge is going to be labour and workforce without a doubt," said De Sousa, since some tradespeople are already in short supply.

Fort McMurray is prepared for a possible oil boom after several years of infrastructure improvements, says Kyle Vandecasteyen, a councillor for the Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

An oil boom will require a plethora of workers from drivers and engineers to mechanics and pipefitters.

The local college is trying to gear up, but it faces a similar predicament in finding enough instructors.

"I'm hoping when this boom happens, we have the manpower," said Shane Ganong, a heavy-duty mechanic and instructor at Keyano College.

He worked in the oilsands during the last boom, including long shifts at all hours of the day.

"We don't need to put people through such extreme workloads that they put in the past," he said.

Housing demand is up about 30 per cent this summer compared to last year, said realtor Paige Cyr, "So we are eating up our housing supply quite quickly."

The real estate market hasn't been this strong in many years, and while prices are rising, Cyr said some houses are still selling $200,000 below when they were purchased 10 or 15 years ago.

"People are coming back to the region. People are ready to invest," she said.

The common sentiment in the community is a need for a slow and controlled pace of growth, since Fort McMurray was unprepared during past booms.

A gold rush-type atmosphere brought workers from across Canada, lured by the highest wages in the country. There were too few houses, daycares and schools. Businesses were poaching workers from each other. Grocery stores had never-ending lineups.

"All of a sudden the bust happens and so many people that are local here are underwater in their mortgages. And that's happened a few times," said Kris Yarish, the chief operating officer of Alcor Facilities Management, which has operated in Fort McMurray for over 50 years, providing construction, work camps and other services.

He remembers the 2006 boom in particular, when it took four times as long to drive to oilsands sites because of so much traffic on the highway.

As he stood in front of his company's booth during a recent oil trade show, the largest such event in nearly a decade with more than 200 businesses, he couldn't help but notice the positive atmosphere.

"Having a new pipeline makes a difference, 100 per cent," he said, providing confidence throughout the industry.

No guarantees

Still, he's cautious knowing how a potential oil boom could always be derailed.

Large oilsands companies have been reluctant to invest tens of billions of dollars and take on sizeable debts to build megaprojects, of which the last one was completed in 2018. Investors no longer prioritize a company's growth as they once did, instead focusing on regular returns of cash and share buybacks.

Past oil booms in Fort McMurray were driven by multiple oilsands companies all building at once, which meant competing for labour, equipment and supplies. These days, there are only a handful of major oilsands producers after several years of consolidation.

There are other factors too, said Yarish, such as the ongoing trade war with the United States and continued turmoil with global oil prices.

An aerial view of Fort McMurray's downtown. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

Major infrastructure work continues in Fort McMurray as heavy machinery moves dirt along the riverbank to better protect the downtown from flooding. The municipality has invested in sewer, water, road and other projects to better position the community for the next wave of growth.

Still, there's more to do, including a continued push by some locals for a new highway to better connect the community.

The $1.5-billion East Clearwater Highway has been discussed since the devastating 2016 wildfire, which highlighted how Fort McMurray only has one highway out of the community.

The proposed project would add a second route to the east, which would also improve access to some oilsands facilities in the region.

"If the oilsands is going to be growing and have a new pipeline, you want to build that highway, not only because it makes business sense for the industry, but for safety as well," said Marty Giles with NorthStar Ford, who has lived in the community for more than 30 years.

His dealership in Fort McMurray sells about 1,200 F-Series trucks each year and he sees all the signs of economic growth.

That's why he is hiring another 30 people to push his staffing level to about 300 workers.

"I haven't seen this much optimism actually in Fort McMurray for the last decade as I do today," he said.

World.title: Ontario trial into boy's death shows need to learn how to 'show up for an Indigenous child:' advocate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story details violence and child abuse.

For Halton Indigenous advocate Jody Harbour, a months-long murder trial in Milton, Ont., shone a light on "the continuing crisis of Indigenous child welfare in Ontario."

In July, two Burlington, Ont., women were sentenced to life in prison for the murder of an Indigenous boy they were trying to adopt, and for crimes against his younger brother, including assault.

Multiple observers have said the trial raised concerns about the child protection system and showcased systemic issues that need to be addressed immediately, including reducing the number of Indigenous children in care and working more closely with Indigenous groups and families to establish appropriate care.

At the July sentencing and other points during the trial, Indigenous community members came to Milton, Ont., to bear witness and support the boys' family. That included Harbour, co-founder of Oakville, Ont., Indigenous organization Grandmother's Voice.

Speaking to CBC Hamilton before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Harbour said that since the sentencing, she's spent hours scrolling through comments and messages written by people who say they've been harmed by the child welfare system.

For her, the case highlighted a need for people at children's aid societies to understand "Indigenous ways of knowing."

"Front-line responders, support workers, the people on the ground [need to] understand what it means to show up for an Indigenous child," she said.

The months-long trial in Milton, Ont., heard the older boy, L.L., died on Dec. 21, 2022, after he was found unresponsive and emaciated in the basement bedroom of the family home. Superior Court Justice Clayton Conlan convicted his prospective adoptive parents Brandy Cooney and Becky Hamber of his murder in May.

L.L. and his younger brother, J.L., entered the child protection system when the older boy was a toddler due to concerns over their home environment that weren't detailed during the trial. CBC is referring to the boys using initials due to a standard publication ban on their identities.

L.L. and J.L. were moved from Ottawa to live with Cooney and Hamber in Burlington in 2017, but remained wards of the Ottawa Children's Aid Society (CAS). The Halton CAS was in charge of supervising the family on a daily basis.

The trial heard Halton CAS received many reports from people concerned about how Hamber and Cooney were treating the boys, yet workers never did unannounced home visits, nor did they interview the boys without Cooney or Hamber present, as is required.

Both CAS agencies previously told CBC they completed reviews for the Cooney-Hamber case and made changes after L.L. died. They haven’t shared specifics about those changes.

WATCH | Advocates called for change during murder trial: Closing arguments start in case of Ontario boy allegedly killed by couple trying to adopt him | Duration closed caption 2:25 Closing arguments are underway in the case of two would-be adoptive parents facing first-degree murder and other charges. The case in Milton, Ont., has raised questions about why the boy and his brother remained in their care despite numerous red flags raised by professionals. The case has advocates calling for urgent changes to the child welfare system.

Halton CAS says it continues to 'engage' Indigenous communities

CBC Hamilton asked Halton CAS to confirm whether it has met or continues to meet with local Indigenous groups and community members about issues raised during that trial. CBC also asked the agency to comment on any specific steps it has taken to help its staff better support Indigenous families and children in their day-to-day work.

In an email, an agency spokesperson who did not provide their name said Halton CAS has "a long-standing commitment and practice of working in partnership with communities, partner organizations and service providers to support the safety and well-being of children, youth, and families."

CAS said it "continues to engage with Indigenous community leaders, representatives, and service providers to strengthen partnerships and enhance supports for Indigenous children, youth, and families.

"We have also expanded Indigenous-focused training and practice supports for staff, with an emphasis on culturally-responsive, relationship-based, and trauma-informed approaches that inform our day-to-day work," the email said.

Former foster mother Heather Walsh, centre, surrounded by supporters, speaks to reporters outside the courthouse on May 5, following the judge's decision in the trial of Becky Hamber, 46, and Brandy Cooney. Walsh and other supporters wore orange shirts to call attention to Indigenous child welfare. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Harbour identifies as an urban Indigenous person with Cayuga and Ojibwa roots. She said the Haudenosaunee grandmothers and Anishinabek elders that guide the work of her organization are passionate about ensuring systems including children's aid societies do the the work they need to keep Indigenous kids safe.

Since L.L.'s death, Harbour said her organization has been in touch with Halton CAS and other local front-line organizations in order to "make change in [his] name."

She said one of those efforts is an ongoing program to provide front-line workers with "cultural trauma training," so they can better support urban Indigenous people.

Harbour said she believes that too often, frontline workers lack the tools they need to do so. She added it's also important for organizations to support any Indigenous workers brought in to educate, so they don't burnout from dealing with trauma.

Making change is “not about pointing fingers because those are human beings that work within CAS," Harbour said. "Reconciliation is saying we want to reconcile. We want to work together."

WATCH | Watch CBC's National Day for Truth and Reconciliation special: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation 2026 | CBC News Special described_video LIVE Canada marks its sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (also known as Orange Shirt Day). CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault is hosting special live coverage to honour residential school survivors and pay tribute to the children who never made it home.

In March, Ottawa-based First Nations child advocate Cindy Blackstock told CBC News the trial brought home the need to implement the first five calls to action from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada. According to CBC tracker Beyond 94 , none of those recommendations focused on the child-welfare system has been completed.

Sherry Saevil, a member of Mistawasis First Nation and a Halton resident shared similar thoughts.

Saevil was part of the Indigenous collective, Circle of Beads, that came together outside the Halton Children’s Aid Society in 2024 to raise awareness about the case.

In May, Saevil said she hopes there'll be an overhaul of the child welfare system and an inquest that examines the role of the Children's Aid Society agencies in this case.

The five TRC recommendations on child welfare are:

Reduce the number of Indigenous children in care. Publish annual reports on the number of Indigenous children in care. Implement Jordan's Principle. Enact child welfare legislation that establishes national standards for Indigenous child apprehension and custody cases. Develop culturally appropriate parenting programs for Indigenous families.

Blackstock said governments need to do more to make changes that are structural and significant or there will be more deaths.

“The biggest price is paid by children," she said, "who pay with their lives and their childhood."

If you’re affected by this report, you can look for mental health support through resources in your province or territory . If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911.

World.title: Alberta independence campaigners go for soft sell, even if they want a hard exit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With polls of Albertans showing the pro-independence side trailing by a nearly three-to-one margin , some activists have been trying a gentler pitch in the referendum campaign’s home stretch.

It’s not a direct vote on independence, they say. This is literally true; the Oct. 19 question gives people the options to stay in Canada or commence the process to hold a future binding referendum on whether Alberta should leave Canada.

Independence advocates go further than this and suggest that the question isn’t really about the goal of independence at all. Which is literally not true, for the above-stated reason.

But darned if Let Alberta Decide co-leader Keith Wilson doesn’t try to frame a future secession vote as just one in a series of volleys in negotiations between Premier Danielle Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

“Even if you want Alberta to stay in Canada, vote Option 2,” Wilson wrote over the weekend on social media.

“It’s not a vote for separation. It’s a vote that the status quo with Ottawa is unacceptable — and it gives Premier Smith real leverage instead of sending Carney a message that everything is fine.”

Keith Wilson leads the group Let Alberta Decide, the best-funded of the many organizations lobbying for the referendum's pro-independence option. (Jennifer Chevalier/CBC)

This has become the lawyer’s key refrain, as he tries to pry loose any votes from the dwindling ranks of undecided voters, or perhaps flip some Albertans in the “stay” camp.

“So even if you don't think Alberta should separate, whatever you think that means, even if you're holding on to a strong emotional and patriotic attachment to Canada, as all of us do, you should still vote for Option 2 because you need to give the premier leverage,” he told one recent forum , and has since promoted this clip repeatedly online.

What else is Wilson promoting heavily these days? A big gathering at the Alberta Legislature on Oct. 17, two days before the vote.

It’s billed as the “Alberta independence rally.” It’s not being advertised as a pro-leverage, or pro-future-vote rally. They’re marketing it as a rally for the objective that Wilson and others speaking there are trying to tell Albertans the referendum isn’t about.

Cory Morgan, a fellow independence activist, is another of the scheduled speakers. He’s also been urging his supporters to make “send Ottawa a message” their pitch to voters. In fact, that’s the message on billboards and lawn signs distributed by his campaign advertising group Pathway to Independence (note the name).

Morgan has urged his followers to campaign on that softer theme of message-sending to the “mushy middle," even if their true goal is separation.

“For the people like me and many of you, it doesn't matter. We're going for independence one way or another, anyways,” he said Saturday on his Youtube channel.

“But that's not what this vote's about. So, let's not campaign on that. We've got three weeks left and we've really got to move that needle with the undecided in the middle.”

The challenge Morgan and Wilson may face with that pitch is that there aren’t many Albertans in that undecided middle.

In the latest Janet Brown Opinion Research poll for CBC News, the “not sure” group was only four per cent of respondents, compared to 72 per cent of people who would vote to remain in Canada and 23 per cent who want a binding referendum.

Prime Minister Mark Carney greets pro-unity campaigners in Banff. The 'stay' side of Alberta's referendum leads by a nearly three-to-one margin, the latest Janet Brown Opinion Research poll says. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Other surveys have delivered similar results , with small pools of undecided voters. That sentiment has not only become “baked in” over time, said data scientist John Santos, but he also points out that when support levels for the pro-independence option stood a bit higher at 27 per cent in the spring, Janet Brown asked the straight stay-or-leave question.

It didn’t appear to make respondents any more likely to say “yes” to the independence option when September’s poll was asked with the current referendum wording; in fact, support dropped.

People vastly prefer the “stay” option, regardless of how it’s asked, Santos said.

“That suggests to me that there isn't a huge market for the soft sell,” he told CBC News.

Smith, the very politician that would wield any supposed leverage that separatists tout, has repeatedly said that she doesn’t want it.

Rather than bring the spectre of Alberta leaving to the federal negotiating table, the premier has said she’d prefer as her bargaining chip a slate of “yes” votes on her other referendum questions on immigration and constitutional reforms.

“I say there is a better way,” Smith said at an event Monday. “If you're mad or you want to give leverage, let's vote to continue working on this relationship. That's what those nine questions are about, is saying things have not been perfect, but we recognize the effort that Canada is making.”

LISTEN | Vote to Stay's leader makes his referendum case: Calgary Eyeopener 9:05 Referendum 2026: Monte Solberg Monte Solberg, founder of the "Vote to Stay," movement, joined us as we kick-off our series featuring referendum campaign leaders.

One of the premier's United Conservative caucus members has also characterized the unity question as something other than it explicitly is.

In a newsletter to constituents Monday, Red Deer-South MLA Jason Stephan disparaged the stay option as one that “affirms the status quo, a nation in decline, dragging Alberta down with it.”

But Stephan stopped short of actually endorsing independence, which no Alberta MLA has done. Rather, voting for a future referendum would “compel Ottawa to fix what is broken,” Smith’s former parliamentary secretary for constitutional affairs wrote to Red Deer-South residents.

He’d previously supported the separatists’ petition to hold a binding referendum, without Stephan himself saying he’d vote yes. But such careful rhetoric hasn’t stopped NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi from calling the government MLA a “full-throated separatist.”

Federalists, meanwhile, don’t believe their rivals’ idea of leverage would actually work. Political scientist Jared Wesley, part of the Lead Not Leave group, said separatists undercut their own message.

“A gambit this big only creates leverage if the other side believes you are prepared and able to follow through on the alternative,” he wrote in a recent Substack post . “The moment you tell the rest of Canada that support for Option 2 isn’t a true metric for independence support, you have killed the credibility of the threat.”

Morgan expresses awareness that many Albertans don’t share his passion for independence, and that polling proves it. But he doesn’t know how persuasive making Option 2 a mere “message” actually will be.

“I haven’t got a clue if we’re moving the needle at all,” he told CBC News in an interview.

An Alberta referendum sign suggests that voting for Option 2 means "we just wanna talk." (Tony Seskus/CBC)

As for Wilson, his campaign efforts are not solely reliant on proposals to convert a secession vote into leverage. He’s also commissioned reports that suggest Alberta independence would bring more prosperity and economic benefits. In another of his latest videos, he’s talked about the changed “constitutional relationship” he foresees down the road if Alberta votes his way Oct. 19.

Alberta becomes “sovereign” and its power resides in Edmonton. “That will become the country's capital, the country of Alberta,” he told listeners.

That’s the sort of message that should go over better at an independence rally, rather than any pro-leverage event Wilson may hold in the campaign’s dying days.

World.title: Canada-wide warrants issued for Edmonton father in alleged abduction of his children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Edmonton father who was reported missing with his young son and daughter five weeks ago is now wanted on charges related to the alleged abduction of his children.

In a news release on Wednesday, the Edmonton Police Service announced that Canada-wide warrants have been issued for 42-year-old Scot Macdermid on two counts of abduction in contravention of a custody order.

The charge is laid when it is alleged that a parent or guardian has taken or hidden a child younger than 14 in violation of a court custody or parenting order.

Macdermid has been charged with one count in connection with the alleged abduction of his son, George, 6, and a second count in the alleged abduction of his daughter, Lesley, 9. Court records show the charges were issued on Sept. 4.

Police continue to seek the public's assistance in locating Macdermid and his children.

Macdermid is wanted on Canada-wide warrants in relation to the alleged abduction of his children. Edmonton police say the background of this image was modified using AI so it could be shared with the public. (Edmonton Police Service)

The case of the missing children first came to light on Sept. 8, when Edmonton issued a news release seeking the public's assistance locating Macdermid and his two children.

Police said he was last seen at Manning Town Centre, a shopping plaza in northeast Edmonton, on Aug. 28.

Since then, investigators learned that Macdermid and his children were seen in Lloydminster, which straddles the Alberta-Saskatchewan border, on the same day, but police said the father and his children's path of travel beyond the border city was unknown.

In Wednesday's statement, police said investigators have assessed the available evidence and determined that this investigation has not met the criteria for an Amber Alert at this time.

"An Amber Alert is one tool available to police, but it is not the investigation itself," Staff Sgt. Robert Davis with the EPS Child Protection Section said in the statement. " Finding Lesley and George remains our top priority.

"We want the community to know that we are working to locate the children safely."

In order for police agencies in Canada to launch an Amber Alert in the disappearance of a child, investigators must have grounds to believe that a child has been abducted and the circumstances must suggest that a child is in immediate physical danger.

Missing children Lesley, 9, and George, 6, were last seen in Edmonton in late August. (Edmonton Police Service)

Court records show Macdermid has previously been involved in a custody dispute with the children's mother.

According to a 2024 Alberta Court of Appeal decision, Macdermid had alleged that the mother had wrongfully removed the children from the Dominican Republic and brought them to Canada.

A lower-court judge had ruled in the mother's favour and determined that the children's habitual residence was in Edmonton, rather than the Dominican Republic. Macdermid appealed that decision, but his appeal was dismissed on June 14, 2024.

The written decision said Macdermid was born and raised in Canada and is a businessman with "corporations in Alberta and business interests in the DR [Dominican Republic]."

According to court records, the children's mother was born and raised in the Dominican Republic but has been a permanent resident of Canada since 2018.

Macdermid and the children's mother married in 2016 in Edmonton and permanently separated on June 26, 2023. During their marriage, they spent time at homes in both Edmonton and Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic.

Macdermid is described as being five feet five inches tall and weighing about 160 pounds, with brown hair and blue eyes. George is described as being four feet two inches tall and weighing 45 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes, while Lesley is described as being four feet four inches tall and weighing about 45 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes.

Police have said said Macdermid has been unreachable, and there is concern for the welfare of his children.

Anyone who has seen the father and his children or who has information on their whereabouts is asked to contact Edmonton police or Crime Stoppers. Police have said the Macdermid and his children should not be approached.
