Sanae Takaichi plans to pledge a nimble response to unexpected economic and market developments at the extraordinary session’s opening, Reuters reported, citing the Nikkei — including setting annual debt issuance with interest-rate conditions in mind.

World.title: Minister of Agriculture identifies Climate-Smart Agriculture and regional partnerships as investment opportunities
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture identifies Climate-Smart Agriculture and regional partnerships as investment opportunities

By Zoila Palma: Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson has identified climate-smart infrastructure, agro-processing, regional transportation and business partnerships as key investment opportunities for strengthening Caribbean food systems.

Ferguson told BBN that private investment will be essential as countries work toward the longer-term objectives of Vision 25 by 2025+5.

One area identified by Ferguson is regional transportation. “A regional cost-effective ferry to facilitate trade particularly within the island territories,” he said.

He said improved maritime links could help reduce transportation costs and make it easier for agricultural products to reach markets across the Caribbean.

Ferguson also highlighted the need for investment in agricultural infrastructure.

“Climate-smart infrastructure to improve production and storage, reduce post-harvest losses and stabilize production and export quality,” Minister Ferguson added.

In addition, he pointed to agro-processing and regional business partnerships as opportunities for investors. “Value adding as in the previous cases shared by Belize,” he explained highlighting Belize’s investments in soybean, sugar and other processing industries.

World.title: Minister of Agriculture calls for ‘One country, one product’ model to strengthen Caribbean Food Security
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture calls for ‘One country, one product’ model to strengthen Caribbean Food Security

By Zoila Palma: Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson is proposing a “One Country, One Product” approach as the Caribbean looks toward 2030 and seeks to strengthen regional food security.

Ferguson told BBN that countries could specialize in commodities where they have strong production advantages while increasing trade among regional markets.

Ferguson said the approach could help countries coordinate production and reduce duplication. “Design a ONE COUNTRY/ONE PRODUCT model and put in place mechanisms to enable success and then launch it,” Minister Ferguson said.

He gave examples of how such specialization could work across the region. “For eg. Guyana will be the rice bread basket of the Caribbean, Belize and Jamaica will be the beef bread basket of the Caribbean, St. Vincent and Dominica will be the root crops bread baskets of the Caribbean, etc.,” he explained.

Ferguson said the model would need to be accompanied by investments in infrastructure and regional trade.

World.title: Belize calls for stronger Regional trade to move Caribbean Food across markets
World.content:
Belize calls for stronger Regional trade to move Caribbean Food across markets

By Zoila Palma: Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson is calling for stronger intra-regional trade and improved transportation systems to help Caribbean countries move more food products between markets.

Speaking to BBN, Ferguson said Belize has the capacity to produce more agricultural commodities but faces several barriers to accessing CARICOM markets.

Ferguson identified high production costs as one of the challenges affecting Belize’s competitiveness. “High cost of labour, electricity, agri-inputs, raw materials, fuel and local transport affect the regional competitiveness of some commodities,” he said.

He pointed specifically to rice, saying Belize can increase production but shipping costs make CARICOM exports difficult.

Maritime transportation is another concern for Belize. “Direct and reliable shipping routes between Belize and the Caribbean islands are not very available, are too costly, and the shipments take too long,” he added.

Ferguson also pointed to non-tariff barriers and sanitary and phytosanitary requirements as obstacles. “Even though Belize is self-sufficient in corn, soybeans, rice, beans, animal feeds, beef, pork, poultry and other food items, apart from the traditional exports of citrus concentrates and sugar, we have great difficulty exporting these other products to CARICOM,” he explained.

World.title: Belize seeks to revive Shrimp and Citrus industries
World.content:
Belize seeks to revive Shrimp and Citrus industries

By Zoila Palma: Belize is pursuing measures to revive two major agricultural industries that have faced significant production challenges in recent years.

Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson told BBN that the shrimp and citrus sectors are showing signs of recovery following major setbacks caused by disease.

Ferguson said the Government has adopted a strategic approach to rebuilding the industries. “A strategic approach has been implemented to revive both the shrimp and citrus industries which were decimated by Early Mortality Syndrome (EMS) and Huanglongbing (HLB), respectively,” Minister Ferguson said.

He added that the shrimp industry is expected to record a substantial increase in production during 2026. “Shrimp production is expected to triple in 2026,” he said.

He noted that the citrus industry is also beginning to recover, although the rebound has been more gradual.

Ferguson said strengthening traditional export industries remains an important part of Belize’s agricultural strategy.

“The citrus industry is slowly on the rebound,” he added.

World.title: Minister of Agriculture says cattle herd surges to 220,000 heads as beef export market expands
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture says cattle herd surges to 220,000 heads as beef export market expands

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s cattle industry has recorded significant growth in recent years, with the national herd increasing from approximately 90,000 head in 2015 to 220,000 as of August 2026.

Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson told BBN that improved genetics, pasture management, husbandry practices and access to new markets have contributed to the expansion.

Ferguson said Belize’s cattle exports have also increased significantly. “Our cattle herd has grown from 90,000 heads in 2015 to 220,000 heads as of August 2026,” Minister Ferguson said.

He said the country exported approximately 14,000 head annually in 2018, compared with more than 40,000 head being exported today.

He added that Belize has developed growing markets in neighbouring countries.

“Our exports have grown from 14,000 heads per year in 2018 to 41,000 heads in 2025,” he explained.

He noted that Belize currently consumes about 10,000 head annually while exporting more than 40,000 head, primarily to Guatemala and Mexico.

Ferguson said the growth presents an opportunity for Belize to play a greater role in supplying beef to CARICOM. “There is a great opportunity for Belize to supply a major portion of Caricom’s beef demand via carcass exports to further process in Jamaica or other Caricom countries,” he further added.

World.title: Belize eyes bigger CARICOM market through Sugar Refinery Investment
World.content:
Belize eyes bigger CARICOM market through Sugar Refinery Investment

By Zoila Palma: Belize is moving to add greater value to its traditional agricultural exports, with a new sugar refinery expected to increase the country’s ability to supply refined sugar to CARICOM markets.

Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson told BBN that the investment forms part of Belize’s broader strategy to move beyond exporting raw commodities.

Ferguson said the refinery represents a major step in adding value to Belize’s sugar industry. “A great example of this is the recent investment made in a Sugar Refinery that will be able to refine all of Belize’s raw sugar and supply 70% of CARICOM’s demand,” Minister Ferguson said.

He explained that refining will take place in Belize while packaging will be carried out in Trinidad, with the investment involving SUCRO Ltd., which has distribution networks in Trinidad and Jamaica. “Refining will be done in Belize and packaging will be done in Trinidad,” he added.

Ferguson said the refinery is expected to come on stream in October and represents the type of regional partnership Belize believes can strengthen CARICOM food systems.

“This investment, which comes on stream in October of this year, was made in partnership with SUCRO Ltd., a company that has distribution networks in both Trinidad and Jamaica,” he further explained.

He added that the project was made “in the true spirit of regional integration” and could contribute to the objectives of the CARICOM 25 by 2025+5 initiative.

World.title: Belize targets greater food self-sufficiency through soybean production and Agro-processing
World.content:
Belize targets greater food self-sufficiency through soybean production and Agro-processing

By Zoila Palma: Belize is expanding agricultural production and agro-processing as part of efforts to reduce dependence on imported food and strengthen its position as a net food exporter within CARICOM.

Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson said that the Government is pursuing import substitution and export expansion under Plan Belize, with support targeted along entire agricultural value chains.

Ferguson highlighted the development of Belize’s soybean industry as an example of the country’s efforts to diversify agriculture and increase local production.

“In the year 2000, Belize imported all of its soybean needs, in 2020 we imported 50% of our soybean needs and since 2022, Belize has been self-sufficient in soybean and soybean meal,” Minister Ferguson told BBN. He noted that research, field demonstrations, technology adoption and investments in processing have contributed to the industry’s development.

Minister Ferguson added that Belize has also achieved self-sufficiency in several other commodities.

“We are also self-sufficient in rice, beans, corn, sorghum and animal feeds, as well as in livestock such as poultry, eggs, beef and pork,” he said.

He said the country has continued moving beyond primary production by investing in processing facilities for products such as corn flour, milk, cheese, coconut oil, soybean oil, wheat flour, noodles and processed meats.

Ferguson said the next phase is to maximize the value generated from agriculture and strengthen export opportunities. “Belize is advancing the CARICOM 25 by 2025+5 targets mainly by implementing Plan Belize which has a dual-purpose platform aimed at import substitution and export expansion,” he stated.

World.title: “It’s about safety”: BFLA pushes to remove criminalization of abortion
World.content:
“It’s about safety”: BFLA pushes to remove criminalization of abortion

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Family Life Association (BFLA) is calling for changes to Belize’s abortion laws, arguing that criminal penalties can contribute to women and girls seeking unsafe care.

Executive Director Joan Burke-Skeen said the organization wants abortion to be addressed as a public health and reproductive rights issue while improving access to safe healthcare services.

“It’s not about just promoting abortion. It is about promoting the safety and in so doing then the removal of the criminalization of abortion,” Burke-Skeen told Love News.

She said advocates want better data, a healthcare system that can accommodate women’s needs and changes to restrictive laws, while also addressing barriers to contraceptive access. Burke-Skeen noted that abortion is not completely illegal in Belize and is permitted under certain conditions.

BFLA is also pointing to Barbados and Guyana as countries whose approaches to abortion laws could be examined by Belize. “Our partnership with Aspire is to create this level of awareness but also to do some advocacy for the necessary changes as we talk about women’s rights and women’s reproductive health and rights,” Burke-Skeen added.

She said Aspire, in collaboration with the University of the West Indies (UWI), has submitted a proposal to the Ministry of Health and is awaiting approval.

Burke-Skeen said advocates are hoping to receive support from the Attorney General’s Office and the Ministry of Health as discussions continue.

World.title: Post match brawl mars Vauxhall’s win over Charlie Smith in Walker Cup
World.content:
Screengrab of video showing crowd gathered on Charlie Smith High School field following alleged brawl following Walker Cup round-of-16 match on Tuesday (Original Video: andrewilliamsmedia Instagram)

Vauxhall High School’s dramatic Walker Cup round-of-16 victory over Charlie Smith High School was followed by a reported post-match disturbance, with videos circulating online appearing to show alleged stone-throwing, fighting and damage to property after the game.

Vauxhall High secured their place in the next round of the competition after overcoming the hosts in a tense penalty shootout, but the celebrations were overshadowed by events that unfolded after the final whistle.

Footage shared online appears to show chaotic scenes at the venue, with reports that students and teachers from Vauxhall High were injured during the incident. There are also reports that the Vauxhall team was unable to leave the venue for more than an hour due to difficulties accessing an exit.

In one video, a man can be heard saying that people at the venue were unable to leave because stones were being thrown.

“They are throwing stones and we cannot leave,” the man said before turning the camera towards another man behind a gate, who he said had refused to open it.

Another video appears to show two men engaged in a physical confrontation on the field, while separate footage shows a coaster bus with shattered windows as students disembarked.

Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) President Keith Wellington said he is aware of the incident but was unable to comment further at this time.

More details to come.

World.title: Sugar tax shortfall
World.content:
The new sugar sweetened drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year.

The Government collected $3 billion less than it had budgeted from the local special consumption tax (SCT) during the April-June quarter, with the Ministry of Finance pointing, in part, to non-compliance following the introduction of the sugar-sweetened drinks tax.

But the country’s fiscal watchdog, the Independent Fiscal Commission (IFC), says the explanation does not go far enough.

The IFC said information provided by the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service (MoFPS) was inadequate to determine whether the explanation for the 35.5 per cent shortfall was reasonable.

According to the IFC’s latest statement on fiscal performance that was tabled in Parliament last week, the Government collected $5.52 billion in local SCT during the first quarter of the 2026/27 financial year, well below the $8.57 billion that had been budgeted.

The resulting $3.04-billion gap was the largest shortfall recorded under the local SCT heading among the production and consumption taxes for the quarter.

The ministry attributed the underperformance to several factors, with the introduction of the new tax on non-alcoholic, sugar-sweetened beverages forming only part of its explanation.

“The shortfall reflects lower-than-expected collections from new revenue measures in Q1 (quarter one), due in part to non-compliance by some firms in remitting SCT for May 2026 following the introduction of the sweetened drinks tax. Changes in production and consumption behaviour in anticipation of the scheduled tax increases announced under the FY [financial year] 2026/27 revenue measures also contributed to the shortfall.

“Lower remittances from Petrojam Limited, together with weaker-than-expected performance in the automotive, petroleum distribution, and beverage/tobacco industries, further reduced SCT collections,” the ministry told the IFC.

However, the IFC was not satisfied that the explanation provided enough information to properly assess the reasons for the shortfall.

The new sweetened-drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year. The Government had initially proposed a charge of two cents per millilitre on non-alcoholic sweetened beverages, but subsequently changed the structure following consultations with industry. The revised measure applies SCT at 22 cents per gram of added sugar or sweetener.

The Government had said the measure was intended not only to raise revenue but also to support public-health objectives. It was originally projected to generate $10.1 billion during the fiscal year.

The implementation itself also encountered administrative challenges. Tax Administration Jamaica extended the deadline for beverage manufacturers to complete licensing under the new SCT regime to May 15, after the tax took effect.

The local SCT shortfall formed part of a wider revenue gap during the quarter. Central Government revenue and grants came in $28.7 billion, or 9.8 per cent, below budget, while tax revenue was $18.8 billion, or 6.9 per cent below target.

The IFC noted that nearly $9 billion of the overall $28.7-billion gap was related to timing differences, including tax revenue that had been projected for April but was collected in March as some companies paid early, and a $2.9-billion transfer from the National Housing Trust that was budgeted for June but was received in September.

The delayed implementation of the Environmental Protection Levy also contributed to the revenue shortfall. The IFC estimated that the delay resulted in approximately $700 million in revenue not being collected during the June quarter and projected a $1.8-billion revenue fallout for the 2026/27 FY if implementation remained delayed.

The legislation for the Environmental Protection Levy was passed by the Senate last Friday with the higher 0.85 per cent levy set to take effect on October 1.

World.title: Road repair ‘blame game’
World.content:
MORGAN... when local authorities demand additional public funds, taxpayers have a right to inspect how existing funds are managed

WHILE Jamaicans continue to express concern over deteriorating parochial roads, central government and local representatives elected on an Opposition ticket are trading barbs, with each side contending that the other is culpable.

At the core of the dispute, minister without portfolio with responsibility for works Robert Morgan insists that municipal corporations are not doing enough to fulfil their responsibility for sustaining roads, while the National Caucus of People’s National Party (PNP) Councillors argue that they are being hobbled by inadequate resources.

In a media release Tuesday morning, Mayor of Spanish Town Norman Scott strongly rejected comments Morgan previously made to the media, regarding poor management of parochial roads by local authorities. Scott argued that the Government should provide municipal corporations with adequate funding instead of engaging in a “blame game”.

He said that of Jamaica’s 25,000 to 27,000 kilometres of roads, municipal corporations are responsible for more than 15,000 kilometres of parochial roads, while the National Works Agency (NWA) maintains approximately 5,000 kilometres. The mayor contended that an annual budget of just over $6 billion across all parishes is simply not enough.

Arguing his point, Scott highlighted disparities in the budget available to works being carried out by the State, including the $45-billion Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to our Road Network (SPARK) programme. Scott also pointed to the $4-billion Relief Emergency Assistance and Community Help (REACH) Programme which addresses road and infrastructure needs in rural communities.

“The Parochial Revenue Fund, from which municipal roads are maintained, is not a personal road fund at the disposal of individual councillors. Resources are allocated through municipal corporations, which must contend with competing demands for road maintenance, drainage, disaster mitigation and other municipal responsibilities as well as being saddled with offsetting the shortfalls in salaries,” he argued said.

“The National Caucus of PNP Councillors is also calling for increased allocations to the Parochial Revenue Fund and a sustainable financing framework that gives municipal corporations the capacity and resources to properly maintain roads for which they have statutory responsibility,” added Scott.

But Morgan was unrelenting in his position, arguing that the issue is not simply a lack of funding but how existing resources are administered.

“When local authorities demand additional public funds, taxpayers have a right to inspect how existing funds are managed. This call for accountability is not coming from the minister of works alone. In her July 2020 audit of Mayor Scott’s own St Catherine Municipal Corporation [covering financial years 2014/15 through 2018/19], the Auditor General [Pamela Monroe Ellis], uncovered severe administrative deficiencies,” said Morgan, adding that the audit magnified flaws in strategic planning, incomplete road inventories, an absence of documented criteria for selecting roadworks, and defective contract records.

He further noted that the caucus failed to disclose in its statement that municipalities collect independent revenue from approximately 30 distinct internal sources, including trade, shop, and market fees, as well as from subdivision, billboard, and parking charges, directly boosting their annual budget.

Against that backdrop, Morgan debated whether an increase in budget would see any changes in the management of parochial roads, arguing that previous increases have only resulted in “close to $2 billion of misappropriation and fraud by municipal corporations under the leadership of the People’s National Party, including the Manchester Municipal Corporation and Mayor Scott’s own St Catherine Municipal Corporation”.

The works minister also sought to put to bed what he deemed an unfair comparison between his ministry’s spending for long-term projects, and funds available to municipalities.

“In the release, they have attempted to compare the municipal corporations’ annual Parochial Revenue Fund allocation of just over $6 billion alongside the $45-billion SPARK allocation to claim financial neglect. This comparison is fundamentally flawed. The Parochial Revenue Fund figure used represents a single year’s allocation, whereas SPARK is a multi-year capital investment programme,” Morgan stressed.

He added that the SPARK programme does not only fund road infrastructure, but also has a portion of its budget dedicated to sewerage, fibre infrastructure, water infrastructure and sidewalks as well as drainage construction.

“The contrast in public disclosure is equally stark. While the central government publishes extensive digital tracking for SPARK and has launched the interactive Jamaica Road Register to map every road, a search of the St Catherine Municipal Corporation website and other municipal portals reveals zero listed ongoing projects. This is not demonstrating accountability and transparency. I welcome Mayor Scott’s call for transparency, and I challenge him and the National Caucus of PNP Councillors to join me in achieving it,” charged the minister.

World.title: Ny-Robii comes into his own
World.content:
Recording artiste Ny-Robii

For years Dowayne J Morrison was comfortable allowing his music to take precedence over establishing his name. Long before he began seriously carving out his own space as Ny-Robii, the St Thomas-born artiste was already putting his pen to work behind the scenes, contributing to songs recorded by dancehall entertainer Pamputtae, including Good Good, Drive Mi Good, Stop It, and Good Gold.

Back then, he was known as Priceless. Today, with a new name, a clearer sense of direction, and an increasing confidence in his own artistry, Ny-Robii believes it is finally time for audiences to know the man behind the music.

“I’m feeling superb and proud of myself,” he said, reflecting on his growth. “I know I mastered the art because I can DJ, singjay, and sing on any rhythm — trap, dancehall or reggae.”

It is the kind of confidence that did not emerge overnight. Now, based in Long Island’s East End in the Hamptons, Ny-Robii’s journey has been one of reinvention, patience, and learning to trust his own ability.

Though songwriting gave him an entry point into the industry, his ambitions have always stretched beyond creating material for other artistes. He wanted his own voice to be heard. That desire eventually gave birth to Ny-Robii, an identity under which he released Clowny in 2019 before following with the seven-track EP Welcome to Ny-Bration in October 2021.

Since then, he has been steadily building his catalogue and refining what he describes as a sound rooted in reggae trap, dancehall, melody, and storytelling.

For Ny-Robii, versatility is one of his greatest strengths. He describes himself as a lyricist with strong vocals and an ability to move comfortably between subjects, rhythms, and styles without losing his identity.

“My expectation as an artiste is to be unique — different — be professional, release quality music consistently, and please my audience to the best of my ability,” he said.

That commitment to individuality appears to be at the heart of the artiste he is trying to become. Rather than simply chasing what is popular, Ny-Robii says he wants his music to reflect his own creative instincts. He refers to that space as his “flow state” — a place where, creatively, he feels unrestricted and able to operate on what he describes as another plane.

The visual for his 2022 single Destiny has accumulated more than 168,000 views onVevo, while Going Crazy has surpassed 205,000 views, taking the combined tally for the two visuals beyond 370,000.

Still, Ny-Robii does not want his journey reduced to numbers. For him, the more important story is the distance travelled between the man who once questioned his own possibilities and the artiste who now speaks openly about becoming a household name. That evolution has shaped much of the message he wants his music and career to represent.

Ny-Robii firmly believes that where a person begins does not have to determine where they end up. It is a lesson he hopes others can take from his story, especially through his latest single, Flight.

But Ny-Robii’s ambitions stretch much further than studio releases. He wants stages, big ones. Among his goals are performances at major festivals around the world and the opportunity to build a catalogue and career strong enough to make Ny-Robii a recognisable name internationally.

Ultimately, he speaks boldly about wanting to become not simply a successful recording artiste, but a music icon and, eventually, a legend. While some listeners may already know songs that his pen helped create, Ny-Robii is hoping this next chapter ensures they remember the name attached to his own voice.

World.title: DERRIMON TAKES US COST-CUT ROUTE
World.content:
Derrimon Trading Company Limited Chairman Derrick Cotterell (right) and Chief Executive Officer Ian Kelly

DERRIMON Trading Company Limited is relocating its US wholesale operation from Brooklyn, New York, to New Jersey as it seeks to slash operating costs and return the business to profitability following a period of sustained losses.

Chairman Derrick Cotterell told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday that the decision was driven largely by the high cost of operating in New York, where expenses including rent, insurance, municipal charges and even waste disposal have weighed heavily on the business.

“We’re trying to save some cost as it was just getting too expensive to operate from that location. We have moved the business to New Jersey, which is way cheaper. And that move will bring the business to profitability much faster,” Cotterell further told the Business Observer.

He said the move to New Jersey is expected to reduce the US operation’s costs by more than 60 per cent, with the company targeting a return to profitability within two to three months of the relocation.

In a notice posted to the Jamaica Stock Exchange on Monday, the company advised shareholders that its “Food Saver New York and Sampars New York stores will cease operations at 402 East 83rd Street in Canarsie, Brooklyn, with wholesale operations expected to restart from New Jersey in November 2026”.

As part of the restructuring of its operations across the tristate area, the company also plans to place greater emphasis on e-commerce, through which it will mainly drive retail transactions, following upgrades to its Sampars online platform.

“Sales will go down a little bit, but we’re going to be profitable a lot quicker,” Cotterell said.

The relocation also follows significant disruption caused by flooding at the Brooklyn property, which forced a prolonged period of closure of the supermarkets and resulted in substantial revenue losses. The US stores serve as both an overseas revenue stream and an export channel for Derrimon’s Jamaican brands, including Spicy Hill Farms products.

The stores, which operated under Food Savers NY and Good Food for Less through Derrimon’s Marnock LLC subsidiary, reopened in August 2025 under the Sampars New York banner after a nine-month closure caused by severe roof and water damage.

“We’re still not 100 per cent satisfied with the repairs that were done, plus the high cost here. So between that and the cost to operate in New York — as everything is higher in New York — we just had to relocate,” Cotterell said.

Despite the restructuring, Cotterell said Derrimon has no plans to exit the US market.

“We’re still good here. We have a lot invested and we still have a lot of customers and bright prospects there,” he said. “We’re not moving out of the US. It’s just that we’re moving from Brooklyn to reduce costs.”

The relocation comes as Derrimon works to recover from a difficult financial period that has seen group revenue decline sharply.

For the six months ended June 30, 2026, consolidated revenue totalled $5.7 billion, down 33 per cent from the $8.6 billion earned in the corresponding period last year, while the group recorded a net loss of $442 million. Second-quarter revenue similarly fell 35.35 per cent to $2.72 billion, down from $4.21 billion a year earlier, while the group reported a loss of $273 million.

Derrimon attributed the revenue decline to supply chain challenges and temporary working-capital constraints that affected the timely availability of inventory during the quarter.

“The group has realigned operations to match the current economic climate while emphasising strict cost management to become more efficient and improve profitability,” the directors said in the company’s recent quarterly report.

Derrimon which has had to be dealing with fall-outs concerning its enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, saw glitches in the system affecting the accuracy of unit costs and units of measurement across its Sampars and Select Grocers supermarket operations throughout 2025,

Cotterell said that though the ERP problems have since been corrected and the group is now seeing signs of improvement, the decision to relocate was also taken as part of proactive measures to contain losses rather than wait for the US operation to recover on its own.

“We couldn’t wait until the business turned around there. We had to pivot,” he said.

With the restructuring and cost-cutting measures expected to produce progressively better results, Cotterell said the company remains optimistic about its recovery despite continued challenges in the global economy.

He said the group expects to see significantly improved performance by next year, although some initiatives could deliver results sooner.

“We see improvements happening already, but I think we should be back to profitability by the second to third quarter of next year,” Cotterell said.

World.title: ‘BIG SETBACK’
World.content:
SPEID... I thought our pressing wasn’t so good tonight, but even when we dropped into a low block, [Honduras] were still finding ways through (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

AFTER the Reggae Boyz lost to Honduras for the first time in 13 years, interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid says he may have to make some personnel changes ahead of their now crucial remaining group stage games in the Concacaf Nations League.

The national senior men’s team suffered a tough 0-1 defeat to the Hondurans on Monday at the National Stadium with Keyrol Figueroa scoring the lone goal in the 14th minute.

Although Jamaica had a man advantage for over 22 minutes following Dereck Moncada’s red card in the 68th minute, they failed to capitalise, managing just three shots on target for the 90 minutes.

It ended an impressive eight game unbeaten streak against Honduras with their last defeat coming in 2013. It was also the first time in two years that Jamaica lost on home soil and the first since 2022 that they lost to Central American opposition.

Speid, who was suffering his second competitive loss since taking over as interim boss last November, believes the team fell flat throughout the contest.

“I think that energy-wise we’re not really there. We’re a bit behind Honduras who I think just wanted it more and played much harder than how we were playing and I think that is what decided the game,” he said.

“Almost everything we need to improve on. I thought our pressing wasn’t so good tonight, but even when we dropped into a low block, (Honduras) were still finding ways through so I think we probably were just too wide apart and we played much tighter.”

With only the top two from the group advancing to the quarter-finals, the result sees Jamaica fall to fourth on 3 points. Suriname lead with 6 points while Guatemala, in second, and Honduras, in third, above the Reggae Boyz due to goal difference and head-to-head respectively.

The team will visit El Salvador, also on 3 points in 5th, on Friday in their penultimate game before playing Honduras again next Monday.

“It’s a big setback for us. It means that we have to win our remaining games to qualify straight from this stage so it’s going to be tough and we’re going away, which makes the team harder for us,” said Speid.

However, Speid says some changes are likely in order to see improved results going forward.

“Football is a game that you have to learn to live with the wins, the losses and the draws. So it’s something that we expect to do. We’ll have some soul-searching with the whole team,” he said.

“We have a big squad, so it is possible that we might have to allow other players who have more energy to play. We’ll have to be rotating the squad, so it’s something we’re going to look at.”

Striker Rumarn Burrell, who missed the contest after scoring in the 3-2 over Guatemala last Friday, will miss the remainder of the Nations League group stage campaign after he returned to his club Queens Park Rangers in England after picking up an injury.

They could also be without winger Renaldo Cephas who pulled up inside 10 minutes of the game and was later substituted.

The team will leave the island today before arriving in San Salvador ahead of Friday’s game.

— Daniel Blake

Starting XI: Andre Blake, Brandon Cover (46’), Joel Latibeaudiere, Richard King, Ronaldo Webster (83’), Isaac Hayden (62’), Karoy Anderson, Kasey Palmer (62’), Kaheim Dixon (46’), Renaldo Cephas (12’), Bailey Cadamarteri

Substitutes: Tyreece Campbell (12’), Miguel Freckleton (46’), Javon East (62’), Courtney Clarke (62’), Dwayne Atkinson (83’)

World.title: Wage bill watch
World.content:
The Government has set aside $42.8 billion to cover new public sector wage rates and retroactive payments, but the Independent Fiscal Commission (IFC) says it cannot determine whether the provision will be enough to settle the outstanding claims across State agencies.

The uncertainty comes even after the Government reached a three-year wage agreement with the Jamaica Confederation of Trade Unions (JCTU), with the fiscal watchdog warning that negotiations with other bargaining groups could add further pressure to the wage bill.

The JCTU agreement, formally signed on August 27, covers the period April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2028. It provides for a one-off, tax-free payment of $80,000 to public servants for the 2025/26 financial year, followed by a five per cent wage increase in each of the next two years, as well as the restoration of the 2.5 per cent performance increment.

The IFC said the settlement was reached well into the three-year period and has introduced uncertainty into a budget that had been prepared on the basis of a smaller wage increase.

“In addition to the IFC being unable to assess the fiscal impact of the compensation agreement in the absence of pertinent information on the cost of the wage settlement relative to the initial offer from the ministry, there is also uncertainty on whether the $42.8-billion contingency allocated to cover wage rates and retroactive payments is adequate,” the IFC said in its latest Statement on Fiscal Performance tabled in Parliament last week.

The Government’s original wage offer, which was incorporated into the 2026/27 Budget, provided for an annual 2.5 per cent increase over each of the three years of the wage agreement.

The final settlement therefore represents a higher rate of increase in the second and third years, while also restoring the performance increment that had been suspended during the implementation of the new public sector compensation structure.

However, the IFC said it was unable to properly calculate the fiscal impact of the settlement because the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service (MoFPS) had not provided sufficient information on its cost compared with the original offer.

That uncertainty is compounded by the fact that the JCTU agreement does not settle the wage position for every public sector bargaining group.

“The agreement covers the contract period April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2028. Nevertheless, the IFC is unable to assess the impact, specifically on the wage bill, and more broadly, on the fiscal programme, due to lack of information from the MoFPS on the cost of the settlement. Of note, negotiations continue with other bargaining groups, which will also impact the overall wage bill,” the IFC added.

The fiscal watchdog’s concern extends beyond the $42.8-billion contingency itself.

It pointed to a claim before the Industrial Disputes Tribunal by the Jamaica Medical Doctors Association for $31 billion in retroactive overtime, compared with the Government’s calculation of $23 billion.

The $8-billion difference between the two figures represents another potential pressure on the public finances.

The wage uncertainty comes against a backdrop of rising public sector compensation costs.

The IFC noted that wages and salaries accounted for 13.2 per cent of gross domestic product at the end of the 2025/26 financial year, up from 8.8 per cent after the abolition of the wage fiscal rule following 2021/22.

Wages and salaries also represented 54.4 per cent of tax revenue in 2025/26, compared with 47.9 per cent in 2024/25 and 45.5 per cent in 2023/24.

Despite those pressures, the IFC noted that actual spending on wages and salaries during the April-June quarter was broadly in line with the Budget.

The concern is about what happens as the new wage agreement and other settlements feed through the financial year.

“Despite the recent wage settlement with the JCTU, albeit 18 months after the starting period for the agreement, the IFC reiterates that the GOJ needs to establish and timely execute a public sector compensation negotiation cycle that aligns with the budget cycle,” the IFC warned.

The commission has also welcomed the Government’s stated intention to reintroduce a fiscal rule for public sector wages and salaries, saying such a move could help contain budget risks and improve fiscal management.

World.title: St Elizabeth student injured by falling boulder still unconscious at UHWI
World.content:
A loosened boulder on the train track in St Elizabeth where three students were injured, one of whom remains unconscious.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The young schoolgirl, Kendra Rose, who was one of three students injured by a falling boulder as they made their way to Merrywood Primary School in St Elizabeth earlier this month, remains hospitalised in an unconscious state at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI).

Member of Parliament for St Elizabeth North West, Andrew Morris, provided the update on Tuesday during his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in the House of Representatives. He also shared that all medical fees for Rose’s treatment have been waived.

Morris noted that the “heartbreaking incident” occurred on the Merrywood to Breadnut Walk stretch. “Three children were severely injured by falling boulders while forced to use an abandoned train track as an alternative route to get to Merrywood Primary School. No child should risk life and limb just to seek an education,” he said.

READ: Three children injured after being hit by boulder in St Elizabeth

The first-term MP told the House that following dialogue with Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon and Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton and his team, “I am relieved to announce that all medical fees related to care for Kendra Rose have been waived…,” Morris said.

He also shared that the other two children were treated and released from hospital but are still undergoing treatment.

“I have made visits to the hospital and their homes and offered support to the families. Furthermore, I have engaged in constructive dialogue with the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries, Minister Floyd Green, concerning the rehabilitation of the road from Merrywood to Breadnut Walk under the Farm Road Programme to ensure this tragedy is never repeated,” Morris said.

He also pointed out that his constituents face dangerous roadway breakaways that threaten to cut off entire communities, specifically in Ginger Hill, Pisgah, Cornwall, Retirement and Jointwood.

— Lynford Simpson

World.title: L’UE accusée de dissimuler l’impact environnemental des datacenters
World.content:
Lighthouse Reports, une ONG basée aux Pays-Bas qui mène des enquêtes dans plusieurs pays sur de potentiels méfaits commis par des gouvernements et des entreprises, accuse la Commission d’ériger un “mur du silence” autour de la question de la consommation d’énergie.

Les décideurs politiques de l’UE seraient déterminés “à refuser ou à dissuader l’accès aux informations relatives aux performances des centres de données, et à en brouiller la compréhension”, peut-on lire dans la plainte déposée au titre de la Convention d’Aarhus, un traité international juridiquement contraignant qui garantit au public le droit à l’information et à la participation aux décisions en matière d’environnement.

Cette procédure affrontera son premier test en novembre, lorsque le Comité d’examen du respect des dispositions de la Convention d’Aarhus se réunira pour statuer sur sa recevabilité. Par la suite, la Convention d’Aarhus pourrait conclure que l’UE a manqué aux obligations qui lui incombent en vertu du texte.

Contactée par POLITICO, la Commission n’a pas répondu à notre demande de commentaire.

Des gourmands en énergie

Alors que l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle entraîne une hausse de la demande énergétique, l’UE a officiellement annoncé son objectif de tripler la capacité de ses centres de données dans les années à venir, afin de rester dans la course face aux Etats-Unis et à la Chine. Parallèlement, face à la hausse des prix de l’énergie, la contestation citoyenne contre les centres de données prend de l’ampleur à travers l’Europe.

Afin de limiter l’impact environnemental, la Commission a présenté la semaine dernière un nouveau label de transparence destiné à orienter les investissements vers des installations plus respectueuses de l’environnement ; des normes minimales de performance devraient suivre.

World.title: ‘No way they can beat us’: Rutte rebuffs Russian nuclear threats to NATO
World.content:
Rutte's unusually strong remarks underscore the growing tensions between Moscow and NATO countries as hybrid attacks and Russian-linked sabotage proliferate across Europe.

In recent days, Russia's embassy in Belgium sent NATO a note alleging the alliance was displaying "reckless and irresponsible" behavior near its Kaliningrad exclave, following alliance exercises involving several reconnaissance planes, ground forces and fighter jets near the region, which is between Poland and Lithuania, last month.

"We have emphasised that Russia possesses the necessary means to repel any potential aggression and is prepared to deploy its entire arsenal to defend its territory should NATO countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of our country," the embassy wrote on social media.

In its letter to NATO, Moscow explicitly mentions the use of its nuclear arsenal and issues specific threats to hit allied territory, according to one NATO diplomat briefed on the letter, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.

NATO has sent a note back to Russian officials in response, the alliance's spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed.

"We have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia," she said in a statement. "We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."

World.title: Macron and Sanchez say UK would be ‘welcome’ back in EU
World.content:
Rejoining would be “a wise decision” and Burnham was “right to show such boldness,” Macron added.

Speaking at the same press conference, Sanchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain's return with open arms.”

Burnham told Labour’s conference in Liverpool yesterday that Brexit had done more “harm than good” and that he would lay out the “different options” available to repair the damage at a forthcoming U.K.-EU summit expected in November.

Speaking to broadcasters the morning after the speech, the PM confirmed the options could include rejoining the single market, the customs union, or even going “all the way” and rejoining the EU entirely.

But the U.K. prime minister’s announcement was met with a more muted response from Brussels itself.

A European Commission spokesperson said: “The U.K. is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the U.K. Government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

World.title: Europe’s energy security has a Black Sea opportunity
World.content:
Kriti Legend at Kulevi with BSP’s first shipment of Libyan crude oil, 30 August 2026. / via Black Sea Petroleum

Europe’s need for diverse fuel supplies

Europe continues to import fuels used in transport and industry. According to Eurostat, EU net imports in 2024 amounted to 15.7 million tonnes of oil equivalent for gasoil and diesel and 11 million for jet fuel. Both are included in the Kulevi Oil Refinery’s expansion plans.

For Kulevi, the opportunity is to supply EU markets alongside Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, drawing on non-Russian crude and the Black Sea’s shipping connections.

Following the Oil Coordination Group meeting on September 8, 2026, the European Commission reported that higher EU refinery production and alternative international supplies were helping meet demand for diesel and jet fuel. Stocks remained sufficient, but developments in the Middle East and seasonal demand could tighten markets in the weeks and months ahead.

Additional refining capacity connected to maritime trade could give Europe more sources of these fuels. For Kulevi, the opportunity is to supply EU markets alongside Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, drawing on non-Russian crude and the Black Sea’s shipping connections. This would add another route through which international crude supplies can reach Europe as refined products.

An operating refinery connected to the sea

Four pipelines run for three kilometres between the Kulevi Oil Refinery and the nearby port and terminal. They carry crude oil, naphtha, gasoil and fuel oil. The port and terminal are separate facilities owned and operated by SOCAR.

World.title: Farage spoils for a Brexit brawl with Burnham
World.content:
Farage is spoiling to address all these fault-lines on Thursday.

“He will talk about Burnham wanting to take us into the Euro, return us to freedom of movement with 500 million people and losing the ability to nationalize key industries,” said the Reform official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the pending speech in Doncaster.

The Yorkshire city voted 69% in favor of leaving the EU in the 2016 referendum, making it one of the most pro-Brexit areas in the U.K. One of its MPs is Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

Burnham has reopened the debate in Labour and beyond by saying he will canvass opinion on several options for Britain’s future arrangement with Brussels and set them out around the time of a EU-U.K. summit later this year.

Those options, he has said, could include rejoining the single market, the customs union, or “go all the way,” which Reform is interpreting as scrapping the Pound in favor of the Euro. Burnham has not made that specific pledge, and Labour resisted Britain joining the single currency when it was introduced.

Farage is meanwhile planning to argue that EU re-entry would curb the ability of British governments to nationalize key industries — a play by the Reform leader that upends the traditional left-right debate in British politics. Burnham has put emphasis on bringing back “public control” of privatized utilities rather than public ownership, but Farage has changed tack from his Thatcherite credentials to express support for nationalization in some sectors.

World.title: Eurozone inflation heats up faster than expected
World.content:
The numbers all came in above forecasts and hit multi-year highs.

The increases were driven in large part by energy prices as the Middle East conflict continues to disrupt oil and gas markets. The ECB has raised rates twice this year, bringing its deposit rate to 2.5% in September.

The next step is considered more challenging as it could push rates from the upper end of neutral into restrictive territory, where they begin to slow economic activity.

Higher rates are also lifting government borrowing costs. Sovereign yields have reached their highest levels since the 2012 debt crisis, adding pressure to public finances.

France has seen the steepest increase in its borrowing cost among eurozone member states as investors demand an additional premium for holding its debt, given massive fiscal and political uncertainty in the run-up to French presidential elections.

The level could still rise should investors be disappointed by the hotly awaited budget announcement in Paris on Thursday.

Eurostat will release inflation numbers for the 21-nation euro zone as a whole on Friday.

World.content:

Die AfD steckt in einem Konflikt über ihre einstige Kernforderung. Während Parteichefin Alice Weidel und der europapolitische Sprecher Peter Boehringer den EU-Austritt als Ultima Ratio ins Spiel bringen, wirbt der Chef der Parteijugend Pascal Hohm für den Erhalt des Euro. Warum dieser Vorstoß für Turbulenzen sorgt, analysieren Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler.

In Sachsen-Anhalt greift die AfD derweil nach den Schalthebeln der Macht: Der Abgeordnete Tobias Rausch soll Landtagspräsident werden, während Ulrich Siegmund im Dezember als Ministerpräsident kandidiert. Ob das Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht dabei zum heimlichen Mehrheitsbeschaffer wird, zeigt der Blick hinter die Kulissen des neuen Landtags.

Für diplomatischen Ärger sorgt zudem der Europaabgeordnete Maximilian Krah mit einer umstrittenen Reise in den türkisch besetzten Norden Zyperns. Sein Treffen mit türkischen Nationalisten erzürnt griechische Verbündete und ruft den AfD-Bundesvorstand auf den Plan. Welche Sanktionen dem Politiker nun drohen, hört ihr in dieser Folge.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: EU and Canada to announce sweeping new partnership pact
World.content:
BRUSSELS — The EU and Canada will use a landmark summit next month to announce an expansive new partnership, ranging from breaking down digital trade barriers to joint support for Ukraine and investing in fighting wildfires.

"The world is rapidly changing with unprecedented geopolitical challenges as well as challenges across trade, energy, technology, climate, and resources," reads a draft joint statement to be issued by the two sides, circulated to EU ambassadors in preparation for the planned summit that begins on Oct. 29, and obtained by POLITICO.

The EU and Canada have been seeking to shore up their strategic ties as they grapple with the fallout from U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen this month proposed inviting Canada to become an associate member of the EU, triggering an immediate threat by Trump to impose tariffs.

World.title: Houthi attacks put Turkey’s new Saudi defence pact to the test
World.content:
Attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia are putting Turkey's new defence pact with the kingdom to its first major test – forcing Ankara to weigh support for its ally against the risk of being drawn deeper into the conflict.

Advertising

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on 7 August, committing themselves to the principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.

The three countries' military chiefs met in the Saudi capital on Friday, a day after the Iran-backed Houthis launched their latest barrage of missiles targeting Riyadh and Saudi Aramco oil facilities in Yanbu.

In recent weeks, Saudi Arabia has reported intercepting numerous Houthi drone and ballistic missile attacks from neighbouring Yemen.

The military chiefs discussed intelligence sharing, military coordination and integrating their capabilities, Saudi and Pakistani statements said. Turkey's defence ministry did not comment on the meeting.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Saudi expectations

Turkey has so far stopped short of committing itself to military action.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said this month that Ankara was looking into providing what he called “technical support”, without elaborating on what that could involve.

Saudi Arabia could look to Turkey for air defence systems, counter-drone technology, radars and maritime security, given the expertise and capabilities of the Turkish military and defence industry, said Amed Khuzaie of the Washington-based think tank N7 Foundation.

“The Mecca Agreement pact will prove its vitality and importance only if it's deemed to be functional,” Khuzaie told RFI.

The Riyadh meeting followed talks in New York on Thursday involving the Saudi and Turkish foreign ministers and Pakistan's deputy prime minister and foreign minister on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

Turkish media citing foreign ministry sources said the meeting focused on ongoing “technical negotiations”.

But providing support to Saudi Arabia could expose Turkey to retaliation from the Houthis.

“By God, if Turkey and Pakistan become involved, we will strike them with an iron fist,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis, said in an Iraqi television interview.

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Risk of retaliation

The warning should be taken seriously given the Houthis' military presence around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical waterway linking the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, explained Amed Nagi, a Yemen expert at the International Crisis Group.

“[The Houthis] targeted US and UK shipping in the Red Sea,” Nagi said. “They could do the same beyond [that] to the Gulf of Aden, because we know Turkey is very active in the Horn of Africa.

"So I think these are the areas that the Houthis will think about if there is any sort of retaliation against Turkey.”

In 2024, the Houthis attacked US military and commercial shipping in the Red Sea, damaging the Gibraltar Eagle bulk carrier with a cruise missile and sinking the British-linked cargo ship MV Rubymar.

Saudi Arabia could also look to Israel for support if its new partners do not provide what it needs, Khuzaie said.

“Who has better intelligence in the region than the Israelis today?” he said. “Diversifying resources, if one fails you, you have another side that could assist.”

The risks for Ankara go beyond possible Houthi retaliation. Turkey must also manage its relationship with Iran, which backs the Yemeni group.

“It is not in the interest of Turkey to have a direct confrontation with any actor in the region, and the Houthis have become a proxy of Iran; Turkey doesn't want a confrontation with Iran directly," said Bilgehan Alagoz, an international relations professor at Istanbul's Marmara University.

"Turkey is trying to solve the issue from a diplomatic point of view.”

In a joint statement last week, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt said that dialogue and diplomacy were the only sustainable way to resolve the region's conflicts, while affirming Saudi Arabia's right to defend itself under international law.

Fidan met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in New York on Friday.

Fidan later said they discussed Iran's negotiations with the United States and conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but that diplomatic efforts had yet to produce a breakthrough.

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Iran balancing act

The diplomatic efforts come as Turkey's relationship with Iran faces other strains.

Turkey-based international relations analyst Soli Ozel said Ankara has for decades walked a “fine line” between rivalry and cooperation with Tehran while balancing its relationships with Iran and Western allies, particularly the United States.

Turkey's banking regulator recently revoked the operating licence of Iran's Bank Mellat branch in Istanbul, although the official notice did not say the move was intended to enforce US sanctions.

The US Treasury also said Ankara had agreed after talks with Washington to stop flights by Iran's Mahan Air as part of efforts to comply with US measures against Tehran. Three Turkish airlines also suspended flights to Iran.

Turkish authorities have also repeatedly accused Iran of hostile operations inside the country, including assassinations and abductions of Iranian dissidents.

In January, security forces arrested six people suspected of spying for Iran and gathering information about the Incirlik air base, which is used by US forces.

Becoming involved in the conflict against the Houthis could upset Ankara's already delicate relationship with Tehran, Ozel told RFI.

“The Iranians who actually have a lot of [intelligence] capabilities in Turkey, we’ve seen that before, then you find yourself in a hot or cold war,” he said.

World.title: Senegal's Youth Olympics makes Olympics in Africa 'logical'
World.content:
The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.

At the end of October 2026, the first ever Olympic event on African soil will take place as the Youth Olympics comes to Senegal.

Around 2,700 young athletes are expected to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports, with many qualifying through the African Youth Games last year.

"We were entrusted with hosting this event and that is why from Johannesburg to Nairobi, from Dakar to Djbouti, it is all of young Africa that is watching you and watching you with pride," Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said at the arrival of the flame.

The moment marks yet another step forward for global sport in Africa. In 2025, the first major road cycling event took place on the continent, and in September this year it was announced the first-ever World Athletics Championships would be held in Kenya in 2029. There are also on-going negotiations about Formula 1 returning. It appears that 16 years on since the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, global sport is finally returning to different parts of Africa.

"This is a victory for Africa. It opens the door for Africa to host major events," Malick Diouf, head of a marketing agency and founder of the Dakar Sport Summit, told DW.

"Africa is in the process of opening up to the world, hosting major events and everything. And all of Africa must celebrate this kind of victory."

Malick Diouf believes Africa as an Olympic host is the logical next step Image: DW

With more major events in Africa, the question around an Olympic Games being on the continent looms.

Sports scientist Kamilla Swart has said awarding Africa a Games would make the world "take Africa more seriously." Diouf believes it's the logical next step.

"The Youth Olympic Games, it's a major test for Africa. And I think this is where we need to succeed in organizing these Games and also in sending a message," Diouf said.

"We, Africa, are ready to host the Summer Olympics, and I think that would be the logical next step after the Dakar Olympics. We have Olympic champions; we have record holders; we have Olympians, so we deserve to host the Olympic Games."

Senegal an attractive option for many reasons

The move to re-use and refurbish existing facilities rather than build whole new ones is likely why Senegal's bid was so tempting for the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

The fear of the white elephant facility appears to have been considered here. The Iba Mar Diop Stadium, the track and field stadium, is expected to be used for athlete training ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

"It’s by using these facilities, by participating in and hosting international events, and by consistently maintaining them to the required standards, that we’ll be able to keep these stadiums up to the standards they currently meet," Diouf said.

There's also the social and economical impacts of the Youth Olympics. Diouf believes the impact is beyond just infrastructure, but into roads, the development of the hospitality, security and broadcasting sectors and the young athletes themselves.

"There's life after the Games. Now we need to figure out how to use the resources we have, we need to develop and capitalize on what we have showcased during the Games," said Diouf.

Senegal gears up for Youth Olympic Games To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Future of Youth Olympics in doubt

The significance of these Games stretch beyond even the history they are making in Africa. In May of this year, IOC President Kirsty Coventry put the brakes on the future of the Youth Olympics, leaving real doubts as to whether there will be any more after the 2028 winter edition.

"We need to pause and have a real reflection on why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games and we realized that across the Movement it's very disjointed. There's not a true North Star of why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games," Coventry told reporters.

"So the EB (IOC Executive Board) decided to pause the 2030 process right now so there will not be an election in June, and rather we need to take a step back and develop a youth strategy."

The Youth Olympics in Dakar might well be the last summer edition of the youth games Image: Nicolas Remene/Le Pictorium/IMAGO

A lot has changed since the Youth Olympic Games were launched in 2010. Initially it was seen as a way to engage a younger audience (athletes were limited by age to between 15 and 18) by trialing new sports as well as testing host country's on a smaller stage. However, with the age of athletes decreasing and the challenges of engaging a younger audience in the modern sports entertainment landscape even more challenging, it appears clear the IOC are reconsidering their options when it comes to investment.

"My only wish is that Dakar be memorable and that people reconsider their decision not to host the Games in 2030," Diouf said.

"I don’t want these to be the last Youth Olympic Games, but if these are to be the last Youth Olympic Games, we need to go out with a bang. Dakar needs to show the world what Senegal is all about, what Africa is all about."

From October 31 to November 13 this year, Senegal will have the chance to do just that.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: African leaders herald $16B Dangote oil refinery in Kenya
World.content:
An oil refinery on Kenya's coast is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, will lead the project.

African leaders on Wednesday broke ground on a new $16 billion (€14 billion) oil refinery off Kenya's coast.

The project is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. The refinery will be constructed at the coastal town of Lamu.

Kenya's President William Ruto, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed were among the leaders who attended an event to celebrate the project, the largest of its kind in East and Central Africa.

The refinery "will strengthen regional energy security, reduce reliance on imports and bolster our foreign exchange," Ruto said on social media.

"But this is more than a refinery. It is an integrated industrial complex featuring a 1,000MW power plant, plastic factory and the manufacturing of fertilizers and chemicals."

Africa's richest man, Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, will oversee the project.

Dangote: Project will reduce refined fuel imports, foster self-sufficiency

Dangote said the refinery will make East Africa more "self-sufficient" by reducing imports of refined fuel.

"For too long, our continent has actually been rich in resources but poor in value creation and addition. We have exported crude oil and imported refined products," Dangote said in his speech.

"Such practice only leads to us exporting our jobs and opportunities that should remain on the continent and lead us into importing poverty into our nations. Africa cannot build lasting prospertiy by exporting what it has and importing what it needs," he continued.

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote (right) inspected earthmoving machinery with Kenyan President William Ruto (left) Image: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

Lamu project faces environmental concerns, legal challenge

The project, however, has faced resistance from environmental campaigners who fear it could harm Lamu Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site which also hosts a fragile and unique marine ecosystem.

The Lamu marine environment is also home to animals such as dugongs, whales and various sea turtle species.

The Lamu region is home to an incredible variety of aquatic life [FILE: October 4, 2011] Image: Thomas Mukoya/REUTERS

Lamu residents have brought a land rights legal case against the refinery, saying the site where it will be built is their ancestral heritage.

Kenya's High Court on Monday ruled that legal proceedings will continue, but the groundbreaking ceremony can take place.

World.title: Flydubai pilot investigated over possible attempt to crash Tel Aviv-bound flight
World.content:
A Flydubai service from the UAE to Israel made an emergency landing after one pilot stabbed another. Officials are investigating whether this was a deliberate attempt to crash the plane.

Authorities are investigating whether a Flydubai pilot tried to crash an Israel-bound flight after it plummeted several thousand feet on Wednesday.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that one pilot had stabbed another pilot mid-flight, forcing the plane to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. Flydubai confirmed that all passengers were safe.

Israel's defense minister, Israel Katz, said that "an attempted jihadist terror attack" had been thwarted after several passengers intervened.

A spokesperson for the prime minister's office said that Netanyahu has ordered authorities to "ramp up" security on both Israeli and non-Israeli carriers following the Flydubai flight incident.

On Wednesday evening, passengers from the diverted Flydubai flight arrived in Israel on a replacement plane, where numerous relatives were waiting for them.

What happened on the Flydubai flight?

Flydubai said flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an "incident" while en route and landed safely in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 8.

"The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for," a Flydubai spokesperson said.

Later, a Flydubai spokesperson said that the reasons for an altercation that "occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073" remained unknown and were under formal investigation.

"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation. We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts," a spokesperson said in a statement published by the AFP news agency.

Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that authorities were investigating whether one of the pilots had deliberately tried to crash the aircraft, with the other pilot intervening to stop him.

Israeli media said one of the pilots suffered a stab wound. Initial reports had described the incident only as a fight between the two pilots, but images later published by Israeli outlets appeared to show a passenger with blood on his shirt.

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 initially showed a second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, FZ1081, diverting back toward Dubai. It later showed the aircraft continuing toward Tel Aviv. There was no immediate explanation for the change.

The plane managed to land safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia, where passengers waited for a replacement flight Image: REUTERS

How far did the plane fall?

The Israeli news portal Ynet reported that the aircraft entered a steep descent and that passengers helped one pilot prevent the other from crashing the plane.

Flight tracking data shows the aircraft suddenly losing around half its altitude as it neared Saudi Arabia's border with Jordan.

The plane dropped from nearly 34,000 feet (10,360 meters) at 05:21 GMT/UTC to below 17,000 feet (5,180 meters) at 05:22 GMT/UTC, according to Flightradar data.

Israel's Kan public broadcaster and Channel 12 reported that the Israeli military scrambled fighter jets amid initial fears of a possible hijacking. That possibility was later dismissed, according to the reports.

Israel-bound flight triggers hijack alert after pilot brawl To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Israeli minister says 'attempted jihadist terror attack' thwarted

Israeli leaders announced that a "jihadist" pilot had attempted to crash a Flydubai plane carrying mostly Israeli passengers.

In a video message, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that "during the flight... one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board."

He added that passengers and crew subdued the attacker, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where the pilot was arrested.

"I salute these heroes who showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage. They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster," Netanyahu said.

The replacement flight eventually brought the passengers to Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport Image: Ammar Awad/REUTERS

Meanwhile, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz described the incident as "an attempted jihadist terror attack" that was "thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers."

Earlier, Netanyahu's office said he had held consultations over the incident and was monitoring developments.

"The incident is under control, and all measures are currently being deployed in order to return the Israeli passengers safely to Israel," his office said.

An unnamed senior Israeli government official told Channel 12 that a major disaster had been averted.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

World.title: Germany raises Deutschlandticket price to €66.80 a month from 2027 under new cost-based formula
World.content:
A new cost-based formula has pushed up the price of Germany's nationwide public transport pass for 2027.

Germany's nationwide Deutschlandticket will cost €66.80 ($78) per month from January 1, 2027, up from the current €63, transport authorities said on Wednesday.

It is the first price increase to be determined using a new cost-based formula rather than through political negotiations between Germany's federal and state governments.

Why is the Deutschlandticket getting more expensive?

The €3.80 increase reflects rising personnel, energy and other operating costs, according to Bavaria's Transport Ministry, which currently chairs the conference of Germany's state transport ministers.

The new formula also takes into account that federal and state subsidies remain fixed at a combined €3 billion ($3.5 billion) a year.

The discounted job ticket will rise to €63.46, while the student semester ticket will cost €40.08.

Rising fuel prices put pressure on German drivers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Federal Transport Minister Steffen Bilger, of the conservative Christian Democratic Union, said the ticket remained "a very attractive offer" despite the increase.

How popular is the Deutschlandticket?

Around 14.5 million people currently use the Deutschlandticket, which covers local and regional public transport across Germany.

It was launched at €49 a month in 2023 and currently costs €63. The new price means the ticket will have become around 36% more expensive since its launch.

North Rhine-Westphalia Transport Minister Oliver Krischer, of the environmentalist Greens, criticized the increase, saying the federal government had promised price stability.
