World.title: Sloped ceilings and narrow halls don’t have to waste space
World.content:
Dutch homes are famously charming – and famously awkward to furnish – for cabinetmakers at Cabinetheroes, that is the whole point. Narrow facades, steep staircases, and rooms that seem to defy right angles: these aren’t quirks, they’re history.

Property taxes in many Dutch cities were once linked to the width of a building’s frontage, and the result can still be seen today: narrow hallways, steep staircases and rooms where standard furniture is difficult to place.

The familiar hooks above many gabled windows are another reminder of these challenging layouts – they were traditionally used to hoist furniture through the windows because getting large pieces up the stairs was often impossible.

Converted attics bring their own challenges. In a typical “zolder”, sloped ceilings and unusual angles can leave large parts of the room unused. Standard wardrobes are made for straight walls and predictable dimensions, and simply can’t use that kind of space. A made-to-measure cabinet, by contrast, can follow the exact shape of the room and turn overlooked corners into valuable storage. The result: rooms that look bigger on paper than they feel in practice, with corners and slopes often written off as wasted.

“You often have more space than you think – you just aren’t using it yet,” says Sven, managing director of the Cabinetheroes franchise network and an experienced carpenter himself.

Planning around the room, not against it

This is where made-to-measure solutions like those from Cabinetheroes come in. With the Cabinetheroes, creating a cabinet built around a room rather than the other way around is straightforward. Instead of adapting a home to fit off-the-shelf furniture, a personal Cabinethero visits, discusses your ideas, measures the room and plans a solution around the space and the way you live.

As an experienced cabinetmaker, he understands both the design and the craftsmanship behind it, and once the cabinet has been individually manufactured, he also takes care of the professional installation. From the first measurements to the finished cabinet, you have one personal point of contact – and every important step is handled by a skilled professional. Two recent projects show us what this all means in practice.

The hallway that finally feels welcoming

Christian’s hallway was more of a narrow passage than an inviting entrance. A conventional cabinet would have made the space feel even tighter, yet leaving it empty meant coats, shoes and everyday items had nowhere to go.

After measuring the hallway personally, Sven planned a fitted cloakroom cabinet that uses the available space down to the millimetre, with an integrated LED strip adding light and a warmer atmosphere.

“Tidy, I’d say,” is how Christian describes the practical result. But the emotional difference mattered just as much: “You feel welcome.” His verdict on the process was equally clear: “It was really professional. I’d recommend it to anyone.” Every step along the way was handled by one point of contact.

An open dressing area beneath a sloped roof

For Jennifer, a sloped ceiling appeared to rule out a spacious dressing area. Standard wardrobes would have left gaps beneath the roof and wasted valuable space in the lowest parts of the room. The made-to-measure design follows the ceiling precisely and uses the space right into the furthest corner.

Instead of doors, the open layout keeps clothing and accessories visible and easy to reach, with socks, belts and other smaller items each getting their own place, helping the room stay organised in everyday life.

“We’d never had such a beautiful cabinet,” Jennifer says. Everything was “matched exactly to the room”, while the personal planning took place comfortably in her own home. Her conclusion: “Quality, style and something completely individual.”

Starting with the room, not the shop

The lesson from both projects: start with the room rather than with the limited dimensions offered by a furniture shop. Slopes, alcoves and awkward corners are not necessarily wasted space – they simply require accurate measurements and thoughtful planning, with lighting, sockets and everyday routines considered from the beginning.

Features such as integrated LEDs are much easier to incorporate during planning than to add afterwards, and even a few centimetres can determine whether standard furniture fits at all.

As Sven puts it: “Your room can do more.”

For anyone facing a similar layout, the Cabinetheroes offer a free, non-binding enquiry: a personal Cabinethero will visit, discuss the possibilities, take precise measurements and guide the process through to individual planning and professional installation.

World.title: Amsterdam urges health minister to rescue crack treatment study
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The mayor of Amsterdam, Femke Halsema, has called on the government to step in to save an experimental programme to treat crack addicts with a medicine usually prescribed for ADHD.

The inspectorate IGJ has halted production of the medicine, dexamphetamine, at a Dutch hospital as part of an ongoing supervisory procedure.

The IGJ did not name the hospital or say how long the investigation would take, but a spokesman told Dutch News: “We are concerned about the quality of the medicine.”

Amsterdam city council said last week it wanted to start giving the dexamphetamine to people addicted to crack cocaine in an experiment similar to the methadone programme for heroin users.

The probe has been backed by the other three major Dutch cities – Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht – after initial research showed it could help ease crack users’ cravings.

Halsema and Alexander Scholtes, alderman responsible for healthcare, said suspending production of the drug would have a devastating impact.

Promising method

They have written to health minister Sophie Hermans urging her to review the IGJ’s decision and come up with a solution to ensure the study can continue.

“What it means is that the only highly promising method for treating these seriously addicted people has gone out of the window,” Scholtes told TV station AT5. “We can’t let that happen.”

The city council said the suspension of production was “unexpected and for reasons that are unclear to us”, but the IGJ said its investigation pre-dated the experimental programme.

A spokesman said the medicine used in the trial was the outcome of 12 years of research and development by the REDUCE project, whose partners include GGD Amsterdam, the city’s health authority, to develop a form of dexamphetamine with long-term effects.

Halesma and Scholtes have asked Hermans to organise a meeting with all parties concerned before November 1 to discuss a solution. “We value the independent position of the IGJ highly and are not impinging on their judgment,” they wrote.

But they added: “Every day we see people in Amsterdam whose lives are being taken over by a serious crack addiction.”

GGD Amsterdam estimates there are between 3,000 and 9,000 crack users in the city, many of whom are homeless or have mental health problems, or both.

The Trimbos institute, which specialises in mental health, and addiction support service Mainline said in a report three years ago that there were around 27,900 problematic crack users in the Netherlands.

World.title: Most major Dutch data centres keep energy usage secret: report
World.content:
Most data centres in the Netherlands do not make their environmental impact public, which conceals water and electricity usage, according to an investigation by Trouw and Lighthouse Reports.

The Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), which collects data on behalf of the EU, lists only 104 data centres but the industry body Dutch Datacenter Association (DDA) says there were 186 commercial data centres at the end of 2025.

These figures cover data centres with at least 500 kW of installed IT capacity, which are required to report their energy and water use, among other things, under the EU’s Energy Efficiency Directive.

The RVO’s list is missing almost half the centres counted by the DDA, and that count does not include the many data centres run in-house by banks, hospitals and other companies. Trouw estimates that public data is available for only around a quarter of large data centres.

Dutch data centre energy

Data centres used 5.1 billion kWh of electricity in 2024, or 4.6% of the national total, according to statistics from CBS – a 37% rise on 2021. Figures for 2025 are not yet available.

RVO figures published this summer showed that Microsoft’s largest Dutch data centre alone uses 1% of national electricity, though the power is said to come from renewable sources. Google, which runs two large data centres in the Netherlands, does not publish its figures.

Grid operator TenneT expects data centres to account for 10% to 15% of Dutch electricity use by 2030. Water use is lower, at an estimated 0.1% of the national total.

Aarhus Convention

Reporters working with Lighthouse Reports spent a year filing freedom of information requests in all 27 EU member states and with the European Commission. Most were refused, with some countries saying they did not have the data, and others citing commercial confidentiality.

The group has now filed a complaint under the Aarhus Convention, a treaty signed by the EU and all its member states that guarantees public access to environmental information. The complaint is before the convention’s compliance committee, which meets four times a year.

Lighthouse Reports says the Netherlands discloses more than most other EU countries, where reporters met what they called a “wall of silence”.

World.title: Two more suspects arrested in Overasselt shooting inquiry
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Two men have been arrested in Amsterdam during the investigation into a fatal shooting at a farmhouse in Gelderland.

Police said they had also recovered guns, including an automatic weapon, during searches of houses in the capital, Diemen and Hoofddorp on Tuesday.

A group of armed men descended on the small village of Overasselt in the early hours of September 1 and opened fire on a farmhouse, killing a security guard and injuring two police officers.

The man living in the house, 28-year-old Jan G., was arrested in Germany two weeks ago on suspicion of trying to smuggle cocaine through the port of Dunkirk.

He is believed to have been targeted as retribution for a stolen drugs shipment, according to a video that police obtained in the days afterwards.

Bolle Jos

The Telegraaf reported that the 1,283kg shipment belonged to “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers, Europe’s most wanted criminal, who is believed to be living in Sierra Leone.

The arrest of the two suspects, aged 24 and 25, takes the total number of arrests to 36. Most of the others have appeared in court charged with murder or manslaughter.

Two of the suspects are minors aged 16 and 17, the rest are men from France, Netherlands, Algeria, Libya, Belgium and Ukraine – all aged between 18 and 32.

A third man, aged 19, was arrested at one of the houses raided by police. His connection to the gang is being investigated.

To mark the occasion, the speaker of the lower-house Sejm, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, personally informed Cobra of the decision. “An application for transfer to retirement?” said Czarzasty, sitting opposite the extremely well-behaved Cobra in a video published by the Sejm. “Impeccable reputation. No disciplinary punishments. You’ve never barked in the Sejm,” he read from her files. “OK, signed. As of tomorrow, you are free.” Cobra idzie na emeryturę! 🐕‍🦺 Decyzję o przejściu w stan spoczynku przypieczętował podpisem Marszałek Sejmu @wlodekczarzasty. 😉 Psy Straży Marszałkowskiej to ważny element systemu ochrony Sejmu. Czuwają nad bezpieczeństwem wszystkich osób w gmachach pozostających w zarządzie… pic.twitter.com/dKRvHOlKxe — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 30, 2026 On a more serious note, the Sejm pointed to the vital role played by dogs in the so-called Speaker’s Guard (Straż Marszałkowska), which is responsible for security in parliament. “They watch over the safety of all people in the buildings managed by the chancellery of the Sejm,” they wrote, thanking Cobra for eight years of “exemplary” service and wishing her well on her “well-deserved retirement”. Two weeks ago, the Sejm announced the arrival of a new dog, Otik, who would serve as part of the Speaker’s Guard. He has worked alongside Cobra and another canine colleague, Hela, until now. State broadcaster TVP reports that Cobra was one of the first dogs to enter service in the Speaker’s Guard. It notes that dogs serving in the force are eligible for retirement after reaching the age of nine. Their handler has the option of taking in the dog after it retires, or they can nominate another person to care for the animal. The chancellery of the Sejm then continues to cover the costs of any veterinary care that the dog requires. It has not been revealed where and with whom Cobra will spend her retirement. In 2021, Poland’s government moved to introduce retirement benefits for dogs and horses who had served in the police force, border guard and fire service, providing them with support after they finished working. The following year, that was extended to the prison service. World.title: Inflation hits 4% in Poland as fuel prices surge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s inflation accelerated to an annual rate of 4.0% in September, up from 3.4% a month earlier, driven primarily by higher fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the end of Polish government subsidies that kept down prices at the pump. The development means that inflation has now risen above the upper bound of 3.5% set by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which aims to keep the figure at 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Analysts say that an interest rate hike by the NBP is now more likely. The new preliminary inflation figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that prices in September were 4% higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since June 2025. On a monthly basis, prices in September were up 0.7% from August. The rise was caused in particular by the price of fuel for private transport, which was up 36.1% on a year earlier and 9.2% from the previous month. Energy prices also rose, with electricity, gas and other fuels up 4.9% year-on-year and 0.9% month-on-month. To shield consumers from the energy crisis triggered by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Poland has twice introduced temporary measures to curb petrol station prices, including daily price caps and cuts in VAT and excise duty. The system was in place from March to June and again during the the last two weeks of August. The government has been under pressure from the opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to reintroduce the subsidies. However, it argues that Nawrocki’s decision to block a proposed windfall tax on fuel companies makes the measures harder to fund Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices provided some offset, falling 0.5% from a year earlier, although they edged up 0.1% from August. Analysts, however, expect food prices to rise later in the year to reflect lower agricultural yields. According to GUS’s own estimates, also published on Wednesday, the grain harvest came in 5% lower compared to the last season. This will, in turn, “push the CPI index higher in the coming months”, wrote Erste Bank. The breach of the upper end of the central bank’s inflation target and the 4% threshold could influence the stance of the NBP’s Monetary Policy Council (RPP), prompting it to hike rates, added Erste Bank analysts. Inflacja CPI we wrześniu w górę do 4,0%r/r (ING: 4,2%; konsensus: 4,1%). Wyraźny wzrost cen paliw (36,1%r/r) odpowiada już za ok. połowę wzrostu cen w ujęciu rocznym. Zahamowanie spadków cen żywności m/m. Inflacja bazowa prawdopodobnie w dół do 3,0-3,1%r/r, co oznacza że wciąż… pic.twitter.com/AqdIXBthFl — ING Economics Poland (@ING_EconomicsPL) September 30, 2026 Economists at ING Bank Śląski, meanwhile, expect the first rate hike – after a series of nine cautious cuts between September 2023 and March 2026 – to come in early 2027. “The RPP may opt to wait, leaving interest rates unchanged in October, with discussions on potential monetary policy tightening beginning in November following the release of the NBP’s new projections,” they wrote on X. Poland’s benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75%, down from a peak of 6.75% reached during the country’s last tightening cycle in 2021-2022, when policymakers were grappling with persistent inflation fuelled by the post-pandemic recovery and the war in Ukraine. Inflation peaked at 18.4% during that period.

We cannot do what we do without your support. The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, has launched a planned new Polish-American Centre to be established in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city. Rose symbolically laid a cornerstone for the new facility and announced a $150,000 (577,000 zloty) grant to restore and preserve the site. The centre, whose website describes it as a “home for all Polish-American initiatives in Poland”, will be established alongside the famous mound in Kraków created in honour of Tadeusz Kościuszko, a hero of both the Polish and American struggles for independence in the 18th century. Proud to announce a $150,000 AFCP grant to help restore and preserve the future site of the Kościuszko Mound’s Polish American Center — a living symbol of the friendship between our two nations. Under @POTUS, we remain committed to preserving the shared history that binds the… pic.twitter.com/5atStUIid2 — Ambassador Tom Rose (@USAmbPoland) September 29, 2026 “This is a tremendous opportunity for me, on behalf of President Donald Trump and the American people, to celebrate what I consider the most important relationship the United States has with Europe today,” said Rose at the ceremony on Monday. “America is fortunate to have many, many good friends around the world. But we have no better friend in Europe,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF. Together with Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska, the speaker of Poland’s Senate, he laid a cornerstone for the new centre and announced the $150,000 grant, which comes from the Ambassadors’ Fund for Cultural Preservation, a programme run by the US State Department. “Tadeusz Kościuszko is a symbol of the historical bond between Poland and the USA,” declared Kidawa-Błońska. “There is no better place for the Polish-American Centre than Kraków and the mound commemorating a hero of both nations.” Tadeusz Kościuszko to symbol historycznej więzi między Polską i USA. Nie ma lepszego miejsca dla Centrum Polsko-Amerykańskiego niż Kraków i kopiec upamiętniający bohatera obu narodów. Niech powołane dziś Centrum dobrze służy naszym relacjom, które budujemy od 250 lat 🇵🇱🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/8nOkCYDLfD — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) September 29, 2026 Kościuszko’s Mound was established in Kraków in 1823, following the pattern of two prehistoric mounds that already existed in the city. It honours Kościuszko, a military officer who had fought against Russian rule over Poland and in the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. Construction of the new Polish-American Centre is being supported by the Kościuszko Mound Committee in Kraków in partnership with USA250PL, the platform for celebrations in Poland of this year’s 250th anniversary of the American Declaration of Independence. The Kościuszko Mound Committee has long been engaged in efforts to preserve the mound against partial collapses caused by heavy rain. Polish hydraulics manufacturer PONAR Wadowice is also listed as a partner of the new centre. The facility says it “will serve as a living symbol of friendship, understanding, and transatlantic cooperation”, providing “a welcoming space for dialogue, creativity, and exchange”. The centre will house event spaces, conference rooms, and offices. In June, the centre acted as a patron of a United States–Central and Eastern Europe Connection Weekend at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. Next year it plans a commemoration of the Battle of Saratoga, where Kościuszko designed fortifications that contributed to the American victory. Poland has long looked to the United States for support and as an example during its struggle for independence over the last two centuries, including during the period of partitions in the 19th century, the reestablishment of the Polish state after the First World War, and during the later decades of communist rule. Since the fall of communism, the US has become Warsaw’s most important security partner – including establishing its first permanent military garrison, named Fort Kościuszko, in Poland in 2023. The US has opened its first military garrison in Poland, and its first anywhere on NATO's eastern flank. "This is a historic moment," says Poland's defence minister. "We have been striving for years for this word 'permanent' and it has now become fact" https://t.co/knJEcqv4MB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 21, 2023 Last week, President Donald Trump, in a virtual address to the Polish-American Congress (an entity unrelated to the new centre in Kraków), praised his Polish counterpart Karol Nawrocki, a close Trump ally, and described himself as a “great friend of the people of Poland”. Shortly before that, Nawrocki had expressed confidence that a planned new US military base in Poland would soon be confirmed, and suggested that it would be named Fort Trump. World.title: EU court rejects Poland’s request to suspend implementation of Mercosur trade deal
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Court of Justice of the European Union has rejected a request from Poland to suspend the implementation of the EU’s recently launched free trade agreement with the Mercosur bloc of South American countries. The CJEU found that the Polish government had failed to prove its claims that the trade deal would cause serious harm to European farmers, consumers or the environment. #ECJ: Order in Case C-460/26 R Poland v Council: should the implementation of the Council’s decision authorising the provisional application of the EU-Mercosur interim trade agreement be suspended pending the Court’s ruling?#CJEU #Mercosur pic.twitter.com/ocb4I4PsE8 — EU Court of Justice (@EUCourtPress) September 29, 2026 Poland has long been critical of the agreement, in particular over the potential negative impact that imports of agricultural products from Mercosur, which includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, could have on Polish farmers, who have repeatedly protested against the deal. In January, Poland failed in a bid to block the agreement at the European Council, where 21 of the EU’s 27 member states voted in favour of the deal. Although the agreement has not yet received final ratification – still requiring approval from the European Parliament and national parliaments – it nevertheless went into provisional force on 1 May. Shortly afterwards, Poland submitted a complaint to the CJEU, calling for implementation of the agreement to be suspended. It argued, first of all, that the process through which the deal had been provisionally implemented violated the EU’s treaties. Second, it claimed that liberalising trade in agricultural products without imposing the same production standards in both the EU and Mercosur created a risk of harm to human and animal health, the environment, the income of farmers, and the functioning of the market in the EU. Poland has filed a complaint to the European Court of Justice against the EU's free-trade deal with the South American Mercosur bloc that recently went into provisional force. It wants the agreement to be suspended until the court issues a ruling https://t.co/wE7DIbDazU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 However, on Tuesday, the CJEU announced that it had dismissed the application to suspend the agreement, finding that “Poland has not provided any concrete evidence to establish the likelihood and imminence of serious and irreparable damage”. The court pointed out that agricultural products from Mercosur could already be imported to the EU before the free-trade deal, and that they were and continue to be subject to food safety and health regulations similar to those for products manufactured in the EU. It also noted that the new trade deal includes tools allowing the EU to bar products that do not meet standards, including emergency measures in the case of a serious threat to human, animal or plant life. Finally, the CJEU said that Poland’s “general and abstract claims” regarding potential harm to farmers and markets did not include “any evidence capable of establishing, with a sufficient degree of probability, that the implementation [of the agreement]…will cause disruption”. In response to the court’s decision, the Polish government’s spokesman, Adam Szłapka, immediately blamed the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) administration, which was in power in Poland from 2015 to 2023. Szłapka said that the details of the Mercosur deal had been agreed during that period and that PiS had “failed to secure Polish interests in any way”. He argued that it was the current government which secured the addition of last-minute safeguards intended to protect farmers. The spokesman also noted that Polish agricultural exports to the Mercosur bloc have actually increased under the new agreement while imports from there have fallen, showing that “Polish farmers are profiting from this”. Rząd i Premier Tusk najpierw mówili, że umowa UE-Mercosur będzie „bezpieczna dla polskich rolników”. Potem nie potrafili zbudować koalicji blokującej w Radzie Europejskiej – choć polityka europejska jest domeną rządu. Politycy KO, PSL i Lewicy nie potrafili nikogo przekonać.… https://t.co/EqOJr4sneP — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) September 29, 2026 However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the foreign policy office of President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the CJEU’s decision showed the impotence of the current pro-EU government. “The government and Prime Minister Tusk first said that the EU-Mercosur agreement would be ‘safe for Polish farmers’. Then they failed to build a blocking coalition in the European Council,” wrote Przydacz. “In the end, under pressure from public opinion in Poland, they filed a complaint with the ECJ. [It was] so weak that they lost the request for interim relief,” he added. “Ineffective policy and ineffective government.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland recovers looted painting that once hung in SS officers’ club in occupied Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish painting looted by Nazi Germany during World War Two, and which once hung in an SS officers’ club, has been returned by its owner, who donated it to the National Museum in Warsaw. “History is coming home,” said culture minister Marta Cienkowska, celebrating the return of Alfred Wierusz-Kowalski’s Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow, which she described as “one of the most significant wartime losses in Polish painting”. Her ministry is responsible for seeking the return of tens of thousands of artworks and other cultural items that were looted during the war and remain missing. Kolejny sukces restytucyjny! Odzyskaliśmy jedną z cenniejszych i najbardziej znanych strat wojennych malarstwa polskiego. Obraz „Zima – Odwrót Napoleona spod Moskwy” Alfreda Wierusza-Kowalskiego trafił dziś do zbiorów Muzeum Narodowego w Warszawie. To efekt naszej współpracy z… pic.twitter.com/Y0wDIBgIGG — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) September 28, 2026 Wierusz-Kowalski, who was active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a renowned realist painter whose work often featured animals alongside people. His Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow had, by the 1930s, become part of the collection of Andrzej Rotwand, a wealthy banker and industrialist. In June 1939, it was featured in an exhibition organised by the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts in Warsaw, which occupied the building that is now the famous Zachęta National Gallery of Art. However, the exhibition was brought to an abrupt end when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The works on display, along with other items from the gallery, were seized by the occupiers, with many used to decorate the offices and apartments of German officials. Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow was displayed in a club for high-ranking SS and police officers located in Warsaw’s Blanka Palace. The same building also housed Warsaw’s German-installed commissioner, Helmut Otto, and mayor, Ludwig Leist. No information has been released as to the fate of the painting in the immediate aftermath of the war. However, it eventually came into the possession of Ewa Tsonis, who has now handed it back. Speaking at a ceremony in the National Museum in Warsaw, Tsonis said that her late father, Michał Stefan Koryzna, had purchased the painting in the 1960s from Desa, a major gallery and auction house, in the city of Kraków. “I grew up with this painting. It was greatly appreciated and loved in our family,” she said. However, after recently conducting research into the painting’s history, she became aware of its provenance and notified the culture ministry. Experts from the National Museum in Warsaw confirmed the identity of the painting, which remains in good condition and in its original frame. Tsonis then donated the work to the museum. “Restitution is not possible without the cooperation of many people and institutions – both on the side of the state and on the part of the owners of the works,” said Cienkowska, who thanked Tsonis for her “incredibly responsible and civic-minded attitude”. “Such attitudes are still rare but, because we constantly talk about restitution – we search for lost works and strive to recover them – we are increasingly approached by people who own lost objects and feel a sense of responsibility for cultural heritage.” Cienkowska noted that the culture ministry has so far secured the return of over 920 works, with around 200 more restitution cases currently underway in 18 countries. Germany has agreed to return to Poland a collection of 73 medieval documents that were looted during WWII. The culture minister has hailed it as "the most important and valuable return of stolen cultural heritage in modern Polish history" https://t.co/GxHQ8A0jyr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 1, 2025 However, that is still just a small fraction of the over 60,000 missing items listed in the ministry’s database of missing works, which includes seven further paintings by Wierusz-Kowalski. Two other works from Rotwand’s collection – Italian Woman by Anna Bilińska and Mother with Children by Kazimierz Alchimowicz – were also hung in the SS officers’ club during the war and today remain missing. Poland has in recent years stepped up efforts to secure the return of historical and cultural items looted during the German and Soviet occupations. In 2022, it appealed to UNESCO for help in securing the return of cultural items that remain missing after being looted by Nazi Germany. It also launched a campaign seeking the return of thousands of items that ended up in Russia after the war. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the “growing threat from Russia”. Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead. The move follows a series of violations of Polish airspace over the last year by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter, as well as Russia’s increasing use of jet-powered drones to attack targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border. Polska zmienia procedury użycia uzbrojenia dla lotnictwa w przypadku zwalczania obcych statków powietrznych. To wnioski Dowódcy Operacyjnego generała Ireneusza Nowaka z ostatnich tygodni. To także odpowiedź na rosnące zagrożenie ze strony Rosji, doświadczenia wojny w Ukrainie… — Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) September 28, 2026 “In the coming days, the defence minister will change the procedures for firing by Polish planes and helicopters at objects flying to us from the direction of Russia,” announced deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk on Monday, quoted by news service Defence24. The change, as Tomczyk explained in a statement later issued on social media, will shift requirements away from requiring visual identification of foreign aerial objects and towards so-called “positive identification”. The latter involves identifying an object based on a combination of several other, non-visual sources of information, such as using radar and other sensors to determine its speed, altitude, trajectory and flight parameters, as well as a lack of IFF (identification friend or foe) from an object. Tomczyk said that the change was being made based on the “conclusions from recent weeks” made by the operational commander of Poland’s armed forces, General Ireneusz Nowak. It is a “response to the growing threat from Russia, experiences from the war in Ukraine, and the emergence of new air attack means – primarily fast jet drones and cruise missiles in the case of which the time for reaction is very brief”, added Tomczyk. The minister said that positive identification would only be issued when there is a “sufficiently high degree of certainty in determining what we are dealing with”. He noted that accurate target identification is particularly crucial in peacetime, when there are civilian aircraft in Polish airspace. The change will mean “not less identification, but a different way of conducting it: faster and based on data from multiple sources”. Poland's government has issued public guidance on how to act in the case of airborne attacks, amid growing concerns over the threat from Russia. It is also preparing evacuation plans and clearer markings for 85,000 shelters across the countryhttps://t.co/vMEMU6mlRx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026 Defence24 reports that the government, military and many experts have found current rules of engagement to be overly restrictive and not suited to meeting the scale and type of threat facing Poland today. It points to last week’s violation of Polish airspace by a Russian helicopter, which crossed the border from Kaliningrad and spent around 42 seconds in Poland before returning. The website also notes that Russia’s growing use of jet-powered drones, which are able to travel much faster than traditional unmanned aerial vehicles, is a further threat. Such drones have recently been used to attack targets along the Ukrainian side of the border with Poland, including a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026 “Until now, we have not utilised these [non-visual identification] capabilities because they are typically reserved for a state of war or martial law,” said Tomczyk. “However, given the threat, and the fact that Poland today struggles daily with the possibility of drones entering our country, we must implement these changes for the benefit of both pilots and national security.” In July this year, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile also entered Polish airspace before landing in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders. Some were shot down but many struck the ground. Earlier this month, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental, says Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk, citing intelligence sources. The aim would be to create a sense of "NATO's helplessness", he says https://t.co/9MFPiEEkIV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 18, 2026 Poland has invested heavily in its air defences in recent years, including buying Patriot batteries and fighter aircraft from the United States, as well as developing a new anti-drone system with Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace. The government has also recently moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters. World.title: Ninth-century Arabic silver coins found near Viking trading centre in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Several early medieval Arabic silver coins have been found in a forest near Elbląg in northern Poland. Experts believe they may have belonged to merchants travelling to or from the Viking Age port of Truso, which was situated nearby. The silver dirhams date back around 1,200 years, to the first half of the ninth century, before the founding of the Polish state. They may have remained in circulation until the turn of the 10th/11th century, the time of the settlement’s collapse. The discovery of the “new treasure” was announced last week by the Archaeological and Historical Museum in Elbląg. It did not reveal who had unearthed them, but said that the find had taken place during a legal search in a forest near the town of Młynary, just east of Elbląg. After conservation and processing work, the coins will be included in the collection of the museum, whose archaeologists will also visit the site hoping for further finds. The museum’s Jakub Jagodziński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the find consists of “six early medieval Arabic dirhams and two fragments of these silver coins”. He said that they are provisionally dated to the first half of the 9th century, but a more precise estimate will be possible after they are processed. The coins could have belonged to merchants travelling along the routes leading to or from Truso or to Prussian guards who later collected tolls on these routes, Jagodziński explained. Truso was a Viking Age port of trade set up by the Scandinavians on the shores of lake Druzno near the Vistula river delta. Established by the late 7th century and active until the early 11th century, its location enabled trade extending towards Kyivan Rus, Byzantium and the Islamic world. Historians knew of Truso’s existence because of the account of the Anglo-Saxon traveller Wulfstan of Hedeby. Centuries-long efforts to find the precise site proved fruitless until it was finally discovered in the early 1980s by the young archaeologist Marek Jagodziński, Jakub’s father. Finds of Arab coins in Poland are not unprecedented. A silver deposit was discovered in 1986 on the site of Truso itself, consisting of 11 complete coins and five fragments. Coins found there were minted in places including Baghdad and Damascus, according to the Medievalists.net website. More recently, in 2024, a fragment of an early medieval Arabic dirham was found during renovations of an old manor house on the Baltic coast in northwestern Poland. In transactions involving dirhams, it was the value of the silver that mattered, so the coins were often broken into pieces, archaeologist Grzegorz Kurka told PAP. “Therefore, when hoards of Arab coins are discovered in Poland, they are divided into several pieces. Whole coins are also found, but much less frequently,” he explained. World.title: Prague Hospitals Warn of Critical Blood Shortages
World.content:
Several hospitals in Prague are reporting critically low blood supplies, prompting the Czech Ministry of Health to urge people to donate blood in the coming days.

The shortage is affecting more than individual blood groups. Hospitals and transfusion centers in several parts of the Czech Republic are reporting a broader decline in available supplies, with some facilities nearing the minimum levels needed to maintain safe operations.



The situation differs from one region to another. Some transfusion centers still have adequate reserves, while others are short of particular blood groups or are approaching critical levels.

The shortage also extends to individual blood components. In Prague, the Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine (IKEM) is currently seeking more platelet donors regardless of blood type.

People planning to donate are advised to check the latest information on the website or social media channels of their chosen transfusion center before visiting.

Why hospitals need more donors

Hospitals depend on regular blood donations not only during emergencies but also for planned medical treatment.

Blood is routinely needed for surgery, childbirth and the treatment of patients who require repeated transfusions. This includes some cancer patients whose treatment can interfere with the body’s production of blood cells.

Blood donations are also essential in cases of severe complications during childbirth. Heavy blood loss can become life-threatening within a short period, and an adequate supply of donated blood can be critical to saving the lives of mothers and newborns.

The demand for blood can increase during the summer and holiday period, when hospitals continue to perform scheduled procedures while also dealing with more injuries and traffic accidents. At the same time, the number of people coming to donate tends to fall as residents leave the country or travel elsewhere.

Number of donors continues to decline

Official figures indicate that the Czech donor base has been shrinking. Around 348,000 people donated blood last year, down from 362,000 the previous year.

Transfusion centers are also losing older regular donors as they reach the age limit, while the number of younger people replacing them has not been sufficient.

In the Czech Republic, adults can generally donate blood until the age of 65, provided they weigh more than 50 kilograms. Additional eligibility restrictions may apply, including for people who have recently travelled to countries where certain infectious diseases are present.

Donating blood in the Czech Republic is voluntary and free of charge. Donors are entitled to time off work on the day of their donation, while some health insurance companies provide additional benefits or rewards for regular donors.

World.title: British Pop Star Robbie Williams to Headline Colours of Ostrava 2027
World.content:
British pop star Robbie Williams will headline the opening day of Colours of Ostrava 2027, organisers have announced.

Williams will perform on Wednesday, July 21, at the Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex, marking his return to the Czech Republic after his recent concert at Prague’s O2 Arena.



The 2027 edition of Colours of Ostrava will run from July 21 to July 24. Williams is the first major act confirmed for the festival’s lineup.

“For me, Robbie Williams is, above all, a personality. He is someone you know, even if you aren’t necessarily a fan,” said Colours of Ostrava artistic director Filip Košťálek.

“Over more than three decades, he has managed to stay relevant, evolve and surprise audiences while remaining true to himself. And those are exactly the kind of personalities we want to bring to Colours.”

Košťálek said the festival is looking for artists with strong stories and songs who can create memorable moments for audiences.

Williams fits that profile after more than three decades at the centre of British pop. Since launching his solo career in the 1990s, following his departure from Take That, he has become one of the UK’s most successful solo artists.

His latest studio album, Britpop, was released in early 2025 after a delay. Williams had originally planned to release the record earlier but moved the date following the announcement of a new album by Taylor Swift.

The delay was also connected to Williams’ ambition to return to No. 1 on the UK album chart. The strategy paid off, with Britpop reaching the top of the chart and extending his record-setting run of No. 1 albums in the UK.

Williams has remained a major live attraction as well. His most recent Czech concert took place at Prague’s O2 Arena, where he combined songs from across his career with the humour and interaction that have become a defining part of his performances.

More artists for Colours of Ostrava 2027 are expected to be announced in the coming months.

World.title: Techno, Art and Live Performance Come Together at Strahov on October 10
World.content:
On October 10, the Prague electronic music collective EDEN will bring Rotten To The Core to Stadion Strahov for one of the collective’s largest and most ambitious events to date.

Running from 10pm until 7am, the night will bring together international and local DJs, dancers and visual artists for an event built around music, performance and visual art.



The lineup includes VLACE, SCHELLT, RiVid, 2NDRA and Mila (5), with the programme focused on techno and acid.

Among the artists, 2NDRA is a Prague-based schranz and techno producer and performer and one of the founders of EDEN Collective. RiVid, meanwhile, is a Czech-Japanese hard techno duo.

The event takes a broader approach to the club experience, combining the music programme with visual elements, art installations and live performances.

That approach comes at a time when electronic music events are becoming increasingly commercialised, while promoters and venues face rising production costs and growing regulatory pressures.

The event will take place beneath Strahov Stadium in Prague 6, continuing EDEN’s connection with unconventional venues and large-scale rave productions.

The collective previously hosted its 40-hour ALT BABYLON weekender in Prague in August, featuring dozens of local and international artists.

The event is for ages 18 and over, with tickets starting at CZK 300.

World.title: Václav Havel Would Be 90 This Year: From Playwright to President
World.content:
Václav Havel was one of the defining figures of modern Czech history.

Playwright, writer, dissident, political prisoner and, ultimately, the last president of Czechoslovakia and the first president of the Czech Republic, his life reflected some of the country’s most dramatic changes of the 20th century.

Born into a prominent Prague family, Havel experienced both privilege and political persecution. He became one of the leading voices of the opposition to communist rule and played a central role in the Velvet Revolution of 1989.



On October 5th, 2026, Havel would have turned 90. Here is a look at his life, political career and some of the places in Prague and beyond connected to him.

From a privileged Prague family to a banned writer

Havel was born in Prague on October 5, 1936, into a wealthy and well-connected family. His uncle, Miloš Havel, founded Barrandov Studios, while his grandfather was involved in construction and real estate.

His family’s position changed dramatically after the Communist Party took power in Czechoslovakia in 1948. Their property was confiscated, and Havel faced restrictions on his education and career because of his family background.

During the political liberalisation of the 1960s, Havel became increasingly involved in Prague’s theatre scene. He worked as a stagehand and later as a dramaturge, while also establishing himself as a playwright. His plays often explored power, bureaucracy and the absurdity of life under an authoritarian system.

The hopes of 1968

The Prague Spring of 1968 brought a period of political and cultural liberalisation to Czechoslovakia. Censorship was abolished, previously banned books began appearing in print and films that had been restricted were shown in cinemas again.

Havel embraced the new atmosphere and became increasingly active in public life. But the reforms ended abruptly when Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia on August 21, 1968.

Havel opposed the occupation and the return to political repression. He was subsequently banned from publishing and working in the theatre. For a period, he worked as a manual labourer at a brewery in Trutnov.

He later became one of the most prominent figures of the Czechoslovak dissident movement. He was a signatory of Charter 77, a civic initiative calling on the communist government to respect human rights, and was repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

From dissident to president

The communist regime collapsed in November 1989 following mass demonstrations across Czechoslovakia. Havel was one of the leading figures of the Civic Forum, the opposition movement that helped negotiate the peaceful transfer of power.

On December 29, 1989, he was elected president of Czechoslovakia.

Havel remained in office after the country split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993, becoming the first president of the newly independent Czech Republic. During his political career, he supported the country’s integration into Western institutions, including NATO, and advocated closer ties with the European Union.

His presidency also left a visible mark on Prague Castle. Parts of the complex were opened to the public, while the South Gardens were restored following their pre-war design.

Life after Prague Castle

Havel left the presidency in 2003 but remained active as a writer and public figure. He continued to comment on political and social issues and maintained friendships with artists, intellectuals and international figures.

Among them was the Dalai Lama, who visited Havel in Prague on several occasions. Havel died on December 18, 2011, at his country house in Hrádeček, near the Krkonoše mountains.

Places connected to Václav Havel in Prague

Several Prague locations are closely connected to Havel and his family.

One is Lucerna Palace on Wenceslas Square, built by Havel’s grandfather. The complex includes the historic Lucerna Cinema, which has been operating for more than a century, as well as the famous Lucerna Café.

Prague Castle is another essential stop. Havel lived and worked there during his years as president and initiated several changes that made parts of the complex more accessible to the public.

Outside Prague, Havel was also closely associated with Lány Chateau, the traditional summer residence of Czech presidents. During his time there, he was known to visit the local pub and meet residents without the formality normally associated with a head of state.

World.title: Prague’s Kramář Villa to Open for Free Visits on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Kramář Villa will open to the public on October 3, giving visitors a chance to see inside one of the Czech government’s official residences.

Admission will be free.

The villa, located on Gogolova Street in Prague’s Letná district, is the official residence of the Czech prime minister. It was also the home of Karel Kramář, Czechoslovakia’s first prime minister, and his wife, Nadezhda.



Visitors during the open house will be able to take guided tours of the building and learn about its history, architecture and former residents. The tour will include parts of the villa that are normally closed to the public, including its living quarters and ceremonial rooms.

Built with a combination of Neo-Baroque and Art Nouveau influences, Kramář Villa has been one of Prague’s government residences since the early 20th century.

Its history is closely linked to Karel Kramář, who became the first prime minister of Czechoslovakia following the country’s establishment in 1918.

The open house will also include access to the villa’s garden. Located above the city, the grounds provide views across Prague and will remain open for longer than the villa itself.

The villa will welcome visitors from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on October 3. The garden will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

World.title: Czech Study Finds Supporting Homeless People Can Save Public Money
World.content:
A Czech experiment in which homeless people received CZK 100,000 with no conditions attached suggests that early financial support can reduce some of the costs associated with homelessness.

The project, known as New Leaf, was carried out by the Czech organization Neposeda in cooperation with researchers from Charles University.



The findings indicate that the state spends an average of about CZK 200,000 a year on each person experiencing homelessness, with healthcare, social services and police work accounting for a significant share of the total.

The researchers concluded that leaving people without support can ultimately be more expensive for public finances than providing targeted assistance.

How the New Leaf experiment worked

The project ran from summer 2024 until the end of 2025 and was inspired by a similar initiative in Canada.

Researchers focused on people who had been living on the streets for no more than two and a half years. The aim was to examine whether intervention at an earlier stage of homelessness could prevent longer-term problems.

Participants were divided into several groups. Forty people received CZK 100,000 without restrictions on how the money could be used. Another 20 were offered the support of a personal social worker instead, while 40 people formed a control group and received no additional assistance.

The study initially involved 100 people. One participant died from a serious illness shortly after the project began, leaving 99 participants in the final research sample.

The researchers tracked participants’ use of public services and their contact with state authorities, including emergency medical services, hospitals, outpatient healthcare, social services and police.

Healthcare accounts for the largest share

The study estimates that the state spends around CZK 200,000 annually on each homeless person.

Healthcare represented almost 43% of the estimated expenditure. Low-threshold services, which provide basic support and a safe place for people experiencing homelessness, accounted for around a quarter of the total.

Police work represented another 9%, or more than 18,000 crowns per person each year.

The wider cost to public finances

Data from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs recorded 11,641 homeless people in the Czech Republic in the previous year.

Based on the estimated annual cost per person, direct public expenditure associated with homelessness amounts to roughly 2.33 billion crowns a year.

World.title: Smartwings Cuts Prague Flights as Winter Schedule Shrinks
World.content:
Smartwings is reducing its winter flight schedule from Prague, with several routes being cancelled, frequencies cut and new connections postponed until spring 2027.

The biggest changes will affect Spain, a popular choice for Czech travelers looking for warmer weather during the autumn and winter months.

The airline will suspend flights between Prague and Valencia from November 2 until the beginning of March.

Flights to several other Spanish destinations will also be reduced. Smartwings will cut its Málaga service from two flights a day to one, while Barcelona will move from daily flights to four to six services a week.

Flights to Mallorca will be reduced from four per week to two. The Prague–Madrid route will continue, but flights will operate on an irregular schedule.

Smartwings is also suspending flights from Prague to Nice until early March.

New Prague routes pushed back

Several routes that were expected to launch this year will now have to wait until spring 2027.

The postponed connections include new services to Venice and Bergen, Norway. Smartwings has also delayed the return of flights to Brussels and Bucharest.

Both Brussels and Bucharest were suspended in the spring, with Smartwings originally planning to restore the routes in October.

Eurowings also reduces Prague services

Eurowings is making changes to its Prague schedule as well. The German carrier has cancelled its planned winter flights to Madeira, Portugal.

The route had been scheduled to return for the winter season, but Eurowings will instead offer tickets to Madeira through a partnership with Smartwings, which continues to operate flights to the Portuguese island.

Eurowings will also suspend its Prague–Stockholm service for most of January.

Higher fuel costs affect airline schedules

The changes come as airlines face higher operating costs linked to fuel prices.

According to Eurocontrol, the European organization responsible for coordinating air traffic management, jet fuel prices in Europe more than doubled between the beginning of the year and mid-September.

Airlines around the world have been adjusting schedules as fuel costs fluctuate amid the conflict in the Middle East. Route cancellations and reduced frequencies are among the measures carriers are using to adapt to changing market conditions.

World.title: Home Baking Returns to Czech Kitchens as Flour Sales Rise
World.content:
Home baking is gaining momentum in the Czech Republic, with online supermarket Rohlik.cz reporting a sharp increase in demand for baking ingredients this year.

Flour has been at the center of the trend. Sales of organic flour have risen by almost 72 percent compared with the previous year, while conventional flour sales increased by around 23 percent.



The change has also affected the balance of sales. Organic flour previously accounted for about 19 percent of flour purchases at Rohlik.cz. That figure has now climbed to almost 25 percent.

The figures suggest that customers are not simply buying more flour but are also paying greater attention to the type and quality of the ingredients they use.

Rohlik.cz CEO Miroslava Vopatová says baking continues to play a role in family life, particularly as an activity shared across generations. The supermarket has responded by offering products at different price points, from private-label options to organic and farm-produced ingredients.

Yeast sales tell a different story

The increase in demand for flour has not been mirrored by yeast.

Sales of yeast have been gradually falling since the surge in home baking during the coronavirus pandemic. One shift remains noticeable, however: shoppers are increasingly choosing fresh yeast rather than dried yeast.

Home baking in the Czech Republic is also strongly seasonal. Christmas remains the busiest period of the year, while a smaller increase usually occurs in March and April. Demand drops during the summer months.

For experienced bakers, the quality of the final product often depends on relatively simple details. Yeast dough needs enough time and warmth to rise properly, while rushing the process can affect the result.

The preparation of the filling matters as well. Curd cheese should be drained thoroughly before being added to a cake or pastry, reducing the risk of excess moisture making the dough soggy. Fruit fillings should also be sufficiently thick rather than watery.

These practical details can make a noticeable difference, particularly in traditional Czech pastries whose recipes are often passed down through families.

World.title: Budapest antifa attack case: Maja T. prison verdict becomes final
World.content:
Metropolitan Court has reduced the prison sentence of German national Maja T., who was convicted over a series of antifa attacks on people perceived to be far-right supporters in Budapest in February 2023.

Maja T.’s sentence was cut from eight years to seven years by the Metropolitan Court on Wednesday. The court also reduced the sentence of fellow defendant Gabriele M. from seven to six years, while upholding a two-year prison sentence for German national Anna Christina M. The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

Antifa attacks targeted people seen as far-right

The defendants were accused of taking part in antifa group attacks between 9 and 11 February 2023, targeting people they believed were far-right based primarily on their clothing. The victims were allegedly identified as people attending events associated with the so-called “Day of Honour” and the Breakout Memorial Tour, gatherings connected with commemorations of a 1945 attempt by Nazi and Hungarian forces to break out of encircled Budapest.

Five antifa attacks were recorded during the period, leaving nine people injured, six of them seriously, according to reports cited in the case. Prosecutors accused Maja T. of attempted aggravated bodily harm causing life-threatening injuries and attempted serious bodily harm committed with a base motive, both allegedly carried out as part of a criminal organisation.

Defence challenged first-instance ruling

The case reached the appeals stage after both prosecutors and defence lawyers challenged the original verdicts. Maja T.’s lawyer had disputed the classification of the group as a criminal organisation and argued that video footage did not show his client actively participating in some of the attacks. The defence also questioned aspects of the medical expert evidence.

Their lawyer had additionally raised concerns about Maja T.’s ability to defend themselves while they were on hunger strike during the proceedings. Judge Géza Szalai said defendants have a right to effective legal defence, but argued that the state cannot compel a defendant to exercise that right. He said Maja T. had effectively chosen to exercise their right to express their views through the hunger strike rather than their right to participate fully in their defence.

Antifa supporters gather outside court

The verdict attracted significant attention, with supporters of Maja T. gathering outside the court before the hearing. Media and antifa supporters formed a queue to enter the courtroom, while a representative of the German embassy was also present. Maja T. entered the courtroom accompanied by officers before hearing their final sentence, writes Telex.

Another defendant, Italian national Ilaria Salis, is currently covered by a separate legal situation after being elected to the European Parliament in 2024. Proceedings against their have been suspended. The appeals court’s ruling in the present case is final.

World.title: EPPO chief Kövesi reveals what could be achieved in Hungary by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office
World.content:
European Chief Prosecutor Laura Codruța Kövesi says the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) could begin operating in Hungary as early as next year, potentially giving European prosecutors powers to investigate EU-fund fraud, corruption and money laundering in the country.

European Chief Prosecutor gives interview to the Hungarian press

Speaking to Telex during a visit to Budapest, Kövesi said she had met Hungary’s justice, finance and interior ministers, whom she described as strongly committed to making the initiative work. She said the sides had agreed that ten European delegated prosecutors would work in Hungary, alongside police officers, financial investigators and customs officials specifically assigned to EPPO cases.

Hungary did not originally join the EPPO, which began operating in June 2021. However, the EU has now confirmed Hungary’s participation, with the office set to become operational after the appointment of the country’s European Prosecutor.

What could the EPPO investigate?

The chief prosecutor said the office would be able to investigate fraud involving EU funds, as well as related corruption, embezzlement and money laundering. The EPPO’s existing mandate covers fraud affecting the EU budget involving more than EUR 10,000, while cross-border VAT fraud falls within its remit when the damage reaches at least EUR 10 million.

She said the office would examine matters falling within its jurisdiction from 2021 onwards once its Hungarian operation is fully functional. Kövesi also warned that Hungary could become a particular target for Chinese criminal networks, although she did not identify specific cases that could be investigated. The European chief prosecutor said the first investigations could start next year, following the establishment of the Hungarian office and necessary legislative changes.

Raids, arrests and asset seizures

Kövesi said European delegated prosecutors would have the same investigative powers as domestic prosecutors, including ordering investigative measures, conducting searches, requesting arrests, bringing charges and freezing or seizing assets. The EPPO’s cross-border structure could be particularly significant when allegedly misappropriated money or assets are moved abroad.

The chief prosecutor cited property purchases elsewhere in Europe as an example, arguing that a national authority can face difficulties tracing and securing assets outside its jurisdiction. The EPPO already operates as an independent European prosecution service, conducting investigations and bringing cases before national courts in participating countries.

Stay up-to-date: Orbán-era ministers arrested as National Asset Recovery and Protection Office and prosecution order detention

‘It is time for them to take back their country’

Kövesi believes some investigations could produce results within a year or two, depending partly on Hungary’s legislative framework and the independence and quality of the prosecutors appointed. She also offered a broader assessment of Hungary’s recent political history, saying: “It is time for them to take back their country,” and arguing that police, prosecutors and judges must be able to perform their duties independently.

Asked about cooperation with Viktor Orbán’s governments, Kövesi said there had been cooperation in some VAT cases, but claimed cooperation became more difficult when investigations involved people close to politicians. The EPPO already has a cooperation agreement with Hungary’s prosecution service dating from 2021, but until now Hungary has remained outside the office’s full operational structure.

World.title: BudapestGO receives useful new update to make metro journeys easier
World.content:
Should you board at the front, in the middle or towards the end of the train? The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has added a new feature to BudapestGO that will now help passengers make this choice.

When planning a metro journey, the app shows passengers exactly which carriage they should board to reach the exit at their destination as quickly as possible, or to make a simpler transfer to another metro line. The new feature will be rolled out gradually and will be available to all users within a few days.

BudapestGO gains another useful feature

BKK is continuously developing BudapestGO to ensure that the app can provide assistance with more and more aspects of everyday travel. One of the key new features in the update released on 29 September – which will become available to all users within a few days – is that, when planning a journey, the app now also shows passengers which part of the metro train they should board.

The new feature can be particularly useful on journeys where passengers have little time to make a connection or are less familiar with the metro station concerned. At the same time, it can also help regular passengers travelling along the same route to reach their exit more directly, avoiding a few unnecessary minutes or detours.

The new feature also plans step-free routes without any additional settings

The new feature works automatically, without requiring any additional settings. If a route recommended by BudapestGO includes a metro journey, the app indicates which carriage passengers should board to reach their destination exit more quickly or make a faster transfer between metro lines.

The app also takes accessibility into account when planning a journey. In such cases, it recommends the carriage closest to the exit with a lift and will only plan routes that are accessible without steps.

BudapestGO continues to evolve

The latest update is another milestone in the continuous development of BudapestGO. When planning new features, BKK takes customers’ needs and feedback into account, and requests for recommendations on which metro carriage to board have been raised in feedback from several customers.

The aim is for BudapestGO to provide travellers with an increasing amount of information to help them choose the most suitable route, making public transport faster, more predictable and more convenient as a result.

World.title: Orbán-era ministers arrested as National Asset Recovery and Protection Office and prosecution order detention
World.content:
Two former ministers from Viktor Orbán’s governments have been caught up in a major corruption investigation, with one ordered into pre-trial detention and prosecutors seeking the detention of another.

The cases involving former national development minister Miklós Seszták and former culture minister Balázs Hankó concern alleged misuse of public funds and bribery. Both politicians deny wrongdoing.

Court orders Seszták detention

A Budapest court on Wednesday ordered Seszták, a Christian Democratic Party (Kereszténydemokrata Néppárt, KDNP, the junior partner of Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz) MP and former national development minister, to be held in custody for 30 days.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal, NVVH) suspects Seszták of accepting bribes and committing other offences. The court said it found no grounds to doubt the reasonable suspicion of corruption offences and ruled that detention was necessary to protect the integrity of the investigation.

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?

Seszták was involved in the so-called Volánbusz case

According to prosecutors, Seszták allegedly accepted bribes worth hundreds of millions or even billions of forints from construction companies during his time as minister between 2014 and 2018. Investigators also allege that Seszták and Norbert Szivek, then chief executive of the Hungarian National Asset Management Company, obtained around HUF 11 billion (more than EUR 30 million) in illicit benefits.

The investigation also concerns alleged losses linked to Volánbusz procurements. Authorities suspect that more than 600 second-hand buses were purchased at inflated prices between 2015 and 2018, causing around HUF 10 billion (EUR 27.3 million) in damage.

Investigators also allege that the purchase of a Volán company headquarters in Kecskemét was overpriced, resulting in losses of at least HUF 550 million (more than EUR 1.5 million). Seszták has pleaded not guilty. His detention order is not yet final and his defence has appealed.

Miklós Seszták (L). Photo: Facebook/Dr. Seszták Miklós

Stay up-to-date: Former Fidesz minister Seszták gives interview before being detained over EUR 34 million bribery scheme

Prosecutors seek Hankó’s detention

Meanwhile, prosecutors in Bács-Kiskun County have requested the detention of Balázs Hankó and another suspect in a separate investigation into alleged mismanagement. Hankó, who served as culture minister, is accused of helping divert funding administered by Hungary’s National Cultural Fund (NKA) away from its legally designated purposes.

Prosecutors allege that a parallel decision-making system was used to distribute funds according to political considerations. Authorities say that 1,079 grants were improperly allocated between 3 September 2025 and 30 March 2026, allegedly causing HUF 17.3 billion (more than EUR 47.25 million) in financial damage to the central budget.

According to Telex’s report, prosecutors cited the seriousness of the alleged offences and the suspects’ extensive networks as reasons for seeking detention, arguing that there was a risk of flight and interference with the investigation.

Former minister Balázs Hankó. Photo: MTI

More on the NVVH: Former Slovak police chief warns Hungary’s asset recovery office as he claims ‘2 years should be enough for accountability’. Also, questions arose whether one of the weakest candidates has been installed at the helm of the all-but-omnipotent NVVH.

He claims a political campaign is ongoing against him

Hankó was questioned for around five hours after being detained and transported to Kecskemét. He denied the allegations and filed complaints against both his detention and the suspicion against him. He has described the proceedings as a political campaign against him and said they were intended to marginalise nationally minded politicians and artists.

The Kecskemét court is due to decide on the prosecutors’ request for Hankó’s detention on 1 October. The legal processes of the Volánbusz case started as Hungary’s newly established NVVH took over several major investigations into alleged corruption and misuse of public assets, while Hankó’s detention was requested by Bács-Kiskun County’s prosecution. Authorities have indicated that further investigative measures are expected in the cases.

World.title: Orbán’s friend Mészáros remains Hungary’s richest as Forbes publishes first-ever top 100 list
World.content:
Lőrinc Mészáros and his family remain by far the wealthiest Hungarians, with an estimated fortune of HUF 1,785.7 billion (EUR 4.87 billion), according to the Forbes Hungary 2026 rich list. This year’s ranking is the magazine’s first to feature the 100 richest Hungarians rather than 50, and is published as Hungary’s political and business landscape undergoes major changes.

Mészáros remains firmly at the top

Forbes Hungary has published its 2026 list of the country’s wealthiest people, expanding the ranking from 50 to 100 individuals and families for the first time. Lőrinc Mészáros and his family remain at the top, with an estimated fortune of HUF 1,785.7 billion.

The combined estimated wealth of the 100 people on the list is now approaching HUF 13,000 billion (EUR 35.5 billion), according to Forbes.

The ranking is based on financial reports from the most recently completed business year. As a result, Forbes notes that the list does not yet fully reflect the effects of the political changes that followed the April election.

The magazine says reviews, criminal proceedings, falling share prices and the establishment of a state asset recovery office are already pointing towards a new period in Hungary’s business world.

Have you read this? Legal threats fly as PM Magyar confronts Orbán-linked billionaire over motorway deal

Csányi, Felcsuti, Veres and Szíjj complete the top five

The five wealthiest Hungarians on the 2026 Forbes list are:

Lőrinc Mészáros and family – HUF 1,785.7 billion Sándor Csányi – HUF 649.7 billion Zsolt Felcsuti – HUF 587.6 billion Tibor Veres – HUF 567.7 billion László Szíjj – HUF 530.6 billion

Mészáros has therefore retained the top position, although Forbes says his estimated wealth increased by only HUF 39 billion this year – the smallest increase relative to his total fortune since he first appeared at the top of the list.

Last year, Forbes estimated his wealth at HUF 1,749.1 billion.

Jellinek ranks seventh, while Garancsi and Jászai remain in the top 15

Dániel Jellinek, owner of Indotek Group, ranks seventh with an estimated fortune of HUF 314.1 billion.

Jellinek was detained and subsequently placed under arrest in September in connection with a criminal investigation. The Forbes ranking, however, is based on the financial data and company valuations underlying its 2026 methodology.

His former wife, Kamilla Hermann, ranks 60th with an estimated HUF 59.8 billion.

István Garancsi, owner of Market Építő and Las Vegas Casino, ranks 10th with an estimated HUF 271.9 billion, while Gellért Jászai, head of 4iG, is 11th with HUF 254 billion.

István Tiborcz, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán, ranks 13th with an estimated HUF 185.6 billion.

The expansion to 100 names has also brought several figures onto the Forbes list for the first time. Árpád Habony ranks 52nd, while Mária Schmidt is 62nd and former defence minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky is 74th.

What could the political changes mean for Hungary’s billionaires?

Forbes describes this year’s ranking as a snapshot taken at the end of an era in which several business groups grew substantially through state-linked contracts and concessions.

The magazine says that the future of long-term state concessions could become a major issue for businesses closely associated with the previous system. It also raises questions about how companies that expanded in sectors heavily dependent on state contracts will perform in a more competitive environment.

Forbes further notes that businesses which previously benefited from preferential state financing, bond programmes or major public contracts are unlikely to be able to rely on the same conditions under the new government.

However, the 2026 ranking largely reflects the previous business year, meaning the longer-term impact of the political transition is not yet visible in full.
