How does Forbes calculate the fortunes?

Forbes Hungary uses a methodology based on that of the US Forbes. Where possible, companies are valued using EBITDA – earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation – multiplied by an industry-specific valuation multiple.

Since its 2023 list, Forbes has used the average EBITDA of the previous three years rather than the latest figure alone. The magazine says this better reflects how companies have recently been valued in the Hungarian market.

For non-production businesses such as property developers, the calculation is primarily based on the value of the assets minus liabilities. Start-ups are assessed partly on the basis of investment received, while investment management companies are valued using their after-tax profit and an industry multiple.

Forbes also applies a standard 10% liquidity discount to private companies. Businesses heavily dependent on state contracts or holding state concessions are assessed on an asset basis with a significant discount, where their state exposure is considered substantial.

The magazine says its calculations were supported by data from company information providers Opten and Dun & Bradstreet, as well as Ingatlan.com, while valuation practices and exceptional cases were discussed with M&A advisers.

World.title: Hungary’s Semmelweis University breaks into world’s top 250 after major leap in global rankings
World.content:
Budapest’s Semmelweis University has climbed to 247th place in the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings 2027, making it the highest-ranked university in Hungary and Central and Eastern Europe.

Semmelweis University has made a major leap in the latest Times Higher Education (THE) global university rankings, entering the world’s top 250 universities for the first time. The Budapest-based medical university ranks 247th in the 2027 THE World University Rankings, up from 272nd last year.

The result also makes Semmelweis the highest-ranked university in both Hungary and Central and Eastern Europe.

The British-based Times Higher Education ranking is one of the world’s best-known university rankings. For its latest edition, THE assessed more than 20,000 higher education institutions from 118 countries and ranked around 2,200 of them.

Semmelweis particularly strong in research quality

THE evaluates universities across five broad areas: teaching, research environment, research quality, industry income and international outlook. Semmelweis performed particularly strongly in research quality, ranking 166th in the world in this category. It was also ranked 242nd for teaching.

According to the university, Semmelweis has placed within the top 25% of institutions worldwide in all five indicator groups.

THE also uses size-adjusted indicators, including the student-to-staff ratio, income per academic staff member and research citation impact. This is intended to prevent larger universities from gaining an advantage simply because of their size.

Semmelweis improved significantly in two of the five indicator groups and increased its score while maintaining its position in another.

More than one-third of students are international

Semmelweis Rector Béla Merkely attributed the university’s progress partly to the close relationship between its education, patient care and research activities, as well as its strong international presence.

The university has almost 16,000 students, more than one-third of whom are international, coming from nearly 130 countries around the world.

The number of international applicants is also rising. According to Semmelweis, applications for its English-language programmes increased by almost 40% this year, while its general medicine programme received roughly three times as many applications as available places.

The university has partnerships with a number of internationally recognised institutions, including the Karolinska Institute, Mayo Clinic, the University of Oxford, Heidelberg University, the National University of Singapore and Harvard University.

How other Hungarian universities performed

Several other Hungarian universities also appear in the THE 2027 rankings. The Óbuda University was placed in the 601–800 range, while the University of Debrecen and Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) were ranked between 801st and 1,000th.

The University of Szeged and University of Pécs both fell into the 1,001–1,200 range.

The Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences (MATE) and Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) were placed between 1,201st and 1,500th.

The Széchenyi István University, University of Pannonia, University of Miskolc and Pázmány Péter Catholic University were all ranked in the 1,501+ category.

Within Central and Eastern Europe, Semmelweis leads the regional rankings. The University of Tartu in Estonia is in the 301–350 range, Charles University in the Czech Republic in the 401–500 range, while Wrocław Medical University and Jagiellonian University in Poland are in the 501–600 range.

Oxford extends its record at the top

The University of Oxford remains at the top of the global ranking, extending its record to 11 consecutive years at No. 1, Telex reports. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) ranks second, while Princeton University and Stanford University share third place.

The top 10 consists exclusively of universities from the United States and the United Kingdom. For the first time, however, Asian universities collectively overtook European institutions in the rankings, with three Asian universities making the top 15.

University rankings come with caveats

University rankings have faced criticism in recent years because different ranking systems use different methodologies and attempt to compare institutions with very different profiles.

György Fábri, a lecturer at ELTE, previously argued that it was unrealistic to expect a Hungarian university to enter the top 100 of global rankings, pointing to the substantial financial gap between the world’s leading universities and Hungarian higher education.

He also described global university rankings as being particularly useful for international positioning and for showing roughly where an institution stands within the international research and higher education landscape.

Semmelweis itself has acknowledged the limitations of university rankings, noting that different methodologies can make comparisons between institutions with very different profiles difficult.

World.title: Hungary takes major step towards joining European Public Prosecutor’s Office
World.content:
Head of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), European Chief Prosecutor Laura Codruta Kovesi, has held talks on the technical details of Hungary’s membership of the EPPO with Justice Minister Márta Görög, Finance Minister András Kármán, Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai and Deputy Prosecutor General István Lajtár at the Ministry of Justice in Budapest, the ministry said on Tuesday.

The EPPO is an independent European Union body tasked with investigating criminal offences affecting the financial interests of the European Union, conducting prosecutions and bringing perpetrators to justice. These offences include budgetary fraud affecting the financial interests of the EU, active and passive corruption, embezzlement, money laundering, cross-border tax fraud and other connected offences.

In criminal cases falling outside the jurisdiction of the EPPO, the Hungarian Office of the Prosecutor General and the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office will continue to act as public prosecutors, while criminal liability will continue to be determined by the Hungarian courts in accordance with the Hungarian legal system, the statement said.

The accession process involves significant professional, institutional and legislative tasks, which must be carried out “as soon as possible”, it added.

Legislative tasks will be carried out in two phases. In the first phase, the system for selecting the European Public Prosecutor and the delegated European Public Prosecutors will be established. This will require amendments to three acts. The relevant legislative package will be submitted to parliament as early as in 2026.

The aim is to establish a selection procedure that ensures the highest possible level of independence, objectivity and professional rigour. Due to the high professional standards required, the legislative process necessitates a longer preparation period, as the aim is to conduct wide-ranging consultations with the organisations concerned regarding the selection criteria and the details of the procedure, the ministry said.

World.title: Magyar government publishes list of 3,598 secretive resolutions issued since 2010
World.content:
The Hungarian government has published a list of so-called 2000-series government resolutions issued between 2010 and 2026, the Prime Minister’s Office told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) on Tuesday.

These decisions were previously not published in the Hungarian Gazette, but were sent directly to the government officials concerned. According to the list, the largest number of such resolutions were issued in 2021, during the coronavirus pandemic.

Most non-public decisions issued during 2021

A total of 3,598 so-called 2000-series government resolutions were issued over the past 16 years without being published in the Hungarian Gazette. These decisions, which were sent directly to those concerned, generally assigned tasks to specific government, law enforcement or other state officials.

The 2000-series government resolutions are not the same as government resolutions containing classified information, the Prime Minister’s Office said.

In recent years, the existence or contents of some 2000-series resolutions could only be learned from media reports. However, a complete annual breakdown of the resolutions had not previously been publicly available in one place.

Number of unpublished resolutions rose steadily

The newly published documents show that the government increasingly classified decisions as non-public over time. During the second Orbán government between 2010 and 2013, the number of non-public decisions ranged from 10 to 20 a year. This rose to 33 in 2014, after which the number continued to increase.

The highest number of non-public resolutions was recorded in 2021, during the coronavirus pandemic, when 679 government decisions were classified as 2000-series resolutions. A similarly high number was recorded in 2023, when 635 non-public government decisions were issued.

Full list available online

The annual lists of non-public government resolutions issued between 2010 and 2026 are now available on the government’s website. The documents can be accessed here.

World.title: Romania’s Crisis Spirals as Parliament Rejects PM-Designate’s Govt
World.content:
Romania’s parliament on Wednesday rejected the programme and proposed cabinet of Siegfried Muresan, a Member of the European Parliament, adding to the country’s political crisis.

The Prime Minister-designate needed 233 votes for his government to be approved. He received only 182.

“The parties that triggered the political crisis have voted to prolong it … We are now waiting to see what position the President … will take,” Muresan said after the result was announced.

His proposed cabinet was backed by the centre-right National Liberals, PNL, and two smaller former coalition partners, but the Social Democrats, PSD, the biggest party in parliament, rejected it.

The far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians, AUR, the second-largest party in parliament, also declined to endorse Mureșan. Party leader George Simion said the AUR would not vote for any government until the far-right politician Calin Georgescu “is freed from prison”.

A court on Tuesday ordered 30 days’ detention for former presidential candidate Georgescu, who is accused of defrauding a businessman of more than 1 million euros.

President Nicusor Dan must now nominate another Prime Minister-designate, who will have ten days to put together a cabinet and seek parliament’s approval.

Under the law, the President may dissolve parliament and call an early election if two prime ministers-designate fail to secure parliamentary backing within 60 days. However, Dan has ruled out an early election, arguing that it would likely fail to produce a strong parliamentary majority.

Since May 5, Romania has been operating under an interim government, following the collapse of the previous cabinet. During this period, Dan has made two previous nominations for prime minister, both of whom failed to secure parliamentary support.

In June, independent Eugen Tomac, the first of them, withdrew before even facing a parliamentary vote. Three weeks later, parliament rejected the proposed programme and cabinet of liberal politician Adrian Vestea.

Romania’s political crisis stems from deep tensions among the parties that previously formed the pro-European governing coalition.

The coalition, formed in June 2025, brought together the centre-left PSD, the centre-right National Liberal Party, PNL, and two smaller centre-right parties. One of its main objectives was to curb the rise of the far-right AUR.

Its mandate included stabilising the economy, which is burdened by the largest budget deficit in the European Union, securing access to 11 billion euros in EU recovery funds and safeguarding Romania’s investment-grade credit rating.

But unpopular austerity measures introduced to cut the budget deficit placed growing strain on the coalition, particularly with the Social Democrats, who withdrew support in May.

World.title: In Serbia, ‘Fictitious’ Corruption Campaign Becomes Tool of Distraction
World.content:
Over the same period, Serbia has slid 11 places on Transparency International’s annual Corruption Perception Index, published in February. It now stands in 116th place out of 182 countries, the worst ranking of any country in the Western Balkans.

Last year, Transparency Serbia published a report showing that for the first time since the fall of Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosevic in October 2000, the Serbian public considers corruption the biggest issue in the country.

“Vucic came to power in 2012 on, among other things, a campaign of ‘zero tolerance for corruption’,” said Draskovic. “That zero tolerance has turned into absolute tolerance of corruption.”

Nemanja Nenadic, programme director of Transparency, questioned the very notion of an ‘anti-corruption campaign’, given fighting corruption is the day-to-day remit of special corruption departments within the public prosecution service.

“Based on what has been announced, it can be concluded that a large number of arrests presented as part of this campaign essentially have nothing to do with corruption, but with other criminal offences,” Nenadic told BIRN.

“For example, cases in which owners of private companies engage in schemes to avoid paying taxes, not in collusion with tax officials, but with other private business owners.”

“In 2025, the number of reported corruption cases and indictments did increase compared with the previous year. For four major criminal offences, the number of indictments was 52 per cent higher than a year earlier, but there were only nine per cent more first-instance judgments.”

Arrests are the least important indicators of success, Nenadic said.

“More important indicators include how quickly reports submitted by citizens are examined, which can encourage more people to report cases; the amount of benefit obtained through corruption offences or the level of damage caused to public property or the public interest; the number and seniority of those indicted; the speed of court decisions; and, finally, the value of unlawfully obtained assets that are confiscated.”

Draskovic said that long-running proceedings without final judgments risk weakening public confidence.

“It sends a signal that it is not worth fighting corruption,” he told BIRN.

World.title: Three Kosovo Serbs Plead Not Guilty Over 2022 Unrest in North
World.content:
Barricades set up by Kosovo Serbs on a road in Rudare leading to the Jarinje border crossing with Serbia, December 2022. Photo: Adelina Ahmeti/BIRN.

Three Kosovo Serbs, Dusan Maksimovic, Nemanja Jolovic and Srdjan Vucinic, pleaded not guilty at the Pristina Basic Court on Wednesday to violating the constitutional order by participating in setting up roadblocks in the north of the country in December 2022.

A fourth defendant, Nenad Orlovic, was not present in court. Judge Rrahman Beqiri said that “every effort has been made to secure his presence in the criminal proceedings but it appears that he is not in Kosovo”.

The charges relate to unrest in December 2022, when Serbs in northern Kosovo set up barricades at the two border crossings with Serbia, parking trucks, ambulances, diggers and other vehicles across access roads in what was cast as a spontaneous outpouring of popular anger after the arrest of a Kosovo Serb on suspicion of attacking election facilities.

Two Kosovo Serbs have already been convicted over the case. Dusan Dobrac and Milos Radosavlevic were given prison sentences of one year and nine months respectively on August 31, 2026, after pleading guilty to charges.

Dobrac was convicted of acts breaching the constitutional order and obstruction of an official in the performance of their duties, and Radosavlevic of violating the constitutional order.

The indictment charged six people – Maksimovic, Drobac, Radosavljevic, Jolovic, Orlovic and Vucinic – with staging violent activity to subvert the constitutional order by blocking roads to two border crossings with Serbia: Jarinje and Bernjak.

The prosecution file, seen by BIRN, claims the unrest endangered the lives of police and customs officers. Those involved also allegedly participated in creating “a tense security situation through the opening of fortified positions and the presence of uniformed and armed persons”, according to the prosecution.

The police discovered a Viber group named “Barricades December 2022” on Maksimovic’s phone, suggesting the incidents were organised and coordinated.

They obtained the phone in September 2023 after Maksimovic was arrested over the armed attack on police in the northern village of Banjska, in which one Kosovo Albanian police officer was killed and a cache of military-grade weaponry was seized. He was sentenced in the first instance to 30 years in prison over the Banjska incident.

The contents of his phone helped prosecutors investigating the unrest in Serb-majority municipalities and the setting up of the barricades of December 2022. The messages it contained included: “Today we’ll all receive ammunition” and, “In the afternoon we could try the weapons in Suvi Dol [local village] with two or three bullets each.”

Prosecutors said the phone evidence undermined claims that local Serbs spontaneously set up the barricades.

World.title: Kosovo’s Kurti Pushes for Deal on President to Avoid Elections
World.content:
Photos of Kosovo’s presidents. Photo: BIRN/Denis Sllovinja

With a court deadline to elect a new President approaching, Prime Minister Albin Kurti on Wednesday called on opposition leaders to take urgent steps to address the issue, which risks triggering another legislative election only five months after the last one.

Last week, the Constitutional Court ordered MPs to elect a new head of state by October 6 to avoid new snap elections – the fourth parliamentary polls in two years.

“The Constitutional Court verdict … has put us in an urgent situation,” Kurti said. “The election of a new President is possible, and subsequently new repeat, unnecessary and costly elections, with heavy consequences, are [then] avoidable,” he added.

Kurti, who was re-elected Prime Minister less than three weeks ago, wants an agreement to be implemented that has already been reached with the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK. This would see Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and diplomat, take the post of president.

But Sejdiu withdrew from consideration on September 14, following disagreements within the LDK parliamentary group over his candidacy.

“We have Bekim Sejdiu as a candidate who withdrew because six LDK MPs did not agree with the deal. But from Vetevendosje’s point of view, we have a political agreement and we respect it. We don’t have a new name,” Kurti said on Wednesday when pressed on a possible new agreement with the opposition on a fresh candidate.

For a vote electing a President to be valid, at least 80 out of 120 MPs must be present in the chamber. If the first two rounds of voting fail, the third round requires only a simple majority of MPs to elect a President – but at least 80 of them still need to be in the chamber.

Kosovo has been without a President since April 4, when Vjosa Osmani’s five-year term ended. Parliament speaker Albulena Haxhiu from Kurti’s Vetevendosje party is serving as Acting President.

While the deal with the LDK hangs in the balance, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK is meanwhile urging parliament to support amendments to the law on the Specialist Chambers, approved in 2015, which would limit the scope of this court before considering any discussion on a President. This comes after the Hague-based court found four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, guilty of war crimes.

On Wednesday, PDK MPs boycotted the work of parliamentary committees in order to press Vetevendosje to proceed with the law change. “Six laws have been brought to the committee today but the Law on the Specialist Chambers is being dragged out because they say it needs expertise. We won’t participate in the committees without proceeding with this law,” Blerta Deliu Kodra, a PDK MP, warned.

World.title: Bosnia Mourns Wartime Co-Inventor of Limb-Saving Medical Device
World.content:
Enes Baralic, who co-created a revolutionary external medical fixator that prevented thousands of limb amputations during the siege of Sarajevo, has died aged 84.

During the 1992–1995 Bosnian war, the city endured a 1,425-day siege by Bosnian Serb forces. Amid relentless shelling, local hospitals faced an overwhelming influx of casualties, with nearly 70 per cent suffering severe limb trauma caused by bullets and shrapnel.

As imported medical supplies were rapidly exhausted under a total humanitarian blockade, two orthopedic surgeons, Dr Sukrija Djozic and Dr Raib Salihefendic, designed a modification for an external fracture fixator.

To manufacture it from raw industrial materials, they partnered with Baralic, a mechanical engineer and factory director at the state-owned industrial conglomerate Energoinvest. The resulting device, named the Sarajevo Wartime Fixator, or “Sarafix”, became a crucial tool for saving shattered limbs from amputation.

More than 4,000 fixators were manufactured inside the besieged city at the Energoinvest facility. As equipment was scarce, devices were routinely recycled and re-sterilized to treat subsequent waves of wounded citizens. The fixators were transported to frontline hospitals via underground tunnels and even by bicycles under sniper fire.

“Enes Baralic was an exceptionally creative man, a massive patriot, and an outstanding friend,” Dr Djozic told BIRN. “Within just ten to 20 days of receiving our initial concepts, he developed the prototype within his factory division. He was tireless, organising the production and ensuring these devices reached trapped enclaves like Srebrenica, Mostar, and Gorazde through the wartime tunnel. He left a profound mark on our history.”

The “Sarafix” earned international acclaim, winning gold medals at global innovation fairs in Brussels and Geneva in 1995 and 1996.

The city administration officially honoured the three co-creators with the high-profile Sixth of April Award in 2001 for their outstanding contributions to science and humanitarian technology.

Dr Djozic said that the legacy of their joint innovation remains permanently preserved across borders.

“I donated one of the original wartime fixators alongside our medals to the Historical Museum in Sarajevo,” he noted.

“Furthermore, a British colleague who volunteered with us later donated another original ‘Sarafix’ to a museum in London, where it remains on display today as a symbol of human ingenuity in the face of total isolation.”

Media reported that Baralic died n Sarajevo on Monday. His funeral was due to be held on Wednesday at the Vlakovo city cemetery in Sarajevo.

World.title: Turkey Freezes Former Minister’s Assets in Market Manipulation Probe
World.content:
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said on Tuesday that it had asked Turkish institutions to freeze all assets belonging to former Family and Social Policies Minister Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, as part of an investment fund investigation.

“As part of the fund investigation conducted by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office’s Terrorism Financing and Money Laundering Crimes Investigation Bureau, relevant institutions have been instructed regarding the freezing of all assets belonging to Ilyas Kaya and his wife, Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya,” it said.

The investigation into dubious capital market transactions has resulted in 51 people being remanded in custody. Turkish authorities previously ordered the liquidation of 130 funds managed by seven portfolio management companies after liquidity problems contributed to sharp market losses.

According to Reuters, the funds’ assets are worth around 18.8 billion euros, involving about 353,000 investors. Turkish television channel CNBC-e estimates the total at about 17.4 billion euros and the number of investors at more than 514,000.

Kaya, Turkey’s family and social policies minister from 2016 to 2018, resigned as a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, after allegations emerged about share transactions by her and her husband.

Following a cabinet meeting, Erdogan said the government would act against wrongdoing in the markets. “We neither violate people’s rights nor turn a blind eye when the rights of our citizens are violated,” he said on Tuesday.

Liquidation of funds does not mean that the investors’ money has been confiscated. Instead, banks are being tasked to deliver citizens’ money in these funds. Is Bank has been appointed to handle the liquidation of funds managed by Tera Portfoy, while state-owned Ziraat Bank will oversee funds belonging to the six other managers.

Opposition politicians allege that the couple invested around 2.9 million euros in shares of shipbuilder Ozata Denizcilik in April and later sold the shares for about 39.5 million euros. The figures have not been published by the authorities.

Media reported on Monday that the couple subsequently transferred around 39.5 million euros to an account designated by the Treasury and Finance Ministry. The reported payment has also not been publicly confirmed.

Kaya comes from a family with extensive experience of public office. Her brother, Omer Fatih Sayan, a former telecommunications regulator chief and deputy transport minister, was appointed to the Energy Market Regulatory Board in July.

Her sister, Ayse Hilal Sayan Koytak, previously ambassador to Kuwait and Bahrain, was appointed ambassador to Finland in September. Another sister, Nazmiye Sumeyye Sayan, previously served on Istanbul’s municipal council.

World.title: Tracing Illicit Cigarette Flows over Mountainous Bosnia-Montenegro Borderland
World.content:
To cross between the municipalities of Gacko and Pluzine, in Bosnia and Montenegro respectively, most local residents must drive at least 100 kilometres, crossing at the Deleusa-Vracenovici border crossing.

Not so for the cigarette smugglers.

They use an asphalt road linking the Gacko village of Lipnik with Ravno in Pluzine. It’s a distance of some 10 kilometres.

“It’s exclusively a smuggling road,” a security source in Bosnia told BIRN on condition of anonymity.

The terrain around the road is too steep for farming, and the road sees almost no other traffic.

According to the case files seen by BIRN, police believe the gangs smuggled the cigarettes from Montenegro into Bosnia via mountain passes and stashed them in and around Avtovac and Lipnik.

“Given that the territory of the municipality of Gacko borders Montenegro, specifically the municipality of Pluzine, it is possible to transport excise goods to stash locations in the areas of Avtovac and Lipnik within a short period of time,” one document states.

With Zirojevic and Miletic allegedly in charge, other members of the group monitored the movement of police or drove ahead of the contraband as reconnaissance, according to the documents. The files name 14 other individuals as involved, all from Gacko and neighbouring municipalities.

They used at least nine different vehicles and often switched licence plates.

“They drive like crazy,” said a source familiar with the police investigation. “They can be over the border and back in ten minutes.” Police nicknamed one of the drivers ‘Phantom’.

“He drives so fast that nobody can catch him in a police chase,” said the source.

The smugglers often targeted an evening gap in patrols when shifts change between 6 and 7 p.m.

According to sources familiar with the investigation, rather than rotating officers directly along the road, border police shift changes take place at fixed points further away, leaving the unofficial mountain crossing unmonitored for about an hour every day.

“And while the shift happens, they have done the job,” a source said.

From Lipnik and Avtovac, the cigarettes are transported deeper into Bosnia for sale through street vendors. This reporter found smuggled cigarettes for sale on the streets of Sarajevo for 4.5 Bosnian marks, or 2.25 euros. The price of the cheapest legally sold pack of cigarettes is 6.2 Bosnian marks, or 3.10 euros.

Overlapping crimes

World.title: HVARMONY, Celebrating Wellbeing on Croatia’s Premier Island
World.content:
September 30, 2026 – Famous for its sun, beaches, heritage and nightlife, a new initiative celebrates another of its gems – wellbeing. Meet HVARMONY.

Soon after I moved to the island of Hvar back in 2003, an island whose existence I had only become aware of two days before I bought my house, I realised that it was a very distinct island of two halves. The most famous, of course, was the tourism side, with its world famous beaches filled with tourists all over the world, as they also enjoyed the fine gastronomy, culture and endless sun.

But there was another side to Hvar, and one that I liked much better – the off-season. No longer warm enough to swim (although some did), devoid of tourists, most businesses closed for the season, but what a fantastic slice of nature to enjoy in peace and quiet. If Croatia made me realise that quality of life, lifestyle and wellbeing were the shortcut to happiness, it was the winters in Jelsa that first pointed the way.

Olive groves, vineyards, growing their own food, while loudly discussing olives and Hajduk Split over timeless coffees, I had never come across a place so contented with itself. And I quickly learned that I was not alone. All over the island, there were Austrians, Norwegians, Americans, Germans living in the hills or smaller villages, some with yoga studios, but all thrilled that they had found such a gem off the radar.

The digital nomad revolution came to Croatia in 2020, enabling a new breed of tourist to spend an extended period in Croatia. One of the first was an American couple who moved to Jelsa and did a great documentary for national tv on why life on a Dalmatian island in January was perfect. Some locals might have thought they were nuts, but I understood perfectly.

And as look around Hvar these days, in addition to the tourism, there is another undercurrent bubbling away – wellbeing. Yoga, pilates, energy healing, retreats – they are all increasing in number and diversity. It is for me an essential part of the Hvar DNA – this is, of course, the island that was nicknamed the Austrian Madeira for its temperate and healing climate, which resulted in it becoming the birthplace of organised tourism in Europe with the founding of the Hvar Health Society in 1868.

But there has been precious little official recognition of this wellbeing aspect. Until now.

Meet HVARMONY, an excellent initiative from the Hvar Tourist Board, which will take place for the first time from October 15-18. And before we get to the concept and programmes, the locations of the event set the tone – the oldest public theatre in Europe, the impressive Arsenal on the corner of the main square, the 1930s colonnade, Bonj les Bains, and the 5-star Maslina Resort, whose slogan is Mindful Luxury.

So what exactly is HVARMONY? An explanation from the dedicated website:

HVARMONY is a four-day gathering built around one simple question: how can we live better, longer and more fulfilling lives?

From 15 to 18 October in Hvar, talks, conversations, workshops and shared experiences will explore what wellbeing really means today, why we seem to need it more than ever, and whether somewhere along the way it has become yet another industry selling us health, happiness and longevity.

Over the four-day event, some 23 Croatian and international speakers will put on an excellent and diverse programme exploring key themes on health, happiness and longevity, with plenty of yoga, pilates and other energy food for the body. You can see the whole programme here.

I really like the direction that Hvar tourism is going these days, it is a much more pleasant experience, and I applaud the organisers of this initiative, which will not only bring together motivated like-minded people, but also showcase some of the magic I first discovered a quarter of a century ago.

Entrance and participation for events is free of charge (with the exception of a few sessions which are paid), although registration is required. You can do this on the official HVARMONY website.

World.title: Uber CEO Comes to Zagreb and Tries Out Rimac’s Robotaxi
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi arrived in Zagreb and tried out Mate Rimac’s famed robotaxi without a safety driver.

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi visited Verne and the Rimac Campus in Zagreb yesterday and rode in a robotaxi without a safety driver, Mate Rimac announced. “Uber is an investor and strategic partner in Verne. Dara tried out the robotaxi without a safety driver in Zagreb and was delighted with the experience. We talked about further cooperation and expanding Verne beyond Croatia with the ‘final’ Verne car without a steering wheel and pedals,” Rimac wrote on Facebook.

Index reports that Uber and Verne have otherwise been cooperating for months now on an autonomous taxi project. Back in March, Verne, China’s Pony.ai and Uber announced a strategic partnership to launch a robotaxi service in Europe, starting in Zagreb. Uber also announced an investment in Verne at that time.

driverless rides are already being tested out in zagreb

At the beginning of September, Verne and Pony.ai began testing rides with passengers in Zagreb without a safety driver or other staff in the vehicle. The tests are taking place on a 22-kilometre route connecting Verne’s headquarters with the area of Zagreb Airport. However, these are vehicles from the Chinese manufacturer BAIC with Pony.ai autonomous driving technology, not the final Verne vehicle without a steering wheel and pedals that Rimac mentions in today’s post. Since August, Uber has also enabled the ordering of autonomous rides via its app in Zagreb. In that phase a licensed operator was still behind the wheel, while fully driverless rides were introduced as separate tests.

the final report for the eu-funded project has been submitted

Mate Rimac’s announcement comes on the same day that Project 3 Mobility, the company developing Verne, submitted its final report to SAFU on the last day of the deadline for the robotaxi project financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. According to what remains unofficial information, the company is not requesting recognition of the remaining part of the already paid advance in the final documentation. Verne had 179.5 million euros in non-repayable EU funds approved for the project, and back in July 2023 it received an advance of 89.75 million euros. SAFU earlier confirmed to Index that of that amount around 8.77 million euros had been justified so far, while around 80.98 million euros had not been justified.

The project formally ended on the 30th of August, after which a 30-day deadline for submitting the final documentation began. SAFU now has 60 days to check the reported costs and documentation, and during the procedure it may also request additional information. Only after the check is completed will it be known how much of the paid advance will be recognised and how much money, if any, Verne will have to return.

the primary contracted goal was not completed in time

The key problem of the EU-funded project remains the fact that by the deadline it was not confirmed that a fully autonomous Level 5 vehicle had been produced and homologated, which was one of the main contracted results of the project. Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said after the deadline expired that the project had not received final homologation from the competent institution in Germany and that it had not been completed by the end of August.

At the beginning of September, Verne revealed that it was ready to return the funds if the final evaluation showed that the contracted obligations had not been fully met. At the same time the company claimed that during the project test prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles had been confirmed and appropriate tests carried out. Mate Rimac’s meeting with Uber’s Dara Khosrowshahi therefore concerns the continuation of Verne’s commercial development and cooperation with Uber, while the final evaluation procedure for the EU-funded project continues separately.

World.title: EU Raises Retirement Age, Here’s What Awaits Croatia
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – As the EU raises its retirement age and multiple countries now expect their work forces to work for longer, what exactly awaits Croatia?

Working life across the European Union is lengthening significantly, and for younger generations the difference could be as much as ten years. Croatia is not currently going to raise its retirement age above 65. The retirement age is rising across Europe, and for some of today’s younger workers a working life could last until the age of 70 or even longer. The OECD estimates that the average retirement age will increase further in the future as life expectancy rises, while numerous countries have already legally adopted gradual increases.

Denmark stands out the most. There it has already been decided that the statutory retirement age will rise to 70 by 2040, while the OECD projects an even higher threshold for generations that have only just entered the labour market if the current method of linking the pension age to life expectancy continues. According to the latest edition of the OECD’s Pensions at a Glance report, the average normal retirement age for people who retired in 2024 is around 64.7 years for men and 63.9 years for women.

For those who have only just entered the labour market, the OECD expects a significantly longer working life. The average future retirement age is estimated at 66.4 years for men and 65.9 years for women.

denmark is taking it the furthest

Denmark is at the top of the European ranking. The current normal retirement age there is 67, and parliament has already adopted an increase to 70 years from 2040. The OECD projects that if the current formula linked to life expectancy continues to be applied, the future retirement age in Denmark could rise as high as 74 years. It is important to emphasise, however, that 74 is not a legally set limit for a specific year, but a projection that depends on whether Denmark continues to link the pension age to increases in life expectancy. The country is already discussing possible easing of that formula after 2040.

High future thresholds are also expected in other European countries. Estonia could reach 71 years, while the OECD projects a normal retirement age of around 70 for Italy, the Netherlands and Sweden. Under current rules, Finland could reach around 68 years and Slovakia around 69, while in a number of other countries the future normal retirement age is approaching 67.

many countries are adopting reforms

The changes are no longer just projections. In several European countries reforms have already been adopted that gradually increase the retirement age or link its future movement to life expectancy.

Belgium will reach a retirement age of 67 years, while the United Kingdom has planned a further increase towards 68. The Czech Republic has also adopted a gradual increase of the statutory age to 67. Slovenia has reformed its pension system and raised the statutory age, but in international comparisons the possibility of full retirement with a sufficient number of contribution years must also be taken into account. The main reason for such reforms is demographics. Europeans are living longer, while at the same time in many countries the share of the working-age population that finances pension systems is shrinking.

Countries are therefore trying to achieve a balance between longer life expectancy, the number of years spent in retirement and the financial sustainability of the system.

men and women are moving towards the same threshold

Differences in retirement age between men and women are gradually narrowing. In most European countries men and women already have the same statutory retirement age, while differences have been retained only in some countries. Some countries where the difference still exists have already decided on its gradual abolition, so the number of systems in which women can take full retirement earlier than men will decrease further.

where does croatia fall here?

Croatia is currently among the countries that do not have a legally determined increase in the regular retirement age above 65. Men in Croatia acquire the right to an old-age pension at the age of 65 with at least 15 years of pensionable service. For women a transitional period is still underway. In 2026 a woman can acquire the right to an old-age pension at 64 years of age and at least 15 years of service.

The threshold for women then increases by three months each year. In 2027 it will be 64 years and three months, in 2028 64 years and six months, and in 2029 64 years and nine months. From the 1st of January 2030, the conditions will be equalised, so both men and women in Croatia will acquire a regular old-age pension at the age of 65. There are also special rules for long-term insured persons. A person who has 60 years of age and 41 years of insurance service in effective duration can acquire the right to an old-age pension for a long-term insured person.

For early old-age pension the general rule is 60 years of age and 35 years of service. For women a transitional period is still underway, so in 2026 they can acquire the right at 59 years of age and 34 years of pensionable service.

will people in croatia have to work for longer?

So far no decision has been taken according to which the regular retirement age in Croatia would be increased above 65. This currently distinguishes Croatia from countries that have already legally linked the retirement age to life expectancy or adopted increases towards 67, 68 or 70 years. Nevertheless, the demographic pressure that is driving reforms in other European countries is also present in Croatia. The population is ageing, and the ratio of the number of employed people to pension beneficiaries is one of the key factors in the sustainability of the system.

That is why the question of how long future generations will have to work before retiring will remain one of the more important topics of European, and also Croatian, social policy. The difference between today’s and future generations can be large. While in a large part of Europe today’s normal retirement age is around 65, in some countries those who are only just starting work could, under current rules, retire only after the age of 70.

World.title: Wellovar – Bjelovar Geothermal Complex Now Open
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – Wellovar, the much anticipated Bjelovar geothermal complex is now open, with the ceremony attended by approximately 600 guests.

The ceremony was attended by around 600 guests, and alongside Mayor Dario Hrebak and Bjelovar-Bilogora County Prefect Marko Marušić, the highest-ranking state guests included Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Gordan Jandroković and Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina.

Poslovni reports that after years of planning, preparation and 23 months of intensive construction, Wellovar opened its doors today. The ceremony was held as part of the celebrations of Bjelovar’s 270th birthday, and the new complex in Veliko Korenovo was presented as the largest project in the city’s history.

The way Wellovar was opened was particularly symbolic. Instead of the classic ribbon-cutting, 18 Bjelovar residents of different generations jumped into the Olympic pool. The youngest was a kindergarten-age girl, and among the participants were also well-known Bjelovar athletes, swimmers and pensioners. This “Generational Jump” was meant to symbolise the decades during which the people of Bjelovar had waited for an indoor Olympic pool, as well as the fact that the project is intended for the generations to come.

Wellovar was built as a geothermal sports and recreational complex and contains a total of 10 pools – five indoor and five outdoor. The complex also has four saunas, a gym, sports and recreational facilities and a restaurant. The outdoor pools will be presented to the public next spring.

Terme Bjelovar Director Zvonimir Žarec emphasised that behind the project were 23 months of intensive work, numerous challenges, but also a large team that in recent months prepared the complex for its first guests. Terme currently employs 47 people, and the number of employees will continue to grow. For Bjelovar, the opening of Wellovar also marks the beginning of a new tourism and economic story. With the project, the city aims to position itself as a destination for geothermal, sports and health tourism, and the new complex should also attract visitors from outside Bjelovar.

World.title: Split to Construct a Totem at the Entrance to the City
World.content:
September the 30th, 2026 – Split is set to construct a totem at the very entrance to the city, with 130,000 euros to spend on it.

Split will announce a public competition for a spatial marker, or totem, with which it wants to mark the entrance to the city. A total of 130,000 euros has been allocated for the project through 2026 and 2027. Index reports that on the 25th of August, Split Mayor Tomislav Šuta issued a conclusion on conducting a competition that should result in a “high-quality, recognisable and feasible design solution” for marking the city entrance.

The competition will seek proposals for the appearance, materials, basic dimensions, method of installation, visual identity and how the marker will fit into the immediate space and urban context. The final appearance, material and dimensions of the totem have therefore not yet been determined. The competition does not cover only the conceptual design. The official conclusion also states that its subject includes the production of the marker itself by the author of the winning solution.

130,000 euros have been allocated

In the budget, 80,000 euros has been earmarked for the activity “Marking the city entrance” in 2026, and a further 50,000 euros in 2027. The competition will be prepared and conducted by the city’s Department for City Development and the Croatian Designers’ Association, with the participation of other city departments. Official documents so far do not indicate exactly how much the production of the totem itself will cost, as other project costs are also financed from the same budget item.

World.title: Nations League: Spain Hand Croatia 4-1 Defeat in Seville
World.content:
Spain and Croatia met in Seville on Tuesday for matchday 2 of Group 3 in the Nations League A division.

The reigning world and European champions opened the campaign with a 3-2 win in England, while Croatia came from behind to beat the Czech Republic 2-1 away. Spain were heavy favorites, both in the group and the competition as a whole. Following this match, both sides return to action on Saturday — Croatia host England at Rujevica, while Spain welcome the Czech Republic.

Slaven Bilić made several changes from Prague, with only five players retaining their places. Dinamo Zagreb duo Dion Drena Beljo and Josip Mišić were handed starting berths, with Beljo leading the attack. Behind him, Ivan Perišić, Marco Pašalić, and Petar Sučić provided support, while Mateo Kovačić partnered Mišić in midfield.

The defensive line also saw significant reshuffling. Joško Gvardiol dropped to left back, while Ivan Smolčić came in on the right to replace Josip Stanišić. Josip Šutalo and Marin Pongračić formed the central defensive partnership.

Spain’s Luis de la Fuente also made notable changes, leaving captain Rodri, Dani Olmo, and Ferran Torres on the bench from the start. However, Lamine Yamal started and immediately posed a threat to the Vatreni.

Lineups

CROATIA: Livaković – Smolčić, Šutalo, Pongračić, Gvardiol – Mišić, Kovačić – Marco Pašalić, P. Sučić, Perišić – Beljo

SPAIN: Unai Simón – Pubill, Cubarsí, Huijsen, Cucurella – Zubimendi, Ruiz, Lopez – Yamal, Oyarzabal, Baena

Match report

The spectacle in Seville kicked off at 20:45, and Spain wasted no time, scoring with their very first attack as Baena and Cucurella combined to release Lamine Yamal on the edge of the box, who fired into the far corner in the second minute.

Croatia struggled to gain any foothold in the early stages. Cucurella and Baena continued to cause problems down the left, with another chance in the fourth minute falling to Baena from 16 meters, only for Livaković to hold comfortably. Oyarzabal also threatened after a slick Yamal assist, and Cubarsí tested Livaković from range as Spain dominated. Pongračić, who had a nervy opening, picked up a yellow card in the 19th minute.

Croatia’s first meaningful attacking moment came in the 17th minute when Perišić crossed to the far post for Marco Pašalić, but his header was comfortably gathered by Unai Simón. The Vatreni gradually found their footing and managed to settle into the match, though Spain remained firmly in control.

The 28th minute brought a moment of Croatian joy. Perišić delivered a pinpoint cross and Dion Drena Beljo rose to meet it with a header that beat Simón, scoring his first senior international goal and drawing Croatia level. The celebrations were short-lived. Within three minutes, Yamal found space on the left and picked out Pubill in the center, who headed calmly into the net to restore Spain’s lead. Pubill’s first international goal put the hosts back in front at 2-1.

Spain continued to press before the break. Fermín López struck the post with a superb effort from the edge of the box, while Oyarzabal had a goal disallowed for offside. Half time arrived with Spain deserving their advantage, Baena fortunate to still be on the pitch after a series of sharp reactions to refereeing decisions.

Bilić made one change at half-time with Luka Vušković replacing Pongračić. Spain began the second half with more of the same, though Croatia created their first real chance of the half in the 50th minute when Sučić played in Marco Pašalić, whose effort was blocked and won a corner.

De la Fuente made his first substitutions in the 57th minute, bringing on Merino and Pedri for Fermín and Fabián Ruiz. Croatia responded three minutes later with a double change of their own, with Ante Budimir and Mario Pašalić replacing Beljo and Kovačić.

The third goal came in the 63rd minute and it was Yamal again. The teenager burst clear of the Croatian defense, rounded Livaković one-on-one, and slotted the ball into the near post where it bounced into the net. Croatia showed spirit and continued to push, with Ivanović — who had replaced Perišić in the 72nd minute — firing narrowly wide from distance in the 77th minute. Pedri also drew a fine save from Livaković late on.

In the 81st minute, Luka Modrić received a warm reception from the Seville crowd as he was introduced from the bench. The veteran captain tried his luck in the 90th minute, getting into the box and shooting from ten meters, but fired straight at Simón.

By then, the result had long been decided. A minute before the final whistle, Nico Williams wrapped up a convincing Spanish victory. Merino played him in on the left side of the penalty area; Williams held off Šutalo and finished precisely past Livaković to make it 4-1.

This was Croatia’s first defeat in the new edition of the Nations League. After two rounds, they hold third place in Group A3. This was also Slaven Bilić’s first defeat since returning to the Croatia bench.

Croatia plays its next match on Saturday, October 3rd, when they welcome England to Rujevica.

World.title: Croatia and USA to Strengthen Ties Across Multiple Sectors
World.content:
September the 29th, 2026 – Croatia and the USA are set to strengthen ties across multiple sectors, from tourism to investments, energy and tech.

The recent Economic Forum in New York, organised by the Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK) and the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ), brought together around 70 American and 35 Croatian companies, including 15 from the tourism sector.

Domagoj Puljizovic reports for Poslovni that over 100 business people from both sides of the Atlantic took part, with the goal of strengthening economic cooperation between Croatia and the USA, connecting companies, opening new business partnerships and creating opportunities for investment and business expansion on the American market. Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković also attended the forum together with entrepreneurs from Croatia and the USA, discussing the further development of economic relations between the two countries. B2B meetings were also in focus, enabling direct company connections and the presentation of opportunities for future cooperation.

important croatian companies took part

President of the Croatian Chamber of Economy Luka Burilović emphasised that some of the most important Croatian companies from the energy, food industry and defence sectors participated in the economic delegation. “The strongest Croatian companies from energy, the food industry and defence are taking part in the economic delegation. Some of them are already present in the USA, including Orqa, Končar, Infobip, HS Produkt, Metamorfoza, Podravka and many others. Interest in cooperation is high, and the potential is even greater. This is confirmed by the impressive turnout, both in number and composition, of more than 100 businesspeople from the American side,” said Burilović.

new business bridges

He added that the partnership between Croatia and the USA is strengthening year by year, and that existing cooperation agreements provide an important framework for its further development. As one of the important steps in strengthening economic cooperation, he highlighted the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, which was signed almost four years ago but has not yet entered into force. Its application is expected to reduce business costs and administrative barriers and further encourage investments, especially in the IT sector.

Prime Minister Plenković emphasised that Croatia wants to further develop its partnership with the USA in areas of strategic importance for future economic development – from energy and technology to industry and innovation. “We see particular potential in energy, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, the defence industry, research and development, and high-tech investments. The expanded LNG terminal on Krk will reach a capacity of 6.1 billion cubic metres per year, and more than two-thirds of the gas arriving at Krk comes from the USA,” said Plenković.

croatia’s blossoming ict sector

He also highlighted the importance of Croatia’s ICT sector, whose globally successful companies confirm the potential of domestic knowledge, talent and innovation. He stressed that Croatia should be viewed not only as a market of 4 million people, but also as a safe and stable base for access to the European Union market of 450 million consumers.

“We want to connect Croatian and American companies, capital, technology and knowledge even more strongly. We want to further develop tourism sustainably, with investments in higher-quality accommodation, infrastructure, services and stronger air connections with the USA. We are building new transatlantic value chains and opening space for an even stronger economic partnership between Croatia and the USA,” the Prime Minister said.

further tourism opportunities

Tourism was one of the important topics of the forum. Croatian service exports to the USA have amounted to almost one billion euros in recent years, and a significant part of the revenue is generated precisely in this area, along with IT and consulting services. HTZ Director Kristjan Staničić said that the American market shows great interest in Croatia’s tourism offer, especially the premium segment and high value-added products.

“The USA is Croatia’s most important long-haul market, with great potential. American guests are among our tourists with the highest average spending, they increasingly visit Croatia throughout the year, and interest in investing in Croatian tourism is also growing,” said Staničić. He added that discussions were also held on continuing cooperation to improve air connectivity between the USA and Croatia. He also highlighted the promotion of Croatia through a new promotional video featuring John Malkovich, which is being shown on Times Square in New York, one of the world’s most famous tourist locations.

World.title: Largest Thermal Baths in Croatia Open As Of Today
World.content:
September the 29th, 2026 – The largest thermal baths in Croatia have opened their doors today, putting Bjelovar and the massive Wellovar project in the spotlight.

Construction lasted 23 long months, and it is the most complex pool complex in Croatia due to its energy, heating, air-conditioning and cooling systems. Poslovni reports that the geothermal baths called Wellovar in Bjelovar will be officially opened today on the occasion of City Day. The thermal baths themselves will be available to the general public in about ten days, Mayor Dario Hrebak announced on Monday.

Today marks 270 years of the city of Bjelovar and the Wellovar project is the largest project in its history, and all of the necessary occupancy permits for the baths have been obtained. The complex has five indoor and five outdoor pools, including an Olympic-size one, four saunas, a gym, sports and recreational facilities, and a restaurant. The outdoor pools will open only next year in May because it’s currently too cold.

According to Terme Bjelovar director Zvonimir Žarec, there are currently 47 employees at the baths, and lifeguards will also be hired shortly. Žarec said that in the last seven to eight months he has spoken with more than a thousand candidates, and a large part of the employees have returned to Bjelovar from other places.

Three hours of swimming on a weekday will cost seven euros, and a full-day ticket 16 euros on weekdays or 21 euros at weekends and on public holidays. Pensioners, persons with disabilities, war veterans, students and secondary-school pupils will pay five euros for three hours of swimming in the morning hours. A full-day family ticket for two adults and two children will cost 44 euros on weekdays or 56 euros at weekends and on public holidays.

Around 600 guests are expected at the ceremonial opening and session, and the arrival of Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Gordan Jandroković has also been announced.
