World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019064/When Surgery Isn’t Enough for China’s MRKH Patients
World.title: When Surgery Isn’t Enough for China’s MRKH Patients
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019064/When Surgery Isn’t Enough for China’s MRKH Patients
World.content:
Twenty-eight-year-old Ada, a pseudonym, and her boyfriend had reached the point of discussing marriage, but she was keeping a major secret from him: she has MRKH.

MRKH, short for Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome and also known as Müllerian agenesis, is a rare congenital disorder of the female reproductive system, affecting approximately one in 4,500 to 5,000 women. Most patients are born without a uterus and with an absent or underdeveloped vagina. In China, women with the condition have long been derogatorily labeled “stone women.”

Ada knew the condition could complicate her sex life, but she believed that was something she could address before marriage. She researched MRKH on her own and eventually found Shenzhen Luohu District People’s Hospital, in the country’s south, where she planned to undergo vaginal reconstruction surgery.

She told no one but her mother about the procedure. And saw little reason to tell her boyfriend. “After vaginal reconstruction, nothing will really feel any different (for him). I can give him the same thing, so why do I need to spell it out? If I did, it would only affect him psychologically.”

Like many MRKH patients, Ada was drawn to Shenzhen Luohu District People’s Hospital by its reputation. Although it is administratively only a district-level hospital, it has become a leading center for MRKH treatment. More than 20 years ago, doctors there pioneered the “Luohu technique,” a form of laparoscopic peritoneal vaginoplasty in which the vagina is reconstructed using tissue from the patient’s abdominal cavity. Since then, the hospital has performed more than 5,000 operations for various congenital malformations of the lower female reproductive tract, treating more MRKH patients than any other medical institution in China.

Many of these patients endure a long, painful search for medical care before finding their way to Luohu. They typically first seek treatment during adolescence because they have never had a period, or because they experience cyclical abdominal pain without menstrual bleeding. At the hospitals they visit, they may be the first MRKH patient doctors have encountered. Some are examined with multiple people looking on, only to be bluntly told that nothing can be done.

But the medical experience is only one source of pain. Patients must also contend with social and cultural pressures that can profoundly affect how they see themselves. Sighs and self-recrimination from family members can gradually lead patients to internalize the belief that they are not “complete women.” The question of whether to disclose their condition to an intimate partner can be equally fraught, bringing self-doubt and inner conflict, whatever they decide.

Research my team conducted suggests these anxieties also shape seemingly ordinary aspects of daily life. Some people with MRKH avoid public baths, swimming pools, and changing rooms. Even walking down the sanitary pad aisle in a supermarket can make them uncomfortable.

At Luohu District People’s Hospital, patients have a good chance of having their physical condition treated. But successful surgery rarely puts an end to their troubles. Dr. Qin, the clinical lead, told me frankly that surgical success marks only a biological transformation of the body. Patients still face the long process of returning to family life and rebuilding intimate relationships. A major gap exists between successful treatment and this broader recovery process, one doctors cannot fill on their own.

Even within this medically advanced team, some unease remains. Team members worry that outsiders could misunderstand reconstructive procedures involving intimate reproductive organs as dubious or unorthodox. Doctors are therefore often reluctant to talk openly about the procedures, while patients can feel they have been left to navigate their implications alone. The silence on both sides reinforces the problem.

This is precisely where medical social work can play a role.

In the autumn of 2025, after spending three months conducting sociological research with MRKH patients and the medical professionals who treat them, I joined Luohu District People’s Hospital’s Gynecology Department 3 as the supervisor of a team of social workers. We began providing medical social services for MRKH patients, helping them rebuild their sense of identity and dignity while encouraging medical professionals to shift their focus from “treating illness” toward “treating the person.”

After all, surgeons can reconstruct the body, but recovery involves more than the physical: patients must also rebuild their sense of self and return to society with dignity.

From the beginning, I knew we were in largely uncharted territory. China has no standardized assessment tools designed specifically for people with MRKH, nor an established, validated model for providing them with social services. Therefore, we had to develop our approach within the constraints of a working hospital, learning from patients and refining our methods as we went.

Our work gradually took shape in three areas.

First, we tried to bridge the gap between physical and psychological care by taking on emotional needs that clinical treatment could not easily meet.

Negative medical experiences have made many patients highly sensitive about exposing their bodies. Even an ordinary consultation room can easily trigger traumatic memories of being examined while others watched. We worked with the department to train medical staff in gender sensitivity and ethics. With their support and cooperation, we also secured private spaces for one-on-one conversations and made small changes to the rehabilitation area to make it feel less clinical and reduce patients’ discomfort when seeking care.

Our individual work with patients focused in part on helping them separate their physical differences from their sense of self-worth. Social workers encouraged them to question beliefs they had internalized, particularly the idea that “without a uterus, I am not a complete woman,” and to develop a healthier relationship with their bodies.

There are limits to what we can do. Because no locally developed assessment tool exists for MRKH patients, we rely on interviews and clinical observation to track changes in their physical and psychological well-being. Budgetary and institutional constraints also limit how much we can change the care environment.

Second, we sought to break the isolation surrounding MRKH by creating spaces for peer and family support.

We organized small in-person patient-sharing sessions and themed support groups. These included highly practical exercises such as what we call “disclosure rehearsals,” which help patients think through conversations with intimate partners in advance. If a partner asks about the condition, how should the patient respond? What are they comfortable disclosing? What risks might different approaches carry, and how might a partner react?

We also experimented with family interventions. Through family meetings, we tried to help relatives move beyond the entrenched belief that a woman’s value is tied to her ability to reproduce. At the same time, we established an online peer-support community where patients could connect.

But these efforts created challenges of their own. Many patients worried about their identities being exposed, so willingness to participate in person varied considerably. Online, we had to strike a difficult balance between allowing members to support one another and preventing the spread of medical misinformation or the amplification of distress. Some families were also deeply reluctant to discuss MRKH at all and refused to participate in family meetings.

Third, we began looking beyond the immediate clinical setting through modest advocacy efforts.

At this early stage, we were not seeking sweeping policy reform. Instead, we focused on specific problems we encountered in our work. Some patients, for example, struggled to afford surgery. We also encountered language in primary medical settings that objectified women or reduced them to their reproductive functions.

In response, our social workers contacted the She Unbinds Asia Foundation to explore dedicated financial support for people with MRKH, prioritizing patients experiencing financial hardship. But securing such dedicated funding is difficult and inherently uncertain. A stable system of financial support remains out of reach.

Despite these difficulties, I am determined to continue. Supervising this exploratory social work project has made me deeply aware that dignity is not restored through a single intervention. It is rebuilt little by little, through interactions between patients, medical professionals, social workers, and families.

Our efforts have also borne tangible results. Patients are testing different ways to navigate everyday life and gradually learning to live with their condition on their own terms. Social workers, too, are learning through trial and error, continually adjusting and refining their approaches.

The lessons extend beyond MRKH. Every year in China, large numbers of people with rare diseases enter operating rooms and leave the hospital with their physical conditions treated but the wounds to their sense of identity still unhealed. Yet social services for these patients remain severely underdeveloped.

Every obstacle we have encountered in Luohu, and every lesson we have learned, can therefore serve as a signpost for those who follow. Our experience may help not only support people with MRKH, but also develop locally grounded approaches to medical social work for other rare diseases and hidden illnesses in China.

As a university educator, I can also bring what we have learned back into the classroom. It shows students that social work is more than textbook theory. It is the painstaking work of helping people whose experiences place them outside the mainstream rebuild their dignity within the very real constraints of the world around them.

With contributions from Yang Feixu and Ni Sihan.

Translator: Gabriel Kwan.

(Header image: iStock/VCG)

World.title: It takes a village: Lady’s Choice leads a parent-kid-school partnership for healthier kids
World.content:
The Baon Buddies School Takeover brings families and educators together to make proper nutrition easier to practice every day

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Lady’s Choice Philippines and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Raising healthy kids has never been the work of parents alone. Children move between different environments every day — from the breakfast table to the classroom, the school canteen, and the people they spend their day with. Each one can influence the habits they form around food and nutrition.

This means that while healthier choices may begin at home, they become easier to practice when the circles they move in reinforce them, too. Parents can prepare nutritious meals, and schools can reinforce nutrition education, but kids also need to understand the choices that keep them fueled throughout the day.

It is this shared responsibility that sits at the heart of Lady’s Choice’s 2026 Baon Buddies School Takeover, bringing parents, kids, and schools together to make proper nutrition something they can practice consistently wherever they are.

The campaign is built around a parent-kid-school partnership designed to support children’s nutrition beyond just the school day.

Making nutrition part of the school day

School takes up a lot of children’s time and energy. Between classes, playtime, and extracurricular activities, a school day can stretch beyond the hours spent sitting inside the classroom. Lady’s Choice’s campaign is rooted in the insight that meals and snacks should do more than simply fill children up; they should also help support them through the demands of the day.

That is why the Baon Buddies School Takeover brings the conversation on nutrition directly into schools. As part of the campaign, Lady’s Choice introduced its Baon Buddies, Sandy and Elsie, in school activations that make nutrition education more engaging for both parents and children. The program includes nutrition awareness explainers, sandwich-making workshops, an “Omega-sigla” quiz bee, and sandwich sampling.

Instead of treating healthy eating as another lesson children have to “learn”, the activities show that nutrition can be educational and enjoyable at the same time.

SAMA SAMA SA NUTRISYON AT SIGLA. Kids in Upper Bicutan Elementary School participate in a sandwich making workshop.

Parents may start the habit, but kids have to be part of it

For parents, baon can easily become another item on their morning agenda — but involving children in what goes into their lunchbox can also help turn food into a conversation. What do you like eating? What can we prepare for tomorrow? What gives you enough energy for the school day?

This kind of participation matters because healthy routines are easier to sustain when children understand and have a role in them.

The Lady’s Choice Baon Buddies campaign brings this conversation into schools through a nationwide roadshow as part of its effort to reach 70,000 school sampling hits. The roadshow is done in collaboration with the Department of Education in celebration of Nutrition Month, positioning schools not just as mere venues, but as partners in making nutrition awareness part of children’s learning.

BAON BUDDIES. Making healthy eating more fun starts with meeting kids where they are.

Highlighted in Lady’s Choice’s back-to-school campaign are its Meaty Spreads, including chicken, ham, bacon, tuna, and plain variants, made with real meat and farm-fresh eggs that contain Omega-3 and 6 nutrients, as part of a proper diet and healthy lifestyle.

The campaign then brings these products into different parts of a child’s day — from breakfast, baon, and to merienda — through sandwich sampling, recipe videos, and digital content that give parents more ideas for preparing everyday meals and snacks.

Lady’s Choice taps into these different moments so healthy eating becomes something children can easily recognize. By showing how nutritious sandwiches and snacks can fit into different mealtimes, the campaign helps make better food choices feel easier to practice —supporting its larger goal of getting parents, kids, and schools to work together in building healthier everyday habits.

Watch how moms and students gave their baon a tasty twist during the Baon Buddies Takeover in Upper Bicutan Elementary School here. – Rappler.com

World.title: EJ Obiena ‘reborn’ after record-breaking Asian Games triumph
World.content:
After two years of career struggles, EJ Obiena now sees pole vault in a different light, with his resurgence reaching a golden high as he claims his second Asian Games title

MANILA, Philippines – EJ Obiena is not only rediscovering his old form but also the joy that drew him to pole vault.

And it showed in his latest golden conquest as Obiena defended his Asian Games crown, delivering a record-breaking performance to repeat as the men’s pole vault champion at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in Japan on Tuesday, September 29.

Obiena established a new Asian Games mark of 5.91 meters, eclipsing the previous record of 5.90 meters he set during his maiden victory in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China.

“I think I was not enjoying the sport as much as I should and I think that took a toll on me, in a way. Like I’m not feeling the excitement, I feel — I wouldn’t say empty — but kind of empty, like without the excitement, without the feeling of the pressure, without what I felt today. It’s been a while,” Obiena told Filipino reporters.

“To be honest, I missed it. With that, I would say it was a bit of a reborn. I see the sport in a much different perspective than it was — a little bit of fun, a little bit of reality.”

After clearing the record height, Obiena screamed at the top of his lungs, thumped his chest, and basked in the cheers of a small but raucous Filipino crowd that witnessed him become only the fourth back-to-back Asian Games champion in the event and the first since Kazakhstan’s Igor Potapovich (1994 and 1998).

Obiena also became the first Filipino to retain an athletics title in the Asian Games since the late great Lydia de Vega won the women’s 100m crown in 1982 and 1986.

The celebratory scenes stood in stark contrast to his heartbreaking fourth-place finish in the 2024 Paris Olympics, where Obiena tearfully apologized to the nation after missing out on the bronze by just a single attempt.

A series of career setbacks followed that Olympic run as Obiena — once ranked second in the world — fell outside the top 10 and failed to produce marks that he regularly achieved at the peak of his powers.

But his recent results, including five first-place finishes in his last nine meets, suggest that Obiena still has more to show.

Obiena is even surprised that he looks forward to getting back to work.

“As long as I’m having fun, I think I’m going to keep jumping. That is something new for me, to be honest. That’s something I never thought I would ever see myself do. With that, I need to understand why exactly am I doing that and kind of regroup myself and see why exactly am I excited to go to training, which I probably shouldn’t,” he said.

“I have this different situation, different aura. It’s difficult to describe because I still don’t know it.”

Obiena has plenty of time to process his emotions as he returned home to the Philippines for some much-deserved downtime with friends and family. – Rappler.com

World.title: In the Public Square: Taking the fight to the dynasties
World.content:
How did Philippine politics get this way? And what can be done to change it?

In the ongoing drama of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the Senate sits as the impeachment court—and also as a representative of the general public. But the Senate also represents the country in a different and darker way: It is the practice of dynasty politics taken to the extreme.

Eight seats in the 24-person Senate are occupied by four pairs of siblings. At least four are held by senators who have family members in national elective or appointive positions. At least two belong to political families.

How did Philippine politics get this way? And what can be done to change it?

It is time to take the fight to the dynasties.

In this new episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by former Supreme Court senior associate justice Antonio Carpio, and lawyer Alex Lacson, the chair and vice chair, respectively, of the People’s Initiative Coalition Against Dynasties.

Watch the episode on Wednesday, September 30, at 8 pm. – Rappler.com

World.title: Chasing her ‘best version,’ Alex Eala reaches Asian Games semis for sure medal
World.content:
Alex Eala knows the risk of losing, but that mindset keeps her at the top of her game as she disposes of Chinese Taipei's Joanna Garland to secure at least a bronze in the 2026 Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – As much as Alex Eala is the favorite to win the gold medal in the Asian Games, she remains mindful of the possibility of losing.

Upsets in tennis are not uncommon, with the world No. 18 Filipina fresh from a surprise exit in the Singapore Open, where she fell to Russia’s Tatiana Prozorova in a defeat that marked the first time she lost to a player outside the world top 100 since she broke into the top 50.

But that understanding has kept Eala at the top of her game as she assured herself of a medal in the 2026 Asian Games after advancing to the semifinals of the women’s singles event following a 7-5, 6-0 win over Chinese Taipei’s Joanna Garland at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center on Wednesday, September 30.

“And at the end of the day, being a professional tennis player and a competitive tennis player, losing comes. You have to understand that losing is part of the job and losing is always a possibility,” Eala said after the match.

“That’s what makes tennis so difficult, that’s what makes tennis so exciting, is that you never know what’s going to happen and you can’t let your guard down. I think that also contributes to my pursuit for excellence and my pursuit for the best version of myself.”

Ranked 143rd in the world, Garland held her own against the top-seeded Filipina in the first half of the match that took 1 hour and 49 minutes to finish, even grabbing a 5-4 lead to move on the brink of stealing the opening set.

But Eala found another gear, winning the next three games to clinch the first set and dominate the rest of the way.

Eala won nine consecutive games in total as she served her second bagel of the Asian Games after opening the tournament with a 6-1, 6-0 shellacking of Thailand’s Patcharin Cheapchandej on Monday, September 28.

“I ended the match playing better than I started, which is always a good thing,” Eala, who secured at least a bronze, told Cignal. “Really happy with the win.”

Eala took home a bronze in the 2023 edition, where she lost in the semifinals to eventual champion Zheng Qinwen of China.

This time, Zheng is not around, as well as other top Asian players in world No. 1 Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan and No. 17 Naomi Osaka of Japan as they opted to see action in the China Open, leaving Eala as the leading gold-medal contender.

Eala shoots for a spot in the final as she battles world No. 49 Wang Xiyu of China next. – Rappler.com

World.title: Leandro Leviste’s ABS-CBN stake is shrinking, and so is everyone else’s
World.content:
The expansion of the equity pie alters the corporate math for all outsiders

ABS-CBN Corp.’s stockholders approved on Wednesday, September 30 the P6 billion that will keep the media company going, and Leandro Leviste, who holds the largest stake in it outside the Lopez family, had no hand in putting the deal together. Five parties are providing the money, and he is not one of them.

The Batangas representative’s stake in ABS-CBN, which launched the political career of his mother, former news anchor Senator Loren Legarda, is heavily diluted. He shares the same fate as other public shareholders outside of the Lopez group and allies. His share of the common stock falls from 10% to 3.54%, while his true voting power drops from 4.74% to 2.54%.

The public did not get a chance to buy these new shares. Instead, this is a private deal arranged strictly between the legacy family and friendly incoming capital. Three Lopez family branch holding companies—Crème Investment, Mantes Corporation, and Presta Holdings—are buying primary common shares directly, alongside top holding vehicle Lopez Inc. Entering beside them is strategic turnaround firm I&C Holdings Corp., which is putting in P3.5 billion for 959 million shares to emerge as the single largest common shareholder.

Together, the Lopez family vehicles (around 61%) and I&C (27%) lock up roughly 88% of total voting power. That gap between owning ordinary shares and holding voting power is the whole point: common shares mainly give investors a claim on future profits and dividends, but voting power decides who actually controls the company.

Outside that circle sit public minority investors and Leviste. Without a single share trading hands, their holdings shrink both in value and in their already tiny say in the company as the share pie expands around them.

What management told shareholders

The capital increase passed on September 30 with 83% of the voting stock behind it, which is what Lopez Inc. at 78.4% and ABS-CBN Holdings at 4.83% add up to. It is likely that the shares being diluted did not vote for it.

The shareholders approved tripling the company’s authorized capital stock to P4.5 billion, and then management directly addressed the changes.

ABS-CBN president and CEO Carlo L. Katigbak defended the move when asked what benefits minority shareholders can expect from the capital increase: “The increase in authorized capital stock will allow the infusion of the P6 billion in equity from our investors. The additional capital is expected to strengthen the Company’s balance sheet, support working capital requirements, and help fund the Company’s turnaround and initiatives. We believe these measures will enhance the Company’s long-term prospects and create value for all shareholders.”

For public minorities who were not invited to take part, company survival and avoiding loan defaults were offered as the reasons for being diluted.

Chairman Martin L. Lopez also made it clear where real control sits. When asked about governance and whether new investors would steer the ship, he drew a firm line: “Lopez Inc., together with its stockholders, Crème, Mantes and Presta, and together with ABS-CBN will continue to determine ABS-CBN’s strategic direction. The new major investor will be consulted and their rights will be respected.”

A Mother’s Day gift

Leviste moved quickly when he built his stake. On April 30, 2024, his investment vehicle LL Holdings reported holding 75.9 million ABS-CBN common shares and 619,000 Philippine Depositary Receipts (PDRs) through parent firm Countryside Investments, giving him an initial 8.5% of the company.

He gave two reasons for buying, and he gave the warm one first: he timed the purchase around Mother’s Day as a nod to her mother, Loren Legarda, who anchored The World Tonight during his early childhood from 1986 until her 1998 Senate run.

“I told her that it was, of course, in time for Mother’s Day,” Leviste said in a May 16, 2024 interview on One News. Asked how she reacted, he replied: “I think that she, like others, would remark that it’s seemingly a risky investment because of the challenges of any media company nowadays but that… even a challenging market at the right price is worth looking, and that it’s very risky and that maybe buying land is a safer bet.”

Pressed on whether the purchase was opportunistic, he agreed: “A large part of ABS’s asset is also in real estate so that’s a good benefit in any company, that your primary business might encounter difficulties but you have some tangible asset underlying the company.” He added: “If there weren’t 10% or so of a company being sold at its all-time low that we wouldn’t have been able to and ended up acquiring that number of shares.”

When Leviste began accumulating in late April 2024, ABS-CBN stock was trading near historic lows in the P3.4 to P4.5 range. Once his initial 8.5% block was disclosed on May 2, the share price surged by 77% to close at ₱7.65 on June 4 as he rounded out his stake to 10%. Across that window, Leviste spent an estimated P300 million to P400 million assembling his position.

In an interview with Bilyonaryo News Channel, Leviste laid out how he snapped up positions being offloaded by foreign investors: “That was more opportunistic, because the price had tanked, and typically companies in the Philippines Stock Exchange don’t have big blocks for sale, but there were foreign investors that were willing to get out at the price… They were actually selling in the market, and then they sold to some other investors, and then those investors were selling in the market as well.”

Part of that came from buying Philippine Depositary Receipts (PDRs). Under Article XVI, Section 11 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, mass media ownership is reserved 100% for Filipino citizens. Foreign funds cannot hold media shares directly. ABS-CBN Holdings issued PDRs so foreigners could collect cash dividends without holding legal title or voting rights.

Foreign institutional investors had been trimming their exposure to the instruments, and Leviste took advantage of that secondary-market liquidity to accumulate 2.3 million PDRs, holding them alongside 87.7 million common shares as of May 28, 2024. That foreign retreat has only continued since, with foreign-held ABS-CBN PDRs falling further from 41.6 million units at the end of 2025 to 26.4 million units by June 30, 2026.

Post-May 2024, Leviste converted those 2.3 million PDRs into direct common stock. Under local rules, only 100% Filipino nationals can surrender PDRs and take delivery of the underlying media shares. By converting, Leviste turned passive receipts into voting equity, bringing his total holding to 90 million common shares—a clean 10% common block.

Why 10% was never in control

Headlines in 2024 trumpeted that Leviste owned 10% of ABS-CBN, but the capital structure was engineered long ago to ensure common shares alone could never take control.

ABS-CBN carries two classes of voting stock: listed common shares with a par value of P1, and one billion unlisted voting preferred shares with a par value of just P0.20. Despite costing one-fifth the par value of common stock, each preferred share carries one full vote.

These preferred shares are unlisted, meaning no outsider can buy them in the open market. Private family holding vehicle Lopez Inc. holds 98.71% of them (987 million shares). The remaining around 13 million shares sit across brokerages and personal holdings. It was not a legal wall, but an unlisted closed door: no outsider could ever assemble a meaningful block of preferred shares.

Because voting power is calculated using both share classes combined (899.8 million common shares plus one billion preferred shares), the total voting denominator stood at 1.9 billion shares.

Against that total, Lopez Inc. commanded 78.4% of the vote. Leviste’s 90 million shares gave him 10% of the common stock, but only 4.74% of the total vote. He held no blocking minority, no swing vote, and no unilateral path to a board seat.

Separating economic returns from voting control has long been the setup in Philippine media. Leviste bought the economics because the economics were the only part for sale.

Why ABS-CBN needed money

What Leviste bought a tenth of was an earnings stream that stopped in 2020 and has not returned.

Since Congress denied its broadcast franchise in 2020, ABS-CBN has posted consecutive heavy losses: P6.09 billion in 2024, P4.72 billion in 2025, and another P1.83 billion in the first half of 2026. While content partnerships with GMA, A2Z, and Netflix generated cash flow, heavy operating overhead, talent payroll, and debt service continued to bleed money.

Common and preferred shareholders have received zero dividends since 2020. Cumulative unpaid preferred dividends climbed past P24 million.

Worse, ABS-CBN hit a debt wall: standstill agreements on P8.5 billion in bank debts with BPI and UnionBank had expired, and past-due liabilities were piling up. Without a primary capital injection, the broadcaster faced severe balance-sheet distress.

The fine print on the P6 billion

When a listed company needs equity, it typically holds a rights offering, giving all existing shareholders the legal option to buy new shares pro-rata and maintain their percentage stake.

ABS-CBN did not do that. Instead, it sold 1.644 billion primary common shares at P3.65 each to 5 chosen subscribers, citing an exception to the rights offering requirement under Philippine Stock Exchange rules. In a solvency crisis, an open rights offering carries heavy market risk: public shareholders, already nursing paper losses, might refuse to put up fresh cash, leaving the rescue underfunded.

The transaction is not P6 billion in instant bank cash, nor is the money sitting in escrow. Term sheets reveal that ABS-CBN has received P2 billion in upfront deposits upon signing:

I&C Holdings paid a P1.5 billion deposit (against its P3.5 billion subscription).

Lopez Inc. paid its full P300 million subscription upfront.

Crème Investment (Geny Lopez line) paid a P100 million deposit (against P767 million).

Mantes Corporation (Manolo Lopez line) paid a P100 million deposit (against P767 million).

Presta Holdings (Prescy Psinakis line) paid no deposit (against P667 million).

The remaining P4 billion is deferred: Crème and Mantes pay their balances “on such date as may be determined by the Board of Directors,” making the remaining cash discretionary rather than an immediate delivery.

Leviste and the other minority shareholders were not invited to participate in the capital raise. In May 2024, he told reporters: “We want to buy more shares. If there will be shares available, then we will buy.” But the new shares were created exclusively for the five subscribers. Outside shareholders were never invited into the room.

How everyone got diluted

The expansion of the equity pie alters the corporate math for all outsiders:

Shareholder Pre-deal common % Post-deal common % Pre-deal voting power Post-deal voting power Leandro Leviste (LL Holdings) 10% 3.54% 4.74% 2.54% Lopez Inc. ~55.8% ~22.98% 78.4% 44.35% I&C Holdings Corp 0 37.7% 0 27.06% 3 Lopez branches’ SPV (Crème, Mantes, Presta) 0.05% 23.7% 0.02% 17.02% Other minority holders (excluding Leviste) ~25.4%% ~8.97%% 12.02% 6.44% Total public float (“Others” in disclosure table) ~44.2% ~15.6% 16.75% 8.98%

Leviste’s common block falls from 10% to 3.54%, and his voting weight shrinks to 2.54%.

Other retail holders suffer the exact same proportional cut: their collective voting strength drops from 12.02% down to 6.44%. The line marked “Others” in ABS-CBN’s regulatory table reads 318 million shares before and after—the exact same shares, compressed from 16.75% of the company to 8.98% purely because the firm expanded around them. ABS-CBN summarized the impact to the stock exchange in six words: “The public float will be diluted.”

The transaction also closes the door on any outside boardroom clout. I&C Holdings comes in with 959 million common shares—more than 10 times Leviste’s 90 million shares. With I&C and the Lopez family vehicles jointly controlling 88% of total voting stock, Leviste’s ability to act as a swing vote or rally fellow minorities is neutralized.

Watching from afar

Leviste is likely watching this unfold from abroad. The Batangas representative has been out of the country since August, while he and Senator Legarda face a preliminary investigation before the Office of the Ombudsman regarding P10.44 billion in unpaid obligations tied to past solar projects—allegations both have rejected as baseless and politically motivated.

Because his shares are held through LL Holdings Inc., an appointed proxy can still vote his stake. But against an 88% insider bloc, the vote cannot change the outcome.

ABS-CBN gets the P2 billion in initial cash it needs to placate bank creditors and keep producing content. But the recapitalization underscores a familiar rule in Philippine business: in companies shielded by constitutional rules and dual-class voting shares, outside minority shareholders absorb the dilution, while the family and its chosen partners keep the keys. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: Industrial Modernization, Investment in Focus of Tokayev’s Business Meetings in Munich
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev began the second day of his official visit to Germany in Munich on Sept. 30 with a series of meetings with senior executives of Siemens AG, Linde and Aurubis AG, focusing on industrial modernization, technological cooperation and new investment projects.

During a meeting with Bernd Ulbricht, vice president for commercial and financial affairs at Siemens AG, Tokayev described Siemens as an important partner for Kazakhstan, noting that its expertise in industrial digitalization, electrification, mobility and smart infrastructure aligns with the country’s economic modernization priorities.

Tokayev welcomed a joint project between Siemens and Kazakhstan’s Silk Road Electronics to modernize equipment at the Qarmet metallurgical plant. He emphasized Kazakhstan’s interest not only in acquiring advanced equipment but also in establishing local manufacturing, engineering and service capabilities, reported Akorda.

The officials also discussed opportunities to apply Siemens technologies in modernizing Kazakhstan’s energy and utilities sectors, environmental monitoring, medical technologies and data center infrastructure.

In a separate meeting with Oliver Pfann, senior vice president at Linde, Tokayev welcomed the company’s plans for new projects in Kazakhstan with potential investments of up to $500 million. The officials noted an agreement between Linde and Qarmet to build a new air separation unit in Temirtau and discussed prospects for cooperation in the petrochemical industry.

Tokayev also highlighted Linde’s carbon capture and storage and hydrogen infrastructure technologies, inviting the company to participate in projects in the petrochemical and chemical clusters in the Atyrau and Mangystau Regions.

During talks with Fritz Vahrenholt, chairman of the Supervisory Board of Aurubis AG, the officials discussed potential investment projects in Kazakhstan’s mining and metallurgical sector. Tokayev emphasized the country’s priority of moving from a raw-material model toward deeper metals processing, advanced technologies and higher value-added production.

The discussions covered processing complex copper-bearing raw materials, recovering associated metals and recycling and localizing downstream production. Particular attention was given to cooperation between Tau-Ken Samruk and Aurubis on processing copper scrap and technogenic mineral formations in Kazakhstan, with the sides considering a joint action plan for prospective projects.

Kazakhstan-Germany cooperation in education and science

During a meeting with German university rectors and research institute heads on Sept. 30, Tokayev called for stronger cooperation between Kazakhstan and Germany in education, research, technology transfer and artificial intelligence.

Tokayev highlighted growing academic ties, noting that 45 Kazakh universities cooperate with around 100 German partners, while nearly 2,000 Kazakh students study in Germany.

He proposed expanding joint education and dual-degree programs, scientific research and technology transfer. He also invited German businesses to establish engineering laboratories and technology transfer centers at joint institutions in Kazakhstan.

Tokayev said cooperation should increasingly connect universities, research and industry and focus on developing technologies and products with higher added value.

World.title: Global Logistics Company Rhenus Advances Plans for Multimodal Terminal in Aktau
World.content:
ASTANA – Rhenus Group, a global logistics and supply chain company, and Aktau International Sea Trade Port are advancing plans to develop a trimodal container terminal in Aktau, designed to connect maritime, rail and road transport and strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a key logistics hub along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), or the Middle Corridor.

The agreement outlining the project’s next steps was signed on Sept. 30 during Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Germany.

The project is part of Rhenus’ long-term strategy to strengthen transport links between China, Central Asia, the Caspian region and Europe, and supports the development of the Middle Corridor as part of the EU’s Global Gateway initiative, Rhenus press service reported.

“The strategic importance of the TITR is now hardly in question. The key challenge is to bring individual infrastructure projects together step by step into an efficient network in which capacity, operational services and strong partnerships work seamlessly along the entire route,” said Tobias Bartz, CEO and chairman of the Management Board of Rhenus Group.

Aktau to strengthen its multimodal role

The planned trimodal container terminal at Aktau International Sea Trade Port will connect maritime, rail and road transport. It will be developed on a site of at least 30 hectares and is expected to provide additional handling capacity of at least 150,000 TEU annually.

The project would increase capacity on the Caspian section of the TITR and strengthen Aktau’s role as a key logistics hub.

Rhenus is also working closely with Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the country’s state railway operator, to expand corridor capacity and build the infrastructure needed to accommodate growing cargo flows.

“Cooperation with Rhenus opens up new opportunities to develop Kazakhstan’s transit potential. The joint terminal project at the Aktau Port will become an important element of our logistics infrastructure and provide a foundation for deepening our partnership,” said Yelzhas Otynshiyev, KTZ chair.

The next stages will include an analysis of expected cargo flows and assessment of the project’s technical and economic feasibility.

Building an integrated logistics network

Rhenus has operated in Kazakhstan for 30 years and has expanded its presence through targeted investments. At the beginning of this year, the company acquired a rail-connected terminal in the Almaty Region, adding terminal, depot and multimodal capacity and strengthening the region’s links to international transport routes.

Beyond Kazakhstan, Rhenus is present in key markets along the Middle Corridor, including Azerbaijan, Georgia, Türkiye and Uzbekistan.

The company’s long-term objective is to integrate terminals, depots, rail and maritime services and freight forwarding activities along the route and connect them with its European logistics and terminal network.

The approach is intended to gradually develop individual infrastructure projects into a more reliable and predictable logistics network between Asia and Europe.

About Rhenus

Rhenus Group is a global logistics company with annual turnover of 8.2 billion euros (US$9.3 billion). It employs 39,000 people at 1,300 sites in more than 70 countries, providing transport, warehousing, customs clearance and other supply chain services.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Energy Hinges on Diversification and New Investment, KIOGE 2026 Experts Say
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s position in emerging global energy value chains will increasingly depend on the resilience of its infrastructure, diversification of export routes and investment in new production and technology, speakers said at the strategic plenary session opening Kazakhstan’s International Oil and Gas Exhibition (KIOGE 2026) in Almaty on Sept. 30.

The session, dedicated to Kazakhstan’s role in new energy value chains, brought together senior officials and industry experts to discuss how geopolitical disruptions, changing trade flows and growing energy demand are reshaping the global oil and gas market.

Karen Oldhoven, moderator of the session, said Kazakhstan has positioned itself as an important link between major markets at a time of significant changes in the global energy system.

“This is a year of tectonic and geopolitical shifts and at the same time the world is getting more hungry for energy and despite all this Kazakhstan positions itself as a reliable partner and also a bridge for dialogue, cooperation and investment,” she said, highlighting that the next stage would require cooperation between industry participants, governments and experts to build Kazakhstan’s future energy ecosystem.

Resilient infrastructure becomes a priority

Suhail Mohamed Faraj Al Mazrouei, the United Arab Emirates’ Minister of Energy and Infrastructure, highlighted the impact of geopolitical disruptions on energy and commodity flows. According to him, countries are increasingly looking at projects that would allow hydrocarbons to be exported through multiple routes rather than relying on a single corridor.

“Something that is very important as well, other than the optionality and building other options, is to ensure the resilience and the security of the critical infrastructure. Because those infrastructures were attacked, unfortunately,” he said.

He also stressed the importance of international cooperation, noting that disruptions to major trade routes can affect markets well beyond the countries directly involved.

“If those veins of trade are restricted, threatened, all of us are going to pay the price. It’s not just one country,” Al Mazrouei said.

The emphasis on alternative routes and infrastructure resilience is particularly relevant for Kazakhstan, whose energy exports depend on several international transportation corridors and whose role as a link between East and West is expanding.

Energy markets face a new era of uncertainty

Philip Mshelbila, Secretary General of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, said the latest energy crisis demonstrated that geopolitical disruptions are likely to remain a recurring feature of global markets. The Gas Exporting Countries Forum brings together 20 countries holding about 70% of the world’s proven natural gas reserves, he noted.

“This conflict and the crisis that’s emanated from it has first of all taught us that geopolitical events are going to continue to happen. They will continue to happen more frequently. And we need to accept them as the new norm,” Mshelbila said.

He pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2022 conflict in Ukraine and the latest crisis as examples of major disruptions that have affected the energy sector within a relatively short period.

“What we just don’t know is what’s going to happen, when it’s going to happen, and where,” he said.

At the same time, Mshelbila said the global natural gas system had demonstrated a degree of resilience during recent disruptions. He cited accelerated projects, additional production from North America, deferred maintenance at energy facilities and increased upstream gas production as measures that helped compensate for supply losses.

“Between March and August, we estimated that about 39 million tons per annum of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) was taken off the market. Mainly between Qatar and the UAE. But, close to 34 million tons of that came into the market,” he said.

According to Mshelbila, this demonstrated that more than 80% of the potential LNG supply gap was compensated through various measures.

“There is already some degree of resilience in the natural gas system globally. It’s clearly not enough. And a lot more needs to be done,” he said, stressing that energy producers ultimately remain dependent on markets, even when they have sufficient resources and production capacity.

“Even if you have all the forms of energy that you need, in the quantity you need, you might actually have a surplus you want to sell to somebody. Which means you’re going to depend on the market,” he added.

Kazakhstan seen as investment and transit hub

Against this backdrop, Mshelbila pointed to Kazakhstan’s geographic position and resource base as factors that could support further investment.

“I think that Kazakhstan gives an example of an investment destination. That could welcome that sort of an investment. Because it is so strategically located between East and West. And it has its own resources in abundance. And it could actually serve as transit even more than it is already doing,” he said.

His comments come as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its role in regional energy and transport chains while attracting investment into both traditional and emerging parts of the sector.

KMG targets higher recovery from mature fields

For Kazakhstan’s national oil and gas company, maintaining production from mature fields remains a key part of the long-term strategy. KazMunayGas First Deputy CEO Kurmangazy Iskaziyev said the company has been working to increase output of refined petroleum products while diversifying transportation routes. However, he said expanding the company’s resource base is a central strategic priority.

“KazMunayGas has 65 producing fields, excluding major projects such as Kashagan and other large developments. About 90% of production from the company’s mature fields comes from 12 fields,” he said.

Iskaziyev said many mature fields have already depleted around 70% of their reserves, increasing the importance of identifying new resources, particularly in Paleozoic formations.

“The company has identified 23 projects and is working with the Ministry of Energy on improving the terms of the relevant contracts. The program includes 3D seismic surveys and the drilling of deep wells,” he said.

A second component involves large-scale exploration using 2D seismic surveys covering areas in the south and east of the Caspian region and the northern Caspian area.

Logistics increasingly shape oil prices

The discussion also moved beyond production to the ability to move energy products to consumers. Global Director for Refined Products, Platts and S&P Global Energy Francesco Di Salvo said current oil market dynamics cannot be explained by supply and demand alone, with logistics increasingly affecting prices and trade flows.

Speaking from the perspective of a company that provides benchmark price assessments, including Brent and CPC Blend, Di Salvo said the ability to transport crude from production sites to end users has become increasingly important.

“It is actually the ability to evacuate these molecules, to bring them from the production point to the delivery and consumption point and that is being made incredibly more difficult,” he said.

For Kazakhstan, this has direct implications for the value of its crude exports, including CPC Blend. He noted that shipping has increasingly become a key component of oil trade economics.

Refined products and changing trade flows

Di Salvo also highlighted the growing importance of refined products, particularly diesel, jet fuel and gasoline, whose values can increasingly diverge from crude oil prices. He linked this trend to the broader issue of diversification, particularly in Europe, where dependence on limited sources and routes has created additional energy security challenges.

Another major development, he said, is the reshaping of global trade flows driven by geopolitical developments and sanctions.

“We are really seeing a paradigmatic shift in the market, and I think it’s quite exciting to see, but also very challenging to have to play in this market,” he said.

The discussions at KIOGE 2026 highlighted a common idea across the different perspectives: Kazakhstan’s future role in global energy markets will depend not only on the availability of hydrocarbons, but also on the country’s ability to develop resilient infrastructure, diversify transportation routes, expand its resource base and adapt to changing global trade patterns.

The 30th KIOGE 2026 is taking place in Almaty on Sept. 30-Oct. 2, bringing together more than 500 companies from 62 countries to discuss the future of Kazakhstan’s energy sector, international cooperation and emerging technologies.

World.title: Hong Kong to Host Major Electronics Fairs in October
World.content:
ASTANA – The Hong Kong Trade Development Council (HKTDC) will host the Hong Kong Electronics Fair (Autumn Edition) and electronicAsia from Oct. 13-16, bringing together more than 3,200 exhibitors to showcase the latest consumer electronics, smart products, electronic components and technology solutions.

The fairs will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Center, providing a global platform for electronics companies, buyers, startups and technology innovators to explore new products and business opportunities.

Last year, the two fairs attracted nearly 60,000 industry buyers from 142 countries and regions, while bringing together more than 3,200 exhibitors.

Focus on AI, robotics and smart wellness

Now in its 46th edition, the Hong Kong Electronics Fair will highlight three key themes: AI and Robotics, Smart Wellness and NEXT Entertainment.

The AI and Robotics theme will feature more than 120 robots, showcasing advances in artificial intelligence, intelligent automation and robotics across industrial, commercial and everyday applications. The dedicated RoboPark zone will offer live demonstrations of robotic technologies.

The Smart Wellness theme will showcase digital health devices, smart wearables, personal care technologies, elderly-care solutions and other technology-enabled wellness products.

NEXT Entertainment will focus on XR technologies, smart gaming devices, digital content creation tools and other immersive and interactive entertainment solutions.

New zones for emerging technologies

The fair will also feature several dedicated zones, including the Hall of Fame, Startup Zone and the new Future Industries Zone, which will showcase innovations in Future Computing, Future Manufacturing, Future Marine & Quantum Technologies, Future Microelectronics and Future Wellness.

A new GoGlobal Connect Zone will provide businesses with one-stop professional support for international expansion and access to overseas markets.

Held concurrently, electronicAsia, organized by HKTDC and MMI Asia Pte Ltd, will focus on electronic components, parts and related solutions.

The four-day program will also include forums, conferences and seminars, where industry experts will discuss market trends and technological developments, while startups will have opportunities to connect with investors and industry professionals.

The registration is available here.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expects Above-Average Grain Harvest as 83% of Crops Collected
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan expects this year’s grain harvest to exceed the long-term average, with farmers having already harvested around 20 million tons of grain from 83% of planted areas, Deputy Agriculture Minister Nazgul Khatepova said at a Sept. 29 government press conference on the harvest campaign.

Kazakhstan’s grain harvest has typically stood at around 18-19 million tons in recent years, reported the Prime Minister’s press service.

The country has sufficient storage capacity to accommodate the new harvest, including carry-over stocks from previous years. Total grain storage capacity stands at 30.5 million tons, including 13.1 million tons at licensed elevators and 17.4 million tons at farms and agricultural enterprises.

Nearly 4.9 million tons of this year’s grain has already been placed in storage.

Potato exports seen at 400,000 tons

Kazakhstan expects a potato harvest of around 2.8 million tons, broadly matching last year’s level. The country exported 388,000 tons of potatoes last year, while this year’s export potential is estimated at 400,000 tons

Nearly 2.5 million tons have already been harvested. In the Karagandy and Pavlodar Regions, potatoes are currently selling for 90-100 tenge (US$0,23) per kilogram.

The Agriculture Ministry, together with local authorities and major retail chains, is working on advance contracting to help farmers export surplus potatoes.

Vegetable storage capacity sufficient

Existing vegetable storage facilities are also sufficient to preserve key produce through the off-season, according to the ministry.

Kazakhstan produces around 2.8-3 million tons of potatoes and 2.5-3 million tons of vegetables annually. The main types of produce require around 2.5-2.6 million tons of storage capacity. More than 700,000 tons of new capacity has been commissioned over the past three years.

Natural losses during harvesting, storage and transportation average 5-10%.

Beef prices remain stable

The domestic market remains fully supplied with locally produced beef, with no grounds for a sharp price increase, Khatepova said.

The average retail price is around 3,800 tenge (US$8,66) per kilogram nationwide, while prices in Astana start from nearly 3,800 tenge.

“Grounds for a sharp increase in prices are not observed. The domestic market is fully supplied through domestic production,” she said.

Kazakhstan produced 434,000 tons of beef last year, with production continuing to grow this year. The ministry said regional price fluctuations occur periodically, but no sustained upward trend has been recorded.

World.title: Tokayev, Merz Take Kazakhstan-Germany Partnership Forward as 30+ Deals Reach $2 Billion
World.content:
ASTANA – More than 30 commercial agreements worth around $2 billion are expected to give new impetus to Kazakhstan-Germany relations, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Chancellor Friedrich Merz discussed expanding cooperation in industry, critical minerals, technology, transport and other strategic sectors on Sept. 29 in Berlin.

Expanding trade and investment

Germany is one of Kazakhstan’s key trading partners and a leading foreign investor. Bilateral trade reached $4.5 billion last year, up 13.4%, while cumulative German investment in Kazakhstan has reached $8 billion over the past 21 years, Akorda reported.

Tokayev and Merz identified significant potential for cooperation in industry, critical minerals, transport and logistics, digital technologies, machinery and chemical production, notably in areas involving high-value-added products.

The joint investment portfolio currently includes 40 industrial projects worth around $54 billion.

Tokayev said Kazakhstan attaches particular importance to creating favorable conditions for German investors.

“Ensuring the security of German investments is under our special control,” he said.

New commercial agreements

On the first day of President Tokayev’s visit, more than 30 commercial documents worth around $2 billion were signed.

Tokayev highlighted the role of the Intergovernmental Working Group and the Kazakhstan-German Business Council in advancing bilateral economic ties and supporting joint projects.

He said effective implementation of the newly reached agreements would strengthen economic cooperation between the two countries.

Cooperation in technology and industry

The talks placed particular emphasis on expanding cooperation beyond traditional trade into technology, industrial production and innovation.

Tokayev is also scheduled to visit Bavaria and attend the Kazakhstan-Bavarian Technology Forum, where they are expected to discuss further opportunities for technological and business cooperation.

President Tokayev said Germany’s industrial strength, scientific expertise and technological capabilities provide a strong basis for expanding bilateral cooperation.

Central Asia-Germany cooperation

Both leaders also discussed regional and international cooperation and agreed to intensify engagement through international organizations, including the Central Asia-Germany format.

Tokayev described Germany as a reliable strategic partner for Kazakhstan in Europe and noted that the two countries would mark the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations next year.

He said bilateral ties have expanded across political, economic, investment and cultural-humanitarian spheres since diplomatic relations were established.

Tokayev and Merz also discussed expanding cooperation in education, science and culture, including joint initiatives in these fields.

Kazakhstan’s position on international issues

The talks also covered regional and global developments.

Tokayev reiterated Kazakhstan’s position that conflicts should be resolved through peaceful and diplomatic means, with respect for the principles of the UN Charter and the territorial integrity of states.

During the press briefing, an ARD correspondent asked Tokayev about his earlier remarks on the war in Ukraine. Tokayev clarified that his proposal to freeze hostilities aimed to create conditions for a transition to diplomatic negotiations.

Merz invited to Kazakhstan

Following the talks, Tokayev invited Chancellor Merz to visit Kazakhstan on a state visit next year.

The invitation comes as Kazakhstan and Germany prepare to mark 35 years of diplomatic relations, with both officials expressing an intention to further expand their strategic partnership across economic, technological, scientific and humanitarian fields.

The same day, Tokayev held talks with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier to discuss the development of bilateral relations and prospects for further cooperation.

World.title: Kazakhstan Rises Eight Places in Global Innovation Index, Posts Best Result in Decade
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has climbed eight places to 73rd among 139 economies in the World Intellectual Property Organization’s (WIPO) Global Innovation Index (GII) 2026, marking the country’s best result in the past decade.

Kazakhstan ranked first among Central Asian countries and second among 11 economies in Central and Southern Asia. Among 35 upper-middle-income economies, it placed 17th, the permanent mission of Kazakhstan to the World Trade Organization reported on Sept. 29.

The greatest improvement came in innovation outputs, where Kazakhstan rose 11 positions from 84th to 73rd. Its ranking in the Innovation Input Sub-Index also improved, from 75th to 73rd.

The GII 2026 results were presented at WIPO headquarters in Geneva during an advance presentation for Permanent Representatives of WIPO Member States.

Kazakhstan’s improved ranking follows systematic engagement between the country’s permanent mission in Geneva and WIPO throughout 2026. The work focused on specific GII indicators, the methodology used to calculate them and the quality of underlying data.

At the permanent mission’s initiative, WIPO experts held an online consultation with relevant government authorities to review Kazakhstan’s indicators, data sources, missing and outdated statistics, and areas requiring further work. The mission subsequently prepared an analytical assessment with recommendations and shared it with relevant government bodies.

The process shifted Kazakhstan’s engagement with WIPO from monitoring its annual ranking to more targeted work on individual indicators, data quality and policy measures.

Further improvement remains possible in areas including research and development expenditure, university-industry collaboration, venture capital, innovation clusters, software, and scientific and technical publications.

The permanent mission said it will continue working with WIPO on individual indicators and methodology, with the next objective being to consolidate the progress achieved and further improve Kazakhstan’s position through systematic work on key GII indicators.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Germany Set Sights on Deeper Economic Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier held talks in Berlin on Sept. 29 to discuss the development of bilateral relations and prospects for further cooperation.

Tokayev thanked Steinmeier for the reception and invitation to visit Germany, describing the country as Kazakhstan’s key strategic partner in Europe. He said bilateral ties are based on mutual trust, respect and shared interests.

The two countries will mark the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations next year. Tokayev noted significant progress across a broad range of cooperation over the past three decades.

Steinmeier, in turn, highlighted Tokayev’s personal contribution to expanding cooperation between Kazakhstan and Germany. He said the visit would add momentum to bilateral relations and take them to a new level.

Economic cooperation takes a central place

The talks come as economic ties have become an important component of the Kazakhstan-Germany partnership. Earlier on Sept. 29, Tokayev met with heads of leading German business associations and financial institutions, where he proposed establishing a Kazakhstan-Germany Investment and Financial Platform to facilitate joint projects and investment.

During the visit, Tokayev also met with executives of major German companies, discussing transport and logistics, industrial localization, engineering, metallurgy and waste processing. Discussions included developing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, modernizing railway and logistics infrastructure, expanding manufacturing in Kazakhstan, developing engineering and service capabilities, and exploring potential projects in metal processing and waste management.

A visit at a new stage of relations

Tokayev’s Sept. 29-Oct. 1 visit includes meetings in Berlin and Munich and comes as Kazakhstan-Germany relations continue to expand politically and economically.

At the same time, the discussions have increasingly focused on moving from political dialogue and existing cooperation frameworks toward specific investment, industrial and infrastructure projects.

The meetings in Germany aim to strengthen this economic dimension of bilateral relations and expand opportunities for German companies in Kazakhstan and the wider Central Asian market.

World.title: From self-defence to political statements: how former Georgian PM Garibashvili’s ‘prison’ letters have evolved
World.content:
Analysis of former Georgian PM’s “prison” letters

Former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has published his eighth letter from prison, which differs significantly from his previous seven. In the letter, Garibashvili looks back on his political career and presents himself to the public as a successful prime minister. The text effectively serves both as a political report and a statement of leadership ambitions.

In the letter, the former prime minister seeks to show that in 2021 he led the government out of a deep political and economic crisis and improved the country’s situation through his work.

At the end of the letter, he asks the public whether the situation has improved or deteriorated since he resigned. Although he does not directly name current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, the question clearly challenges his administration.

“Almost three years have passed since then [my resignation], and I want to ask the people: has the situation in the country improved or deteriorated, both in domestic and foreign policy?”

About former PM Giorgi Gakharia

Garibashvili begins his account with February 2021, when he returned as prime minister for a second time after Giorgi Gakharia resigned. He says Georgia faced several serious challenges at once: a political crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, a shortage of vaccines, an economic downturn, a large budget deficit, rising public debt and a weakening lari.

In his view, Gakharia abandoned the country and the ruling team under these circumstances. Garibashvili’s position on Gakharia echoes the Georgian Dream party’s narrative:

“Gakharia left the country and the team in the middle of an acute crisis, committing an act of unexpected betrayal by resigning. The government stood on the brink of collapse, the ruling party had lost morale, the team was divided, and the party’s approval rating had fallen to 35–37%.”

Garibashvili portrays his return as, essentially, a rescue operation for the government. He says that after taking office as prime minister, he strengthened the team, stabilised the situation, reopened the country and the economy, secured vaccine supplies and lifted restrictions introduced during the pandemic.

The former prime minister stresses that the government abandoned what he calls a “Covid dictatorship” and gave people complete freedom to choose whether to get vaccinated.

“In the shortest possible time, we restored balance, strengthened the team and stabilised the situation. Together with the team, we took bold, decisive, effective and — at the time — risky steps.”

In his view, these measures secured Georgian Dream’s victory in the 2021 local elections. Garibashvili credits himself not only with helping the party clear the 43 per cent threshold and win 47 per cent of the vote, but also with preventing a potential revolutionary scenario after Mikheil Saakashvili returned to Georgia.

“We prevented destabilisation and an attempted revolution involving Saakashvili, put all destructive forces in their place and brought the political crisis to an end.”

Showcasing economic results

A significant part of the letter focuses on economic indicators. Garibashvili claims that Georgia’s economy grew by 30 billion lari (about $11,516,310,000) during his three years as prime minister. He says the economy recorded double-digit growth in 2021 and 2022, putting Georgia first among EU member and candidate countries in terms of growth.

Garibashvili lists the following among his government’s achievements:

cutting the budget deficit from 9 per cent to 2.8 per cent;

reducing public debt from 60 per cent to 38 per cent of GDP;

stabilising the lari exchange rate at between 2.6 and 2.7;

bringing inflation below the target level;

reducing unemployment and poverty to historic lows;

creating tens of thousands of new jobs;

raising pensions and salaries for public-sector workers.

The former prime minister attributes lower medicine prices to the opening of the Turkish pharmaceutical market and the introduction of a reference pricing system for medicines.

EU candidate status and the issue of being “dragged into war” with Russia

Garibashvili also devotes considerable attention to foreign policy. Here again, he echoes Georgian Dream’s rhetoric. He says Georgia faced intense pressure after the war between Russia and Ukraine began, but his government managed to protect the country from the threat of war and destabilisation.

“From the very first days of the war between Russia and Ukraine, despite enormous pressure, we firmly and uncompromisingly defended our country’s national interests, preventing destabilisation and the real threat of war.”

Garibashvili thus repeats one of Georgian Dream’s key political arguments: after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia faced the risk of being dragged into the conflict.

The former prime minister lists his foreign visits and diplomatic initiatives in the letter. These include applying for EU membership, developing strategic relations with China, signing free trade agreements with several countries, mediating between Azerbaijan and Armenia, and hosting a meeting of the three countries’ prime ministers in Tbilisi.

Garibashvili considers Georgia’s achievement of EU candidate status in December 2023 his main foreign policy accomplishment.

“Without bowing to anyone — either inside the country or abroad — and solely through our uncompromising defence of our country’s national interests and the joint efforts of our team, we secured EU candidate status in December 2023.”

The letter says these results came without political subordination to external forces.

Approval ratings and resignation

Garibashvili claims he left office with high levels of public support. According to him, in January 2024, approval of the government’s performance and support for Georgian Dream both reached 60 per cent.

“Thanks to the results we achieved — and, most importantly, thanks to democratic methods — we politically neutralised the entire radical opposition, leaving no one with any grounds for criticism or complaint.”

Garibashvili presents not only his government’s record but also the neutralisation of the opposition as a political achievement. He effectively equates this “democratic success” with the ruling party’s dominance and the opposition’s removal from the political arena.

The letter does not explain why Garibashvili resigned as prime minister at a time when, according to his own account, the government enjoyed high approval, the economy was growing and the opposition had suffered political defeat.

From self-defence to political statements: analysis of former Georgian PM’s “prison” letters

Garibashvili’s eight letters form a coherent political narrative. At first, he sought to protect himself and his family. He later accused the authorities of orchestrating political persecution. He subsequently began raising questions about the government’s actions and several other issues. In his eighth letter, he defends his political legacy and criticises the current government. Political analysts say the latest letter points to political ambitions on Garibashvili’s part.

The first stage — Ivanishvili loyalty and self-preservation

In his first letters, Garibashvili described the pressure against him as the main source of the conflict. He said he did not plan to return to politics, but the authorities demanded that he admit guilt to new corruption charges, fearing a “one per cent risk” that he might return to politics.

He firmly reaffirmed his loyalty to Bidzina Ivanishvili, while holding him personally responsible if anything threatened his family.

“I am not fighting or battling anyone — I am only defending myself and my family!”

Garibashvili took a defensive position, seeking to show that he had not chosen this confrontation and that the authorities had forced him to defend himself.

The second stage — accusing specific individuals

In his subsequent letters, it became clearer who exactly Garibashvili was targeting with his criticism. His focus shifted from Ivanishvili to Prime Minister Kobakhidze and former regional development minister and former State Security Service chief Mamuka Mdinaradze. Garibashvili accused both of them of organising the pressure against him.

By presenting the situation this way, the former prime minister clearly left the door open to reconciliation with Ivanishvili. He continued to describe Ivanishvili as someone for whom he had “enormous love, respect, boundless gratitude and absolute loyalty”, while placing the blame for what was happening on people around him.

The third stage — systemic accusations

In his fifth and sixth letters, Garibashvili broadened the scope of the conflict. He publicly questioned the circumstances surrounding the death of human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze and linked the incident to other suicides that occurred while Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze held power.

The convicted former prime minister later accused the government as a whole of conducting systematic propaganda, using investigations for political purposes, and trying to link Garibashvili to the United National Movement or foreign agents.

Garibashvili moved beyond his own criminal case, criticising the government’s methods and presenting himself as a victim of political persecution.

The fourth stage — creating an alternative to the current government

In his seventh letter, Garibashvili claimed that the authorities had arrested him to destroy his political future. He accused the government of creating an atmosphere of endless chaos, crisis and impoverishment.

The most significant point came when he compared Georgian Dream with Mikheil Saakashvili’s administration:

“You are already following in Saakashvili’s footsteps and bringing back the methods of governance used by the National Movement…”

For years, Georgian Dream has built its political identity around contrasting itself with Saakashvili’s rule. Garibashvili’s accusation that the current government uses the same methods therefore directly challenges the ruling team’s legitimacy.

Analysts say the eighth letter takes a more political tone than his previous statements in his own defence.

Garibashvili has not officially announced a return to politics. However, the logic of his letters points towards a political comeback.

Analysis of former Georgian PM’s “prison” letters

World.title: ‘Transparent and competitive, but also cause for concern’: PACE report on Armenia’s elections
World.content:
PACE report on Armenia’s elections

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe’s election observation mission has published a report on the parliamentary elections, which took place in Armenia on 7 June.

“The elections were competitive, and citizens had a genuine choice between different political forces and alternatives,” the report says.

Observers also found the process well organised and transparent, with no serious incidents.

At the same time, they identified several serious problems. In particular, they expressed concern over a post-election dispute involving the invalidation of voting results at polling stations 10/51, 35/65 and 12/13. PACE experts believe that if officials had counted those votes, the opposition Prosperous Armenia party could have crossed the four per cent threshold and won seats.

Meanwhile, the Central Election Commission said the annulment of the results at these polling stations did not affect the election outcome. It therefore decided not to hold repeat voting there. However, PACE described the decision as “unsatisfactory, given the significance of its consequences”.

“A perfectly acceptable option would have been to hold repeat voting at the relevant polling stations. The CEC rejected this without providing serious justification. Authorities should base such an important decision on strong, transparent and verifiable grounds. Unfortunately, that did not happen,” said Swiss politician Damien Cottier, one of the report’s authors.

Armenian journalists also noted that MPs from the ruling party and the opposition selectively presented PACE’s assessment to the public. They quoted and highlighted the parts of the document that supported their respective positions.

“Politicians often resort to such tactics. In English, there is an expression for this: cherry-picking. Politicians select and present only the findings that portray them in a positive light, while ignoring or downplaying the negative ones,” Factor TV said in a report.

Main concerns

“Interference by the Russian Federation and foreign information operations in a Council of Europe member state have reached unprecedented levels,” the report says.

According to the PACE mission, Russia used economic restrictions and tough diplomatic rhetoric to influence the election results in favour of the pro-Russian opposition.

The report also identifies the following problems:

abuse of administrative resources,

biased coverage on public television and by key opposition media outlets,

some Karabakh Armenians being unable to vote because bureaucratic delays prevented them from obtaining Armenian citizenship,

unprecedented external interference and geopolitical pressure.

PACE recommendations

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe has called on Armenia to amend its electoral code:

“The law should clearly require repeat voting whenever the fundamental right of a political force to have representation [in parliament] comes into question. It should also establish a clear threshold and procedures for such cases.”

The observation mission also recommends that the Armenian authorities take the following steps:

strengthen the resilience of the electoral process and democratic institutions, particularly by increasing national capacity to identify and counter Russian information operations and economic pressure tools;

broaden the range of people who can challenge electoral disputes in court, extend appeal deadlines and introduce more flexible remedies for violations;

ensure the independence of the process for appointing members of electoral commissions;

fully regulate the use of administrative resources and effectively punish any abuse of them;

end the selective prosecution of opposition figures and guarantee compliance with all procedural rules in election-related court proceedings;

guarantee the right of all political forces to hold peaceful assemblies;
