World.title: ‘Be prepared’: Victorians warned of thunderstorm asthma risk ahead of intense pollen season
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaHealthcare ‘Be prepared’: Victorians warned of thunderstorm asthma risk ahead of intense pollen season Henrietta Cook October 1, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victorians are being urged to prepare for potentially deadly thunderstorm asthma as health experts warn of an intense hay fever season following a wet and warm winter. Ten years ago, Victoria experienced the world’s largest and most catastrophic thunderstorm asthma event, one which led to the deaths of 10 people and caused breathing issues in thousands of others. Thunderstorm asthma is expected to affect more Victorians this year, after a warm and wet winter. Chris Hopkins Chief Health Officer Dr Caroline McElnay said a relatively warm and rainy winter had led to a lot of grass growth around the state, contributing to an early start to the pollen season. “We can’t control the weather or the pollen, but we can reduce exposure,” McElnay said.



From today until December 31, the VicEmergency website and app will provide three-day forecasts of thunderstorm asthma risk for each of the state’s nine weather districts. Related Article Good Weekend Thunderstorm asthma: the night a deadly storm took Melbourne's breath away It will do this using seven high-tech pollen counters distributed around the state. McElnay said people with asthma and hay fever were particularly vulnerable to thunderstorm asthma and should follow the forecasts, continue taking prescribed medication, and comply with their asthma action plans. They should also close windows and avoid being outside during storms and when it’s windy. Thunderstorm asthma occurs when there is a sudden change in weather, which can lead to grass pollen grains absorbing moisture in the air and bursting. This releases thousands of allergenic particles, which can be inhaled into the depths of the lungs, triggering asthma symptoms.



People with hay fever can unexpectedly develop asthma symptoms when this occurs. Related Article Health People suddenly get asthma after moving to Australia and researchers don't know why McElnay, who suffers from hay fever, recently bought an inhaler ahead of thunderstorm asthma season. “It’s better to be prepared,” she said. McElnay developed the common condition when she moved from the UK to New Zealand. The thunderstorm asthma forecasts are also used by health services so they can prepare for a potential rise in people turning up to emergency departments.



“What we’re trying to minimise is the number of people whose asthma would be triggered or would be so severe that they need to seek emergency care,” McElnay said. Dr Naghmeh Radhakrishna, a respiratory and allergy physician at St Vincent’s Hospital and The Alfred, treated patients who wound up in intensive care following the catastrophic thunderstorm asthma event on November 21, 2016. “There was one patient I saw who ended up needing resuscitation,” she recalled. “He was a young guy in his late 30s or early 40s. He had a severe episode and also had allergic rhinitis.” She advises people with hay fever to also get tested for asthma.



“The people who died during the thunderstorm event were the people who basically had undiagnosed asthma, or they had asthma but it wasn’t well controlled,” she said. Dr Naghmeh Radhakrishna Paul Jeffers Radhakrishna said immunotherapy and desensitisation treatments could gradually retrain a person’s immune system to tolerate pollen, reducing hay fever symptoms. Since the events of November 2016, the state government has invested in and expanded Victoria’s world-leading Epidemic Thunderstorm Asthma Risk Forecast System. The system was modernised last year with automated pollen counters, which use advanced imaging to deliver faster and more precise data, replacing manual traps. Health Minister Ingrid Stitt described the sophisticated pollen counters as a nation-leading tool that kept Victorians healthy and safe.



Related Article Exclusive

Illness Why your hay fever might actually be spring asthma “We want every Victorian to be safe this pollen season – that’s why we’re encouraging everyone to be prepared,” she said. Edwin Lampugnani, chief executive of AirHealth, which provides daily pollen counts to thousands of Australians through the Melbourne Pollen and Sydney Pollen websites and apps, said satellite data showed verdant landscapes, particularly in north-west Victoria. “Everything is looking very, very green,” he said. “It’s much greener than it was in 2025.” He said this led to the grass producing more pollen.



“We’re looking at a stronger season, or a more intense season than we saw last year,” he said. National Asthma Council Australia spokesperson and respiratory physician Professor Peter Wark said effective day-to-day control of asthma was the best defence during the pollen and thunderstorm asthma season. Related Article Healthcare Nothing to sneeze at: Why so many Australians suffer from hay fever National asthma guidelines changed last year, with doctors urged to move away from solely prescribing blue puffers as a standalone treatment for those aged over 12. It’s now recommended that people with asthma use anti-inflammatory relievers. “Even people with hay fever who have never had asthma should see their GP if they experience symptoms such as breathlessness, wheezing and tightness in the chest. These symptoms do not occur with hay fever alone,” Wark said.



About 11 per cent of Australians have asthma, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare says. One in four Australians suffer from allergic rhinitis, the scientific name for hay fever. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: House prices slump extends to six months
World.content:
NationalProperty market House prices slump extends to six months Matt Wade October 1, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Home values in Australia have fallen by 5 per cent from their peak in March, with Sydney and Melbourne leading the downturn. The national property slump has stretched to six months after a 1.1 per cent fall in September, Cotality’s Home Value Index shows. Values fell in every capital city except Darwin last month. Home values in Australia fell for the sixth straight month in September. Wolter Peeters Sydney’s property market has taken the biggest hit, with prices now 8.6 per cent below their February peak. The city’s median dwelling value is $1,198,596, Cotality’s figures show. Price declines in Sydney are now a little deeper than the equivalent stage of the previous 2022-23 downturn “highlighting how rapidly demand has weakened across the nation’s largest housing market”.



Melbourne property values are now 7.2 per cent below their peak in November 2025 and 7.5 per cent lower than the record high for property prices registered in March 2022. But Cotality, a property analytics firm, said the Melbourne property market is now showing a “milder rate of decline” with prices down 0.7 per cent in September, the smallest monthly fall among the state capitals. Property market sentiment has been hit by multiple interest rate hikes this year, along with changes to the taxation of housing investment and lingering economic uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East. On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank lifted official interest rates by 0.25 of a percentage point to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent in a bid to dampen inflationary pressures in the economy. That followed hikes in February, March and May.



Cotality’s report said housing market conditions are likely “to remain under downward pressure over the coming months with the latest interest rate increase adding to a formidable set of demand-side headwinds.” The federal government’s overhaul of capital gains tax and negative gearing, legislated earlier this year, has also contributed to weaker conditions in the property market. “Less favourable negative gearing and capital gains tax arrangements have already seen a sharp reduction in investor demand,” Cotality’s report said. Brisbane recorded the sharpest decline in September, with house prices down 1.5 per cent in the month. Property prices in the city have fallen 5.4 per cent since peaking in May. House prices in Perth fell 0.5 per cent in September to be down 6 per cent since their April peak.



Tim Lawless, Cotality’s research director, said property values have fallen in more than 90 per cent of capital city suburbs over the past three months, “highlighting the broad-based scope of this negative housing cycle”. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates To avoid another rate rise, things might have to get worse “The housing downturn reflects a combination of affordability constraints, higher interest rates, elevated living costs, and weaker consumer sentiment, all of which have reduced purchasing capacity and dampened buyer demand,” Cotality’s report said. There has also been a sharp decline in housing turnover which threatens to hit stamp duty collections, an important source of state government revenue. Cotality’s estimates of the number of home sales over the past three months nationally are nearly 20 per cent lower than a year ago and 13.3 per cent below the previous five-year average.



The volume of home sales compared to a year ago was down most sharply in Brisbane (minus 27.2 per cent) and Sydney (minus 26.5 per cent). “The sharp drop in sales has implications for the broader economy, with lower sales likely to hit some retail segments as well as stamp duty revenues for state governments,” Lawless said. Separate figures released by Housing Australia, the federal government’s housing delivery agency, show 102,000 first-time buyers have taken up Labor’s 5% Deposit Scheme to purchase a home. The scheme was expanded to all first home buyers a year ago, and the government estimates one in two first home buyers nationally are now using it. Cotality’s report said regional property markets have proved more resilient than in capital cities. Regional dwelling values fell by 0.7 per cent in September but are still up 5.6 per cent annually.



Darwin was the only capital city to register a house price increase in September (0.4 per cent). Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.content:
(MA15+) 114 minutes

I’ll say this for Verity, the latest film adaptation of a Colleen Hoover novel (after It Ends With Us, Regretting You and Reminders of Him): it lays its cards on the table, right from the title.

Verity means truth (from the Latin veritas). It also happens to be the name of a bestselling crime fiction author, Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), whose novels tap into her own thoughts and longings and anti-social impulses to such a degree that her husband Jeremy (Josh Hartnett) stopped reading them after the first one, because he didn’t want his perception of the woman he loves to be tainted. Is the book version of her the truth, or the version he knows?

Dakota Johnson in Verity. Amazon/MGM Studios via AP

The story isn’t Verity’s, though; its narrator and central character is Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson), also a novelist, but very much at the other end of the publishing mountain. We first meet her as she’s doing an apologetically hushed-voice reading in a sparsely attended book store, interrupted when one of the attendees gets a phone call. “Sorry,” the woman says. “Sorry,” responds the timorous Lowen.

World.title: Wheelchair-bound Nathan Cleary wins Dally M Medal at end of horror week
World.content:
Nathan Cleary could never have imagined collecting his first Dally M Medal while seated in a wheelchair at home.

Cleary has been at the centre of some brilliant moments on the field this season, but the image of him being crowned the game’s best player last night while recovering at home from a badly broken leg will not be forgotten any time soon.

Panthers halfback and Dally M winner Nathan Cleary. NRL Photos

The 28-year-old capped a whirlwind 72 hours by collecting the award that had so far eluded him during his brilliant career.

Brisbane’s Tamika Upton took out her third Dally M as the game’s best female player, and can cap an outstanding season with another premiership on Sunday.

Upton finished on 31 points, polled a full six points in the penultimate round, then one in the last round to beat Wests Tigers’ Raecene McGregor (29 points).

Cleary was the red-hot favourite to take out the Dally M in 2020, only to be pipped by Canberra’s Jack Wighton. But nothing was going to stop him as he polled 67 votes, 14 clear of Cronulla’s Braydon Trindall, with Dylan Edwards a further vote back in third.

The game’s best player suffered a double compound fracture of his leg in Sunday’s preliminary final loss to Newcastle as a result of a tackle that led to Newcastle’s Phoenix Crossland being handed a four-match ban. If Cleary wearing the Dally M Medal around his neck in his lounge room was a lovely touch, so was Crossland’s heartfelt teary apology a night earlier when he received his ban, and told those at the judiciary hearing he felt guilty for taking the gloss off the grand final.

The Penrith halfback was earlier this week handed the Rugby League Players Association’s Players’ Champion, which complemented the Brad Fittler Medal he won for being NSW’s best player and the Wally Lewis Medal, which is awarded to the standout player in the Origin series.

Cleary was also one of three Panthers included in the Dally M team of the year with Edwards and winger Tom Jenkins.

Andrew Webster was crowned coach of the year, fellow New Zealand Warrior James Fisher-Harris the captain of the year and Canberra halfback Ethan Sanders the best rookie.

Sunday’s grand finalists, the Sydney Roosters, had centre Rob Toia and prop Naufahu Whyte named in the team of the year. Newcastle, however, failed to have a player included in that side.

South Sydney’s Jai Arrow was forced to medically retire after being diagnosed with motor neurone diseases this season, and the heart-warming scenes he was involved in on several occasions, including being allowed to bring up his 100th game for the club in the final round before being brought from the field, earned him two awards, the Provan-Summons Medal, and the Peter Frilingos Headline Moment.

World.title: Bogongs change their tune
World.content:
Paul Duncan of Leura has been experiencing first-hand the return of the bogong moth (C8): “In the mornings the front and back fly-screen doors are covered with them, and one needs to use the leaf blower to move them on or they will fly inside. In earlier times they would swarm around the nearest street light, which in turn attracted the local owls, but they seem to have disappeared. Hopefully they, too, will return.”

For Central West locals, there are issues. Just ask Donald Hawes of Peel: “We are welcoming the current fluttering of bogong moths at our place outside Bathurst but they’ve played havoc with the organ at All Saints Cathedral in town. The trumpet, bassoon, trombone and clarinet pipes, which all have a large reed at the base, have become jammed with errant moths and are unplayable. After the great number of pipes, ranging from about 70 millimetres to nearly five metres, have been taken down, cleaned, returned and re-tuned, a screen will have to be installed to keep the moths out, just as we do for the blowies at home.”

Sticking with nature, Janice Creenaune of Austinmer notes that “my middle child has had a big week watching multiple diamond pythons copulating in his front garden in Bulli. One large and beautiful female and multiple males ‘balled in ecstasy’. An amazing sight.”

Andrew McPherson of Tathra “can’t help but wonder if AI (C8) would have squashed the millennium bug”.

“The mention of Lady Marmalade reminds me of Je t’aime … moi non plus, the seductive, oh-so French song from Serge Gainsbourg and Jane Birkin, from 1969,” writes Pauline McGinley of Drummoyne. “It was in French, with much suggestive, heavy breathing and less-than-coy lyrics. It had us high school French students furtively translating away! It was played freely for a short while on the radio but the censorship and controversy had kicked in by the time it reached No.1 on the pop charts, and then only the music, sans lyrics, was permitted.”

World.title: Hutt South electorate seen as a bell-weather for the election
World.content:
In the Wellington region, election day in the Hutt South is shaping up to be an existential one for incumbent National's Chris Bishop - but could a haircut secure the seat?

Why is it interesting?

Hutt South - sweeping from the western hills north of Wellington across the Hutt Valley to the east - is an electorate with working-class roots that is slowly gentrifying.

According to pundits, Hutt South typically leans left. With enthusiasm declining for the major parties, it means the electorate could be a significant player in the make-up of Parliament after 7 November.

For more than 20 years from 1996, the electorate was held by former Labour Party stalwart Trevor Mallard. After he stood down in 2017, National's Chris Bishop took the seat and has traded it with Labour's Ginny Andersen ever since.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Consultant Neale Jones - a Labour Party member and former chief of staff to Labour leader Jacinda Ardern - attributes the volatility to a boundary change in 2014 that saw the Labour-leaning suburb of Naenae absorbed into the Remutaka electorate.

"That turned Hutt South into a marginal seat with a slight Labour lean, and it's been seen since as a bit of a bell-weather.

"When National's doing well in its party vote nationally, Hutt South has gone to National and vice versa for Labour."

Ben Thomas - a former National government press secretary and public affairs consultant - agrees with Jones that this year's election could be "existential" for Bishop, who is number three on the National Party list.

Both major parties are polling under 30 percent, which puts Bishop "in the firing line", according to Thomas.

"Because National is struggling in terms of its party vote, it's looking at bringing in fewer - and on some projections - maybe no list MPs," he said. "That creates a big problem for the party at the top of the list... they could all be gone."

Jones puts it simply: "I think [Bishops's] going to have a bit of a nail-biter of an election night."

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What happened last election (and what might happen this time)

Just over 1300 votes separated the Hutt South incumbent from his Labour rival in the 2023 election.

Each party secured more than 30 percent of the vote in the undisputed two-horse race, with the Green Party coming in third on 15 percent.

That was notable, Thomas said, who argued that a vote for change this year could scoop up Green voters and send Bishop packing - adding it would be a "heroic" effort if he retained it.

Jones put 75 percent odds on Andersen claiming the seat, citing three reasons: a recent boundary change that brought the Labour-friendly Newlands suburb into the Hutt South; the decline in National Party polling since it won 38 percent of the vote in 2023; and the prevalence of public servants in the electorate who help prop-up local businesses.

"I'd say it's harder for Chris Bishop to run as a local champion when he's a senior figure of a government that's been seen to harm the local economy," he said.

So, who's standing?

Alistair Boyce, New Zealand First Party

Ben Wylie-van-Eerd, Opportunity Party

Chris Bishop, National Party

Courtney White, Green Party

Ginny Andersen, Labour Party

What do the locals say?

If you want to know what the electorate's thinking, head to the barber or the hairdresser - they've got all the goss.

Inside the salons in the Hutt South, the election was largely met with indifference and indecision - some were engaged, others a little disillusioned.

"I don't really care," No Good Barbers owner Eheng Chin told RNZ. "I don't think anything has ever changed has it? Has an extra $5 in your pocket made a difference?"

Brooke Brown. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In Eastbourne, one man getting a trim accused politicians of "throwing around policies to buy votes", while in Wainuiomata Rizwan Shaikh was looking for an easier path to residency, and stylist Brooke Brown wanted help for the squeezed middle.

"It's really hard to get ahead," the 28-year-old said, confessing she didn't know who to vote for. "Might draw a name out of the hat at this point."

Rizwan Shaikh. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

While access to healthcare was the biggest election issue for one retiree, her 18-year-old hairdresser lamented the lack of jobs for her peers.

Opinions differed on who could solve cost-of-living pressures, but affordability was a unifying theme.

Morgan Collins. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"People are really struggling," Morgan Collins said at Chocolate salon. "Some people can't afford to come in and get their hair done because of the cost-of-living right now."

Although those around her were on the fence, Collins was optimistic and confident in her vote on 7 November.

"I'm paying attention. I'm ready to vote. I'm looking for a change, so hoping for that."

Susan Cowpland. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Hedz for Hair owner Susan Cowpland was demanding solutions for the languishing economy and homelessness, and wanted to know if her industry would be included in the apprentice subsidy scheme.

The scheme helped with cashflow, she said, until the apprentice brought in money.

"National took that off us, so for me it pulled me taking on an apprentice. So that's a big one for me.

"I get that they're trying to pull everything back, but at what cost?"

Franky Fan. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Back in the Hutt, Catch Hair Co owner Franky Fan was looking for business support.

"New Zealand is really about small businesses. I'm quite keen on the National [Party] because I think they're the ones that are really looking after the people that are working hard."

Next door at No Good Barbers, Mitchell Morton felt disillusioned, at the age of 17, with politics in general.

"I saw this analogy on TikTok the other day that resonated with me... the left and the right wing belong to the same bird."

His barber Tahjae Sage had just one piece of advice for the Hutt South incumbent. "Come through for a hair cut. I've seen the signs - could do with a touch-up, mate."

World.title: Fears Southland's urology service could collapse as surgeries cancelled
World.content:
Health New Zealand is transferring patients as far as Christchurch and offering $3000 a day to locums while Southland lacks a permanent full-time urologist, documents released under the Official Information Act reveal.

Following the resignation of two specialists earlier this year, the organisation said it would only defer surgeries and procedures where absolutely necessary and if it was clinically safe to do so.

At the same time, internal briefings show health bosses moved a risk rating to 'extreme', with warnings of adverse patient impacts and the potential "collapse of the Southland service".

Health New Zealand said 48 Southland patients had been transferred to other regions and 13 operations had been cancelled by 21 June.

By September just five of those had gone ahead, with the remainder rescheduled.

The briefing documents showed the cancelled treatments included cancer surgeries, and patients were being sent to either Dunedin or Christchurch.

The situation was compounded by the fact the Dunedin urology service was "already under-recruited and struggling to meet demand", health bosses wrote.

The briefings showed Health New Zealand had approved pay rates of $3000 a day for locums to fill the gap.

The organisation later confirmed four had been supporting the Southland service.

Health New Zealand acknowledged patients were waiting longer than it wanted but said patients were being triaged according to their need and wait time.

It comes after RNZ spoke with a Winton man who faced weeks of delays for cancer surgery.

Southland Hospital. Google Maps

Patients sent out of region

Invercargill resident Ashley Fulton said her long-awaited endometriosis operation was abruptly cancelled because the urologist had quit.

The call came right as she walked into hospital and grabbed the door handle for day surgery.

"It had already took two years for my case to work its way up through the system ... and so I went back into the mind games of being back in limbo," she said.

She said four months later she was eventually able to receive treatment in Dunedin, but the wait was far from ideal.

"I was on 35 pills a day just to be able to get out of bed and even that didn't stop the pain. That was just me being able to get up and just walk around," she said.

"That four months of not knowing and then getting the date to go - and then I'm in a whole different town. I had no support people … which was hard as well."

Health New Zealand declined RNZ's interview requests but sent a statement from Southland general manager Simon Donlevy.

He said the organisation was prioritising patients with the greatest clinical need or who had been waiting the longest.

"We know that people requiring less urgent treatment may wait longer than we would like, and we acknowledge their frustration," he said.

Senior doctors and specialists were in demand across health systems internationally - and New Zealand was not immune to that trend, he said.

Prostate Cancer Foundation networker Trish Wright said the situation was dire.

"I think they're surely absolutely panicking to offer somebody $3000. I think it goes back to the whole situation of medical students - whether there's not enough medical students being trained or they're not being encouraged to stay in the country," she said.

"The fact that [patients] are being referred to Christchurch, to me shows that everybody's panicking because they've got nowhere else to send them."

Southland Kidney Society president Nobby Clark. RNZ / REECE BAKER

Southland Kidney Society president Nobby Clark said he agreed with Health New Zealand that there was no quick fix.

"The dilemma I guess they face is there's no magical way to find urologists or surgeons that can do urology surgery … there is no magic bullet," he said.

However, the region was already beset by waiting lists due to a shortage of hospital beds and operating rooms, he said.

"In Southland, for example, we know that we're short of about one and a half operating theatres. If an urgent case comes in on a helicopter, those people get the operating theatre, not necessarily the specialist," he said.

Union urges retention push

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton said she rejected any framing of the resignations as normal turnover.

She said Health New Zealand should be looking after its existing staff better, with specific recruitment and retention allowances for hard-to-staff regions like Invercargill.

"I'm kind of gobsmacked that Health New Zealand don't just put their hands in their pockets and get their best efforts at recruitment and retention underway, because it's costing everybody. It's causing patient harm. It's leaving doctors unhappy, frustrated," she said.

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton. RNZ / Nick Monro

She said if a specialist services collapsed, remaining doctors and general surgeons would be forced to step in and work beyond their normal clinical scope.

"You get a domino effect where a service reaches that tipping point, people throw up their hands and say 'this is not safe, I can't work like this', and they go and work somewhere else."

World.title: 'Stakes could not be higher': Concern over claim NZ breached FTA climate commitments
World.content:
International relations experts are warning a case claiming New Zealand is not meeting EU trade agreement climate commitments could seriously impact the country's reputation.

Lodged by Dutch environmental group Both ENDS at the European Commission's Single Entry Point complaints body, the case has the backing of New Zealand climate activists including Mike Smith and Jane Kelsey.

The complaint hinges on legal commitments in the EU-NZ free-trade agreement (FTA) not to weaken environment protections and meet Paris Agreement commitments, and aims to encourage compliance rather than suspend trade.

However, University of Canterbury professor of political science and international relations Bronwyn Hayward said it was a "high stakes" and "very serious landmark case" that would be watched very closely by trade partners and countries around the world.

She said the government prided itself on securing trade, but was now being called out internationally for not playing fair.

"Until now the New Zealand government has been able to have it both ways, appearing to take action on an international stage over climate by making speeches about supporting the Paris climate agreement but significantly rolling back local climate action and policy.

"The stakes could not be higher for us as a nation and I am deeply concerned that our government has put our country's reputation and trade at risk."

She said the case noted many climate rollbacks in New Zealand but the "most serious trigger" appeared to be the move to prevent tort lawsuits like Mike Smith's against big greenhouse gas emitters, and the revelations of secretive lobbying that came alongside it.

"These actions have tainted New Zealand's reputation as an honest broker and added to the seriousness of this case," Hayward said.

What's more, the Trump administration was also looking to block litigation against the oil and gas industry.

Dr Alexander Gillespie Wayne Mead

University of Waikato law professor Al Gillespie said New Zealand had made "clear promises to the Europeans, which will now be held up to the light" and the United Kingdom and members of the CPTPP trade agreement would be watching with interest.

He said even before government-to-government consultations it could mean negative publicity for New Zealand that could impact the country's "green" brand or lead to consumer boycotts, and was not just about climate change but testing how free trade and environmental sustainability had been woven together.

"It is an open question whether NZ is currently in breach of its obligations with regards to the promises we made to effectively implement the Paris Agreement. Although our broad goals remain in place, the architecture around them (from stopping the Smith case, weakening targets, and reversing earlier exploration goals) is collapsing - and where it is more likely we may be found in breach of our second commitment in this area of non-regression (backsliding)."

The debate back in New Zealand meanwhile would be coloured by the larger political debate about whether New Zealand should exit the Paris Agreement, he said, "while highlighting, if we leave, we risk undermining complimentary free trade agreements".

"This is a very complicated knot to untangle."

Trade Minister Todd McClay. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Trade Minister Todd McClay has argued it was not for overseas countries, organisations or lobby groups to tell New Zealand how to meet its obligations and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon asserts New Zealand is "fully compliant" with its international obligations.

World.title: Auckland sellers get real: Asking prices below $1m
World.content:
Audio player for " Is a loan on my home the best way help my kids? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/business/1665146%2Fauckland-sellers-get-real-asking-prices-below-1m

Is a loan on my home the best way help my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

Auckland's average asking price on Realestate.co.nz has dropped below $1 million for the first time in six years, although its median sale price has been there for some time.

The website's average asking price for the city in September was $993,562, about a quarter of a million dollars below the January 2022 peak of $1.274m.

It means the asking price is coming closer to what might be achievable - Real Estate Institute data put the median sales price for the city in August at $950,000, the same as a year earlier.

Realestate.co.nz spokesperson Vanessa Williams said the asking price was usually more than the sale price.

"The average asking price, as we all know, we come to the market hoping that we will get a premium price for our product as a vendor so we have years and years' worth of data to suggest that that average asking price typically, depending on which market but give or take, is about 15 to 20 percent above the actual sale price of the … I'm just sort of generalising there but usually the average asking price sits above the selling price just because as I said people wanting to come to the market hoping that in that first couple of weeks they're going to get a premium price for their property."

Realestate.co.nz spokesperson Vanessa Williams. Supplied / Realestate.co.nz

She said the drop signalled that there could be more urgency among people listing now, to get their properties sold before the election. "Vendors are coming to the market being very realistic with what they are asking for their properties to get the deal done."

Williams said Auckland buyers had a lot of choice. There were 3500 new listings on the market in September, 7.7 percent more than a year earlier. The total amount of stock available in Auckland increased 13.8 percent to 13,958 homes.

Across the country, the available stock rose 10.7 percent year-on-year in September, to 34,001. Only Southland had fewer properties for sale than a year earlier.

Nelson and Bays' average asking price dipped below $800,000 for the first time in five years in September, to an average $791,917. Wairarapa recorded the largest annual decline of all the regions, down 9.2 percent to $667,375.

The national average asking price remained steady in September at $855,245, down just 0.2 percent year-on-year.

Four regions bucked the trend and recorded record average asking price highs for the month of September. Canterbury's average asking price lifted 1.3 percent year-on-year to $736,585. Southland's average lifted 5.9 percent to $593,723. Central Otago's lifted 4.6 percent to $1.586m and the West Coast's average increased 0.8 percent to $514,013.

World.title: Cities sinking due to too much groundwater extraction may eventually lift again - study
World.content:
Cities that are sinking because too much groundwater is being extracted may eventually lift again if the water is allowed to replenish, new research shows.

The study found the Japanese city of Osaka is rising again after decades of strict groundwater regulations, introduced after over-extraction caused some areas to sink by nearly three metres.

New Zealand earth scientist and co-author Jesse Kearse said the research had important implications for coastal cities in particular, because of accelerating sea-level rise and coastal flooding.

That included New Zealand, where nearly 80 percent of the coastline was already sinking, and pressure on freshwater - which was currently abundant - would grow as the climate warmed.

"We're not quite at that same stage as other countries around the world - I can't really point to a particular city in New Zealand and say, this city's sinking because we're using way too much groundwater," Kearse said.

"But the key message is, as we move into a world where we're getting more and more reliance on groundwater resources, we just need to be aware that that's one of the implications."

The link between over-extraction and land subsidence had long been known, but researchers had not been sure if allowing groundwater to replenish would reverse the subsidence over time.

The study used Osaka as a natural laboratory, because of its long history with groundwater and vertical land motion, Kearse said.

"The city realised in the early part of the 20th century that they were taking far too much water from underneath the ground, running out of water, and the city dropped by close to three metres in some places - which is really extreme subsidence - as a response to groundwater extraction."

Osaka put strict regulations in place in the 1960s and groundwater had gradually replenished over the last 50 or 60 years, he said.

The researchers combined long-term groundwater monitoring data from wells as deep as 500m with repeated satellite observations to measure the effect on land movement.

"The city has bounced back up again... Osaka is actually rising."

Kearse described the effect as "a gigantic water balloon" beneath the city.

"When we take up water from underneath the ground, that balloon deflates and the city sinks. But as the groundwater is replenished, that balloon reinflates and the city pops back up again - so it works in both directions," he said.

The patchiness of the subsidence meant it could cause great damage, Kearse said.

"If you've got pipes under the ground and some bits are moving differently to others, that can cause stress on the infrastructure. Roads are cracking, building are tilting, it's not a good thing."

The research showed it was possible to predict "quite precisely" where the damage would occur.

"The sharp barrier between uplift and subsidence tends to occur along the known mapped faultlines - they are acting as underground dams," he said.

That created corridors of damage - "not because of earthquakes, but because of how they're disrupting the groundwater flow."

The same subsidence could occur with any sub-surface fluid, such as oil and gas extraction, he said.

"It's essentially the same geomechanical process... The physical relationship there is really well-understood."

New Zealand's coastal subsidence had been mapped in detail as part of the NZ SeaRise project, which projected sea-level rise out to 2300.

World.title: Investigation highlights safety gaps after Air NZ plane flew below safe altitude
World.content:
The Transport Accident Investigation Commission says a series of systemic failures led to an Air New Zealand plane descending more than 2500 feet below its planned flight path into Timaru.

The Q300 aircraft, carrying 33 passengers and three crew was travelling from Wellington to Timaru in June 2023, when it deviated from its programmed flight path, which was around 1000 feet below the minimum safe altitude, before the captain corrected course and landed safely.

The Civil Aviation Authority notified the Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC), and opened an inquiry.

Chief investigator of accidents Louise Cook said it wasn't the case that the crew had a bad night - the investigation identified six similar events on Q300 aircraft, and another two after the inquiry was opened, showing it was not an isolated event.

The commission found the way the aircraft's systems were set up meant pilots had to rely on remembering to reverse a manual step partway through descent.

The error went unnoticed because both pilots were fixated on visually identifying the runway lights, which made their instrument monitoring less reliable.

Cook said TAIC's opinion was that an appropriate response would have been for the pilots to do a go around, to gather themselves and check everything was in accordance, before starting the descent again.

She said while it appeared to be a simple flight crew error, the commission found the error was known to both the operator and to the regulator, and the systems in place should have prevented it from turning into a serious incident.

The inquiry found there were a number of contributing circumstances; issues around crew training, the safety culture within Air New Zealand, issues with the aircraft autopilot design and the regulatory oversight by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA).

Cook said one of the key messages in the report was that regulators needed to scale their oversight to match an operator's changing risk profile.

"The commission identified that in 2019 Air New Zealand went through some pretty major changes, particularly around the merger of its regional carriers and then there was also Covid-19.

"Those factors introduced new significant risks and that should have triggered close scrutiny by the Civil Aviation Authority."

TAIC chief investigator of accidents, Louise Cook. RNZ/Baz Macdonald

The inquiry also found the regulatory relationship was too close in nature, which likely "impeded the regulator's ability to impartially oversee" Air New Zealand's safety management system.

TAIC Recommendations

Cook said the commission identified nine safety issues and seven had been addressed.

"Air New Zealand and the CAA have taken on board the commission's findings and made important changes to training, procedures, safety culture work, and how the CAA structures its oversight. We're satisfied those actions address seven of the nine safety issues we identified, so we haven't needed to recommend further action there."

The remaining two recommendations were around the flight management system design and the cockpit voice recorder.

The commission recommended that Air New Zealand work with the aircraft manufacturer De Havilland Canada on the design of a flight management system that calculated a smooth descent pattern, and avoided the need for a work around that increased the likelihood of human error.

It also recommended that the Civil Aviation Authority push for a change to international aviation rules so that all transport aircraft that were required to carry a cockpit voice recorder must also meet modern recording requirements.

Air New Zealand chief safety and risk officer Nathan McGraw said safety and a strong safety culture were fundamental to the national carrier.

Air New Zealand chief safety and risk officer Nathan McGraw. Supplied / Air NZ

"When something doesn't go as it should, our job is to understand why and learn from it."

He said the airline began its own investigation after the incident and strengthened its procedures, training, monitoring and safety culture, before the TAIC inquiry was completed.

McGraw said work was underway on the recommendation to work with Q300 manufacturer De Havilland Canada to find a technical solution that enabled the flight management system to calculate a smooth descent flight profile through transition.

"Independent investigations, regular audits, and being open about what we can do better are all essential parts of a safe aviation system. We're very confident in the training, systems and safety culture we have in place today."

A Civil Aviation Authority spokesperson said it accepted the recommendation relating to cockpit voice recorder requirements and planned to raise the issue through the appropriate International Civil Aviation Organization forum.

"The report looks at events and regulatory approaches from 2023 and earlier. Since then, CAA has strengthened how it brings together safety intelligence, monitoring, certification and regulatory decision-making, with a more coordinated and risk-based approach to oversight."

The New Zealand Air Line Pilots' Association president Andrew McKeen said the comission's findings reinforced that aviation safety was a shared system responsibility.

"Operators need to identify and manage emerging risks, regulators must have the capability and independence to provide effective oversight, and pilots must maintain disciplined monitoring and recovery decision-making."

McKeen, a 787 pilot, said the report highlighted how safety depended on recognising and acting on precursor events.

World.title: Rare umbilical disorder missed on 'successive occasions' led to baby's death - Coroner
World.content:
A coroner says a rare umbilical cord condition that led to the "deeply sad" death of a baby just after birth was missed on successive occasions.

Sage William Mana Lewis was born on 14 November, 2019 and died on 16 November.

A coroner has found that a rare pregnancy complication was missed on successive occasion and that at no point were the risks associated with the condition remaining unresolved discussed with the baby's mother.

"This is a deeply sad case, in which two parents and their family have suffered the devastating loss of their baby boy almost immediately after his birth," coroner Ian Telford said.

"Although Sage lived for only a short time, it is apparent that he was cherished for every second of the one day, 15 hours and 42 minutes that he was with those who loved him."

Telford said he had met Sage's mother and maternal grandmother and was struck by their "dignified calm in the face of such profound and enduring grief".

"Most particularly I was struck by their focus on what could be learned from what had happened to them, and how those lessons might help to prevent a similar tragedy from occurring in the future."

Hannah Nicholson's labour was induced at Rotorua Hospital on the evening of 14 November, 2019 at 38 weeks plus one day gestation.

In his findings, Telford said labour progressed normally until there was a sudden drop in Sage's heart rate.

The decision was made for an emergency caesarean section and Nicholson was transferred to theatre for the operation. Sage's heartbeat was still low, and he was delivered "in poor condition and was not breathing".

Resuscitation started immediately and the baby was transferred to the Special Care Baby Unit before being transferred to Waikato Hospital.

"Sage's condition continued to deteriorate. Ultimately, it was assessed that he was unlikely to survive, and a decision was made to cease active treatment," Telford said.

His death was formally recorded at 12.15pm on 16 November, 2019.

Specialist perinatal pathologist Dr K Bartlett said Sage suffered significant blood loss, with a lack of oxygen to his organs.

Examination of the placenta showed the umbilical cord was abnormally attached to the membranes surrounding the placenta, instead of directly to the placenta.

This is known as a velamentous cord insertion, which Bartlett said was a very rare condition that occurred in about 1 percent of placentas.

It meant umbilical blood vessels travelled through the membranes for some distance without the usual protective tissue, making them vulnerable to being compressed or torn during labour.

Bartlett found that in Sage's case, one of these unprotected blood vessels, the umbilical vein, was torn.

"The tear caused significant bleeding, and this was the likely source of the severe blood loss that left Sage in such poor condition at birth."

Telford said as was usual in these circumstances, Health New Zealand Lakes conducted a learning review to consider what happened, how, and why.

The review noted that, at 20 weeks and two days' gestation, an ultrasound identified an additional section of placenta, together with blood vessels running close to and overlying the cervix (vasa praevia).

It was planned that if this persisted, an elective caesarean section at 36 weeks would be recommended.

Then, during week 25 of pregnancy, Nicholson was admitted to Rotorua Hospital with a small antepartum haemorrhage.

"Scanning reported succenturiate placenta (as before) but no signs of vasa praevia. The review states that this was assessed to still meet some guidelines for diagnosis of the condition, concluding that this scan showed evidence of vasa praevia, but it was not recognised."

Transabdominal and transvaginal scans were performed at 30 weeks' gestation, with that report again saying no placenta praevia.

However, the review said measurements obtained in the scan indicated that a vasa praevia was still present according to some guidelines, but this was not explicitly stated.

At 30 weeks and one day of gestation, Nicholson was then referred to hospital with high blood pressure, where the 30-week scan report was noted but not commented on again during visits by medical staff on two consecutive days.

The review of the scan showed Nicholson's condition still met the definition of vasa praevia under some guidelines.

"The presence of a vasa praevia at 30 weeks does not appear to have been recognised by the medical staff during this admission," Telford said.

Nicholson was discharged and admitted to Rotorua Hospital again at 32 weeks and one day.

Telford said the doctor recorded, in relation to the 30-week scan, that it showed "no vasa praevia". Nicholson was discharged the next day.

At 33 weeks and five days gestation, an ultrasound scan report stated, "vasa praevia identified at 20 weeks, not present at 25 and 30 weeks".

Nicholson was not seen again before going into labour.

He said the review report made a large number of recommendations which should help minimise the risk of similar events occurring in the future.

"I particularly note that HNZ Lakes has now developed and implemented a care pathway for prenatally diagnosed vasa praevia and socialised this with staff. This condition has also been added to the list of conditions that are now referred to the High-Risk Clinic."

Updated guidelines had also been published that provided greater clarity of the diagnostic criteria.

World.title: Politicians clash on climate commitment trade risks at rural issues debate
World.content:
Agriculture Minister Todd McClay is sparring with the Green Party's Steve Abel around claims New Zealand is failing to meet its climate commitments under the European Union free trade agreement.

New Zealand-based climate activists and environmental organisations have joined Dutch NGO Both ENDS in its complaint to the European Commission, claiming Aotearoa has failed to comply with climate and sustainability causes in the agreement, that came into effect in 2024.

Complaint co-sponsor, Greenpeace Aotearoa said the complaint identified recent policy decisions as areas of concern, including weakening biogenic methane targets, removing agriculture from the Emissions Trading Scheme, and legislation around tort liability against polluters.

At a rural issues debate organised by agriculture sector groups in Waikato on Wednesday, McClay defended New Zealand's commitment to achieve the net-zero greenhouse gas emissions target by 2050, under the Paris Accord.

"We are within our obligations. We take our obligations seriously. We will be net zero by 2050," said McClay to the audience of around 350.

"But we're only asking farmers to do what they need to, not more. And I'm not going to sit here and tell them how they should run their farms."

Federated Farmers president Colin Hurst, Agriculture Minister Todd McClay, Associate Agriculture Minister Andrew Hoggard and DairyNZ chair Tracy Brown. RNZ/Monique Steele

McClay said farmers would be in partnership with the Government of the New Zealand people.

"It is for the New Zealand Parliament, the New Zealand Government to decide how we meet our obligations. Not you [Abel] and your mates overseas who don't care about New Zealand exporters."

The NZ-EU FTA required both parties to recognise the "importance of taking urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts".

"Each Party shall effectively implement the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, including commitments with regard to nationally determined contributions," the text read.

Furthermore, both parties must also commit to "effectively implement the Paris Agreement", including the "obligation to refrain from any action or omission that materially defeats the object and purpose" of it.

Abel, the Green Party's agriculture spokesperson, disputed claims that the party was involved with the Both ENDS complaint.

"Not supported by the Green Party ... we're not part of that complaint."

Although Abel said it had warned the Government in Parliament on numerous occasions that its environmental policies risked non-compliance with the deal.

"We flagged for some time that there was a risk of a complaint because New Zealand has failed in its obligations in the EU agreement to not backtrack on environmental commitments," he said.

"A lot of environmental advocates have been pointing out that our free trade agreement with the EU had these environmental commitments, and we said we wouldn't backtrack on them."

The rural issues debate held at Mystery Creek near Hamilton on Wednesday night. RNZ/Monique Steele

Abel said that changed once the Government came into power.

"We are dreaming if we think that the rest of the world doesn't care about us playing our part in the challenge of climate change and of broader environmental change," he said.

"The existential challenge of our time is climate change, and if we don't think we want to be part of it and we want to back away from those commitments, can I just put it to you, Minister? Are you backing away from our climate commitments?

"And if not, what have you got to be afraid of?"

McClay said the Greens should be backing New Zealand exporters.

"Absolutely not [backing away from climate commitments]. Well, I am afraid you're going to go and tell someone else we're doing something that we're not to harm New Zealand exporters."

Furthermore to Greenpeace, the Both ENDS complaint was also backed by the Environmental Law Initiative, climate campaigner Mike Smith, Ngāti Pūkenga Iwi ki Tauranga Trust, OraTaiao New Zealand Climate and Health Council, and Professor Emeritus Jane Kelsey.

The political debate held at Mystery Creek near Hamilton on Wednesday night was organised by Beef and Lamb New Zealand, DairyNZ and Federated Farmers.

World.title: Stawell Gift winner suspended for 12 months after positive drug test
World.content:
This year's Stawell Gift men's winner, Olufemi "Femi" Komolafe, has been suspended for 12 months after testing positive for ADHD medication.

The 21-year-old set a new personal best to claim his first major title in April this year, and also claimed the $40,000 prize for placing first in the annual 120-metre handicapped sprint.

Komolafe was given a 5-metre handicap in this year's race, starting behind all but one of his opponents in the final.

But Sports Integrity Australia has handed down a 12-month ban, confirming Komolafe had tested positive for the banned medication.

ADHD medications are banned in sport for their potential performance-enhancing effects, with athletes only able to use them if they have a medical diagnosis and it is part of treatment.

Stawell Gift organisers have not confirmed whether Komolafe will be asked to return his winnings or whether he will be stripped of his title.

The ban comes as Sports Integrity Australia expresses concerns over the prevalence of athletes using ADHD medications without a formal diagnosis.

In July, its chief executive, Sarah Benson, said she was seeing a "significant number" of inadvertent doping violations from high-level Australian athletes using ADHD medication.

Dr Benson said the consequences are severe for athletes found breaching the rules.

"Since these medications could be abused by athletes for performance improvement reasons, the tough reality is that they are banned under the World Anti-Doping Code if the athlete does not have a formal diagnosis," Dr Benson said.

"Under the Code, this is true even if they establish their diagnosis after the positive test, and they face a ban of one to four years."

World.title: Nathan Cleary accepts maiden Dally M Medal from his dad's couch
World.content:
Injured Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary has accepted his maiden Dally M Medal from his couch, while Brisbane fullback Tamika Upton took out the NRLW award for the third time in four seasons.

After years of being the consensus best player in the men's game, Cleary finally made it official by romping clear in the Dally M count, securing the award with two rounds remaining and ultimately finishing 14 votes clear — 67 to Braydon Trindall's 53.

Trindall made a late push to cause a major upset before injuring his shoulder in round 24, while the rest of the top five — Dylan Edwards, Haumole Olakau'atu and Scott Drinkwater — failed to poll in round 25, when Cleary got a maximum six votes in a 22-14 win over Melbourne.

Having suffered a gruesome compound fracture of his left leg in the Panthers' preliminary final loss on Sunday, Cleary was not at the awards ceremony on Sydney Harbour, instead accepting the award via video message.

"I want to start by saying how grateful I am for everyone's support the past few days," he said from a couch with his injured leg propped up in a cast.

"I can't thank everyone enough for the messages they've sent through."

He thanked his parents, who he has been living with this year while his house has been being renovated.

He credited his Panthers teammates for making him a "10,000 times" better player, while he also paid tribute to girlfriend Mary Fowler, who is currently playing for Manchester City in England.

"It's tough doing the long distance but she always makes me feel supported and loved. That's all I could ever ask for," he said.

Tamika Upton will play for her sixth NRLW premiership on Sunday. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The NRLW count was much closer, with 2022 winner Raecene McGregor pushing Upton to the 11th and final round of the season, but the Broncos gun finished with 31 votes to McGregor's 29.

Upton is preparing to play for her sixth NRLW premiership when the Broncos face the Roosters for a second straight year on Sunday, when the league will honour Jai Arrow after his MND diagnosis earlier this year.

The tribute is set to occur in place of traditional pre-game entertainment after negotiations with Tones and I fell apart.

NRL boss Peter V'landys on Monday promised "surprises" and said on Wednesday night that a number of Australian artists would be part of the tribute, although Arrow said earlier in the night that V'landys had told him "nothing yet".

Look back at every moment of the NRL Awards night in our live blog below.

World.title: Ten years after their lowest ebb, Newcastle are one win from salvation
World.content:
The outpouring of emotion following Newcastle's return to the grand final after 25 years is proof you can't understand how good winning can feel until you've lost a few times.

The Knights know it better than most because in the quarter-century since their glory days they've lost hard and lost plenty.

Before this season there'd been more wooden spoons than finals wins over the past two decades, survived financial turmoil that threatened the club's very existence and persevered through other struggles that proved there's more to life than football, even in Newcastle.

But on the field the times were never harder than ten years ago, when the club won just a single game for the entire 2016 season, the equal fewest victories for a team in the past 60 years.

There's two men left standing from that leanest of winters and while Jacob Saifiti will miss Sunday's grand final through suspension, Dane Gagai has the chance to bury the old pain under a mountain of grand final glory.

Dane Gagai is the only grand final player who appeared in the 2016 season for the Knights. (Getty Images: Ashley Feder )

The 2016 season was the lowest point amid three-straight last-placed finishes, but what Gagai remembers most is the indomitable hope of the faithful, against all odds and good sense.

"The fans still kept turning up. There was still 20,000 people at a game, Knights jerseys on, even after back-to-back spoons," said Gagai.

"To be able to be in this position now and give these fans what they deserve, I couldn't be more proud to be a Newcastle Knight."

It's a similar story for Trent Hodkinson, who captained the Knights that season after arriving from Canterbury as the incumbent New South Wales Origin halfback

"I was excited to get there, I really like that it was a one-team town, seeing how they got behind their team — I wanted to be a part of that," said Hodkinson.

"The first thing that comes to mind is the loyalty from the fans. No matter how tough we were doing it on the field they'd rock up in numbers.

"We were trying our best to win for them, we really were, but we were deep in that rebuilding phase. The times on the field were so tough but the fans got us through it."

Hodkinson joined the Knights from Canterbury as the incumbent New South Wales halfback. (Getty Images: Tony Feder )

Both men are right about the support never wavering given the Knights had higher average crowds that season than three teams who made the finals.

They also, somehow, experienced an overall lift in crowds from the year before and had a higher average attendance than the club did in their 1997 premiership season.

All the players and fans had was their faith, which is just another way of saying they had one another, and few teams have ever needed it more.

Only six of their games were decided by less than one score and they conceded 24 points or more in 19 of their 24 matches.

There were special horrors that would rear their heads up from time to time that made the campaign seem like less of a bad season and more of a divine punishment, like an ironic torture dreamed up in the sick mind of a wicked and vengeful God.

The Newcastle people still showed up in droves for their team. (Getty Images: Ashley Feder )

Their sole win came in Round 6 against Wests Tigers, when a fan threw a ball on the field and prop Korbin Sims toed it through to force an error from Tigers winger Jordan Rankin as he tried to field a bomb.

The Knights scored from the ensuing set to claim an 18-16 victory but the next month was a taste of hell, as if they were being tormented for their one day of good fortune, for daring to have one happy day.

They lost their next four games by a combined margin of 179-10 and were kept scoreless three times.

The final match, a 62-0 loss at home to Cronulla, was the second heaviest defeat in club history.

Gagai played despite his grandmother passing on the morning of the match and broke down in tears in Sims's arms afterwards after he was racially abused by a member of the crowd.

Tariq Sims, who began the season as one of the club's co-captains, left on a mid-season transfer to St George Illawarra a few weeks later and Jarrod Mullen, the club's most experienced player, had his NRL career end months later after testing positive to steroids.

Newcastle couldn't find a win to save themselves in 2016. (Getty Images: Matt Blyth )

There were some days that were closer than others, but only close enough to make it sting all the more and show there can be no true despair without a little piece of hope.

Newcastle took Canberra, who finished the regular season second and ended up in the preliminary final, to extra time twice. They did manage, as a squad, to outscore Raiders centre Jarrod Croker, who finished as that year's top point-scorer but given it was 306 to 296 it was a close run thing.

In their last game of the season, when a win might have meant most of all, the Knights conceded a last-second penalty to lose to St George Illawarra and confirm their status as one-win wonders.

There was talent enough on the Knights roster to be competitive — Gagai was a Queensland regular by that point and won the club's player of the year award, his first taste of being a stand-out soldier for a hopeless cause.

"Back then he was exactly like he is now — a true competitor who worked his backside off at training and always tried to help the young guys through," said Hodkinson.

It was a season of constant sorrow for the Knights. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan )

"He'd try so hard, he'd do whatever it took to try and get a win for the team and the town."

Gagai and Hodkinson were just two of 12 players on the roster who would play Origin or for Australia or New Zealand at some point in their careers.

But none of the timelines matched up. Some of them were too young — Mitch Barnett and the Saifiti twins were in their first year of first grade.

Others were too old — Kade Snowden, Jeremy Smith and Mullen were all in the final year of their NRL careers and under coach Nathan Brown the mix was never right.

"The new guys, they were up for it, they were next in line, but they were just young," Hodkinson said.

No end in sight for ageless wonder Gagai He has already played more NRL matches than any other outside back in the history of rugby league but ahead of yet another finals campaign Dane Gagai is certain there are still great days to come.

"They did everything they could and I feel for a few of them but some of them have gone on to great careers — Josh King down at Melbourne, Jack Cogger is going great at Penrith, both Saifiti's turned into great players.

"But when you have more youth than experience it makes it hard, especially when the roster and combinations keep changing."

Given the team was unable to give back to the community in glory, Hodkinson worked hard to find other ways to repay the love that meant so much.

His work in the community with ill children, including escorting 15-year old Hannah Rye to her high-school formal while she had terminal cancer in 2017, served as a constant reminder that rugby league could be bigger than winning and losing.

"That made some tough times on the field a lot easier, it put things in perspective when you know kids out there are doing it much, much tougher than anyone who's playing football for a living," said Hodkinson.

"The fans and the club were so great to me. In a tough time they were such a positive part of my life.

"Me and my wife still speak about it now, because we loved Newcastle, we loved the people. Off the field, we wouldn't change a thing."

It's been a winding way back for the Knights, who went to the finals and back to last place over the course of the next ten years.

Gagai is so close to the ultimate reward for his years of loyal service. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Hodkinson was released at the end of 2017, just before Kalyn Ponga arrived and the long march to Sunday began.

Saifiti is the only player on the roster who's been there all the way after Gagai eventually left for South Sydney at the end of 2017 in search of winning football.

His return four years later to the club he'll always call home was that of a prodigal son and a premiership would be a reward he's earned a thousand times over, just like it would be for the fans who were with the team during those darkest days.

Ten years after one win was all they had, one more win can mean everything and would prove that true salvation comes to they who can suffer the most without losing the faith.

"I want it. I want it bad. But that's the end product of what needs to be done," said Gagai.

"A lot of people have been putting us as the underdog. But we've never done that, we've had that belief throughout the whole year.

"To be able to come back and play in a grand final here, I couldn't be more proud to be a Novocastrian."

World.title: Neale set to join Magpies as Lions confirm exit
World.content:
Collingwood says it "looks forward" to Lachie Neale joining the club in 2027 after it was confirmed the three-time premiership player is leaving the Brisbane Lions.

Neale's departure was no secret, as he revealed he was going to miss the Lions "very much" when speaking immediately after Saturday's AFL grand final at the MCG.

This morning, the Lions confirmed the 33-year-old would leave the club as an unrestricted free agent.

"Lachie has been a great player for the Brisbane Lions, and we thank him for his incredible contribution over his eight seasons," Lions list manager Dom Ambrogio said in a club statement.

"We understand Lachie's reasons for wishing to explore free agency and we wish him all the best for the next chapter of his career."

Lions break Dockers' hearts The Brisbane Lions launch an incredible fightback late in the grand final to edge Fremantle by seven points and win a third consecutive premiership.

The Lions said they would "further celebrate and recognise Neale's contribution to the club in the coming days".

The Magpies did not waste time announcing Neale's intention to move south.

"Three-time premiership player and two-time Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has decided to exercise his free agency rights with a move to Collingwood," a Magpies statement read.

"The club looks forward to welcoming him … when the AFL trade and free agency period commences on Friday."

The AFL is expected to confirm the suitable free agency compensation the Lions will receive during the trade and free agency period.

Speaking after the Lions clinched a third straight flag with a remarkable seven-point win over Fremantle in the grand final, Neale said he owed the club a lot.

"It doesn't feel real at the moment, but I'm sure it will sink in," Neale said on Saturday.

"I've absolutely loved my time at this footy club, they're an exceptional organisation from top to bottom and I can't thank them enough.

"It's been an incredible ride and the best eight years of my life."

Neale moved to the Lions from the Dockers at the end of the 2018 season.

He won his two Brownlow Medals (2020 and 2023) while playing 186 senior matches for the Lions.

Neale, a four-time All-Australian selection, played 135 matches for the Dockers between 2012-18.

World.title: Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters grand final specialist
World.content:
The Roosters boast a galaxy of stars for Sunday's NRL decider against Newcastle, but veteran winger Daniel Tupou might be the only one who can call himself a grand final specialist.

Not that he ever would. The 35-year-old has for many years now been a firm believer that actions speak louder than words, and those actions demand his automatic inclusion in any discussion about an all-time Roosters XVII.

A win over the Knights will make Tupou, already the club's highest-ever tryscorer and only a few games shy of being their most capped player, the first Rooster to win four premierships with the club since the 1940s.

He's the only player to have appeared in all three grand final wins under coach Trent Robinson, although calling what Tupou has done merely "appearing" sells him short.

Back in 2013, in just his second year of first grade, Tupou went skywalking to score a spectacular try in the Tricolours' win over a Manly side containing future teammate Daly Cherry-Evans.

Tupou has been making his mark in grand finals for more than a decade. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Back then, Tupou was like so many of his teammates are now — young and hungry in his first grand final, with everything to prove.

"I can't remember much, to be honest it's a bit of a blur, it was such a long time ago. Most of these boys are where I was in 2013 — I was the same age then as Rob Toia is now," said Tupou.

"He's (Cherry-Evans) has never brought it up. I might not bring it up this week, not until after the game on Sunday at least."

That try was just the 17th of Tupou's career, and his 199th in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins is proof he can still fly.

But that and his calm demeanour are about the only things that are still the same after all this time, with Tupou himself having become one of the best wingers of the modern era in the years since.

His performances in the club's back-to-back premiership wins in 2018-19 are living proof of that transformation from skinny aerial specialist to a truly complete flanker.

In the first victory, a comprehensive win over Melbourne, he scored the opening try and worked like a dog from the backfield, running for the second-most metres of any Roosters player.

In the second, a 14-8 war with Canberra, he was unlucky not to become the first winger to win the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.

Tupou ran for a team-high 185 metres from 17 carries and saved several tries with perfect defensive decision-making before making the break and throwing the final pass for James Tedesco's premiership-winning score.

It's as good a game as a winger has ever played in a grand final, but when Tupou explains how he finds his best form on the season's biggest day, he makes it sound maddeningly simple.

"You have to stay calm and collected. Enjoy the week and the hype around it, enjoy the atmosphere once we hit the field but embrace the vibe, embrace the energy," said Tupou.

"There's a lot of stuff to tick off, but you have to enjoy every bit of it.

"Just stay present. Don't overthink, be where your feet are."

It's the advice he'll give the grand final rookies on Sunday, even though the Roosters have plenty of premiership experience on hand.

Victor Radley and James Tedesco both played in 2018-19, Nat Butcher and Angus Crichton were both there for the latter and Spencer Leniu won three titles with Penrith.

This Rooster has been the NRL's best forward in 2026 Fresh off another act of blunt-force artistry, there can be no doubt that Roosters prop Naufahu Whyte has been the best forward in the NRL in 2026.

But given 15 of the 22 players named on Tuesday have yet to play in a grand final, they have a fair share of first-timers.

None could ask for a better example of how to make the most of it than Tupou, whose deeds under the brightest of lights have made him a stone-cold living legend of the club he'll once again try to bring to glory on Sunday.

"It's in the preparation. We've worked so hard during the year to earn this moment," said Tupou.

"It's nothing less than what we've already done, we just have to stay consistent."

World.title: Aussie skipper Molineux a chance to play home series despite injury
World.content:
Australia will give captain Sophie Molineux every chance to play in white-ball matches against Bangladesh and New Zealand, as she battles a hip injury.

Molineux was named to captain Australia's side for one-day internationals against Bangladesh and T20s against New Zealand next month, despite the injury.

Fast bowler Darcie Brown has been sidelined with a back injury that also has her in doubt for the WBBL, while fellow quick Lucy Hamilton will miss the ODIs with a quad strain.

Molineux proves inspired choice Sophie Molineux is praised for her leadership ability after guiding Australia to its Women's T20 World Cup victory.

But it is Molineux's fitness that is of most interest ahead of the opening ODI in Brisbane on October 9.

The Victorian put aside a history of frustrating blows to have a stellar first six months as captain, culminating in Australia's T20 World Cup win in England.

"Sophie has been named in the squad but has been managing a hip injury," chief national selector Shawn Flegler said.

"Her involvement in the series will continue to be assessed over the coming days.

"Lucy suffered a mild quad strain at training, but we're hopeful she'll recover in time to be fit and firing for the T20 series."

If Molineux is ruled out, selectors will have to make a call between vice-captains Tahlia McGrath and Ashleigh Gardner to lead the side.

Australian squad:

Sophie Molineux (c), Ashleigh Gardner (vc), Tahlia McGrath (vc), Nicola Carey, Kim Garth, Lucy Hamilton, Alana King, Phoebe Litchfield, Beth Mooney, Ellyse Perry, Megan Schutt, Annabel Sutherland, Georgia Voll, Georgia Wareham

AAP

World.title: Biles undecided about competing at 2028 LA Olympics
World.content:
Simone Biles understands the constant speculation about whether she will compete at another Olympics.

Mostly because the American gymnastics icon is still kind of wondering about the prospect herself.

So much so, there will be times when the question wakes the two-time Olympic all-around champion up in the middle of the night.

"I don't know what the decision [is) I should make, but I don't necessarily have to make it just yet," Biles said.

"But I feel like it's kind of in the works which way I'm leaning towards."

After competing at the Rio de Janeiro, Tokyo and Paris Olympics, the lure of performing on the world stage at home in Los Angeles in 2028 is real.

Simone Biles has won seven gold medals across her Olympic career. (Getty Images: Tom Weller)

Olympic teammates Suni Lee, Jordan Chiles and Jade Carey are already pointing toward LA.

So is Katelyn Ohashi, who returned to elite competition in July following a staggering 13-year break from the sport's top level.

"I know [athletes] are going a lot longer … It's going to be like a big reunion if I did," Biles said.

"It would be so much fun. But I still have to weigh the options."

Biles, who has won seven Olympic gold medals, will be 31 by the time the flame is lit at the Los Angeles opening ceremony in July 2028.

The sacrifices of trying to make a fourth Olympic team would be far different than what she faced in Rio a decade ago.

Biles and her husband, Indianapolis Colts NFL player Jonathan Owens, would like to start a family at some point.

"I am getting to the age of 30 where we start to talk about, 'What does your reproduction cycle … what's going on in there? Biles said.

" I think these are major things that are on the table at my age that I have to take in consideration and weigh those options and what that looks like and when we want to start a family."

Still, the "FOMO", or fear of missing out, when it comes to LA is only too real.

"Like a home Olympic Games … how could you not?" she said.

"It's absolutely incredible."

AP

World.title: Aussie breaks 24-year-old world record at national short course swimming titles
World.content:
Two-time Paralympic gold medallist Rowan Crothers has set a men's S10 world record for the 200 metres freestyle at the Australian Short Course Championships in Sydney.

Competing in the 200m freestyle multiclass event, Crothers stopped the clock in 1 minute and 49.93 seconds.

Canada's Philippe Gagnon had held the previous world record of 1:52.83 since 2002.

Crothers's Australian teammate Alex Tuckfield also dipped under the mark, swimming 1:50.79 to finish second.

"I did not see that coming at all. Not even close," Crothers said.

"Unfortunately, the 200m freestyle isn't a Paralympic event for my classification (S1), but we're going to keep working on it and keep building on the 200m because it's just great training and it's going to help my 100m massively.

"That swim just gets me really excited for the future."

Tuckfield was full of praise for Crothers.

"Rowan is someone I definitely look up to," Tuckfield said.

"I take every opportunity to race him with heart. He's a lovely, lovely man. I want to be like him when I get to his level, and I will.

"Every time I race him, I get a bit better, and it shows with tonight's PB (personal best) that is under the world record … I couldn't be prouder that we both went under the world record."

Among other results, Maddie McTernan broke her S14 women's 200m freestyle national record, swimming 2:07.68.

Ed Sommerville and Ben Armbruster also set national records in the men's 200m freestyle and 50m butterfly respectively.

Sommerville swam 1:40.16, while Armbruster recorded a time of 21.90, becoming the first Australian to go under 22 seconds for the event.

Lani Pallister continued her outstanding 2026 season with an Australian all-comers record in the women's 1,500m freestyle.

Pallister, who won eight gold medals across the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacific Championships earlier this year, swam 15:18.68.

She won the 200m freestyle final earlier in the evening, with a time of 1:51.99.

Tech.title: The Halide camera app now offers full control of the iPhone 18 Pro’s aperture
