Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A new update to Lux Optics’ anti-algorithm Halide camera app for the iPhone and iPad adds two new photography looks and support for the variable aperture on the new iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera. Halide isn’t the first alternative to the native iOS camera app to add support for the new feature, but it offers more finite control over aperture settings than other third-party apps.

The iOS camera app limits aperture adjustments to just four presets, but both the BlackMagic Camera and Moment Pro Camera II apps expand that to 10 presets in 1/3 stop increments, similar to what most digital cameras offer. Halide Mark III goes even further by letting you select any f-stop setting from f/1.48 down to f/4.0. Although it’s hard to imagine you’ll see any noticeable difference between f/4.0 and f/3.99, the option is available. The Halide developers are also considering adding f-stop presets in future updates based on user feedback.

The new Dawn look (left) adds warmth to images while Quicksilver (right) mutes colors and boosts contrast. Image: Lux Optics

Halide Mark III launched earlier this year with added features including a new film simulation engine and multiple looks that can be applied to photos. Today’s update adds a new Dawn look to the collection that applies “filmic warmth in the mid-tones and highlights with gentle, rich shadows” and Quicksilver, which “pairs high contrast with muted color, inspired by silver-retention processes.”

Tech.title: All the latest news on Meta’s cute, creepy Muse AI agent
Tech.content: Meta launched a new Muse AI agent it claims can help you with everything from firing off emails to buying stuff online. Muse can be surprisingly effective at delivering on those promises — if you’re willing to trust Meta with your data and hand Muse your credit card. Since the launch, Meta’s also announced plans for a Tamagotchi-like Muse Charm device for its cuddly AI mascot.

Tech.title: Google reportedly tests paying publishers for AI search results
Tech.content:
Google has launched a pilot program that pays publishers for their contributions to its AI-powered search features, according to a report from The Information . The pilot program reportedly includes around 100 publishers and comes as Google faces scrutiny over the impact of its AI features on web traffic.

Digiday first reported on the pilot program, which began less than a year ago. As part of the test, Google is reportedly paying participating publishers for how much their content contributed to AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search, as well as its Gemini chatbot. One publisher that joined the program when it first started earned over $1 million in a year, while another that joined a few months ago has earned around $50,000 to $60,000, The Information reports.

Tech.title: Instagram is adding an AI ‘assistant’ to tell you how to post
Tech.content:
Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts. The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change.

Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience. The tool pulls in data and metrics such as likes, views, retention on videos, and shares. Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide. Creators can also ask for ideas for content, how to hook viewers, what captions to use, which audio tracks are trending, and how to script videos.

I want to hear from you about your experience. Contact me at mia@theverge.com or at miasato.11 on Signal.

If that sounds familiar, it’s because YouTube also just announced updates to its sprawling AI-powered dashboard that tells creators how to maximize engagement. (YouTube’s version, which it initially announced in 2025, also has AI editing and A/B testing capabilities.) If you’ve been online for a while — and especially if you’ve ever had to pay attention to social media metrics — you’ll know that this is quite a shift. Historically, many platforms have limited or even hidden detailed metrics about how your own content is performing. The platforms certainly have not been open about why a video or post performed poorly. Tools like CrowdTangle, which researchers and journalists used to monitor the most popular content on Meta platforms, have been shut down or restricted. Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm.

It’s in both the platforms’ and creators’ best interest to shape content for maximum engagement. As I wrote earlier this month, though, what happens when everyone is perfectly optimizing their content? Will content become even more similar as creators adjust to one another? Is there no ceiling for the amount of time audiences are willing to spend on the platforms? The shift also raises interesting new questions about the relationship between tech companies and the creators that fill the platforms with things to look at: How does this dynamic change when platforms are straightforwardly giving creators instructions on how to post?

The new feature is free for creators to use, up to a point. Meta says “power users” will be able to buy a Meta One subscription for more usage. This, too, speaks to the changing winds: Meta needs to finance its lofty AI ambitions, and it’s already signaled that premium social media features may be part of how it does it. It’s not hard to imagine a future where meaningful feedback and AI-driven analytics and insights are for paying subscribers. In the end, it may end up re-creating the same frustrations and opaqueness that have plagued content creators for years — but this time, behind a paywall.

Tech.title: Amazon’s new Fire TV Stick 4K can pull power directly from your TV
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The new Fire TV Stick 4K will be a little easier to set up than Amazon’s previous 4K streaming sticks since it no longer requires a power adapter. You can power the device directly from your TV’s USB port, like the updated entry-level Fire TV Stick Amazon launched earlier this year. The Fire TV Stick 4K, available starting today for $59.99, runs on Amazon’s refreshed TV OS and includes Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, and Bluetooth Low Energy.

Amazon’s also simplifying its streaming stick lineup, which now includes four devices instead of five: the Fire TV Stick HD, Fire TV Stick 4K, Fire TV Stick 4K Max, and Fire TV Cube. The new Fire TV Stick 4K is replacing Amazon’s earlier “Select” and “Plus” 4K streaming sticks.

Amazon’s Fire TV streaming device lineup no longer includes the 4K “Select” and “Plus” sticks. Image: Amazon

A redesigned Fire TV Remote is launching alongside the new streaming stick, featuring a new asymmetrical shape and “more tactile controls.” The new remote is compatible with all Amazon Ember TVs and Fire TV streaming devices from 2019 onward. It will be available standalone for $14.99 and starts shipping late October. Amazon says it also plans to launch a “Plus” version of the new remote early next year, with an aluminum design, backlit buttons, and a “Find My Remote” feature.

Fire TV is getting a few software updates, as well, including an Alexa Plus Hub and an Alexa Plus integration in the Fire TV mobile app. Amazon says its AI “now draws on real-world context” like awards and events, helping it answer more complex prompts for show and movie suggestions. Amazon Music is also getting a new Fire TV app later this fall, with an Alexa Plus integration users can prompt for music and podcast recommendations.

Tech.title: The Sonos Ace Ultra are the headphones Sonos should have made the first time
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

The original Sonos Ace headphones should have been a triumphant entry into a new product category. Instead, they were overshadowed by Sonos’s disastrous app redesign. And while the original Ace are well built, sound good, and are incredibly comfortable, they weren’t good Sonos headphones: Their flagship feature let you reroute audio from a Sonos soundbar to the Ace headphones so you could listen to your TV audio without disturbing anyone. But it was glitchy, and at launch it only worked with the $1,000 Arc soundbar, and only with one pair of Ace headphones at a time (Both of those have now been fixed). It also couldn’t connect to the rest of the Sonos system for music streaming.

Now the Ace Ultra are here, at the same $449 release price as the Ace (which are now $349). They’ve improved on what the Ace did well, while finally adding the ability to pass audio from your Sonos system to the headphones and back (although it’s in “early access”). They’re what the Ace should have been the first time.

The Sonos Ace Ultra have the same clean, understated look of the original, which I appreciate. They’re incredibly comfortable for hours on end, even while I’m wearing my glasses, and though they’re ever so slightly heavier than the Ace — 0.69 pounds to 0.71 pounds with the Ace Ultra — that weight was never a problem. The ear cups are squishy and spacious, and like the Ace’s ear cups, they’re also magnetic and easily removable; Sonos sells extras for $39 a pair. The battery is also user replaceable (a kit costs $25), although a statement on the battery kit listing does warn that “swapping out the battery requires disassembly and tools, plus some time and patience.”

The headphones also keep the tactile buttons and Content Key volume slider of the Ace instead of using capacitive buttons like the Sony XM series or Bose QuietComfort Ultra. I loved this setup and I’m glad Sonos kept the real buttons on the Ace Ultra. The Content Key reacts quickly and is easy to find while wearing the headphones. And its button functionality allows you to access the Sonos-specific features of TV audio swap and headphone linking.

The Content Key control acts as both a slider and a button, and it’s very intuitive to use. The Ace Ultra support lossless audio over USB-C.

While the original Ace came with TV audio swap, that was the extent of their Sonos system integration. The Ace Ultra have rectified that, albeit with a caveat, by adding headphone linking. The headphones now show up in your system list, and with a press of the slider button, you can move your music from any Sonos speaker or speaker group — not just TV audio from the soundbar — to the headphones and vice versa. That includes audio coming into the Sonos system from a record player or CD player or anywhere else. Both TV audio swap and headphone linking use a Wi-Fi connection.

It’s not flawless; sometimes I’d have to press the button a couple times to get the transfer to happen. If you pull the audio from your speakers to the headphones and decide to send it back later, it only goes to the closest speaker in your system, not whichever speaker or group was playing before. Adding it back to a speaker group has to be done in the Sonos app. The headphones also cannot be grouped with any speakers. I suppose the thinking is, if you’re listening to music on your headphones you don’t need it also playing from your speakers. One nice touch is that if you have different music playing on different speakers, pulling the music to the headphones from one doesn’t affect the rest of them. Headphone linking is in early access, according to Sonos, so it’s possible the experience will change.

As Sonos’ own Wi-Fi vs. Bluetooth explainer points out, one of the main benefits of Wi-Fi audio streaming is that the higher bandwidth allows for hi-res and lossless audio. But right now, the Ace Ultra don’t take advantage of that. During the headphone linking early access period, audio over Wi-Fi with headphone linking is lossy. (Sonos has not said how long the early access period will last). Senior director of product management Andrew Sutherland told The Verge via email, “our focus right now is making sure the core experience is genuinely solid and reliable for listeners by using a high-quality, lossy-compressed stereo audio stream optimized for listening over WiFi. We’ve been really happy with the results. We’ll continue to build out its capabilities from there.” I appreciate the cautiousness in making sure headphone linking works properly, but it’s disappointing that Sonos shipped a product with one of its flagship features still in beta.

There’s a magnetic pouch in the case to hold the included USB-C-to-USB-C and USB-C-to-3.5mm cables.

At the moment, the Ace Ultra only support lossless audio over Bluetooth with aptX Lossless and a compatible device, or over USB-C. The wired USB-C or 3.5mm connection maxes out at 16-bit/48kHz, though, so there’s no high-res audio. There will surely be lots of debate on the forums about the tragic lack of high-res support, but the reality is most people won’t be missing anything.

Newly designed 40mm drivers sound better than those on the original Ace, and an adaptive EQ makes real-time adjustments based on fit and any obstructions — such as glasses’ temples or earrings. The bass is richer without overpowering vocals, which is most evident in songs with a thumping low end, like Billie Eilish’s “Bad Guy” (one of my go-to bass tests). The kick drum through the verse and chorus has weight and drives the energy forward while the rhythmic bass line supports the voice. There’s also good stereo separation on “Killer Queen” by Queen with lead guitars to the left and right of the soundstage.

I do wish the Ace Ultra had better midrange clarity, especially on busier tracks like Radiohead’s “The National Anthem” and its cacophonous middle section. The 8-band EQ Sonos added to the Ace Ultra (sorry original Ace owners, this isn’t for you) helps this a bit when I boosted the mids at 460Hz and 1kHz a little. While in there, I also added more high frequencies to open up the sound. With the tweaks, I got the Ace Ultra to a place where I enjoyed my listening across genres. It’s a good step forward from the original Ace, although I still prefer the Sony XM6’s default sound profile.

Streaming music can be moved from a Sonos speaker to the headphones with a press of a button or through the Sonos app.

The Ace Ultra’s active noise cancellation (ANC) is better than the Ace’s and now includes an adaptive version. It’s still not as strong as the ANC on the Sony XM6, Bose Ultra Headphones, or Apple AirPods Max 2 — it lets in more midrange and a few higher frequencies, as well — so if you’re mainly using them to block out ambient noise, those three options are better choices. But if you’re using ANC paired with music playing, the Ace Ultra perform well.

Call quality is also better. When I was on a video call while my wife was having a phone conversation 20 feet behind me in the kitchen, the Ace Ultra kept her voice and other ambient noise quieted. They had a bit more trouble keeping out the noise when I went outside to a busy street — the Sony XM6 are much better at this — but I still sounded clear and easy to understand.

Sonos has upped the battery life, from up to 30 hours on the Ace to up to 35 hours with the Ace Ultra. They come with the same felt-covered case with a magnetic removable pouch that stores the USB-C to USB-C and USB-C to 3.5mm cables.

Sonos has taken a great first shot at headphones and followed up with an even better pair. They have improved sound, better ANC, and Sonos-specific features. And they’re one of the most comfortable pairs of headphones I’ve worn in a while.

The Sonos Ace Ultra come in four colors — black, white, agave, and sand.

But to get the most out of the Ace Ultra, you need to be an existing Sonos user, or be ready to spend hundreds more dollars. The cheapest Sonos soundbar that works with TV audio swap, the Ray, is still $219. And headphone linking is only useful if you have Sonos speakers.

If you do have a Sonos soundbar and speakers and you’re looking for headphones, the Ace Ultra are an easy recommendation, especially over the original Ace — even though those are down to $350. If you’re not in the Sonos world, though, the Sony WH-1000XM6 (or even the older XM5) with their better ANC and sound quality for less money, are a better bet.

Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

Tech.title: Potato by air
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Wing Hummingbird 7000W-B delivery drone weighs less than 15 pounds. It has 16 propellers — four for horizontal movement and 12 for vertical — a top speed of 60 miles per hour, a carrying capacity of up to 2.7 pounds, and a delivery radius of about six miles. It is authorized by the FAA for beyond-line-of-sight piloting. As a feat of engineering, it is impressive.

So far I’ve mostly used it to send people potatoes.

It all started a few Sunday mornings ago when my neighbor Will added me and a half dozen other local dads to a group chat. I only recognized a few of the numbers.

“Anyone looking for dumb stuff to entertain the kids?” he wrote, under a video of a drone lowering a blue doggie bag into his backyard. He’d discovered that we were now in the delivery range for drone service Wing’s partnership with Walmart, and could get household items dropped onto our lawns in 25 minutes. “Hopefully liquor store will get on board soon.”

Ever since I saw the video of an Amazon drone dropping a package in someone’s pool, I’ve needed to know one thing: Do you have to order drone delivery to your own yard? I raised the question in the chat.

Turns out: no and yes. Image: Nathan Edwards / The Verge

Will, a few minutes later: “Nathan I just ordered you a potato to see if I can send to other people. 8 minutes out.”

Two minutes after that, a neighbor named Rick: “Will just want you to know you’re going to get your potato first.”

Rick and Will had each scanned the list of deliverable items — over two thousand of them — and independently arrived at the same conclusion. “There is currently an air strike squadron of potatoes headed to our neighborhood,” Rick wrote.

It’s a bird! It’s a plane! It’s a cropped still from a video! Image: Nathan Edwards / The Verge

At 12:14PM, a drone dropped a doggie bag in my yard. It contained a single russet potato and a bottle of water. Three minutes later, another arrived in Will’s yard, also containing a single potato and a bottle of water. (The water bottle seems to have been added as ballast; every Wing order I’ve placed came with one.)

Someone posted “The drones are everywhere.” Those of us who hadn’t met introduced ourselves. An apparently more practical dad named Jason ordered himself a pair of gloves. Dev, who lives in the next development over, was just out of drone range and could only watch in envy. Eventually, a storm rolled in and the potato drones tapered off.

My child voluntarily peeled and cooked a potato. This is huge. Photo: Nathan Edwards / The Verge Slice consistency could use some work but A for effort. Photo: Nathan Edwards / The Verge

My sixth-grader turned our sky potato into oven fries; Will baked his.

The wild thing — aside from the fact that you can just order a drone delivery to someone else’s yard — is that each potato delivery cost 82 cents. Total. Each order came from the Walmart Supercenter a few miles away. Wing is absolutely losing money on this. There’s no minimum order, there’s no delivery fee, and the prices are the same as in-store. Wing’s not even collecting sales tax. Welcome back, millennial lifestyle subsidy!

At these prices, if you’re not using drones to send potatoes to your neighbors you’re leaving money on the table. That evening, I remembered that my friend Bill had been going through a rough time lately.

I sent him a potato.

Okay, technically, Wing’s terms of service state “You will not use the Service to engage in any unlawful behavior, or to cause harassment, nuisance, annoyance or inconvenience to Wing, its users or any other person.” And I can definitely see ways you could abuse the system to do that.

While I lacked actual permission to land a drone potato in Bill’s yard, based on our relationship, I was confident I had spiritual permission. (This was confirmed a couple of days later when he asked me to drone deliver some candy for his kids. I sent the candy, and then another potato, and then the link to the Wing app.)

So what’s stopping someone from using this to harass people, beyond your own moral compass and the fact that they ask you not to? When I asked what safeguards the company had in place to prevent unauthorized deliveries, Wing spokesperson Jessie Poole-Strang wrote:

Wing has safely completed over 1 million residential drone deliveries, averaging thousands per day. Customers must be physically present for their first order, and every order requires a verified account and confirmation of a clear delivery zone. Just like traditional delivery or mailing a package, customers can choose to send an order to a friend or family member’s address that lives in eligible service areas. In the rare event a resident ever has a concern about a delivery to their property, our support team can help (support@wing.com).

Now, is drone delivery wasteful? If you’re only buying a single lightweight item — like a stick of deodorant, a bottle of sunscreen, or a potato — it seems more environmentally friendly than driving to the store. And as long as it’s subsidized, it’s way cheaper than DoorDash or whatever people use. I could see situations where it would be genuinely useful, especially if you can’t leave the house but you desperately need a bottle of ibuprofen and a Gatorade (for example). And of course it would be preposterous to DoorDash someone a single raw potato.

Of course, once you order more than a pound or so of stuff, that math goes off the rails. One afternoon, my wife ordered a box of frozen horchata mochi and a pint of gelato — among the few frozen desserts on the list. They arrived in two separate drones, three minutes apart, and each came with a small bottle of water. They held up surprisingly well during their 7-minute trips in the full Texas sun, considering the total lack of insulation. But it did feel silly to get two drones for two items.

That’s how they get you, of course. They hook you with convenience while hiding the true cost of the service. Drone delivery further squeezes gig workers in an already shrinking labor market, and it’s one more excuse for big companies to suppress wages. You don’t have to pay a drone, and you don’t have to tip it, either.

It’s been just over three weeks since we found out we had access to subsidized drone delivery. Aside from the two desserts and a couple of bags of gummy Nerds clusters, I’ve only used it to send potatoes to the dads. I sent three last week, plus one to myself to throw them off the scent. I’ve probably blown my cover now.

The other day someone — not me — escalated and sent Rick a broccoli potato soup. I’m pretty sure it was Will.

What have I learned from all of this? Well, I now know a few more people in my neighborhood. I’ve learned that drone delivery is way more useful to me than agentic AI has ever been. And that given the opportunity to airdrop subsidized potatoes to my friends, I’ll take it.

Tech.title: You can text DoorDash’s AI bot to ‘order my usual’ and it will figure the rest out
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DoorDash is launching new ways to use the local delivery platform, including text message ordering, drone deliveries, and retail returns. The new message ordering feature builds on capabilities that the Ask DoorDash AI chatbot introduced to the DoorDash app in June, allowing you to get recommendations and offload your browsing while skipping the app entirely.

“Ordering is now as easy as sending a text,” DoorDash said in its press release. “Whether you’re requesting a specific dish, asking for a local recommendation based on your mood, or telling DoorDash to ‘order my usual protein bowl to the office,’ it searches local spots, suggests a cart, and handles checkout right inside the text thread. It learns your preferences and remembers them for future orders.”

This is all just a preview for now because ordering by text isn’t available yet — iOS users in the US can join a waitlist from today to try the experience in beta. We’ve asked DoorDash for information about the rollout timeline and Android availability.

The first location for DoorDash Air, the company’s drone delivery service, has also been revealed. It’ll be piloted in an unspecified part of northern California with local food services, including Chipotle and Popeyes. DoorDash says around 80 percent of typical restaurant orders are “light and small enough for the aircraft to carry safely,” and that food arrives at customers’ doors within five minutes based on initial testing. DoorDash hasn’t announced when the drone deliveries will actually be available to consumers.

The limited capacity for drone orders means you probably won’t squeeze any massive takeout splurges in there. Image: DoorDash

Finally, a returns feature will be expanded across the US in November that allows customers to pay DoorDash couriers to send items back to local retailers. It’s only available in select cities right now, and costs $7.99 to schedule an eligible return. No box or shipping label is required — the item just gets collected from your door, taken back to the store, and then your return is processed for you.

The idea is to prevent you from missing the return window for unwanted products purchased on DoorDash due to other commitments that prevent you from shipping or taking it back yourself. TikTok announced its own version of this feature via UPS yesterday.

Tech.title: Meta disputes claim that Muse read a user’s private messages without permission
Tech.content:
Meta is refuting a journalist’s claim that its AI agent Muse read the user’s private messages without permission. Following an earlier report from Inc. columnist Jason Aten that detailed the issue, Meta VP of Communications Andy Stone pushed back, making it clear that the company does not believe its product did this without the user’s consent.

“The Messages integration in the Muse app for Mac is entirely opt-in,” Stone wrote on X in response to the claims made by the piece. “You have to enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content. It can’t read your Messages unless you do this.”

Despite Meta’s denial, many people are still suspicious that Meta isn’t being truthful.

That’s not surprising, given the tech giant’s years of mishandling consumer data, which has led to lawsuits, FTC violations, and fines. Just days ago, for instance, a New Mexico jury determined the tech giant had misled users about its data practices in a case that resulted from the 2018 Cambridge Analytica data breach scandal.

Whether users can trust Muse will be a deciding factor in whether or not Meta wins the consumer AI market. Although its app is faring well now, and remains No. 1 on the App Store, Meta’s reputation may not recover if more reports like this emerge, true or not. If anything, the company should be engaging with the journalist directly to determine how this could have possibly happened, instead of just denying that it did.

Stone’s official statement from Meta follows a more technical reply from Meta Superintelligence Labs executive David Singleton, who responded directly to Aten on Threads, explaining that the set of permissions a user must grant to let Muse read their messages on the Mac involves “three separate steps of application-level permissions and built-in macOS system-level protections.” He said these “can’t be circumvented even if the Muse application had a bug.”

The steps involve explicitly choosing to grant Muse Full Disk Access, which would then allow the user to choose what level of access Muse is being granted to the Messages app (i.e., None, Read only, or Read). If Full Disk Access is not enabled, these options are grayed out.

In addition, when allowing Full Disk Access, the dialog invokes the macOS Settings user interface, where the user has to again manually confirm that they intend to take this action. Doing this triggers a full restart of the Muse app, Singleton wrote, which makes it even less likely that such a choice could be made accidentally without the user’s knowledge.

However, Aten’s report claimed that when Muse read his messages, Full Disk Access was off. He also said that when he asked Muse to explain how this occurred, the AI said that it was syncing his “device notifications.” That means, Aten believes, that Muse was passing along the text of his incoming banner notifications on the Mac to the AI agent.

Singleton disputed this, too, saying that the AI was confused and gave an incorrect explanation of what happened. He then pointed to Meta’s page about Muse’s security architecture and bug bounty process.

In short, the company’s response is essentially that what Aten said happened did not and could not have happened.

This is not the only incident where Muse has allegedly overstepped and won’t likely be the last. Another user, YouTuber Matt Robb, recently said that Muse mishandled a task in which he was selling things on Facebook Marketplace, leading to his address being shared and a buyer showing up when he wasn’t even home. Singleton is apparently looking into that one, per his response on Threads, suggesting that the company believes this one, at least, could be its fault.

Tech.title: DoorDash launches an AI agent you can text to order food
Tech.content:
In Brief

DoorDash announced on Wednesday that it’s launching a text-to-order AI agent that lets users place orders through Apple Messages. The new tool allows users to send prompts like “order my usual,” and the agent will understand that they mean their Friday night order.

DoorDash says users can also ask for a specific dish and request a local recommendation. The agent will then search local spots and suggest a cart based on the prompt, and even text photos of the food it recommends. When ordering for a group, DoorDash says the agent can handle mixed dietary preferences and different quantities in one order.

By launching an AI agent for food ordering, DoorDash is looking to gain an edge over rivals Uber Eats and Grubhub. The launch also comes amid a growing push to adopt personal AI agents that can handle tasks without requiring users to navigate apps or websites themselves.

DoorDash is opening up a waitlist for users in the U.S. to try out the new feature.

In addition to the new AI agent, DoorDash announced that it will begin testing its delivery drones with select restaurants in Northern California.

Tech.title: Destro AI’s secret sauce is getting robots and humans on the same page
Tech.content:
The best path to successfully deploying a robot is not building one at all, according to Destro, a startup that came out of stealth Tuesday with an $8 million seed round.

Most new robotics companies are focused on finding the right form factor or developing an AI model that can put metal hands to work. Destro has instead built an AI intelligence layer that lets robots work effectively in logistics settings, in part by also telling the human workers what to do.

“A lot of robotics companies started from robotics engineers [asking] ‘What cool things I can do?’” Destro founder Manthan Pawar, a veteran of the industry, told TechCrunch. “One of the biggest reasons we are winning against robotics companies is because we are not a robotics company.”

Pawar, who earned a master’s degree in robotics at NYU Tandon and has spent roughly eight years in the U.S. supply chain and robotics industry, explains that “our mindset is, we know our customers’ problems so damn well, and we are actually on path to be cash flow positive at the end of this year.”

Richard Brunelle, the director of automation for the American logistics group at Yusen Logistics, a South Korean shipping giant, helped get the startup pointed in the right direction. Brunelle is responsible for automation across about 30 facilities in the U.S. There, Yusen uses fixed automation, like conveyors and sorters, but it is still piloting new technology like trailer-unloading robots and autonomous floor scrubbers.

Finding more ways to put technology like that to work is Brunelle’s priority: Yusen’s UK subsidiary has built out a fully autonomous facility and now a similar plan is in the works in the U.S. When Brunelle met Pawar, Destro was focused on a different challenge in the space—picking and pack, the process by which various goods are sorted into single packages.

Brunelle realized his primary challenge was “fundamentally the same problem.” His job involved cross-docking: unloading goods from one truck and sorting them into mixed loads for other trucks that make the final delivery to customers.

“I asked whether Destro would be willing to adapt their solution to fit that cross-dock environment, because I don’t think anyone was doing that,” he told TechCrunch. “They went away, thought it through, and came back excited. They agreed nobody was addressing that space and that they could modify their tool to support it. Since then, they’ve gone all in.”

Destro started with a pilot program at one Yusen facility in the Pacific northwest, using three cart-moving robots built by Miva Robotics and operated by Destro’s Vision operating system based on open-weight vision-language-action models (AI systems that interpret camera images and instructions to control a robot’s movements).

As human workers unload goods from one truck into different carts, the robots find the full loads and bring them to their destinations. What makes this efficient, in the estimation of Brunelle and Pawar, is that the human, the cart, and the trucks are all directed by Destro’s Mothership operating system.

“We make that operation less labor intensive, and we get away from the paper,” Brunelle said. “Everything is now systematic.”

That matters because Yusen also talked to two other big-name robot startups in this space, and neither could fit into their workflow. One offered a robot that could move the carts point-to-point but could not manage loading or unloading. The other came with fleet management tools, but required a person to handle all the orchestration. Destro won because of its ability to apply autonomous direction to the whole process.

Now, Destro is expanding its initial pilot to a full deployment of 26 robots and launching another pilot with 17 robots at Yusen’s facility in Southern California. Pawar plans to take this cross-dock loading workflow and “copy-paste” across thousands of other warehouses that handle this kind of labor. It’s that plan that convinced Base10 Partners and Bonfire Ventures to lead Destro’s seed round, with additional investment from CoFound Partners.

Destro may face a challenge with workflows that require more dexterity and manipulation. Generic robot bodies and open-source models haven’t proven capable at these tasks yet, and it’s not clear if companies building foundation models, ultra-dexterous hands, or general-purpose humanoids will make those tools available to a company like Destro rather than trying to capture that business themselves.

Pawar remains confident that he’s found the part of the stack where value will accrue, and that his company will be able to take advantage of the research dollars pouring into new AI models and robot components.

“Robots are a platform. Every layer model is a platform. But we build a harness around it,” Pawar told TechCrunch. “That harness is just so complex and value-added that without that harness, these workflows are completely impossible, right?”

For now, competing with futuristic robot-builders is probably not an issue. Brunelle says he has yet to find a good use case for a bipedal humanoid robot, though he is evaluating a potential pilot with a wheeled humanoid.

“At the end of the day, we’re not putting automation into a building just because the technology is interesting,” Brunelle said. “It must solve a real operational problem. If it can make the operation more efficient, consistent, and flexible, that’s ultimately going to benefit our customers.”

Destro will be making its case for the non-robot robot company at TechCrunch Disrupt in just a few weeks. Join us in October to see Destro in person, along with the rest of our Battlefield competitors.

Tech.title: Instinct’s new product recommendations are giving some users the ick
Tech.content:
The buzzy AI startup Instinct has just revealed a new potential revenue stream: product recommendations. Unfortunately for the company, the rollout is already rubbing some users the wrong way.

Overnight, the AI agent began pushing product suggestions to users as part of a new feature called Instinct Selections, an effort to curate personalized lists for users in areas like dining, travel, and shopping.

Founder Noah Shinn announced the feature’s debut later Tuesday, explaining that the idea is to partner with “local chefs, designers, architects, travel guides,” and others to bring “human taste” to its product.

In other words, instead of only relying on what the AI could suggest based on its training data gathered from the wider web, the company is partnering with people to offer human-curated suggestions, too. (Instinct didn’t share who, exactly, those human partners are.)

“The next time you’re looking for a restaurant, Instinct can pull from a list handpicked by chefs who know the hidden gems in your area,” Shinn wrote on X.

“If you want to find a new trail to explore, Instinct can draw on recommendations from local guides and suggest a few routes that fit your preferences. And if you’re looking to add some color to your home, Instinct will find pieces from independent designers that match your style, space, and budget,” he continued. “Our goal is to deliver world-class recommendations that are differentiated in quality from what you might find on the internet, and from what other chatbots produce,” he said.

But the initial reaction to these seemingly unsolicited product pushes as not been fully positive.

“I didn’t need to buy carry-on luggage, sunglasses, or a brim hat. This feels so disappointing. At least make me a personalized shopping list of things I actually need!!,” Shruti Gandhi, a general partner at the AI-focused investing firm, Array VC, wrote on X.

Instinct became shitty Amazon recommends app overnight.



I didn’t need to buy carry on luggage, sunglasses, or a brim hat. This feels so disappointing. At least make me a personalized shopping list of things I actually need!! https://t.co/hmH2iiE8lF pic.twitter.com/TNQIEwK9z2 — Shruti Gandhi / Array VC preseed rounds (@atShruti) September 29, 2026

Another entrepreneur, Andrew Yeung, confirmed on X that he also received product recommendations that he hadn’t asked for, which can feel off-putting.

A third user, Chat Joglekar, the founder of a business-buying marketplace, wrote, “I had my first ‘ewwww’ moment with an AI assistant when Instinct started to suggest products that I should buy based on what I had in email and upcoming trips.”

I had my first "ewwww" moment with an AI assistant when Instinct started to suggest products that I should buy based on what I had in email and upcoming trips.



– suggested a to-go coffee flask b/c we have a Blue Bottle coffee subscription?

– some travel accessories b/c we have… — Chat Joglekar (@joglekar) September 30, 2026

The trick to making curated suggestions useful is to make sure they’re something the user is actually asking for, or at least fit in naturally within the current conversation. That way, it feels like the assistant is trying to be helpful, not advertising to you.

If the product suggestions are going to arrive at random intervals, as Instinct’s have been, then they need to be highly personalized, excellent picks — otherwise the user will feel like they’ve been spammed.

That’s not likely to endear users to the AI agent at a time when it’s competing agents from bigger companies, like Meta and, now, OpenAI, which don’t do this.

Nice that it is curated and hopefully it’s good but ask me whether I want the recommendations. I just got a random notification for additional equipment based on a future trip which I didn’t ask for and don’t need. Also allow me to curate my own sources as well as the ones you… — Ash Thaker (@ashthaker1) September 29, 2026

Instinct didn’t share whether it’s currently making money from these recommendations or plans to, but the feature seems ripe for some sort of advertising, commerce, or affiliate play.

TechCrunch has asked the company for further comment.

The product suggestions launched shortly after Instinct confirmed its most recent financing, a $1 billion Series C round that values the company at $10 billion. The company has not yet said how many people actually use its product, a figure that would help justify that valuation, but in a recent podcast, Shinn noted that the agent regularly handles transactions for its users.

In that same podcast interview, with investor Patrick O’Shaughnessy, Shinn said the platform is approaching a billion dollars in annual transactions made through the agent, and that more than 50% of them are related to travel.

Tech.title: FedEx orders 2,000 electric trucks from Harbinger in $300M deal
Tech.content:
In Brief

FedEx is ordering 2,000 electric trucks from EV startup Harbinger in a deal worth $300 million. Harbinger, which already has trucks in production, plans to deliver all 2,000 by the end of next year, the company told TechCrunch.

It’s the largest bulk order yet for Harbinger, which was founded in 2022 by former employees of Anduril, defunct EV startup Canoo, and Quantumscape. Bloomberg News first reported the new order Wednesday morning. FedEx led a $160 million Series C funding round for Harbinger late last year.

Harbinger’s pitch since its inception has been to make one main product: an electric medium-duty commercial truck chassis. That simplified approach appears to have paid off, as the company is in production and generating revenue despite being just a few years old. It has already delivered 53 trucks to FedEx as part of an order that the shipping giant placed alongside last year’s fundraise.

That said, Harbinger has started to look at other possible revenue lines. The company is getting into hybrid emergency vehicles, acquired an autonomous driving company in February, and is selling the battery packs it developed as energy storage. The company is also getting into defense use cases. All this comes as Axios reported in May that the company is considering an IPO.

Tech.title: Pledge signed by President Trump and top AI leaders misspells the United States
Tech.content:
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump and top AI leaders announced a signed pledge called a “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” — a voluntary promise to implement more controls and safety measures as the rapid development of artificial intelligence continues.

But there seems to be a catch — namely that the “United States” was misspelled as “Unites States” in a photo of the signed agreement the President shared to Truth Social. The spelling error appears right beneath the president’s signature, though the other signatories and their companies are spelled correctly. Gizmodo reporter Matt Novak was one of the first to point out the snafu, and we’ve reached out to the White House for comment.

The spelling error shows, perhaps, how much time and attention went into drafting the document before it was signed and released to the public. Its announcement came after top AI leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, once again descended upon the White House to talk about advancements in AI. The gathering came just weeks after OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Amodei, and even Elon Musk called for a deceleration of AI advancements, calls that President Trump and Huang rejected. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” the President previously said.

It seems the meet-in-the-middle was this pledge, which mapped out the ways that companies training and deploying frontier models should “ensure that their technology behaves as intended and that any issues are promptly identified and resolved.” This includes tapping an independent board for oversight and implementing internal controls. The pledge is voluntary, and there don’t seem to be any legal or regulatory ramifications if any signee breaks it.

At a press conference after the gathering Tuesday, Zuckerberg called the accord a “start” that the “whole industry could come to,” adding that “it was sort of a historic conversation.”

Via an executive order, the President is also mandating that all government departments and agencies now change their phrasing from “artificial intelligence” to “superintelligence” or “SI.”

Tech.title: Google launches Fitbit Air in India, though its high price might deter the masses
Tech.content:
Google on Wednesday launched the screen-less Fitbit Air fitness tracker in India, but is pricing at ₹13,999 (roughly $146), ostensibly positioning it as a premium device. Comparatively, the device costs $99 in the U.S.

Unveiled in May, the Fitbit Air features health and fitness tracking, like 24/7 heart rate monitoring, heart rhythm monitoring with A-fib (atrial fibrillation) alerts, blood oxygen level, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep stages, and duration.

The device’s screen-less form is a bid to tap into the growing popularity of screen-less devices as people shy away from screens, opting for distraction-free health gadgets like Whoop’s fitness bands and Oura’s rings — though the new Fitbit is more pocket-friendly.

The health tracking space now has screen-less devices from Garmin, Fitbit founders’ new company, Luffu Link, as well as from Indian startups like Noise and Urban, which have been trying to undercut their Western rivals on price.

Research firm IDC noted in its global wearables report that despite a declining number of wristband shipments, screen-less trackers are carving out a niche. Tech.title: Instagram rolls out an AI video assistant for creators
Tech.content:
Instagram announced on Wednesday that it’s bringing an AI video assistant tool to Edits, its CapCut competitor.

This conversational AI chatbot is intended to provide personalized feedback to creators, rather than generic advice.

“The assistant knows your account’s Instagram metrics, things like follows, views, video retention, likes, shares and combines them with your comments, what’s trending on Instagram and what your audience is into,” Brett Westervelt, who leads the Edits app, said. “It can spot patterns in your performance over time and surface actionable insights that are hard to see from the metrics alone.”

Westervelt added that Edits worked closely with a group of creators in developing the tool.

“One thing we heard consistently: creators want a tool that handles the analysis, not one that does the creative work for them,” he wrote. “Edits assistant does the digging for you. The creative calls are still yours.”

Image Credits:Instagram

Meta first previewed the Edits AI assistant in June at an invite-only creator event, where it also said it was working on an Edits desktop app. It’s not the only company working on tools like this, though. YouTube announced last week that it is also working on a conversational video editing tool, which should be available early next year.

From what we can tell so far, it looks like Meta is taking a more analytics-driven approach with its AI assistant than YouTube, which suggested creators would use its AI to help with the actual editing process.

Creators will have a limit to how much they can use the AI tool, but they can unlock more usage with a Meta One subscription.

Tech.title: A Biotech Founder Makes the Moral Case for Gene-Editing Human Embryos
Tech.content:
When the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced in 2018 that he had created the first gene-edited babies, the experiment was widely condemned as reckless and premature. It ended with He in prison.

But that hasn’t stopped the push for gene-edited human embryos, with biotech entrepreneur Cathy Tie arguing that doing so isn’t just urgent—it’s a “moral imperative.”

Tie is the 30-year-old founder of Origin Genomics, a company that launched in March with plans to bring gene-edited embryos to IVF clinics. In a new commentary published in the journal Trends in Genetics, she argues for public funding and new regulatory pathways to advance gene-edited babies and eventually move into clinical use.

But questions remain about what evidence researchers will need to determine whether gene-edited embryos are safe enough to attempt a human pregnancy—and what risks might remain for the resulting children.

“There are cautionary tales of first human trials where there was really no flashing red light, and people died,” says Hank Greely, a law professor and director of the Center for Law and the Biosciences at Stanford University.

So-called germ-line gene editing involves modifying cells involved in human reproduction, like embryos. Any changes made could be passed on to future generations. That could mean, for example, correcting a devastating genetic mutation for good. But accidental DNA edits elsewhere, known as “off-target effects,” could introduce new health risks that could also be passed down. Those high stakes are part of why dozens of countries have banned gene-editing of human embryos intended for pregnancy.

People at risk of passing a genetic disease on to their children can use IVF combined with genetic screening to identify disease-free embryos before transfer to the womb. Critics of embryo editing argue that screening tools make the need for it very small. Gene-editing embryos, Greely says, would be helping “a fraction of a fraction of a fraction.”

The drawback of the current approach is that IVF is inefficient; viable embryos can be hard to come by, even for people without an inherited disease risk. Ian Watts and Cheyenne Ziegler, for example, underwent three rounds of IVF in their attempt to have children that do not carry the genetic variant responsible for Watts’ Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, a degenerative neurological disorder that impacts fine motor skills and mobility. With any IVF cycle, eggs regularly don’t fertilize, and those that do often stall in development or have chromosomal abnormalities. Adding additional screening for disease means that some viable embryos also don’t make the cut.

In Watts and Ziegler’s case, three rounds of IVF have produced eight chromosomally normal embryos, but only three without Watts’ variant. Those three embryos are likely not enough to give the couple the three or four children they hope to have one day.

“The choices currently available are either not having children or doing lots of IVF,” says Watts, a 36-year-old engineer in Long Beach, California. Gene editing could give people like him more chances at a future family. It could also help couples in the extremely rare situation where every embryo would inherit a disease-causing mutation, such as partners who each have two copies of a harmful variant.

“We’re here to treat these diseases, not just exclude embryos and call it a day,” says Tie, a former Thiel fellow who’s alluded to herself as “biotech Barbie.”

The invention of CRISPR raised the possibility of gene-edited babies more than a decade ago, and newer forms of gene editing offer increasing precision. In June, researchers at Columbia University revealed that they had edited early-stage human embryos using a technique called base editing with incredible accuracy. Tie cites this work in her commentary, arguing that precision editing is now well within reach.

Tech.title: The Best Gaming Routers (2026): Tested By a Family of Gamers
Tech.content:
Few things are more frustrating than packet loss or high ping causing in-game lag. It always seems to happen at the worst possible moment, when you’re about to snipe an unsuspecting opponent or screech into a hairpin bend. While there are other potential causes, your substandard router could be doing you dirty. The best gaming routers promise rock solid connections and can usually prioritize game-related traffic to reduce the risk of issues. They also frequently feature fancy designs and customizable lighting to fit your gaming room.

Now, you don’t necessarily need a special gaming router. A good router is a good router, and you’ll find tons of them in my guides to the Best Routers and Best Mesh Systems. You can also get a better connection simply by running an Ethernet cable from your router to your gaming PC. That said, I have tested several gaming routers, and my top pick is the fastest router I have ever tested.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Best Asus Gaming Routers

The brand I recommend as the best for gamers is Asus. The Taiwanese company has a long gaming history and dedicated sub-brands like Republic of Gamers (ROG). It produces fast, highly configurable routers with free security software and many gaming extras. Ports are usually generous, there’s no need for a subscription, and you can combine different Asus routers that support AiMesh into a mesh system to extend your coverage. The potential downsides are the relatively high prices, occasionally buggy firmware, and the need to dig into configuration settings to get the best performance.

Best Gaming Router

Topping my testing charts, the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BE98 Pro is a supremely capable, quad-band Wi-Fi 7 gaming router. In terms of raw speed, this is the best router I have tested to date. That alone makes it feel worthy of the “gimmick” of being designed explicitly for gaming. It is very similar to the RT-BE96U in my regular router guide, but with the ROG model, Asus has added a second 6-GHz band on top of the existing 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands. This massively increases the available bandwidth, affording you plenty of space for multiple gaming streams, or giving you an extra band for wireless backhaul if you decide to set up a mesh using Asus’ AiMesh connectivity. It also has an extra 10-Gbps LAN port, giving you one 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, two 10-Gbps LAN, four Gigabit LAN, one USB 3.2, and a USB 2.0 port. The USB ports come in handy for NAS devices. You must pay extra for these additions, so if you don’t have multiple gaming streams or a NAS, you can save money with the RT-BE96U and still get great performance.

This is also easily the biggest router I have ever tested at nearly 14 inches across, with eight huge antennas, and it weighs 4.4 pounds. It is far from subtle, won’t blend in, and could prove tricky to place due to its size. Because it’s a gaming router, Asus has included Aura RGB lighting, so you can pick the colored lighting you want and make it a feature.

AiProtection Pro security software and parental controls, powered by Trend Micro, are bundled into the cost. This comprehensive security combo includes a firewall, intrusion prevention, malicious site blocking, automatic updates, and more. Parental controls include scheduling, website filtering by age, and usage stats. You also get VPN support with the option to connect remotely when you are out and about. You can redeem a free year of NordVPN service with this router. Naturally, there are some gaming-focused features, with game acceleration enabling you to prioritize gaming-related traffic through ports and packet analysis. If you have Asus’ ROG gear, it can be prioritized with a click, and Asus includes server acceleration to minimize latency through the third-party WTFast service.

Apart from the size and cost, there isn’t much to complain about here, but it is worth considering that the range on the 6-GHz band is limited and struggles to penetrate through walls, so you will need Wi-Fi 7 devices nearby to take full advantage of this router. Ideally, have it in the same room as your gaming PC or laptop. This router was originally touted to get Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) support, but it never did (look at the next pick if that’s something you want).

Asus ROG Strix GS-BE12000 for $400: If you don’t want to spend as much, but you’re set on a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router, and you want lots of ports, this model could make sense. I found it stable and seriously speedy on the 6-GHz and 5-GHz bands. It boasts 320 MHz channels on the 6-GHz band, Multi-Link Operation (MLO), and 4K-QAM (read my How to Buy a Router and Wi-Fi 7 guides for a breakdown on these terms). It has a 2.5 Gbps WAN and seven 2.5 Gbps LAN ports, two of which are dedicated gaming ports, and a USB 3.2 Gen 1 port. You get mostly the same excellent software and gaming options as my top pick. This is a scaled down version of the BE18000 ($530), and has 2 x 2 MIMO on the 6-GHz band instead of 4 x 4, but I think it’s a better buy for most folks, especially if you see it on sale. It’s worth noting that both models have official Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) support, which extends the range of the 6-GHz band to make it more comparable to the 5-GHz band range. I can’t test this here in the UK, as it’s only available in North America and requires your precise real-world location so local regulators can authorize it.

Asus TUF Gaming BE9400 for $265: The cheaper end of Asus gaming routers, this model is still a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router, and it doesn’t make too many compromises. It has one 2.5 Gbps WAN, three 2.5 Gbps LAN ports, and a USB 3.2 Gen 1 port. You miss out on some ROG-exclusive gaming features, the design is not as nice, and it lacks RGB lighting. But this router performed far better than the price would suggest, keeping pace with my top pick at close range, though coverage doesn’t extend as far.

Tech.title: Black Twitter Is Thriving—on Threads
Tech.content:
Last week, after a Mississippi grand jury declined to bring criminal charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the 18-year-old Black college student who disappeared on Horn Island while traveling with a group of white friends and was later found dead, Black users on Threads demanded justice.

“Just so it’s abundantly clear: The state of Mississippi is covering up the murder of Nolan Wells,” user @_taexoxo posted two days after the September 21 decision. The case has incited racial tensions nationwide.

“This year a grand jury handed down an indictment for a pool of water turning green, but didn’t indict when a black kid was found floating face down in water!” commented comedian D.L. Hughley.

Black Americans have never shied away from calling out America’s racial hypocrisies—Twitter served as an indispensable tool as the Black Lives Matter movement swelled in the 2020s—but the chatter on Threads was uniquely charged for Wells. It was the latest bit of evidence showing that the platform has emerged as a vital artery of the Black social media ecosystem, at times even rivaling the influence Black Twitter once personified.

In 2021, when I first explored the cultural expansiveness of Black Twitter, I wrote that it was “all the things: news and analysis, call and response, judge and jury—a comedy showcase, therapy session, and family cookout all in one.” Five years later, Threads is proving to be its spiritual successor, a robust digital universe where no conversation, no matter how ugly or awkward, is off limits.

Tech.title: How Israeli Checkpoints Choke Palestinian Life in the Occupied West Bank
Tech.content:
Some nights, he doesn't get home at all. He sleeps at the factory, in an arrangement Sama built during Covid-19: Two offices hold a bed and a dozen mattresses for whoever can’t make the trip home.

After October 2023, delay times at checkpoints across Nablus spiked to levels beyond anywhere else in the West Bank. Commuters in Nablus spent an average of nearly an hour and 50 minutes avoiding checkpoints. Ali Haj Ali has worked at Sama Pharmaceuticals, a medicine factory east of Nablus city, for over a decade; now, at 37, he supervises the maintenance of the company’s production lines. When he leaves at the end of his shift at 4:30 pm, he has stopped expecting to reach his home before 8:00 pm, even though it’s only 16 kilometers away.

"Nothing is guaranteed, that's just how it is here. It's like a lottery," Ali said.

On a recent afternoon, Ali sat in a room at Sama Pharmaceuticals, along with his colleague, Ohood Khatatbeh. In minutes, they were filling in the details for one another, recounting what they call “Nablus’ checkpoint crisis” in 2024 and 2025. Ali would sometimes reach the checkpoint, sit there for hours, then just turn around and go home.

“My three kids, my wife, my mother, my father, I’d barely see them,” he said. “And forget about seeing friends.” But this is the best job he thinks he can find, so he keeps going.

Ohood, the factory’s quality assurance manager, is 38 years old, and the mother of three sons. Her town, Beit Furik, is southeast of Nablus. It has a single gate, in or out. Her whole day is dictated by that gate.

The town has had to come up with its own protocol, as Ohood calls it: For every three private cars, one shared taxi gets through. What they cannot control is the pace, interrupted by the soldiers’ change of shifts.

Best case, if the Beit Furik gate is open and traffic is moving freely, the drive home can take 15 minutes. But for a year and a half, it routinely took her more than 5 hours daily. On the worst day, it took 10 hours. In 2024, Ohood's teenage son had finished a final exam in biology at his school in Nablus just before she was finishing her shift. They found each other at the Beit Furik gate at 4:30 pm, in a line that packed the road several cars wide, all heading for the single entrance to a town of almost 16,000.

Ohood and her son waited in line together until 3 am the following morning.

"The regular employee, the one not separated from work by a checkpoint," she said, "would be home, eaten, showered, asleep, and already dreaming, while I'm still at the checkpoint."

Across the West Bank, checkpoints have begun to reshape how businesses like Sama operate. The company has started rejecting highly qualified candidates after assessing the checkpoints they would have to cross to get to work, Ohood said. It’s even started writing it into the job postings, as a requirement: Candidates must live in Nablus. About half of people polled said checkpoints have impacted their or their spouse’s ability to get a job.

In late 2025, Ohood’s one-week-old baby, Aws, came down with jaundice. She and her husband drove him out of town to the hospital. But on the way back, as she remembers it, they found the soldier already closing the gate.

"Go back," the soldier yelled in Arabic from the other side of the gate in Beit Furik.

"Go back where?" her husband asked. "We have a sick child with us."

The soldier raised his rifle and pointed it toward them. "For God's sake," Ohood told her husband, "let's just go back." He tried once more anyway, offering to turn around himself if the soldier would just let Ohood and the baby cross the gate on foot. The soldier lost his temper. "I'll shoot you," he said.

They turned around, the baby crying in their arms, and waited in line for an hour and a half until the soldier opened the gate again.

Tech.title: The 6 Best Laptop Docking Stations to Unlock the Full Desktop Experience (2026)
Tech.content:
Other Laptop Docking Stations to Consider

We test a lot of laptop docking stations and, quite frankly, most of them are … fine. They're fine! We get into the nitty-gritty for specific use cases to find the best, but that leaves a bunch of devices that are great options even if they don't make our top picks. Here's a selection of some of our favorites, past favorites, or just alternatives to our picks above.

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Baseus Spacemate Air 12-in-1 Mac Docking Station for $200: This is a really great budget option to the Plugable 5-Display USB-C dock above. While that one offers a faster and more full-featured way to get extra external displays, the Spacemate Air 12-in-1 gives you two 4K displays. That's especially helpful if you own an older MacBook Air or just appreciate the ease of use of connecting all your peripherals, displays, and accessories over a single USB-C cable. But I don't love the integrated cable; there are no card slots, and some of the USB ports aren't very fast.

Belkin Connect Pro Thunderbolt 4 Dock for $300: This one is a bit expensive for a Thunderbolt 4 dock, but it gets you 12 ports, including support for up to two 4K displays at 60 Hz and 90 watts of power delivery to your laptop. Like the Spacemate Air, it also includes some slower USB-A ports, though.

Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Slim Pro Hub for $200: Sometimes, simpler is better. This docking station from Satechi is small, made of sturdy aluminum, and comes with just three Thunderbolt 4 ports on the rear, each of which is capable of up to 40 Gbps. Nothing else. This layout is surprisingly clean, with only a few cables coming out of the back, and one running to your laptop. If all you need is to connect to a couple of monitors or high-speed data storage and you like to keep your desk free of clutter, this is a great option. —Eric Ravenscraft

Satechi Triple 4K Docking Station Photograph: Eric Ravenscraft

Satechi Triple 4K Docking Station for $300: Satechi's Triple 4K Docking Station supports three monitors, and while the first display output is HDMI-only, the two others can be connected via either HDMI or DisplayPort. Each display supports up to 4K resolution at 60 Hz, which is more than enough for most office or media work, though don't expect it to support the high frame rates you might want for gaming. —Eric Ravenscraft

Kensington Triple Video Mobile Dock for $90: A mobile docking station might sound like a contradiction, but in the case of the tiny Kensington Triple Video Mobile Dock, it makes a lot of sense. Using the included two HDMI ports and the DisplayPort, this little device can power three 1080p displays or two 4K displays—all at 60 Hz. It also has a USB-C port with 85 watts of pass-through charging, which is enough to charge most laptops. The downside is that it only supports a single 4K monitor on MacBooks, as the dual 4K support is only for Windows devices.

Satechi Dual Docking Station and Stand for $170: It's tough for laptop docking stations to stand out—most of them are simple boxes that add extra ports to your laptop—but Satechi's Dual Docking Station and Stand breaks the mold. It sits neatly under your laptop and elevates it slightly, putting it at an angle that has better ergonomics. A collection of three USB ports and three monitor output ports on the rear are conveniently placed so your desktop setup can stay connected while cables are tucked out of the way. A hardware switch on the back lets you turn the dock on or off. There's also a small strip of rubber on top and a built-in NVMe solid-state drive. While no SSD is included, you can plug in your own (something like this will work) to give your dock storage to offload files from your laptop.—Eric Ravenscraft

Sonnet Echo 13 Thunderbolt 5 Dock Courtesy of Luke Larsen

Sonnet Echo 13 Thunderbolt 5 Dock for $460: Sonnettech’s Echo 13 was one of the first Thunderbolt 5 docks out on the market. As it turns out, it's also one of the most unique offerings out there, including just about every port imaginable as well as an integrated M.2 storage slot with a Kingston SSD inside. While handy, I don't like that the drive isn't user accessible. The cheap plastic chassis is disappointing for the price, too.

Ivanky FusionDock Max 1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station for $330: It's hard to overstate how excessively luxurious this dock is. It's specifically for MacBook Pro users and can tackle up to four 6K screens, something only recent MacBook Pros support. The Ivanky FusionDock Max 1 accomplishes this via four USB-C Thunderbolt 4 ports, each capable of 40 Gbps data transfer speeds. If you're building the beefiest media workstation you can for the most powerful MacBook Pros on the market, this is it. Just put it on the company card, because it's expensive. —Eric Ravenscraft

Ugreen Revodok Max 213 Thunderbolt 4 for $300: Few people need an 8K display—or multiple 4K displays—but those who do know how difficult it can be to find gear that supports one. Fortunately, the Revodok Max 213 from Ugreen fits that bill. The DisplayPort 1.4 port can handle up to an 8K display at 30 Hz. It also comes with a Thunderbolt 4 upstream port that runs to your laptop, and, more importantly, a pair of downstream Thunderbolt 4 ports, which is another rarity among the docks I've tested. If you need to transfer a ton of media from various sources into one machine, connected to seriously high-res displays, this is the dock that can handle it all. —Eric Ravenscraft

Do You Need a Docking Station or a USB Hub? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron This is the big question you'll want to answer before moving forward. Chances are you know if you need a full-on docking station rather than just a USB hub, but I'll explain the differences in case you're on the fence. A simple USB hub will handle most people's needs, as it will expand the potentially very limited ports of your laptop. If you own a MacBook Air, for example, a USB hub functions as a multiport adapter to get you HDMI, USB-A, and more. They're intended to be portable, and many of these hubs even include HDMI to connect an external display. A laptop docking station will do quite a lot more. These devices are meant to be stationary on a desk, enabling you to access your entire workstation setup with just a single USB-C cable. The docking station is meant to stay put and have all your monitors and accessories plugged into it. Because of that, they require significantly more power and are often bundled with a large power brick. They are often quite expensive. So, while both accessories connect your laptop to more ports, they serve two different functions. There are now lots of docks and hubs that blur the lines, offering multi-monitor support in a very small package. These can be useful, but a full docking station will still give you the fastest transfer speeds, the most ports, and better external display support all through a single cable. What Ports Should Your Docking Station Have? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Figuring out the right connections you need for your setup can be daunting, and the confusing, arcane USB terminology only makes it worse. You can check out our explainer on parsing USB terms here. For the short version, here are the basics you should keep in mind: Check your ports' speeds, and don't rely on version numbers. For a lot of confusing reasons, ports labeled as USB 3.0, 3.1, and 3.2 can all have the same speed or wildly different speeds. For this reason, docking station manufacturers have recently started opting to add speeds (usually written like “5 Gbps”) directly onto individual ports. Use the faster ports for transferring data, and slower ports for things like your keyboard and mouse. Thunderbolt is best for lightning-fast data transfers or high-res displays. Thunderbolt is like a supercharged version of USB, and it even uses USB-C ports. However, Thunderbolt ports are also capable of transferring massive amounts of data. This makes it ideal for tasks like moving uncompressed video files around, as well as 4K (or even 8K) displays or lower-resolution monitors with extra high refresh rates. Keep in mind your power needs. Most laptop docking stations will have some form of power connector and USB Power Delivery (or USB-PD) that can send power through to your laptop. You'll also sometimes see this referred to as “pass-through charging.” Most devices you connect will require their own power as well, especially if you want to connect monitors or charge your phone and tablet. If you plan to connect a lot of power-hungry devices, make sure your docking station can handle your needs. Upstream and downstream ports. You'll often see USB ports labeled either as upstream or downstream. The data either flows up to the source (your PC or docking station) or down from the source. An upstream USB port means it's meant for transferring data from a peripheral (like an external drive) to your PC, whereas a downstream USB port only works in the opposite direction. Mac-Compatible Docks AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron All the docks in our recommendations are compatible with both Mac and Windows, unless otherwise noted. But there are lots of hubs and docks out there that have certain limitations on Mac, such as only supporting mirroring mode in dual monitors. That's not a problem on Windows. On lower-end Macs, there is a limitation on the number of screens. There is a way around this if you use a dock that supports DisplayLink. This software can create a “virtual GPU” that tricks the system into allowing for additional displays so you can drive more displays than are typically allowed on a MacBook Air, for example. In my experience, however, the performance can be shoddy, and you may run into issues with latency. Is Thunderbolt 5 Worth It? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The first Thunderbolt 5-capable PCs, docks, and accessories came out in 2024. Thunderbolt 5 can now handle three 4K displays at 144 Hz (or two 4K displays at 240 Hz) and can deliver up to 240 watts of power. That's dramatic, up from the 100 watts of Thunderbolt 4. Thunderbolt 5 allows you to fully juice up more powerful devices, such as gaming laptops or the 16-inch M4 Max MacBook Pro. Thunderbolt 5 docks are all backward compatible, so there's no worry about outdoing the peripherals you currently own. As is true in many scenarios, buying the latest specs is often worth it to avoid having to upgrade later. However, the adoption of Thunderbolt 5 has been slower than I'd hoped. And if you don't have a Thunderbolt 5 laptop to connect to, you won't get the full benefit that Thunderbolt 5 offers. While there's a breadth of Thunderbolt 5 docks out in the world (many of which you'll see on this list), the biggest disappointment has been in the lack of Thunderbolt 5 accessories. It's still very difficult, for example, to find a Thunderbolt 5 SSD to achieve those faster speeds. Thunderbolt 5 docks are sometimes only marginally more expensive than previous-generation options, so they're often worth buying for the improved display support or higher power delivery. For example, CalDigit's TS5 is only $20 more than the TS4.
