Tech.title: Can Air Purifiers Clear Wildfire Smoke From Your Home? What Our Lab Data Reveals
Tech.content:
On the morning of June 7, 2023, I walked out of my Brooklyn apartment and noticed the skies were hazier than usual, but I chalked it up to a change in weather and headed to work. When I arrived at my Manhattan office that overlooked the Hudson River, though, I knew this was something very different.

On a normal day, I’d have a clear view of New Jersey on the other side of the water, but on this day, it was merely a blur. As I inspected the thick fog, it dawned on me: This wasn’t fog at all. It was smoke from wildfires that were raging in Canada. The air quality monitor on my phone’s weather app confirmed it.

Although there was a thick plume of smoke over the city, I could still see the blue skies peeking through, so I continued to work. But by the end of the day, the sky had turned completely dark with an ominous orange tint. This experience was a first for me, so I was alarmed about having to go back outside to return home, and I wasn’t alone, as people in my office began passing out dust masks. I wasn’t sure if they’d help much, but I took one just in case.

More from CNET

Even in the subway system, the smell of smoke was undeniable. I made it home, took my dog for the shortest walk possible, then immediately went inside, opened my laptop and ordered an air purifier. I’ve had one running ever since.

The view from my office window in the morning, left, and the view from the same window at the end of the workday, right. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

A perfect storm

Although the smoke cleared relatively quickly, and the New York skyline bounced back after two days, not every area is as lucky. Texas and the West Coast are particularly vulnerable to these recurring disasters due to their dry climates and the intensifying effects of climate change. Similarly, the 2023 Canadian wildfires occurred during the country’s driest period since 1980, according to NASA.

Data from the National Interagency Fire Center underscores the increasing threat of wildfires. There were 64,897 wildfires in 2024, a sharp increase compared with 77,850 in 2025. Rising temperatures, reduced rainfall and earlier snowmelt around the world create the ideal setting for wildfires to run rampant.

These types of statistics can feel overwhelming, and while you largely can’t stop a wildfire from happening, you do have control over the air you breathe indoors. To see if air purifiers can make your home’s air safer and cleaner during wildfire season, we tested more than a dozen models to find out.

Key takeaways:

According to our exclusive lab data, air purifiers can help clear smoke from a home, but some do significantly better than others.

After testing 18 air purifiers, the Coway 450 was the best overall in our 2026 tests. It had the best overall average results in our particle-removal test and received an Editors’ Choice award.

The Coway 400S was selected as the best air purifier for wildfire smoke because it cleared T90 fine particles in 39 seconds on high fan, earning it a CNET Lab Test award for that performance.

Best Air Purifiers of 2026 See at CNET

What our testing revealed

To conduct our particle-removal tests at our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, our technicians built a custom smoke chamber to test how quickly an air purifier can remove particulate matter from the air. They created a homemade smoke bomb made from potassium nitrate (KNO3), sucrose (sugar) and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), then placed it in the smoke chamber along with the unit being tested and a particle counter.

This test showcases how well each air purifier works at clearing both coarse and fine particles. When determining which unit is best for wildfire smoke, we paid close attention to the fine-particle result, since, according to AirNow, “approximately 90% of total particle mass emitted from wildfires consists of fine particles.”

Fine particles are also the most detrimental to human health because they are tiny, less than or equal to 2.5 microns, so when they are inhaled, they can embed deep into your lungs and cause numerous health issues.

Our lab data revealed that two Coway air purifiers and one Dreame air purifier especially excelled at clearing fine particles.

The Coway 400S is our top pick for clearing smoke from your home because of its exceptional performance at high fan speed. In our 2026 test, it cleared T90 (the time it took for 90% of particles to be removed) fine particles on high fan in just 39 seconds.

The Coway 450, CNET’s choice for best overall air purifier of 2026, was close to matching the 400S’s performance on high fan, but outperformed it on low fan, taking 1 minute and 53 seconds to remove T90 fine particles.

However, the Dreame Furcatch was the top performer in terms of low fan performance. It cleared T90 fine particles on low fan in 1 minute and 24 seconds, winning a CNET Lab Test award in the process. But it did not perform nearly as well as the Coway options above when set to high fan.

While all three models are great options for different reasons, your choice ultimately depends on how you plan to use the air purifier.

If you need quick bursts at high fan speed in the event of sudden smoke, go with the Coway 400S. If you prefer a unit that does particularly well on low fan and you plan to always keep it on that setting, opt for the Dreame Furcatch. For the most consistent performance at both high and low fan speeds, the Coway 450 is the best option.

In addition to our particle-removal tests, we also tested energy usage and loudness. The Dyson HushJet earned two CNET Lab Test awards for being the quietest and most energy-efficient option on our list.

From left to right, the Dreame Furcatch, the Coway 450 and the Levoit 200S-P, three winners from our 2026 air purifier testing. Zooey Liao/CNET/Coway/Dreame/Levoit

Air purifier use in real life

CNET’s wellness editor, Anna Gragert, has experienced wildfires firsthand. In 2025, California’s Eaton Fire forced her to evacuate her apartment, but luckily, it stopped five miles short of her home.

“Despite taping up our window seams before deciding to evacuate, we returned to an apartment that smelled of smoke, and everything was covered in a thin layer of ash,” Gragert says. “We relied on two air purifiers to filter the air and remove the smoke smell, and wouldn’t have been able to comfortably live in our apartment without them after experiencing a wildfire so close to home.”

While an air purifier won’t protect your home from a wildfire and you should always pay close attention to evacuation orders in your area, it can provide an important line of defense if smoke hits your city so you can breathe easier, both figuratively and literally.

Tech.title: I Visited Lightship’s AE.1 EV Travel Trailer, and Now I Want to Take an Off-the-Grid Road Trip
Tech.content:
I’m approaching the age where I’m supposed to start desiring RV life. I’m not planning to retire anytime soon, but the older I get, the more appealing the idea of abandoning yard work, home repairs and geographic permanence for a life on the open road in a big old house on wheels becomes. My neighbors have an RV they park in the space between our houses, keeping both a permanent location and a home they can travel in; they still have yard work and house repairs, but few complaints.

So it was with some curiosity that I visited a pop-up for Lightship, a Colorado company making EV trailers for RV enthusiasts, outside the flagship Yeti outdoor-recreation store in Austin, Texas. The company’s eye-catching AE.1 trailer was parked and open to the public. (AE.1 refers to Aero-Electric 1.)

The Lightship AE.1 includes lots of modern design touches, like a kitchen area with a two-burner stove, a fridge and freezer, microwave and a hidden compact dishwasher. Omar L. Gallaga for CNET

Lightship staffers handed out brochures, stickers and pins to visitors who climbed into the trailer, some of whom seemed surprised by the sleek, air-conditioned interior. The demo model boasted a cushioned lounge area, appliances including a hideaway dishwasher, microwave, full sink and stovetop, a full bathroom and shower area, and plenty of storage. It can sleep up to six.

More from CNET

The selling point of the highly customizable AE.1, which starts at $157,500, is that it offers a more modern design than most RVs and trailers. It includes thoughtful design touches and an electric-powered motor called TrekDrive that kicks in when in motion to lighten the load on whatever’s pulling the trailer. If it’s an EV truck or SUV, that could significantly extend the range between charges.

Pushing back on decades of RV design

Ben Parker, Lightship’s co-founder and chief product officer, worked at Tesla in California as a battery engineer and was inspired while traveling in an RV during the pandemic. Parker started the company with Toby Krauss, another former Tesla employee who worked in finance and product management and serves as Lightship’s CEO.

Parker said there’s a gigantic market of Americans who want to travel in camper RVs, but their options have been limited to a few highly consolidated manufacturers offering unchanging designs. So far, he said, customers interested in Lightship are a mix of EV owners and longtime enthusiasts who want “greater capacity, comfort and independence.”

“Our customers are people who love spending time outdoors and want more freedom in how they travel,” Parker said.

Ben Parker, chief product officer and co-founder of Lightship, stands next to the company’s AE.1 EV camper trailer at a pop-up event in Austin, Texas on Sept. 26, 2026. Omar L. Gallaga for CNET

The AE.1’s most notable design feature is that it compresses from a 10-foot-tall Camp Mode with lots of windows and headroom to a Road Mode that lowers the roof to under 7 feet, making the AE.1 more aerodynamic in motion. Most of the trailer’s features, from the lighting to extras like an auto-leveling system and a motorized awning, are controlled by an app. A solar array on the trailer’s roof helps keep power flowing.

If you limit your A/C and power use, the AE.1 can last for about a week off the grid before it needs additional charging, Parker said. The AE.1 has hookups for EV charging as well as the kind of 220-volt hookups found at RV parks. It can hook up to external devices with vehicle-to-load power capabilities.

Some of the more interesting option features include a pull-down bed that attaches to the trailer’s ceiling and a setup for a 4K video projector that can be mounted inside the trailer for viewing on a pull-down screen.

“The demand we’ve seen reflects a broader appetite for innovation in the RV space,” Parker said. “Customers are excited by the idea of an RV that combines modern technology, energy independence and a dramatically improved towing experience in a single product.”

The co-founder said his company wants the buying and using experience of an AE.1 to wow customers enough for Lightship to gain a foothold in a market that’s not very open to newcomers.

“Breaking into any established industry requires earning trust,” he said. “We’ve focused on building a high-quality product that solves real customer pain points and delivering an experience that people can immediately appreciate once they see it and use it for themselves.”

New trailer players

Lightship is headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado. It’s expanding its manufacturing center there to accommodate additional trailer production, as well as production of a carriage-minus-trailer product called PowerSled, which it’s been selling to businesses like movie productions that need a mobile platform with electric power.

Lightship’s mission to disrupt the RV market is not unlike that of another company, Pebble, that has also been making EV trailers in California.

Parker said the main difference between Lightship and Pebble is that Lightship is sourcing more of its materials domestically. Parker estimates that about 75% of the materials used to make an AE.1 are sourced domestically, and all assembly is done in-house.

Pebble, however, is undercutting Lightship on price. Lightship originally planned to offer a lower-priced $125,000 base model without the self-propelled TrekDrive motor. However, the company has since changed its strategy, moving to a single standard base price with a standard 77 kWh battery and various add-on options and upgrades.

Possible retirement plans

For me, a non-RV person, the AE.1 feels design-forward and includes features like a built-in auto-hitch, an auto-leveler, and lots of charging ports and stations, all of which appeal to someone like me who has no idea what they’re doing. The interior feels spacious, but not so much that it makes the exterior look oversized. The ability to shrink down to a smaller size — the AE.1 performs safety checks before compressing to ensure windows aren’t open and nothing will break — brings the wow factor.

It doesn’t take much time in the trailer to imagine traveling in it and using Lightship’s trailer as a mobile workstation (satellite internet service is not included, but it can be hooked up).

The AE.1 isn’t cheap, but it might be worth putting on the retirement wish list. You will still have to wait: the company’s waitlist for delivery is currently about a year long.

Lightship began shipping AE.1 trailers last year and said it’s producing about 30 per month for the rest of this year. By sometime in 2027, with its expanded factory floor, it plans to ramp that up to 40 per month.

If you want to check out the AE.1 for yourself, the company maintains showrooms north of Denver and in San Francisco and will host a pop-up event in Las Vegas in late November.

Tech.title: Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Simplifies Streaming Options, and I Went Hands-On
Tech.content:
Amazon has unveiled a new Fire TV Stick 4K as part of a simplified lineup for the popular streamers, and it has 4K HDR10 playback.

The $60 Fire TV Stick 4K, which replaces both the Fire TV Stick 4K Select and 4K Plus, comes with a new remote and support for HDR10 and Samsung’s HDR10 Plus. It has 8GB internal storage, a quad-core 1.7 GHz processor and support for Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3 and Bluetooth Low Energy. The company says the Stick 4K is 20% to 40% faster than the similarly priced Roku Streaming Stick Plus.

While it’s not consequential, as it’s going to spend all of its time behind your TV, the Fire TV Stick 4K feels solid in the hand. It seems much more luxe than any other Fire TV Stick I’ve ever used. The device comes with a USB cable, and it no longer needs to be plugged into the wall; it can be powered by your TV’s USB port.

More from CNET

The new remote no longer has a dedicated Alexa button.

I found the “upgraded” experience extends to the redesigned remote, which, unusually, no longer includes a prominent blue Alexa button. Instead, the most obvious button features a bright red home icon, and the microphone is now relegated to the top right.

Amazon also said that a new premium remote is coming in 2027, which features backlighting and a “find my remote” feature.

The streaming device is designed to be used in conjunction with Alexa Plus, and one impressive feature the representatives showed me was the forthcoming ability to plug articles into the app. They showed me how to load a “10 best movies about…” article into the Fire TV app and have the TV add the movies listed to a watch-next list.

The Fire TV Stick 4K home screen Ty Pendlebury/CNET

In general, the setup and use of the Fire TV Stick 4K felt very familiar, but since it was fresh out of the box, I didn’t notice any blazing speeds. This will likely improve over time as the device learns the apps I use most.

The best part about the Fire TV Stick 4K’s release, however, is the simplification of the range for buyers, and this stick should now be the go-to device for most people. Enthusiasts who want to make the most of their home cinema should get the $85 4K Max model for Dolby Vision and Atmos, or support for add-on speakers via Alexa Home Theater.

The range is now just four main devices:

Fire TV Stick HD $40

Fire TV Stick 4K $60

Fire TV Stick 4K Max $85

Fire TV Cube $199

The Fire TV Stick 4K is available now for an introductory price of $30, and this will likely continue until Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week.

Tech.title: This Might Be the Only Hair Straightening Tool You Need
Tech.content:
CNET’s key takeaways

The Bluvol I11 Apex cordless hair straightening comb retails for $90.

The I11 Apex is a perfect travel companion for easy touch-ups.

You’ll get up to 45 minutes of styling per charge.

After more than 10 years of wearing my natural curls, I started straightening my hair again. I spent countless hours searching for the best tools and products that would deliver sleek, frizz-free results while protecting my hair from heat damage. The Tymo Ring hair straightening brush stood out to me, and it’s been a good addition to my hair care kit. However, it may have just been replaced by the Bluvol I11 Apex cordless straightening comb.

When the Bluvol I11 Apex arrived, I wasn’t expecting much. I figured it would be good for the occasional touch-up on travel days or even quick fixes if I ever got caught in the rain, but it proved me wrong. It’s lightweight and fits nicely in the hand. From holding it, you can tell it’s well-made. I just couldn’t imagine that something that compact could pack so much heat.

What the Bluvol I11 Apex looks like straight out of the box.

Putting the Bluvol I11 Apex to the test

To really put the Bluvol I11 Apex to the test, I enlisted my cousin’s help. She’s Gen Z, an expert at all things hair and nails, and most importantly, she has an amazing, thick head of hair. After unboxing the straightening comb, I charged it, and we got started.

More from CNET

It has three heat settings: 320, 365 and 410 degrees Fahrenheit. There’s an LCD screen, which shows the temperature and battery percentage. Switching to a lower or higher setting is simple, using the power button. Once you’ve chosen your temperature, the display will blink as the comb heats up. When it stops blinking, you’re ready to go.

On the first pass, we were impressed with how effortlessly it took my cousin’s hair from curly to straight. The I11 Apex has upgraded ceramic glazed plates throughout the teeth of the comb, which prevent singes and allow multiple passes without damage. Its wide heating area provides even heat distribution for consistent coverage across strands.

Bluvol says the straightener releases “200 million negative ions to smooth hair and reduce static and frizz.” While I can’t test that accurately, I can attest that it left her hair far smoother than a similar flat iron and required fewer passes to achieve the desired results.

The results on curly hair.

Battery life and charging time

Bluvol includes a charging cable and suggests using a 15-watt or higher adapter when powering up. With the adapter, you’ll go from zero to a full charge in about 2.5 hours. A full charge will give you up to 45 minutes of styling time. We managed to make it about 80% of the way through her hair before needing to recharge.

Who’s the Bluvol I11 Apex for?

This is by far the most impressive cordless straightener I’ve tested, but it might not be for everyone. For folks with shorter hair, this won’t be ideal because the layout of the comb’s teeth doesn’t allow it to really hold super short strands to straighten. The company also notes that if your hair is “very curly,” you might need to use professional styling products for the best results.

The I11 Apex is the perfect styling companion for when you’re on the go. There are no wires, so you never have to search for an outlet. It’s easy to slip into your handbag, backpack or luggage. There’s even a physical lock switch that prevents it from turning on while it’s stashed away.

Price

This straightening comb typically retails for $90, but Amazon is currently offering a 22% discount for Prime Members.

The specs

Price: $90 retail, but often on sale for less

$90 retail, but often on sale for less Battery life: 45 minutes

45 minutes Wattage: 33 watts

33 watts Estimated charge time: 2.5 hours from 0 to 100 with a 15-watt adapter

2.5 hours from 0 to 100 with a 15-watt adapter Number of ports: 1 USB-C port

1 USB-C port Max temperature: 410 degrees Fahrenheit (210 degrees Celsius)

410 degrees Fahrenheit (210 degrees Celsius) Weight: 1.46 pounds

CNET’s buying advice

Whether you want effortless touch-ups on the go or a full straightening solution at home, the Bluvol I11 Apex can get the job done. Want the best of both worlds? Tymo has a new two-in-one straightening brush with a built-in traditional flat iron. If you don’t need the portably of I11 Apex, then it’s worth considering.

Tech.title: It’s Official: You’ll See a Pickle Emoji and More on Your Device Next Year
Tech.content:
It’s official: We’re getting a pickle emoji next year. On Sept. 16, the Unicode Consortium approved nine new emoji that you’ll see on your device in 2027. One new emoji is the pickle, which could claim the eggplant’s crown as the go-to emoji for male anatomy.

Here are the nine new emoji you’ll see on your phone next year:

A cracking face

A leftward thumb sign gesture

A rightward thumb sign gesture

A monarch butterfly

A pickle

A lighthouse

A meteor

An eraser

A net with a handle

The Unicode Consortium originally proposed a squinty face emoji in 2025. However, the Unicode Emoji Standard & Research Working Group recommended changing that emoji to a cracking face in January.

Honestly, the cracking face emoji feels more relevant to today than the squinty face emoji. The squinty face comes across as suspicious while the cracking face emoji screams, “I’m putting on a brave face in these trying times.” If that’s not the most relatable sentiment these days, I don’t know what is.

While the Unicode Consortium approved these emoji, companies like Apple, Google and Samsung will still need to design and then implement their versions of the emoji. Those companies usually add the emoji to devices as part of a software update in the spring, so you likely won’t see these emoji on your phone until 2027.

If you have an idea for an emoji, the Unicode Consortium will begin fielding proposals for the next round of new emoji in 2027. Anyone can submit an idea for a new emoji, and the Unicode Consortium usually uploads proposed new emoji to a public document late in the year. For example, the upcoming emoji were originally accepted in October, 2025.

For more on emoji, here’s how to decipher every emoji and the latest emoji on your iPhone and Android.

Tech.title: An Egg Genius Urged Me to Strain Before Poaching. The Results Were Astounding
Tech.content:
Perhaps no other form of egg cookery has so much rhetoric and written words dedicated to it as the elusive poached egg. Poached eggs are humble, but surprisingly complicated to master. Perhaps even more so than the omelet. (In this egg-loving, frequent-egg-cooking author’s opinion.) Even with water as the only other procedural requirement.

If you’ve tried other methods for delivering a perfect poached egg — electric egg cookers, nonstick poaching pans or the seemingly infallible microwave method — and still left unfulfilled or underwhelmed by the outcome, there’s one more pro trick you can try. And here’s a pro tip: Lisa Steele is a fifth-generation chicken keeper and author of Fresh Eggs Daily and In Season: 125+ Sweet and Savory Recipes Celebrating Simple, Fresh Ingredients. She talked me through the single, foolproof step that makes stovetop egg poaching dead simple.

The reason poached eggs are challenging

An egg’s complex structure makes poaching difficult. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Picture it: a pot full of water, maybe with a dash of distilled vinegar, at the gentlest simmer so you don’t subject your delicate egg to a tornado of activity once submerged. You painstakingly crack the egg into a shallow bowl first, and carefully slip it into the pot. Regardless of your good intentions, the egg then clouds the water and turns all wispy, like some sort of blond dementor.

More from CNET

You haven’t done anything wrong here; you’ve just failed to understand an egg’s basic structure. “There are actually two components of the egg white, or albumen,” Steele explains. “There’s the thicker part of the white which encases the yolk, and then there’s a separate, thinner layer of egg white around that. It’s the thinner part of the egg white that will spread and turn wispy when you drop an egg into the water.”

The wispy white of an unstrained egg. Pamela Vachon/CNET

To prevent your poached egg from spreading? Strain it

The thing is, you can easily get rid of the thin, watery white part of your egg using one simple tool you’ve probably got in a drawer somewhere and about a minute of your time. Set a small mesh strainer over a cup or bowl, crack the egg into it, and wait.

Pamela Vachon/CNET

“Straining an egg removes the thinner whites that likely won’t adhere to the rest of the egg and result in shaggy, wispy threads,” Steele says. “It won’t affect the flavor outcome of your poached egg, but it is purely for appearance’s sake.” (And potentially your sanity’s or sense of accomplishment’s sake, I might add.)

While the egg’s flavor stays unchanged, for Benedict lovers, straining the egg first slightly improves the white-to-yolk ratio in the poached result and makes the texture more consistent, while also creating a tidy, photogenic package.

Some patience is required

The thin white will slowly strain itself out. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Once your raw egg is in the strainer, you may notice nothing happens right away, and you may feel the urge to move the egg around a bit to get things going. But don’t zhush, which threatens to scramble the egg. Simply wait for gravity to do its thing; it takes about a minute. It’s akin to what happens when separating whites from yolks, except here you’re separating whites from whites.

Fine mesh strainer $6 at Amazon

“Let the thin part of the egg white drip down into the bowl,” Steele says, “then gently slide the egg into the simmering water.” The strainer can also serve as a handy vessel for transferring the egg, especially if you’re only making a single one. If you’re doing multiple eggs and don’t want to risk cooking any remaining white onto the mesh by submerging it, place the strained egg in a small, shallow bowl as usual before easing it into the water. Without the thin, watery white part, you’ll notice a discernible textural difference in the egg even when raw.

Best poaching practices

A gentle simmer, not a rolling boil, is best for poaching. Pamela Vachon/CNET

The straining step alone can almost completely change your poached egg game in an instant, but for the best results, follow the best poaching protocol. You don’t want a full pot of water at a rolling boil like you would for pasta. “Fill a pot or saucepan with a few inches of water and bring to a boil, then turn the heat down to low so the water is just barely simmering with small bubbles floating to the surface,” Steele advises.

A strained egg simmering like a tidy package. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Creating a little whirlpool will further help your remaining egg white stay snug. “Using a wooden spoon or silicone spatula, swirl the water, then gently slide the egg into the center of the whirlpool as you keep swirling for another few seconds around the egg until the egg white turns milky and starts to set up around the yolk,” Steele says. “At this point, you can push the egg to one side, add another egg into the center and repeat the process.”

An unstrained egg on the left versus a strained egg on the right.

A soft-poached egg takes about three minutes, and because you’ve removed the watery part of the egg white, you’ll get a nice firm structure to hold the still-runny yolk — the poached egg ideal.

Since poaching is a delicate process, no matter your new straining habit and how strictly you follow the recommended procedure, “using the freshest eggs possible is very important when you are poaching because the egg white gets even more thin and watery as the egg ages,” Steele says. “The membrane holding the yolk together also weakens, making the yolk more susceptible to breaking.” So if you don’t have them on hand already, get yourself a strainer and some fresh eggs and put this newfound tidbit to the personal test.

Want more cooking hacks?

Cooking bacon in the oven is a great way to make a large batch, but the air fryer method might be even better — and it’s definitely faster. Here are nine more cooking hacks that save time and energy.

Tech.title: Apple Skipped the iPhone 18 This Year. Is the iPhone 17 Still a Good Choice?
Tech.content:
Rumors hinted that Apple might split its new iPhone launches this year, and it became official when the company’s fall event revealed only the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. For people who don’t need the pro features — or don’t want to pay top dollar for Apple’s first foldable iPhone — the year-old iPhone 17 will continue to anchor the phone lineup for several months at least.

The iPhone 17 closed the gap between Apple’s entry-level phone and the pricier Pro models last year with long-overdue display upgrades, alongside nifty camera and durability improvements. Apple also made new features like Center Stage (its new selfie camera) and Dual Capture available across the entire lineup, making the iPhone 17 an even better value.

A year later, it will have to compete with newer models till March 2027, since the iPhone 18 won’t launch until then alongside the iPhone 18E, according to the rumors.

So what if you need a new iPhone before March or don’t want to pay $1,199 or more for an iPhone 18 Pro? I charged up my iPhone 17 and revisited Apple’s standard model to find out if it’s still worth buying.

Display, durability and camera upgrades keep it strong

Reading on the iPhone 17 is a pleasant experience. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 arrived last year with multiple major upgrades, many of which you’ll appreciate daily.

The screen is finally on par with Apple’s Pro models and every other Android counterpart. It runs at a smooth 120Hz refresh rate, which also adapts to the on-screen content to save battery. I compared it to the iPhone 15 and the smoother visuals were immediately noticeable when scrolling through the home screen. It makes the phone feel faster and more responsive.

The display is also brighter and less reflective than its predecessor. It is immediately noticeable when you’re navigating outdoors or need to do anything on your phone under bright lights. I put it against the new Pixel 11, which is equally bright, but iPhone 17’s smaller bezels make its screen more pleasing to look at.

Apple said its 2025 iPhones were more durable than ever. While I haven’t used the iPhone 17 for a year straight, I have daily driven the iPhone 17 Pro Max without a case during that time. (Yes, I’m that guy.) Compared to my 2024 iPhone 16 Pro, the 17 Pro has fared better against scratches and drops thanks to its Ceramic Shield 2 glass, the same found on the iPhone 17.

The auto framing feature, combined with better stabilization, has been a godsend for recording myself using the front camera. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Some might dismiss it as a minor feature, but the 17’s selfie camera is the best upgrade, in my opinion. The new 18-megapixel square sensor is more of a quality-of-life upgrade than just a mere number bump because it lets you shoot landscape selfies without needing to rotate your phone. The viewfinder automatically repositions its framing based on the number of people in the photo.

I love the camera for two reasons. First, it enables Center Stage, which tracks you (even if you’re moving) on video calls (both on FaceTime and third-party apps like WhatsApp). It’s a handy feature for when I need to move around doing chores, but the camera keeps me in the frame and helps me be less annoying for my girlfriend.

Second, the square sensor improves stability in selfie video recording. I live with a condition that causes constant hand tremors, which makes it difficult to record myself on phones. The iPhone 17 has been helpful as I’m less self-conscious and more confident that I’ll get stable footage instead of a blurry video.

As for the two cameras on the back, they are far more capable than its predecessor. The iPhone 17 has two rear cameras: a 48-megapixel wide-angle camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide, which is an upgrade over the 12-megapixel ultrawide camera on the iPhone 16. You’ll get sharp photos, better indoor shots and a smooth video experience. It misses out on a telephoto camera that the 17 Pro has, so there’s no optical zoom, but these are all the cameras most people would ever need.

iOS 27 fixed the most annoying flaws in iOS 26

iOS 26 (left) displaces the Control Center settings in landscape orientation. iOS 27 (right) has fixed this issue. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 shipped with iOS 26, which offered more translucent controls, customization options and Apple Intelligence features. However, my experience was buggy since the beginning. On multiple occasions, I missed calls and alarms because my iPhone automatically lowered its system volume to a minimum. I didn’t put it in Do Not Disturb or Focus modes. Other times, the keyboard started lagging out of nowhere, and whenever I needed to access the Control Center while watching a video in landscape mode, my controls were all over the place.

Some of these issues are thankfully fixed in iOS 27, which I’ve been running on my iPhone 17 Pro Max.

For starters, I can set different volume levels for the call ringer, alarms and media. The Control Center is now better optimized for horizontal orientation, keeping my customizations right where I want them. Then there are smart features, like spatial reframing in Photos for using generative AI to “change” the camera’s position when an image was taken. There’s also an all-new Siri mode in the Camera app.

In CNET’s 45-minute endurance test, which includes streaming, scrolling through social media, joining a video call and playing games, Apple’s entry-level iPhone went from full to 98%, which matches the results of the iPhone 17 Pro. It has the second-longest battery life of any phone CNET has tested in the past 12 months, tied with the OnePlus 15 and Motorola Razr (2026); behind the first-place phone is the iPhone 17 Pro Max.

It has fared well, but what about six months from now?

The iPhone 17 has aged well and stacks well against its 2026 Android rivals. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The baseline model stacks well against the competition. The iPhone 17 launched at $799, but Apple bumped the price up to $899, which is now comparable to the $899 Samsung Galaxy S26 and the new Google Pixel 11.

As for those willing to wait for the iPhone 18, it is unlikely to be a major upgrade. Apple is expected to reserve the most prominent changes like a reduced Dynamic Island and newer cameras for its Pro models. Moreover, a recent rumor on Weibo suggests that the iPhone 18 could align more closely with a lower-cost iPhone 18E model. It might not receive a similarly powerful chip as its Pro siblings, for instance. It’s a similar move Google has made with its base Pixel 11 and budget Pixel 10A.

Given the lukewarm rumors regarding the upcoming model and despite the iPhone 17’s increased price tag, I think last year’s model is still an excellent deal. And for the first time in my career, I’d say if you want a new iPhone before the new year, it is totally fine to get the iPhone 17 now rather than wait and see what the iPhone 18 may bring.

Tech.title: Google Pixel 11A Leak May Have Revealed a New Color and Spec Bumps
Tech.content:
Google’s next lower-cost flagship phone, the Pixel 11A, appears to have been leaked for the first time through a series of renders posted on Tuesday by Android Headlines and OnLeaks.

Exclusive: Google Pixel 11a Official CAD Renders Leak https://t.co/WcjlvvWKh4 — Androidheadline (@Androidheadline) September 29, 2026

The images suggest that the Pixel 11A will come in a new purple color, but otherwise continue to have a simple flat design without a camera bump — much like the $499 Pixel 10A. That purple color would join black, silver and green variants, all of which will likely get renamed with something artsy from Google’s marketing department in due time.

While the design might be the same, the Pixel 11A is apparently expected to get the Tensor G6 processor — the same as the one in Google’s $899 Pixel 11. If this pans out, that’d be great to see, since the prior Pixel 10A used the same Tensor G4 processor as the Pixel 9 series. And while I did find in my Pixel 10A review that the phone was still feature-packed with one of the best cameras out there for its price range, it notably did not have access to several Pixel 10 features like Magic Cue for contextual assistance.

More from CNET

Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Pixel 11A is likely still months away from an official unveiling; for reference, the Pixel 10A was announced in February.

It’s also unknown how the ongoing RAM shortage would affect the initial pricing for Pixel’s A-series. While the Pixel 7A through 10A also started at $499, it would not be surprising to see the Pixel 11A get its starting price bumped up to $599, much like the rest of the Pixel 11 lineup. If that happens, hopefully it follows the cue of the base Pixel 11 by simply eliminating the $499 128GB model while retaining a 256GB model at $599 — much like the current Pixel 10A.
